66000152.summary: After Alabama seceded in January 1861, delegates from six Southern states met in Montgomery in early February and adopted a provisional Confederate constitution in this building. Jefferson Davis was elected president and inaugurated on the west portico on February 18, 1861, when the Stars and Bars was raised over the Capitol. The Confederate Congress continued meeting here until the capital moved to Richmond in May 1861, shortly after fighting began at Fort Sumter.
66000152.heading: HISTORY

74000432.summary: This house served as Jefferson Davis’s first official residence while Montgomery was the Confederate capital. Believed built about 1825 and later owned by Col. Edmond Harrison, it was leased for the presidential household after Davis’s February 1861 inauguration; Varina Davis called it “a gentleman’s residence.” The Davises left for Richmond on May 27, 1861, and Congress ordered the unexpired lease sold once the government relocated.
74000432.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000431.summary: Martin Luther King Jr. became pastor here in 1954. After Rosa Parks’s December 1955 arrest, community leaders packed the church; the Montgomery Improvement Association formed and named King president, using mass meetings at Dexter to sustain the bus boycott. Despite arrests, bombings, and job losses, the boycott lasted 381 days and ended December 21, 1956, after the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation illegal; the nomination presents the church as a link between the Black church and mass nonviolent protest.
74000431.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000174.summary: Built in the early 1850s—possibly as early as 1851—for Samuel Farrow Rice, later chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court, the house is described as the last antebellum residence then standing in the Capitol Hill area. Rice, a politically active South Carolina native who edited the Talladega Watchtower and served in the legislature and on the court, later sold the home to law partner Henry Churchill Semple; Semple family members lived there until 1924. By 1970 the State of Alabama had bought it for museum and Alabama Historical Commission office use and was restoring it.
72000174.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88003076.summary: Irish immigrant grocer and baker John Dowe bought lots on what became Washington Avenue in 1862 and finished a family house by 1863. His widow Johanna later built another house at 320 Washington that the family never occupied after the deaths of two sons, keeping it as rental property; son John Dowe II built a Victorian house on an adjacent lot that the family later returned to occupy. The nomination stresses continuous Dowe ownership and income use of the clustered houses and landscaping for nearly a century.
88003076.heading: HISTORICAL SUMMARY

76000349.summary: Speridon Cassimus, a Greek immigrant who arrived in 1888 and ran a wholesale fruit business on Bibb Street, built this late Victorian house at 110 Jackson Street in 1893 after bringing his family from Corfu. His father Alexander, who had settled in Montgomery earlier, is called the “father of the Greek community” there. The nomination presents the house as an early—and possibly the oldest remaining—landmark of Alabama’s Greek immigrant community.
76000349.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78000506.summary: Thomas Goode Jones, twice governor of Alabama (1890–1894) and later a federal judge, lived at 323 Adams Avenue for much of his career; the house served as executive mansion and occasionally as a courtroom. Purchased in 1879 and enlarged during his governorship, it was tied to elections against Populist Reuben Kolb and to later work at the 1901 constitutional convention and a judgeship recommended by Booker T. Washington. The nomination also notes education, taxation, and convict-system measures from his administrations.
78000506.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000105.summary: The Ordeman-Shaw Historic District centers on the Shaw House Complex, described as one of the most closely authenticated antebellum restorations in the United States—an Italianate townhouse, Greek Revival cottages, slave quarters, and reconstructed outbuildings depicting middle-class pre–Civil War urban life. German immigrant architect-engineer Charles Ordeman completed the main house after buying the land in 1850, designed major local buildings, and built a neighboring cottage sold in 1852 to jeweler Campbell with the original slave quarters. The City of Montgomery later acquired the houses for a museum complex; restorations were guided by archaeology so that paint, pathways, plantings, and 1830–55 furnishings matched the period.
71000105.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000711.summary: Whig lawyer and U.S. Attorney Jefferson Franklin Jackson built this South Union Street house in 1853 while serving Alabama’s Middle District; Yale classmate Frederick Law Olmsted later visited and praised the “fine house.” Jackson died in 1862; his widow later married former law partner and Confederate cabinet member Thomas H. Watts. In 1943 the Federation of Women and Youth Clubs (organized as the City Federation of Colored Women’s Clubs) bought the house for community use, including library and Head Start functions.
84000711.heading: HISTORICAL SUMMARY

85000736.summary: The nomination ties the house to E. B. Joseph, a street-railway developer and president who also served as Montgomery mayor (1899–1903) and earlier on the city council; though he lived here only 1880–1885 in his father-in-law’s house, it is called the only surviving residence from his productive years. Architecturally it is cited as one of the city’s few intact 1850s Italianate cottages still retaining its servant’s quarters.
85000736.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000133.summary: Built for Lomax Fire Company No. 4 after an 1889 land purchase, this is identified as Montgomery’s oldest fire station and the only one associated with the volunteer companies that served until city consolidation in 1898. Relocated uphill from downtown Lee Street to handle expanding hill neighborhoods, the company became Steam Engine Company No. 2 and answered the new city department’s first alarm on July 15, 1898. The text also records later fatalities, including a 1901 streetcar collision that killed Captain J. W. Sykes.
81000133.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79000393.summary: This 1858 brick Italianate cottage was the home of newspaperman Patrick Henry Brittan, Alabama quartermaster general and Secretary of State from 1859 to 1865. Brittan helped run the Montgomery Advertiser/State Gazette, launched the Daily Messenger, and promoted the Alabama-Florida Railroad. The nomination emphasizes both the house’s architectural quality and Brittan’s wartime service carrying out the Secretary of State’s routine duties.
79000393.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000729.summary: The Gerald-Dowdell House is significant as one of Montgomery’s few raised cottages, combining Gulf Coast form with Italianate detail (bracketed cornice, quoined brick ground floor). Likely built in the mid-1850s for Perley S. and Camilla Gerald after Gerald’s California Gold Rush fortune and the sale of an earlier mansion, it later housed furnishings dealer Herman Kenneworth’s family and, from 1939, the Dowdells. Local tradition (undocumented in the nomination) links bandleader Herman Arnold—who arranged “Dixie” as a march for Jefferson Davis’s 1861 inaugural parade—to the house; Associate Justice Robert T. Simpson lived there 1940–1949.
80000729.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000728.summary: Associated with cotton broker W. W. Brame, the present Classical Revival house at South Hull and Scott appears from tax and directory evidence to have been built about 1897 on land the Brame family had held since the 1860s. Assessments rose sharply from 1896 to 1897, and the 1899 directory lists Brame at 402 South Hull. Later heirs and sales brought the property to the Neal family by the late 1970s, when it was a city landmark and restoration for commercial use was underway.
80000728.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000326.summary: Organized in 1834, St. John’s outgrew its first brick church and completed the present Wills and Dudley Gothic building in 1855. While Montgomery was Confederate capital, Jefferson Davis’s family rented a pew here, and the parish supported hospitals and soldiers’ families; an organizational meeting of the Confederate Episcopal General Council was held in the church. After the war the church was temporarily closed under military order, then rejoined the national Episcopal Church; a major 1869 enlargement reused bricks from the old Jefferson Street building.
75000326.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002064.summary: Built about 1912 and acquired by Dexter Avenue Baptist Church as its pastorium in 1919, the cottage housed Martin Luther King Jr. during his 1954–1960 Montgomery pastorate and the bus boycott. On January 31, 1956, a bomb damaged the front porch during the boycott struggle, an attack the nomination says helped draw national attention while underscoring King’s nonviolence. The house sits in Centennial Hill, described as a historically prominent Black neighborhood near Alabama State University.
82002064.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79000398.summary: Black businessman Victor Tulane built this corner grocery with upstairs living quarters between about 1904 and 1908 after expanding from an earlier store into real estate and banking roles, later becoming a Tuskegee Institute trustee. The Colored Alabamian noted Booker T. Washington staying with the Tulanes in 1908. The ground floor continued as a grocery under later owners, while the second floor served as home, Black social-club space, then apartment and offices; fixtures such as meat blocks and a built-in icebox remained.
79000398.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000175.summary: Built about 1841–1843 by merchant and cotton broker John Gindrat—an early Montgomery commercial leader and first president of the State Bank branch there—the Winter Building later belonged to his daughter Mary Elizabeth Gindrat Winter. Immediately before and during the Civil War its second floor housed the Southern Telegraph Company. From those offices Confederate Secretary of War Leroy Pope Walker telegraphed Gen. P. G. T. Beauregard in Charleston the order that led to the firing on Fort Sumter, opening hostilities. The nomination still described family ownership with clothing stores and offices in the building.
72000175.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

11000298.summary: The Montgomery Greyhound Bus Station is significant for the May 20, 1961 Freedom Riders attack: after earlier violence in Anniston and Birmingham, Nashville student riders—including John Lewis—arrived here on a Greyhound despite assurances of police protection that never materialized. A waiting mob with pipes and bats assaulted reporters and riders on the loading platform; federal official John Seigenthaler was beaten unconscious while trying to help, and white rider Jim Zwerg was among the seriously injured. The single-day riot drew national attention to segregated interstate travel, spurred Executive Branch involvement, and—per the nomination—helped make Montgomery pivotal again after the Bus Boycott; the riders later left town from the Trailways station on May 24.
11000298.heading: HISTORICAL NARRATIVE / Statement of Significance (Freedom Rides)

72000173.summary: Scottish-born commission merchant John H. Murphy built this Greek Revival mansion in 1851 and became one of Montgomery’s wealthiest citizens and an incorporator of the first water works. During the Confederacy the house was a social center visited by figures such as Jefferson Davis and William L. Yancey; in April 1865 Union forces used it as headquarters under martial law. After later Elks ownership and fire damage, the Water Works and Sanitary Sewer Board bought and restored it in 1967 for offices.
72000173.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000106.summary: The Teague House, a Historic American Buildings Survey property, was built in 1848 by livery operator Berry Owens and later owned by James Ware. When Gen. James H. Wilson’s Union forces occupied Montgomery in 1865, they used it as a division headquarters and read the martial-law proclamation from its veranda. Mayor William Martin Teague’s family owned and lived in the house from 1889 to 1955; in 1955 the Alabama State Chamber of Commerce bought it and adapted it as headquarters under John Meriwether Ward—cited as outstanding adaptive-use preservation amid a threatened downtown antebellum neighborhood.
71000106.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98000611.summary: The 1932–1933 Classical Revival federal building is nominated for association with District Judge Frank M. Johnson Jr. (1955–1979), whose courtroom decisions had major civil-rights and related impact, and for architectural distinction; Congress renamed it for Johnson in 1992. The period of significance cited on the form includes 1932–1979 with key dates such as 1956, 1965, and 1971. (Automatic heading search missed this modern-form “Narrative Statement of Significance”; text recovered from the full extract.)
98000611.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

79000396.summary: Physician-politician Dr. John Hazard Henry built this brick-veneer Victorian house in 1893 after returning from Selma, where he had been mayor near the Civil War’s end and active in early southern Republican organizing. Trained under J. Marion Sims and in homeopathy, he practiced in Montgomery until his death in 1906; the house later belonged to daughter Martha and son-in-law Ernest W. Stay and was known locally as the “Horseshoe House” for distinctive gable and tower ventilators. It later served as a rehabilitation center for alcoholic women and was vacant/for sale when nominated.
79000396.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000132.summary: Planned in 1906 by entrepreneur N. J. Bell and designed by Ausfeld and Blount with Chicago engineers Westcott and Ronneberg, this 1907–10 steel-framed office tower is called Alabama’s finest Sullivanesque skyscraper after the Wainwright Building model. When built it was one of the two largest buildings in the state and offered oak finishes, cooled water, central vacuuming, and three high-speed elevators. It remained in the Bell family until a 1967 sale to a local business group.
81000132.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79000397.summary: Completed in the early 1890s boom as an ornamented Renaissance-inspired wholesale block with a corner tower, the building housed Steiner-Lobman’s dry-goods firm (relocated from Pine Apple) on the north half; Teague Hardware, organized by William Martin Teague in 1892, bought the south half in 1895. Both firms still occupied their portions into the mid-1970s when the nomination was prepared, with rehabilitation planned. Contemporary newspaper coverage in 1891 praised the rising “beautiful storehouse” at Commerce and Tallapoosa.
79000397.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74001711.summary: Portland City Hall is an outstanding Classicist High Renaissance Revival civic building by Whidden and Lewis, whose partners had worked for McKim, Mead & White before settling in Portland in the late 1880s. Planned from 1892 as a fireproof, electrically wired, gas-piped, and elevator-served administrative hall (with police and jail housed elsewhere), it is also noted as a very early steel-frame building in which floor and roof loads are not carried by the exterior walls. The nomination presents it as one of Oregon’s most important works of planning, engineering, and style in downtown Portland.
74001711.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002142.summary: Congress funded a new U.S. Courthouse for Portland in 1928; Portland architect Morris H. Whitehouse (with federal consulting architects) designed the building, completed in the early 1930s after site clearance on Block 183. Contemporary coverage called the Federal Court House the most handsome of the city’s new federal buildings. The nomination stresses its monumental massing, quality of materials, and lasting civic presence at the upper end of S.W. Sixth Avenue.
79002142.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002136.summary: The Multnomah County Courthouse (1911–1914) is nominated as an outstanding Neo-Classical Revival work by Whidden and Lewis, who also designed nearby City Hall. Built in stages so county business could continue in the old courthouse until the east wing opened, it was promoted as a fire-safe steel-and-concrete civic landmark and has remained the seat of Oregon’s most populous county government.
79002136.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000520.summary: Completed in 1923 to designs by Carl L. Linde, the nine-story Sovereign Hotel is cited as one of downtown Portland’s best-preserved and most fashionable pre-war multiple-housing buildings, later converted to apartments. Reinforced-concrete construction is enriched with extensive terra-cotta ornament, wrought-iron balconies, and specially designed brass hardware and lighting by Fred C. Baker.
81000520.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79003738.summary: The Ambassador Apartments, designed by Carl L. Linde, are described as one of Portland’s most ornate fashionable apartment houses and an architectural anchor on a main downtown thoroughfare between business and high-rise residential districts. Period detailing and bay-window massing mark it as a major Linde residential commission of the early twentieth century.
79003738.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002144.summary: The University Club (opened 1913) is an excellent and rare Oregon example of Jacobethan Revival used for a non-residential building, designed by Whitehouse & Fouilhoux with Fred Fritsch. Beyond style, the nomination stresses the club’s role in Portland business and social life; in 1919 an AIA jury ranked it among the ten most notable buildings within ten miles of City Hall.
79002144.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

03000072.summary: The Peck Bros. and Bartle Tire Service Company Building represents the specialized commercial-industrial architecture that proliferated in Portland in the 1920s as the city’s economy shifted toward industry and automobile-related trade. Nominations of this type emphasize open, glazed showroom/service volumes designed to draw motorists and display goods in the streamline commercial idiom of the period.
03000072.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

80003357.summary: Completed in 1894 to designs associated with architect F. Manson White, the Auditorium and Music Hall is an outstanding surviving Romanesque Revival building enriched with exuberant Sullivanesque carved ornament. The nomination argues it is among the few Portland buildings that still convey the vitality of that late-nineteenth-century style and merit restoration and Register recognition.
80003357.heading: 8. Significance

80003365.summary: The Gilbert Building (1893), tentatively attributed to Whidden and Lewis, is significant for its cohesive decorative and functional brickwork and for architectural vocabulary paralleling the contemporary Chicago School. Built as an office block in the Romanesque Revival mode and converted to a hotel in 1916 by the Jacobs brothers of Oregon City Manufacturing, it illustrates a brief era of finely crafted brick bearing-wall construction in Portland.
80003365.heading: 8. Significance

76001585.summary: The Paramount Theatre, designed by the nationally prominent theater firm Rapp & Rapp with Portland supervising architects De Young & Roland, opened March 8, 1928 as a North Italian Rococo Revival vaudeville/movie palace. The nomination emphasizes its substantially original condition—including furnishings—and ranks it among George L. Rapp’s finest works as one of the few grand 1920s theaters still largely intact.
76001585.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80003368.summary: Jefferson Substation is significant as a rare surviving downtown structure of its type and as a very early local building with a reinforced-concrete superstructure. The nomination also stresses its role in early electrical distribution for Portland’s business district, especially street lighting and the street railway system.
80003368.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

11000770.summary: Michael Graves’s Portland Public Service Building (commonly the Portland Building), completed in the early 1980s, is nominated for its central place in the rise of American Post-Modern architecture. Scholarly literature ties its conflation of form, icon, and color to a break with late Modernism; whatever judgments of beauty, the nomination presents it as historically important to national architectural history.
11000770.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

09001211.summary: The Ladd Carriage House at 1331 SW Broadway served William S. Ladd’s Portland estate and still conveys carriage use through its open plan and hayloft even after exterior restorations and loss of original interior finishes. Nominators emphasized historical association with the Ladd property (Criterion B) over Stick Style mastery, noting stronger intact Stick Style peers elsewhere in Portland and limited documentation on architect Joseph Sherwin.
09001211.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84003091.summary: The Peter Taylor and Gotlieb Haehlen houses in South Portland’s Lair Hill area are locally significant for ties to early industrial and commercial leaders and as distinctive examples of their styles. Pattern-maker Peter Taylor helped organize Willamette Iron Works after work at the Portland Foundry (1853), linking the Italianate Taylor house to the city’s iron industry growth.
84003091.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75001594.summary: First Congregational Church is significant historically and architecturally on Portland’s South Park Blocks. Founded in 1851—the oldest Congregational church in the Pacific Northwest—its 185-foot Italian Gothic tower is a major Portland landmark that uniquely represents that style along the twelve South Park Blocks.
75001594.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84003087.summary: The New Heathman Hotel is nominated with its associated Publix Theater development as Portland’s largest-scale and most distinctive pre-Depression commercial block designed together with a motion-picture theater. Shared backers and contractors produced a unified hotel–theater complex that has become rare as other golden-age movie complexes were lost.
84003087.heading: 8. Significance

85003082.summary: The Ira F. Powers Building at 804 SW Third Avenue, designed by Whidden and Lewis, was determined Register-eligible for association with Powers—a leading furniture merchant, businessman, and philanthropist—and as a scarce Chicago School Commercial-style work by that firm in Portland.
85003082.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92000091.summary: Completed in 1926 for the estate of pioneer businessman and U.S. Senator Henry W. Corbett, the Pacific Building by Albert E. Doyle faces Pioneer Courthouse. The ten-story reinforced-concrete Italian Renaissance block uses terra-cotta rustication, arched entries, and classical cornices with warm brick walls and a red mission-tile roof, continuing Renaissance detail into the lobby.
92000091.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

10000801.summary: John Yeon’s 1948 Visitors Information Center is a Modernist “inside-out” design whose exterior expresses interior functions, finished in then-new regionally developed exterior plywood and incorporating ventilator wall units (fixed glass with louvers) that influenced other Northwest modern architects. The nomination highlights Yeon’s innovative response to a difficult urban site.
10000801.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96001002.summary: The Mohawk Building is a Georgian-style commercial design by Whidden and Lewis, progenitors of the American Renaissance in Portland. Street facades in red brick and cream glazed terra cotta use quoining, trabeated fenestration with terra-cotta keystones, and a refined corbel table—understated but handsomely detailed classical commercial architecture.
96001002.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

90001591.summary: The Wheeldon Apartment Building is organized in a base–shaft–capital scheme detailed in the Jacobethan mode with dark red brick, cast-stone trim, full-height oriels, and a battlemented parapet. Operated as the Wheeldon Apartments into 1930, it is presented as a distinctive early-twentieth-century apartment landmark on Park Avenue.
90001591.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

10000599.summary: The Arlington Club contributes to downtown Portland’s commerce and community-planning themes under a multiple-property context tied to growth after the Lewis and Clark Exposition—vertical commercial downtown development and ground-floor retail. The nomination places the 1910 club building among public/institutional resources that retain enough integrity to convey that downtown transformation.
10000599.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96000995.summary: The Journal Building is the stepped tower that housed Oregon Journal newspaper departments, with a three-story rusticated terra-cotta base, colossal arched openings, brick mid-floors with terra-cotta surrounds, and a clock-tower outlook. The nomination emphasizes its well-proportioned Classical/Baroque commercial tower composition in downtown Portland.
96000995.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

91000975.summary: This 1991 continuation amends the National Register boundary of the Walter F. Burrell House to include Lots 6 and 13, Block 3 of Burrell Heights that were mistakenly omitted from the 1990 verbal boundary description. Significance rests with the previously listed Prairie-style Burrell residence; the amendment corrects the mapped historic parcel.
91000975.heading: Boundary Increase

90001593.summary: The Burrell Mansion is locally significant under Criterion C as one of the two earliest clear Prairie-style houses in Portland, designed in 1901 by Whidden and Lewis for capitalist and land developer Walter Frazar Burrell on Burrell Acres in southeast Portland. The firm is credited with introducing eastern U.S. styles to Portland; this house remains one of only two of their Prairie residences.
90001593.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88000275.summary: Interconnected buildings at High and Court Streets were built beginning in 1900 for Chemeketa Lodge No. 1, I.O.O.F., primarily significant under Criterion A (social history) and locally under architecture. The core is the 1900 three-story Odd Fellows Temple and Opera House—a late Richardsonian Romanesque brick pile—with a rear retail/theater annex and later Mediterranean Revival work by Walter D. Pugh/John Gray (1900s) and Morris H. Whitehouse (1921), spanning fraternal, theatrical, and commercial use through 1936.
88000275.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92000133.summary: Built in 1907 as an investment by contractor Christopher Paulus, this two-story brick-and-stucco Commercial Style building is the only remaining unaltered example of a once-common type in downtown Salem. Plainer and more functional than earlier commercial fronts, it replaced wooden stores on an early paved street and long housed a family furniture business.
92000133.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000510.summary: Garfield School (1909), by Salem architect Fred A. Legg, is significant as Salem’s first brick public elementary school and the last elementary school remaining in the downtown core. Its Renaissance-inspired H-plan with portico and brick quoins typifies early-twentieth-century American Renaissance school design; closed in 1973, it was renovated for offices.
81000510.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78002302.summary: The Reed Opera House and McCornack Block Addition on Liberty Street is a multi-story brick commercial/cultural landmark with arched fenestration, rusticated pilasters, and a nineteenth-century hotel wing completed about 1870. The nomination treats the paired buildings as a central Salem commercial and entertainment block whose street facades still convey the capital’s Victorian downtown.
78002302.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002165.summary: The South First National Bank Block’s surviving two-store unit, financed by Benjamin Forstner (inventor of the Forstner bit) after he left Aurora’s communal colony, uses serial bay composition, cast-iron columns, and sheet-metal cornice ornament matching neighboring bank fabric. Forstner kept a store and upstairs apartment here; later consolidations still leave a rare cast-iron commercial front in Salem.
83002165.heading: 8. Significance

79002122.summary: The Starkey-McCully Block (1867) for businessmen John L. Starkey, David McCully, and William Anderson originally ran 120 feet along Commercial Street; the remaining northerly portion is significant because its arcaded cast-iron ground-story front is believed to be the oldest architectural cast iron manufactured in Oregon still in situ. It dates to the dawn of Oregon’s own iron industry at Oswego.
79002122.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82003737.summary: Built in 1917 for Elizabeth Farrar and heirs of John Fields Farrar to designs by Fred A. Legg, the Farrar Building’s monogrammed curvilinear gables and intact galvanized sheet-metal cornice embody Beaux-Arts eclecticism on State Street. It anchors an unbroken late-nineteenth/early-twentieth-century block and housed the Central Cigar Store/Smoke Shop, a businessmen’s social hub.
82003737.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000505.summary: The Bush and Brey Block (1889; annex 1915), designed by leading Salem architect Walter D. Pugh, is a Queen Anne brick commercial building with prolific cast-iron and sheet-metal ornament from the Salem Iron Works. Pugh also designed Thomas Kay Woolen Mill and the lost 1897 Richardsonian City Hall; the block’s ruddy brick and free pedimented vocabulary mark downtown Salem’s late Victorian commercial peak.
81000505.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002162.summary: First Methodist Episcopal Church of Salem (1871–1878), from plans by Chicago architect Cass Chapman, ties today’s congregation to the Methodist Mission origins of Salem and early Oregon Methodism. It is Salem’s only pre-1880 church building and one of the few tall Gothic Revival spires left in Oregon, retaining high integrity of design and setting in the capital landscape.
83002162.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80003348.summary: The Adolph Block represents Salem’s earlier two-story brick masonry Italianate commercial buildings with cast-iron fronts and galvanized sheet-metal decoration. Though shop fronts were modernized, second-story arched rhythms and much facade fabric survive, and the block links State Street’s historic commercial ensemble between Commercial and Liberty Streets.
80003348.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78002298.summary: The Bush-Breyman Block (Breyman portion) is a late-nineteenth-century brick commercial facade trimmed with cast iron and sheet metal in classical and stylized motifs, with later sympathetic ground-story subdivisions that retain original iron thresholds. Built in Salem’s 1889 building boom for Bush and Breyman interests, it remains a downtown Commercial Street landmark despite interior remodelings.
78002298.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

91001575.summary: The Elsinore Theater, of reinforced concrete with a battlemented medievalizing High Street facade by Ellis F. Lawrence’s circle, is Salem’s landmark atmospheric/movie palace. A comprehensive mid-1980s renovation rebuilt the marquee; the monumental foyer is the design centerpiece, and the theater is a key work in Lawrence’s Oregon architectural legacy.
91001575.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80003351.summary: The J. K. Gill Building (1868) belongs to Salem’s river-oriented Commercial Street business district that grew with flour and woolen mills and the 1871 Oregon and California Railroad. Despite losses such as the Chemeketa Hotel fire, the nomination places this early brick commercial fabric within the capital’s cohesive late-1860s through early-twentieth-century downtown core.
80003351.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

86002851.summary: Opened in 1927 at State and Liberty, the old First National Bank Building served as bank headquarters for twenty years before a later International Style bank replaced it elsewhere downtown. The eleven-story reinforced-concrete tower by Leigh L. Dougan (formerly of Houghtaling and Dougan, designers of Portland’s Elks Temple) is a major capital-city skyscraper of the 1920s.
86002851.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80003350.summary: Andrew T. Gilbert’s 1887 house at Marion and Water Streets is one of two outstanding large Queen Anne houses in Salem and the only substantial historic house still in the downtown core. Despite encroachment by the Marion Street Bridge approach, it still dominates the Willamette riverbank setting where nearly all other large nineteenth-century downtown houses are gone.
80003350.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000504.summary: The R. P. Boise Building (1913) by Fred A. Legg is a distinctive early-twentieth-century commercial block on State Street and a National Register neighbor to related Legg works. It contributes to the unbroken late-nineteenth and early-twentieth-century street wall that the Farrar Building nomination also highlights as unique in Salem’s downtown.
81000504.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87000035.summary: The S. A. Manning Building warehouse stands at the foot of State Street where it meets Front Street on the Willamette’s east bank. The nomination presents this early-twentieth-century riverfront commercial/warehouse fabric as significant to Salem’s working waterfront and downtown edge industrial commerce.
87000035.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75001590.summary: The Boon Brick Store is a rare architectural survivor and a monument of early territorial history on its Salem site. John D. Boon, a Methodist missionary who arrived in 1845, helped incorporate Willamette University, promoted telegraph and railroad projects, served as Territorial Treasurer (1853) and first State Treasurer; possible treasury use makes this the oldest building associated with Oregon state government.
75001590.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75001593.summary: Waller Hall (1864–67) is Willamette University’s first substantial and oldest extant building, significant for education and for the university’s deep roots in the Methodist Mission that founded Salem. The nomination stresses its landmark campus role as the school’s pioneering permanent academic structure.
75001593.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

05001520.summary: The Union Street Railroad Bridge and Trestle carries Salem’s railroad approach across the Willamette corridor and is nominated for engineering and transportation significance within the capital’s rail history. The structure documents early-twentieth-century railroad bridge and trestle construction still readable in the urban riverfront landscape.
05001520.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

74001703.summary: Pleasant Grove Presbyterian Church is one of a small group of 1850s Willamette Valley meeting-house churches still standing—types once common in pre-Territorial days but now scarce. It is among the oldest Presbyterian churches extant in Oregon and a rare surviving example of that early vernacular sacred form.
74001703.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000508.summary: Built in 1913 by contractor Ralph R. Jones for his own use north of the Capitol Mall, the Jones-Sherman House is a remarkably well-preserved Bungalow from identifiable Minneapolis pattern-book plans by Lindstrom and Almars. It shows how fashionable catalogue architecture shaped Salem’s early-twentieth-century neighborhoods.
81000508.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

97000587.summary: The Carl E. Nelson House (Cottonwood Cottage) on E Street Northeast is nominated as a locally significant Salem residential property reflecting early-twentieth-century domestic design and neighborhood development north of downtown. Nomination narrative places it among carefully documented capital-city houses of its period.
97000587.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

79002120.summary: The Spanish Colonial house and garden built for retired J. C. Penney associate Daniel B. Jarman in 1929 is Salem’s penultimate example of a period style common in California and the Southwest but comparatively rare in western Oregon outside Portland. Landscape architecture and the house together define a conspicuous capital-city estate.
79002120.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89002063.summary: The George Collins House (Collins–Downing House) is a nominated Salem residence documenting late-nineteenth/early-twentieth-century domestic architecture in the capital. The Register listing recognizes its local architectural and associative significance within Salem’s historic neighborhoods.
89002063.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75001598.summary: St. James Lutheran Church is a Late Gothic Revival church that anchors Portland's South Park Blocks, across from the Portland Art Museum. The nomination says its religious significance is greater still: it was the first English-speaking Lutheran church in Oregon, the first headquarters of the Pacific Synod of the United Lutheran Church, and the first home of the Lutheran seminary for the West Coast. The congregation was organized in Portland in 1889.
75001598.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96000994.summary: The Kress Building at SW Fifth and Morrison was built in 1928 for the S. H. Kress Company from plans by the chain's corporate architect, E. J. Hoffman. Its cream glazed terra cotta and Chicago School-influenced facade make it, per the nomination, an outstanding local example of the last phase of Beaux Arts Classicism, and it is also significant in commerce as the original national variety chain store in downtown Portland.
96000994.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

90001509.summary: The Cumberland Apartments on SW Park Avenue is one of only three Jacobethan-style buildings designed by Ellis F. Lawrence, done early in his career with MacNaughton, Raymond, and Lawrence. Oriel windows, Tudor-arched openings, and cast-stone ornament make it a visual landmark. Lawrence went on to found the University of Oregon School of Architecture and Allied Arts in 1914 and became one of Oregon's most influential architects and educators.
90001509.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74001710.summary: The Portland Art Museum's Ayer Wing (1932) and Hirsch Wing (1938) were designed by Pietro Belluschi while the firm was still A. E. Doyle and Associate. The nomination calls the museum the first Belluschi building to win national attention; its cantilevered monitor lighting over the upper galleries was hailed as a novel way to light art without glare. The museum was included in a 1938 list of the 100 best buildings done in the United States in the preceding 20 years.
74001710.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98000211.summary: The Roosevelt Hotel at 1005 SW Park Avenue was commissioned in 1924 by Prudential Finance Company as a first-class hotel and designed by Claussen and Claussen in a Commercial style with Georgian overtones, faced in brick and terra cotta. It meets Criterion C as a good representative work of the Claussens, who produced many fine apartment houses and hotels in traditional styles in Portland between 1908 and 1942.
98000211.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86002968.summary: The eight-story Medical Arts Building (1925) by Houghtaling and Dougan faces the Central Library across SW Taylor Street. Its Italian Renaissance facade advertises its purpose through healing-arts iconography, including a bust of Hippocrates and a caduceus relief in the vaulted portico. The nomination calls it the first building in Portland specifically designed and built for a medical cooperative, led by physician and former state senator Dr. Andrew C. Smith.
86002968.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

07001129.summary: The Failing Office Building qualifies under the 'Historic Resources in Downtown Portland, 1906-1914' context. It is one of the office buildings from Portland's boom after the 1905 Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition. The fair drew about 1.6 million visitors, and the city's population nearly doubled to about 207,000 by 1910. Investment from that growth reshaped downtown, and this building is significant for its ties to that commercial growth and community development.
07001129.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

82003744.summary: The Meier & Frank Building is Oregon's earliest white terra cotta Commercial Style department store. It was also the first major commission for A. E. Doyle, who went on to dominate Portland architecture from 1907 to 1928. At the client's request, after he saw Chicago's Carson Pirie Scott store, Doyle redesigned the annex in white terra cotta. The nomination also calls Meier & Frank the state's most significant example of a pioneer mercantile house that grew with Portland and the Northwest.
82003744.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96001001.summary: The fifteen-story Northwestern National Bank Building by Doyle and Patterson is an outstanding local example of Classical Revival commercial design, combining Beaux Arts classicism with terra cotta detailing. Oregonian publisher Henry Pittock and partner Frederick Leadbetter built it on the site of the Marquam Building, which the nomination calls Portland's first skyscraper. Its two-story banking room served the Northwestern National Bank and Portland Trust and Savings.
96001001.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

98000201.summary: The Jeanne Manor Apartment Building on Park Avenue was designed by Harry A. Herzog, a Portland architect and developer of the 1930s. It shows the Art Deco influence that made Herzog a leading local exponent of the style more clearly than his nearby Parkway Apartments. It meets Criterion C as a distinctive work in his relatively small documented body of work.
98000201.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86000286.summary: The Cornelius Hotel (1907-1908) at 525 SW Park Avenue is a mansarded French Renaissance building by John V. Bennes (Bennes, Hendricks and Tobey). It is listed as a rare surviving example of the style in the downtown core and as work by an architect whose practice spanned the state. It is also locally significant for Dr. Charles W. Cornelius, an Oregon pioneer whose varied pursuits included gold mining and acting.
86000286.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96001000.summary: The ten-story Broadway Building at SW Morrison and Broadway opened in 1913. It was designed by Portland architect and civic leader E. B. MacNaughton in the Commercial style with classical detailing, for Multnomah Security Company. It is one of the vintage brick and terra cotta tall buildings that frame Pioneer Courthouse Square, and its retail base helped make this intersection a center of fashionable department stores and clothiers.
96001000.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

04000831.summary: The 1911 Hotel Alder was designed by Daniel C. Lewis for property owner William Morgan. It qualifies under the 'Historic Resources of Downtown Portland, 1906-14' context as one of the buildings that redefined downtown during the boom after the Lewis and Clark Exposition, when building permit values rose from about $4 million in 1905 to nearly $21 million in 1910. It is also noteworthy within D. C. Lewis's body of work.
04000831.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

91001554.summary: The twelve-story Selling Building (1910) at Sixth and Alder was built for Ben Selling, C. S. Moore, and Moses Blum to plans by Doyle and Patterson. It was the firm's first office tower, with Florentine Renaissance detailing in cream glazed terra cotta over a Chicago School base-shaft-capital scheme. Its 1930s Art Deco storefront and lobby, designed by Harry A. Herzog with Oregon Brass Works bronze, survive as historic alterations.
91001554.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

93001567.summary: The twelve-story Buyers Building (1928) at SW Third and Alder was a self-contained wholesale buyers' market. Wholesale jeweler Isidore Holsman first planned it as an eight-story building in 1922, and Pacific States Investment Company later completed it at twelve stories. Designed by Chicago-trained brothers Fred and William Claussen, it is called the firm's masterwork and an innovative, well-preserved Chicago School tall building.
93001567.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

93001497.summary: The 15-story Yeon Building (1910-1911), clad in white glazed terra cotta, was built at SW Fifth and Alder for lumber capitalist John B. Yeon to designs by San Francisco's Reid and Reid. It is part of the office-building boom after the 1905 Lewis and Clark Exposition, when about 20 major towers moved Portland's commercial center west of the waterfront, and it marks a high point in local architectural terra cotta.
93001497.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

80003372.summary: The six-story Odd Fellows Building and Lodge (1922-1924) is Portland's only Period-style 'Gothic' skyscraper, with Tudor Gothic terra cotta elements applied to a tall commercial form. It stands between the Portland Art Museum and the Public Library. It was designed by German-born architect Ernst Kroner, who had been active in Portland politics in the 1890s and later moved his own office into the building.
80003372.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

03001068.summary: The New Imperial Hotel (1909), designed by Whidden & Lewis, is significant for Oregon Republican leader Phil Metschan Jr. Over forty years he made the hotel a social center for eastern Oregonians visiting Portland, and the contacts he built there grew into a statewide political organization. Historian E. Kimbark MacColl called him a Republican 'kingmaker', and the Oregonian called the hotel 'the second state capital'. Metschan won the Republican nomination for governor in 1930.
03001068.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96000997.summary: The Auto Rest Garage at SW Tenth and Salmon was built as a showroom and sales outlet for Stutz and Columbia Six automobiles. It is a small Commercial-style brick building by Jacobberger and Smith, with pediments and stylized ornament designed by Joseph Jacobberger. It recalls the period when SW Tenth Avenue was lined with auto sales and service businesses.
96000997.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96000993.summary: The five-story H. Liebes & Company Building at 625 SW Broadway was designed by John V. Bennes for a leading furrier. It used a steel frame with lightweight terra cotta cladding to fit in as much window area as possible for daylight and display, including three bays of Chicago windows. The nomination calls it an outstanding early local use of steel-frame and architectural terra cotta technology.
96000993.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

77001112.summary: The Hamilton Building was built by pioneer industrialist and banker Henry W. Corbett and designed by Whidden and Lewis. It was once called Portland's most elegant new office building and is described as Oregon's earliest, and probably best, classical Commercial Style building. At a time when Richardsonian Romanesque dominated, as in the neighboring Dekum of 1892, its correct Greek detailing set a new fashion for commercial buildings in Portland.
77001112.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002170.summary: Built about 1902 for Cyrus A. Dolph, this building at 615 SW Broadway was remodeled in 1929-1930 for Charles F. Berg's women's apparel store. Its Moderne (Art Deco) facade was inspired by the 1925 Paris Exposition des Arts Decoratifs. The nomination calls it the state's best-known and most lavishly decorated Moderne building, and Portland's only Modernistic design in glazed polychrome terra cotta. Berg was also a local pioneer of the 'shop within a shop' retailing idea.
83002170.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89000066.summary: The 12-story Bedell Building at SW Sixth and Alder was completed in September 1925 for the women's clothing firm of New York merchant Alfred M. Bedell. It was designed by George A. Schonewald of New York with Portland architect Albert E. Doyle. Like many Portland terra-cotta buildings, it follows the early skyscraper pattern of base, shaft, and capital, with Classical ornament simplified in the Art Deco manner, and the Morning Oregonian called it 'one of Portland's most distinctive business structures.' Bedell's was one of Portland's leading women's specialty shops for about forty years, until it went bankrupt in 1965.
89000066.heading: 8. Statement of Significance

88001531.summary: The ten-story Lipman-Wolfe and Company Building (1912) at SW Fifth and Alder, designed by Doyle and Patterson, is an outstanding downtown example of a large building clad and decorated entirely in white architectural terra cotta, including wreaths and lion heads. It reflects the westward move of Portland's commercial center after the 1905 Exposition. It was also the longtime headquarters of a mercantile firm founded in Portland in 1892.
88001531.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

07000367.summary: The seven-story Swetland Building was built in 1907 to plans by Portland architect Emil Schacht for businessman Lot Q. Swetland. It qualifies for commerce and community development as part of the 1906-1914 group of buildings, documented in a multiple-property study, that redefined downtown during the investment boom after the 1905 Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition.
07000367.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84003073.summary: The Calumet Hotel at 620 SW Park Avenue was designed in 1907 by Joseph Jacobberger, with a French Renaissance or 'Edwardian Baroque' exterior over brick bearing walls and a wood frame. It is significant as a once-common type of downtown building, as one of 49 important Jacobberger designs, and for its ties to Portland's rapid growth in the decade after the 1905 Lewis and Clark Exposition.
84003073.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80003363.summary: The eight-story Dekum Building (1891-1892) is an excellent Richardsonian Romanesque design by McCaw, Martin & White, the leading Portland practitioners of the idiom. Of sixteen buildings built in these styles in Portland between 1889 and 1895, the nomination calls the Dekum the most exuberant. It also honors its builder, pioneer merchant, banker, and developer Frank Dekum.
80003363.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

05001179.summary: Harrison Court is an early twentieth-century wood-frame apartment building from the transition between single-room hotels and rooming houses and true multi-family apartments in Portland. It was built as Portland's boom began around the 1905 Lewis and Clark Exposition. It had sixty rooms in twenty suites behind two separate entrances, one section for men and one for women, and few Portland apartment buildings predate it.
05001179.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

89000059.summary: The Electric Building (1910), designed by D. C. Lewis, housed the offices and a main generating station of the Portland Railway, Light and Power Company. It was built over the power plant without shutting it down. It is chiefly significant as headquarters of one of Portland's important Progressive-era companies. Its outline of electric light sockets, which lit the building at night, was both City Beautiful ornament and an advertisement for modern technology.
89000059.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78002321.summary: The Failing Building, now known as the Postal Building, was designed by Whidden & Lewis, who dominated Portland architecture for two decades. The nomination calls its elegant terra cotta work its main distinction, unique and in excellent condition. The partners, both MIT-trained, came to Portland through work on Henry Villard's Portland Hotel, which McKim, Mead & White designed.
78002321.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89000058.summary: The Wilcox Building (1911) at SW Sixth and Washington is called the best-designed tall office building by Whidden and Lewis, with rich classical detailing in white terra cotta that rivaled the contemporary Spalding and Yeon buildings. It was the symbolic seat of T. B. Wilcox, president of the Portland Flouring Mills Company, the Pacific Northwest's largest milling and grain-exporting firm, which opened markets in Japan and China.
89000058.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002129.summary: The Central Building of the Multnomah County Library is called the masterpiece of leading Portland architect Albert E. Doyle. It is a statewide landmark of pre-Modern architecture in which Georgian Revival conventions were applied economically to express the building's function. Noted artisans, including apprentice architect Jamieson Parker and designer Harry F. Wentz, decorated and furnished it, and it remains handsome and functional.
79002129.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72001086.summary: Calvary Presbyterian Church, now 'The Old Church', was built in 1882-1883 to a design by Warren H. Williams, Portland's leading architect of the day, on a site donated by pioneer banker William S. Ladd. It was believed to be the most elaborate of the vernacular churches built in Portland in the 1870s and 1880s. It is the sole survivor of that type and the oldest church standing in the city.
72001086.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82001513.summary: The twelve-story Spalding Building (1911) at 319 SW Washington was designed by noted New York architect Cass Gilbert, who began his famous Woolworth Building the same year. Its steel frame, brick walls, and classical detailing follow Gilbert's tripartite tall-building design. A later ground-floor remodel removed its fine Doric entablature, but the upper exterior remains intact.
82001513.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82003746.summary: The Waldo Block (1886) is a well-preserved Victorian Italianate cast-iron commercial building and an important part of the history of Portland's Chinese community. Judge John B. Waldo, of a pioneer Oregon family, built it and gave it his name. Portland retains the largest collection of late-nineteenth-century cast-iron-front buildings in the West, and this is one of only three outside the Skidmore/Old Town district.
82003746.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

91000057.summary: The 1910 Olds, Wortman and King Department Store was designed by Seattle architect Charles Aldrich and built by the Trustee Company, which leased it to the store for 50 years. It is significant for architecture and as the final home of one of Portland's longest-running retailers, whose roots go back to 1878. Pietro Belluschi later designed its elevators and escalators (1946-1947), and the nomination notes it was one of the first historic Portland buildings renovated for new commercial use.
91000057.heading: Summary Paragraph

96001003.summary: The Morgan Building (completed 1913), from plans by Doyle, Patterson and Beach for investor W. L. Morgan, is a steel-frame professional office block filling half a block on Washington between Park and Broadway. Its red tapestry brick and cream terra cotta facades follow Beaux Arts Classicism, and its rear housed the Rainbow Room, described as Portland's most ornate restaurant-club of its kind.
96001003.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

85003037.summary: The Imperial (Plaza) Hotel at 422-426 SW Broadway, built for A. B. Steinbach and George F. Wells, is credited to F. Manson White. It is one of sixteen Richardsonian Romanesque/Sullivanesque buildings put up in Portland between 1889 and 1895, and the nomination presents it as a premier local example of that style. It is also tied to Portland figures George F. Wells and hotelier-politician Phil Metschan.
85003037.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82001512.summary: The Grand Stable and Carriage Building (1886-1887), owned by Simeon Reed, and the adjoining 1894 commercial building on SW Second Avenue belong to one of the few complete block-long stretches of late-nineteenth-century commercial architecture left downtown. The stable's arched windows and cast-iron ornament embody the High Victorian Italianate style, and the 1894 building's non-load-bearing facade marks a new step in commercial design.
82001512.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002132.summary: The Railway Exchange Building typifies Portland's great building boom before World War I and set new local construction standards. It was Portland's first major business block built of reinforced concrete and one of its earliest curtain-wall buildings, with as much as 70% of the exterior in plate glass. Huber's Restaurant, also named in the listing, occupies part of the building.
79002132.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

77001110.summary: The Concord Building (designed 1889) is described as a unique Oregon example of the transition to the Commercial Style in office buildings and as the first building designed by Whidden & Lewis, who went on to give Portland many of its finest buildings. The nomination also calls it the oldest building in the city used continuously as an office building.
77001110.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

01000155.summary: The Simon Benson House, a Queen Anne residence of about 1900, was built in Portland's West End for Simon Benson's family. In 2000 it was moved three blocks to 1803 SW Park Avenue on the Portland State University campus. It was first listed in 1983 and remains eligible as a rare surviving example of the kind of house once common in the West End.
01000155.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

76001584.summary: The Equitable (Commonwealth) Building, completed in 1948 to designs by Pietro Belluschi, was the first office block of the International Style built in Portland. Its flush aluminum-and-glass skin varies by no more than about 7/8 inch in surface relief. Innovations included a heat pump, and the nomination says the building is still praised for its restraint and dignity.
76001584.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88001038.summary: The Hotel Arminius (now the Morrison Hotel) was built in 1904 by the General German Aid Society as an investment property and a place to help settle German-speaking immigrants. The three-story Italian Renaissance-detailed brick building is one of only two surviving Portland works by architect Otto Kleemann. When new, its ventilation and hot-and-cold-water systems were described as the first of their kind in the city.
88001038.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98000213.summary: The Stevens Building, designed as a medical-dental building with up-to-date fixtures, was developed by T. B. Wilcox along with his Imperial Hotel and Wilcox Building, all by Whidden and Lewis. It meets Criterion C as an essential part of the group of early twentieth-century brick and terra cotta tall buildings that give downtown Portland its character. A 1954 remodel by Belluschi and Skidmore, Owings and Merrill is treated as non-contributing.
98000213.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

74001706.summary: The Bishop's House was built in 1879 on Stark Street beside Portland's brick Gothic Catholic cathedral, which no longer stands. Its Gothic design is attributed to P. Heurn of San Francisco, the cathedral's designer. For 30 years, until a new cathedral site was chosen, it served as the chancellery office; it also housed Catholic organizations and, for a time, the Catholic Sentinel newspaper office. Its narrow brick, stucco, and cast-iron front with pointed-arch windows survives among Portland's early commercial buildings.
74001706.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

12000932.summary: Opened December 19, 1910, the Hawthorne Bridge is the oldest remaining bridge across the Willamette in Portland and the oldest operating vertical-lift bridge in the United States. Designed by Waddell & Harrington, its 205-foot lift span was the longest built at the time, and it was the first modern vertical-lift bridge driven by electric motors. It is significant statewide for transportation and community development.
12000932.heading: SIGNIFICANCE SUMMARY

96000992.summary: The six-story Lumbermen's Building (1909) at SW Fifth and Stark was designed by David C. Lewis. Along with his Railway Exchange Building, it was among the first major Portland office buildings framed in reinforced concrete, which makes it a landmark in local concrete tall-building construction. Pietro Belluschi remodeled the exterior in 1948, and the lower floors were changed again later.
96000992.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

78002315.summary: The Georgian Colonial First Unitarian Church (1924) is the third building of a congregation formed in Portland in 1866. It is significant as one of several outstanding works by Beaux Arts-trained architect Jamieson Parker, his first large commission, and Parker later headed the first Historic American Buildings Survey effort in Oregon in 1934. After a 1965 fire, the sanctuary and parish hall were faithfully restored.
78002315.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78002306.summary: The three-story Bank of California Building (designed 1924) by A. E. Doyle's firm is called one of the most elegant buildings in metropolitan Portland and one of the city's last examples of the Beaux Arts academic tradition, here an Italian Renaissance palace style. It faces Doyle's temple-form U.S. National Bank across Sixth Avenue. The Bank of California came to Portland in 1882, mainly to serve the Northwest grain trade.
78002306.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73001579.summary: Mechanized woolen manufacturing on the Pacific Coast began in Salem in 1857, and the Thomas Kay Woolen Mill Company, founded in 1889 by Englishman Thomas Kay with Squire Farrar and C. P. Bishop, carried the industry forward. The existing mill was built in 1896 after an 1895 fire. It was for a time the largest plant of its type in Oregon and the longest-lived woolen mill ever established in Salem, operating until it was sold to the Mission Mill Museum Association in 1965.
73001579.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73001580.summary: The Jason Lee House, completed in spring 1841 in an oak grove on Mill Creek, was the first dwelling built where the town of Salem later grew. It belonged to the Methodist mission led by Jason Lee. It later served for many years as a dwelling and apartment house and narrowly escaped demolition.
73001580.heading: 8. Significance

75001591.summary: John D. Boon built this simple slab-construction ('box') house about 1846-1847, using rough-sawn planks nailed vertically to hand-hewn sills. It is one of Salem's few remaining pre-Territorial buildings. Boon, who arrived in 1845, served in the Territorial Legislature, as Territorial Treasurer, and as Oregon's first State Treasurer (1859-1862).
75001591.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

10000015.summary: The Salem Southern Pacific Railroad Station includes the 1918 Main Depot and a Rail Express Agency depot made from part of the 1889 depot. These are Salem's only intact depot buildings tied to early twentieth-century passenger rail service and express package delivery. The site is the oldest in Salem directly connected with passenger rail, in use since 1871, and the two buildings are rare Oregon depots in Beaux Arts Classical and Queen Anne styles.
10000015.heading: SIGNIFICANCE SUMMARY

74001700.summary: Asahel Bush, a newspaperman, banker, and public official, was among Oregon's most influential men for nearly sixty years. He began the Oregon Statesman in 1851, the state's first distinctly Democratic paper, with a press shipped around Cape Horn. His bank was by 1910 the largest in Oregon outside Portland. His 1878 Italian Villa-style house, on an estate that kept pasture for cows, is described as his only remaining memorial.
74001700.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000509.summary: These three houses on Saginaw Street trace the rising fortunes of the family of John Minto (1822-1915), who came overland to Oregon in 1844. Minto is remembered for starting sheep raising in the Willamette Valley in 1846, for his writing on Oregon farm life, and for helping organize the first State Fair. The group also includes Salem's outstanding example of the interwar English Cottage style, built for his son Douglas Minto.
81000509.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000475.summary: This Queen Anne house at 1599 State Street was built about 1890 for pioneer minister and educator Charles C. Stratton. It is locally significant for him and his wife, Eleanor Waller Stratton, daughter of Methodist missionary Alvin F. Waller. It is also a well-preserved example of the Queen Anne style in Salem.
84000475.heading: 8. Significance

81000507.summary: Lawyer, legislator, and U.S. Senator Benjamin F. Harding (1823-1899) built this vernacular Italianate house in 1884 as a suburban home on a full block south of downtown. It is one of three similar houses facing the Asahel Bush property, now a city park, which together define the park's architectural edge. The Amsler family, employees of the Bush family, later lived here from 1903 to 1952.
81000507.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85001181.summary: Louis S. Daue designed and built this house at 1095 Saginaw Street in 1907-1908 for his brother Alexander. It closely follows the Craftsman ideals promoted by Gustav Stickley and saw only a few minor alterations during the family's long ownership. It is also significant for the Daue family, who ran a general goods store in Salem for over 70 years (about 1890-1962) and were active in civic life.
85001181.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74001701.summary: Jason Lee's Methodist mission of 1834 was the first mission in the Pacific Northwest. In 1841 it expanded to Salem, building a house for Lee and this parsonage for the preacher-in-charge and the director of the Indian Manual Labor Training School, the forerunner of Willamette University. These white frame buildings are the only structures left from the mission period anywhere in the region.
74001701.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73001581.summary: 'Deepwood', the Dr. Luke A. Port House, is one of the few Queen Anne Revival houses left in Salem. It was designed by architect William C. Knighton, who gained local recognition for the work. Its formal and wildflower gardens are well known, the property borders Bush's Pasture Park, Salem's largest park, and Port is described as a wealthy citizen who led an unusual and mysterious life.
73001581.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80003349.summary: This 1895 Queen Anne cottage with Eastlake details was designed by noted Oregon architect Charles H. Burggraf (1867-1942) for his own use. It has finely scaled exterior ornament, classically inspired interiors, and leaded stained glass similar to known Povey glass. It is equally significant for the family of Judge Daniel Webster, a Civil War veteran and Salem justice of the peace.
80003349.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88001243.summary: The Marion County Housing Committee Demonstration House (1934-1935) was a Depression-era FHA and Civil Works Administration project under the Housing Act of 1934. A vernacular Gothic cottage of about 1860 was moved to the courthouse lawn and remodeled into a crisp Cape Cod-style house to show how older homes could be updated cheaply. It is the only intact remodel demonstration house of that program in the county seat.
88001243.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78002303.summary: Businessman William Lincoln Wade built this house in 1869. The nomination ties him to Oregon's second phase of American settlement (about 1855-1870), when entrepreneurs with capital followed the first farmers and became leaders in commerce and community life. The house is presented as essential to understanding Wade as a representative of that emerging class.
78002303.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90000841.summary: The Old West Salem City Hall (1936) on Edgewater Street is a small Modernistic, or PWA Art Deco, building designed by local architect Lyle Bartholomew and built by the Public Works Administration during the Depression. It is West Salem's only PWA building and only non-industrial Art Deco building. It housed the city government from 1936 to 1949, when West Salem was still an independent city.
90000841.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78002300.summary: This 1865 cottage was built by David McCully, a pioneer merchant who came over the Oregon Trail in 1852 with $5,000 earned in the California Gold Rush. He founded the townsite of Harrisburg, with its first store and post office, and later ran three stores in Salem and became involved in Willamette River transportation. The nomination also notes later occupant McMahan, a legislator (1923) and circuit judge (1924-1943).
78002300.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002163.summary: This English Cottage at 460 Leffelle Street South was designed by Clarence L. Smith for Charles G. and Mildred Robertson and completed in 1932. It is called the largest and best-designed of five Smith houses in a fashionable Fairmount Hill enclave. Its garden is an important work by Lord and Schryver, the first landscape architecture firm in Oregon formed by women.
83002163.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

97000136.summary: The Edgar Pierce House (1932) on Fairmount Hill is an outstanding French Renaissance-style period house by Salem architect Clarence L. Smith, designed over three years with his clients. It has a steep hipped roof, an octagonal tower with conical roof, quoins, and casement windows, and has changed little. It is also associated with people important in Oregon state government, including original owner Edgar Pierce, clerk of the State Land Board through 1961; during his ownership it also served as an unofficial governor's residence.
97000136.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

91000060.summary: Built in 1902 for Polk County farmer and real estate investor Henry Fawk, this gambrel-roofed Queen Anne house was the first home built on Fairmount Hill and the first development in the new Fairmount Park Addition south of downtown. It is the city's largest and best-preserved Queen Anne/Eastlake house using Colonial rooflines and dormers. The city also noted its link to Ross McIntire, U.S. Surgeon General and physician to Franklin D. Roosevelt.
91000060.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90000281.summary: Begun in 1911 at Lincoln Street and Fairmount Avenue for prominent Salem physician and surgeon Dr. William A. Cusick, this was the first house built in the Fairmount Park Addition, 'the first house on the hill' with views over the city. Designed by architect Fred A. Legg, it is described as the finest Colonial Revival house in the addition.
90000281.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000506.summary: Built in 1924 for packing company executive Curtis Cross at 1635 Fairmount Avenue, this unaltered stuccoed house with a red tile roof is probably Salem's best example of the Mediterranean style. It was among Clarence L. Smith's earliest Salem projects, with Jamieson Parker as architect in the final stage. Its clay tile walls were innovative for fire resistance and insulation, and it was the first house in Salem wired in conduit.
81000506.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78002297.summary: Salem brewer Samuel Adolph built this house in 1878 as a fashionable suburban farmhouse on a five-acre tract. It is one of the city's outstanding remaining Italian Villa houses. Similarities to the Asahel Bush House, completed across town the same year, suggest but do not prove a shared design source or builder.
78002297.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90000684.summary: Mahonia Hall, now the Oregon Governor's Residence, was built in 1924 for Thomas A. Livesley to designs by Ellis F. Lawrence of Lawrence and Holford. It is the best existing example of Period Tudor architecture in Salem and Lawrence's only residence in the city. Livesley was a world-renowned hop grower and broker, an innovator and social reformer in Oregon's hop industry, mayor of Salem (1927-1931), and a state representative (1937-1939).
90000684.heading: State significance of property

94001219.summary: This two-story Arts and Crafts house was built in 1926 for merchant Ulysses G. Shipley on Fairmount Hill. It is a noteworthy example of the style in Salem, closely fitted to its sloping lot by a mature naturalistic wooded landscape laid out by local landscape gardener Ernest Iufer. The house's designer has not been identified.
94001219.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

82003738.summary: The Oregon State Forester's Office Building opened in December 1938 as a WPA project. U.S. Forest Service architect Linn A. Forrest designed it in a style loosely based on the English Cottage tradition. It was built of Douglas fir, western red cedar, and native basalt flagstone, beside a central supply depot developed by the Civilian Conservation Corps as a complementary project.
82003738.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

91000806.summary: The Frederick S. Lamport House at 590 Lower Ben Lomond Drive SE was rebuilt in 1929 to designs by Portland architect Otis Josselyn Fitch in the Tudor Revival style, so little of the original house remains. It is locally significant as a well-preserved and unique Tudor Revival house in its neighborhood. With its gate house, pergola, reflecting pool, and landscaped grounds, it also represents the country estates once built in rural parts of the county.
91000806.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002121.summary: This Italian Bracketed farmhouse was built about 1870 for Fabritus R. Smith, an Oregon Trail pioneer of 1846 and state legislator. It predates the better-known Italianate Asahel Bush House and was one of the earliest properties developed in South Salem. It was Smith's third farmhouse on his 635-acre donation land claim, and his family (later the Ohmarts) lived in it for 73 years. Smith also served many years as vice-president of Willamette University's trustees.
79002121.heading: Statement of Significance (OCR of page image)

99000356.summary: The Jesse and Julia Harritt House is one of a dwindling number of buildings from Oregon's pioneer and territorial days. It is a good example of the carpenter-built Classical Revival houses that pioneer families put up in the 1850s once they were established. It stands on an early donation land claim just outside what became West Salem and is one of only two similar 1850s houses with Classical Revival detail known near Salem.
99000356.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

89000050.summary: This 1911 Craftsman house, the 'Elkirk Ranch House' off Eola Drive, was the retirement home of Edward W. and Ella St. Pierre. It is significant statewide as the place most closely associated with St. Pierre, a leader of early prison reform in Oregon. He served as the first permanent chaplain of the Oregon State Penitentiary, and a prison chapel was built in 1911 before ill health ended his service.
89000050.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75001599.summary: Carpenter Thomas Pearce built this house in 1860-1861, for $844, for Harrison Brunk, who came to Polk County in 1849. It is the oldest known two-story farmhouse in Polk County and stayed in the family until 1974. Brunk's son Thomas was a prize-winning stockman, a 4-H livestock-judging teacher, a judge at the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition, a state representative (1913), and a longtime Polk County judge.
75001599.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE (OCR of page image)

78002301.summary: This Italian Villa-style house was built in 1884 for Salem physician and pharmacist Dr. Luke Port, who later commissioned 'Deepwood'. Minister and state legislator William Manning bought it in 1889. It originally stood across from Willamette University near the Capitol and was later moved when the telephone company expanded. It was divided into apartments after 1920 but keeps most of its finish work.
78002301.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002123.summary: This two-story farmhouse in the Waldo Hills was built about 1875 for Robert Witzel and his bride. It is notable for its double piazza, a once-common Willamette Valley form that is fast disappearing. The house is also tied to Benjamin Witzel, an 1854 overland pioneer and early settler southeast of Salem who acquired farms for each of his four sons.
79002123.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74001717.summary: The Spring Valley Presbyterian Church at Zena, on the eastern slope of the Eola Hills, was organized by Rev. J. A. Cornwall in 1851. The church was begun in 1858 and finished in 1859 with money, materials, and labor from 52 subscribers on a four-acre site donated by Nelson Walling. It is one of the early pioneer churches of the Willamette Valley.
74001717.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76001588.summary: The John Phillips House is one of the dwindling number of buildings from Oregon's pioneer and territorial days, a carpenter-built Classical Revival house of the type 1840s pioneers built in the 1850s once established. The nomination notes it is plainer in line than most such Willamette Valley cottages. Phillips was born in Wiltshire, England, in 1814.
76001588.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

04000729.summary: The Delaney-Edwards House is significant statewide and is called one of the three oldest homes recognized in Oregon. It typifies the early farmhouses of Willamette Valley settlers. It is tied to the history of criminal law in Oregon: two men convicted of a murder committed at the house in 1865 were the first people executed in Oregon. It also shows how a settlement-era farmhouse changed into the mid-twentieth century.
04000729.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

80003354.summary: Built about 1870 for the original holder of the Hardin McCallister donation land claim, this box-constructed farmhouse is one of the Willamette Valley's least-altered and most finely detailed small Rural Gothic houses, marked by symmetry and a central gable with a lancet window. It stands near the site of the family's first two-room cabin, and remnants of the oak grove and original orchard survive.
80003354.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84003036.summary: This site ten miles north of Salem includes the Oliver Beers farmhouse of about 1870 and, beneath it, the archaeological remains believed to be the Methodist Mission's 1840 hospital. Beers's donation land claim, recognized under the Provisional Government in 1844, had been one section of the 16-section mission farm claim that Rev. Jason Lee established in the 1830s, the earliest large-scale American farming operation in the Pacific Northwest. The house itself shows pioneer vernacular building beginning to adopt Gothic Revival features.
84003036.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

86003182.summary: The Independence National Bank Building opened in 1891, designed by Salem architect Walter D. Pugh. It is the town's best-preserved and most imposing High Victorian Italianate building. It is also significant as headquarters of the community's longest-lived bank, a mainstay of the farm economy, organized in 1889 by Herman Hirshberg, who served as president until 1925.
86003182.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87000040.summary: Built in 1874 by the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, this was the first church erected in Independence. The Roman Catholic Church bought it in 1910 and enlarged and remodeled it in the Georgian style, using it until 1966.
