As St. Patrick's it was the first Roman Catholic church in Polk County, and it is the town's only Georgian-style church.
87000040.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

86003177.summary: This two-story L-shaped farmhouse at 386 Monmouth Street was built for J. A. Wheeler, manager of the Independence Sawmill, when he arrived in 1880. It is the oldest, most distinguished, and best-preserved vernacular farmhouse in Independence, with Italianate features and porches with decorative bracing and original wrought iron cresting. Its southwest corner tower blew down in the 1962 Columbus Day Storm.
86003177.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88000092.summary: This T-plan balloon-frame house, probably built about 1875 for developer Dr. John Davidson, is a rare and distinctive local example of the Gothic Revival style once common in Independence. Banker and politician James S. Cooper (1841-1921), founder of the First National Bank, mayor, and state legislator, lived in it from 1883 to 1913. It was then moved two blocks south to its present site.
88000092.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88001040.summary: Built about 1914-1915 (the nomination gives both dates) for prosperous dairyman Kersey C. Eldridge, this two-story house is called the largest and best-designed Craftsman bungalow in Independence. It has many low-pitched gables with deep eaves on outriggers and knee braces, and it keeps its original bracketed window planter boxes. The architect is unknown.
88001040.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85000371.summary: This house at 887 Monmouth Street, apparently from the late 1870s and updated in the Queen Anne/Eastlake style about 1890, is a locally distinctive Rural Gothic house with refined craftsmanship. It stands on the donation land claim of Dr. John E. Davidson, a physician and merchant who arrived in 1850. Davidson and his wife Mary held the property until 1881, after which it passed to later owners.
85000371.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80003353.summary: The R. C. Geer Farmhouse of 1851 in the Waldo Hills is a historic farm group on land settled in 1847-1848 by pioneer nurseryman, flax grower, and territorial legislator Ralph Carey Geer. Meetings about Oregon statehood were held here before 1859. It is the most direct link in Oregon, apart from his Silverton burial site, to Geer's grandson Homer Davenport, the famous political cartoonist who wrote 'The Country Boy'.
80003353.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90000373.summary: Walter J. Domes built this Craftsman farmhouse in 1919 in rural Polk County between Bethel and McCoy, near Rickreall. It is significant for its architecture, combining a vernacular Craftsman house type with 'high style' touches such as columns on brick bases, half-round pediments, and a porte cochere, giving it the air of an elegant country house. It stands beside a filbert orchard among fruit trees and mature plantings.
90000373.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89000054.summary: Built about 1900 on North Craven Street in Monmouth for Eleanor Sherman, this balloon-frame house originally faced the trolley line linking Monmouth and Independence. It is a vernacular version of Queen Anne/Eastlake architecture and, in scale and state of preservation, clearly the most distinctive of three recorded examples of its type in Monmouth.
89000054.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98000210.summary: This Vernacular Gothic house in Monmouth, believed built about 1869, is one of the town's oldest houses and its only Gothic Revival building. It is associated with Polk County farmers Joseph and Priscilla Craven. Some have noted that its trim resembles Campbell Hall (1872), the oldest building at Western Oregon University.
98000210.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002118.summary: James Mechlin Anderson built this house in 1855 with savings from the 1849 California Gold Rush. It is an early, distinctive, and very well-preserved Greek Revival house, with an unusually original adaptation of a Virginia-style plan and additions from about 1878. It is also tied to the first wave of farm settlement in the mid-Willamette Valley and to Methodist members and clergy important in Oregon's early development.
79002118.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85001336.summary: Built in 1891-1892 for Glenn O. and Mary Ann Graves and deeded to Edward Webster Strong in 1907, this house at 391 E. Jackson Street in Monmouth is the town's most distinctive surviving example of the Stick/Eastlake style, with surface detailing possibly drawn from pattern books over Queen Anne massing. It has been restored as closely as possible to its appearance in a photograph taken by 1914.
85001336.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87001536.summary: Monmouth carpenter-builder John W. Howell built this Queen Anne/Eastlake house in 1891 for his family and ran it from the start as a boarding house for students of the Christian school that became Oregon Normal School and later Western Oregon State College. It is the oldest and best-preserved building historically tied to student housing at the college and one of Monmouth's two finest Queen Anne/Eastlake houses.
87001536.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000978.summary: Mount Gilboa Chapel has served the same Black community in the Oella/Catonsville area since the eighteenth century and remains its central landmark. The nomination remembers the A.M.E. church as where free Black scientist Benjamin Banneker worshipped and attended school, standing near his farm as a symbol of honor to that community.
76000978.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78001467.summary: The Emory Jail—also called the Howard County Jail or “Willow Grove”—is a five-bay, 2½-story granite block structure built in 1878 at 1 Emory Street in Ellicott City. The nomination highlights Romanesque Revival features such as the tall Roman window in the projecting central bay and fine stone lintels. Executions by hanging were held between the courthouse and jail until 1916; when nominated the jail was still in use, with hopes it would be preserved once a new correctional facility opened.
78001467.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76002221.summary: The Patterson Viaduct (Ilchester Bridge) ruins, built May–December 1829, were part of the early Baltimore & Ohio Railroad’s engineering works on the Patapsco. The nomination cites the stone viaduct as an important surviving fragment of pioneering American railroad civil engineering.
76002221.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79001114.summary: Summit survives from Catonsville’s era as a summer retreat for Baltimore’s wealthy merchants and bankers, who from the 1840s built large seasonal homes here. Begun in the 1850s as an Italianate villa and unfinished or Civil War–damaged by 1860, it illustrates that mid-century suburban villa landscape.
79001114.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

06001126.summary: Linnwood, about 2¾ miles north of Ellicott City, shows national architectural fashion replacing local building traditions. In 1901 an existing farmhouse was thoroughly remodeled into a large Queen Anne-influenced frame house from designs by D. S. Hopkins, a nationally known author of pattern books. It has a hip roof topped by a belvedere and a wraparound porch. The land is tied to James S. Gary of the nearby Alberton (later Daniels) textile mill on the Patapsco, who bought it in 1864. The property keeps the outbuildings of a small family farmstead: a stone springhouse/greenhouse, a cold-storage annex, a smokehouse, and a privy. Surviving farm accounts and family papers document its history from about 1865 to 1920.
06001126.heading: Summary Statement of Significance

04001382.summary: MacAlpine is a well-preserved post-Civil War country house of the Howard County gentry, built about 1868 for attorney James MacKubin about 1½ miles west of Ellicott City. The 2½-story frame house has a mansard roof and a two-story wing linked to it by a hyphen. Country estates once surrounded Ellicott City, but few survived development after World War II. MacAlpine has changed little and keeps comforts that had appeared in city houses before the war and reached country houses after it, such as heat-saving fireplace devices and a system of bells for calling servants. The period of significance runs from about 1868 to 1946, when the house left the original family's ownership.
04001382.heading: Summary Statement of Significance

87001568.summary: Old Catonsville High School (built 1878, enlarged 1898) is important for association with Catonsville’s growth as a Baltimore suburb, especially after the Baltimore and Catonsville Passenger Railway began in 1862. The brick school met expanding educational needs in an unincorporated Baltimore County community.
87001568.heading: 8. Significance

77000683.summary: Old Salem Church and Cemetery reflects mid-nineteenth-century German immigrant craftsmanship; stonemason Johann Moessmeringer’s plans produced a Gothic-inspired church consecrated June 16, 1850, praised then as a beautiful little church with rising tower. It symbolizes early German Lutheran/Reformed congregational life near Catonsville.
77000683.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

95001522.summary: The Brick House on the Pike is a well-preserved Federal-period house with a side-passage, double-pile plan, built about 1817 on a knoll facing the Baltimore National Pike west of Ellicott City. Charles Worthington Dorsey probably built it soon after his father, Caleb Dorsey, deeded him the land in 1817. The service wing may include an earlier, possibly mid-18th-century building. Only about half a dozen houses of this type survive in Howard County, and this one stands out for the exceptional quality of its interior woodwork. The decoration becomes plainer as rooms become more private, from the richly detailed entrance hall and front parlor up to the attic. Colonial Revival changes made after 1907 left the early interiors essentially untouched.
95001522.heading: Significance Summary

80001794.summary: Hilton is an elegant early-twentieth-century Georgian Revival mansion built within the walls of a large early-nineteenth-century farmhouse and now the focal point of a college campus. Constructed of specified high-quality materials with richly ornamented interiors, it is a well-preserved adaptive landmark of the Catonsville area.
80001794.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

01001374.summary: Dorsey Hall in Howard County is nominated for architectural and associative significance within the historic Dorsey family landscape near Columbia/Ellicott City. The narrative statement of significance supports its listing as a major local historic house.
01001374.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

85000583.summary: St. Mary’s Episcopal Church, Woodlawn, is significant for Gothic Revival rural frame church design influenced by Richard Upjohn’s Rural Architecture—one of fewer than ten surviving Maryland churches of that pattern—and for construction in 1873 to designs of Baltimore architects Dixon and Carson.
85000583.heading: SIGNIFICANCE SUMMARY

85001613.summary: Lorraine Park Cemetery Gate Lodge, designed by Baltimore architect Henry Brauns, embodies late-nineteenth-century picturesque eclecticism with stone-and-frame construction, irregular massing, and elaborate Stick-style detail. It is among Baltimore County’s most expressive Queen Anne buildings and retains excellent integrity.
85001613.heading: SIGNIFICANCE SUMMARY

06001127.summary: The Curtis-Shipley Farmstead on the old Annapolis Road (MD 108), south of Ellicott City, is a well-preserved example of the farmsteads typical of rural Howard County from the late 1800s to the mid-1900s. The Shipley family farmed this land from the colonial period, and their family cemetery still stands in a grove northeast of the house. John and Louisa Curtis bought the 90-acre farm in 1890 and built the frame farmhouse in 1891. It mixes Queen Anne shingled gables with Colonial Revival symmetry and a projecting central front gable. Eight contributing buildings survive, including a stone dairy/smokehouse, a bank barn, a granary, a wagon shed/corncrib, a hog barn, and a chicken house. The farm reflects an agricultural heritage now under heavy development pressure.
06001127.heading: Statement of Significance

78001446.summary: Owings Upper Mill is probably the oldest and largest mill surviving in Baltimore County and the last known project of Revolutionary patriot and merchant Samuel Owings. It exemplifies post-Revolutionary merchant mills built for Baltimore’s overseas trade and still shows massive millwright framing, pegged joints, and belt/axle fabric.
78001446.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

11000820.summary: Oakland Mills Blacksmith House and Shop is nominated for its association with rural craft industry and vernacular architecture in Howard County. The paired house and shop document blacksmithing as a community service trade in the historic Oakland Mills vicinity.
11000820.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

75002093.summary: Smithsonian bridge historian Robert Vogel called the Lombard Street Bridge unique: a bifurcated water-main form integral to a Bollman-truss support system rather than an arch. Self-taught engineer Wendell Bollman’s 1852 truss was a major nineteenth-century advance; this bridge is cited as the only one of its kind.
75002093.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85002174.summary: Schwartze Mansion (1845) is a well-preserved mid-nineteenth-century estate house with Greek Revival form, proportions, and detailing, retaining nearly complete interior decorative fabric after careful restoration. Additional significance comes from association with the Schwartze family and Baltimore’s industrial elite.
85002174.heading: SIGNIFICANCE SUMMARY

66000388.summary: Still in use, the Thomas Viaduct where the B&O crosses the Patapsco is the world’s oldest multiple stone-arched railroad bridge and America’s earliest major railroad bridge of its kind. Designed by Benjamin H. Latrobe, Jr., it was for its day the country’s largest masonry work and has needed no major structural changes.
66000388.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76002185.summary: The Weiskittel-Roehle Burial Vault illustrates inventive late-nineteenth-century cast-iron use: stove founder Anton Weiskittel created an impressive vault that appears to be stone, with Victorian renderings of Greek architectural detail, tying Fells Point industry to Loudon Park cemetery art.
76002185.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96000655.summary: Loudon Park National Cemetery in Baltimore is nominated under the National Cemetery MPS for its Civil War–era and later national cemetery significance—military burial landscape, architecture, and commemorative design. (NARA files this PDF under an NPS_AL medialz path though the property is in Maryland.)
96000655.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

00001084.summary: Howard Park Public School 218 is significant under Criteria A and C for association with community educational development and as a distinctive example of its school type/period in northwest Baltimore near Catonsville. The nomination links the building to broad patterns of public education and neighborhood growth.
00001084.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90000635.summary: Elkridge Furnace Complex on Furnace Avenue documents iron-making and related housing/industrial buildings in Howard County. The multiple contributing resources interpret the furnace community that served regional industry along the Patapsco corridor south of Catonsville.
90000635.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000958.summary: Waverley’s recorded history begins about 1703 as part of Ranter’s Ridge; the house fabric is judged more likely circa 1800–1820 than the traditional 1780 Nathan Dorsey attribution. The nomination presents the property as a significant Howard County plantation/dwelling landscape.
74000958.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

10000868.summary: The Hebrew Orphan Asylum in Baltimore is nominated for its architectural and social-historical significance to Jewish philanthropic care for orphans. The narrative statement documents the institution’s role in Baltimore’s Jewish community and the building’s distinctive institutional design.
10000868.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100007638.summary: Completed and dedicated in 1939, the State Library of Oregon was the first building on the Capitol Mall after the Capitol itself. It was built as a New Deal relief project with Public Works Administration and Works Progress Administration funds, giving work to architects, builders, and other workers. At the time it was the only library serving all Oregonians, through local libraries and its Oregon history collection. The nomination calls it the most important New Deal-era design by Whitehouse & Church and an outstanding example of Modernist architecture in Oregon, with carvings by sculptor Gabriel Lavare.
100007638.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

100005014.summary: Built in 1914 to designs by Oregon State Architect William C. Knighton, the Supreme Court and Library Building was the first building in Oregon built solely for the state Supreme Court. It escaped the 1935 Capitol fire and is now the oldest government building on Salem's Capitol Mall, still home to the court. It is Knighton's best Beaux Arts work and the first documented use of terra cotta in Oregon outside Portland. Its interior keeps marble floors, a grand stair, and a Povey Brothers stained-glass skylight over the courtroom.
100005014.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

14000895.summary: Gaiety Hollow was the home, studio-office, and garden of Elizabeth Lord and Edith Schryver, who founded the first woman-owned landscape architecture firm in the Pacific Northwest. They ran the practice for forty years, from gardens to large civic projects, and worked hard to professionalize landscape architecture in Oregon. The 1932 Colonial Revival house is a finely detailed work by Salem architect Clarence Smith. The garden, which they used to try out and showcase their ideas, embodies all of Lord and Schryver's design principles.
14000895.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

100002097.summary: The Spring Valley School, built in 1907 north of Zena in rural northeastern Polk County, replaced an 1868 school serving farm families. It taught children until 1952, when it was consolidated into the Salem School District, and it has served since then as a neighborhood gathering place. It is significant for the history of rural education before consolidation in the mid-Willamette Valley. It is also an excellent, well-preserved example of an early twentieth-century 'third generation' one-room schoolhouse.
100002097.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

74001697.summary: 'The Willows', the Sam Brown House near Gervais, was built in 1856-1858 in the Classical Revival style as a temple form with flanking wings, a design used in the East and Midwest but rare in Oregon. It was designed by another Sam Brown (no relation) and is said to be the first architect-designed house in Oregon. Builder Samuel Brown came west in 1846 and made money in the California gold rush before settling on a donation land claim. The grand house also served as a stop on the Oregon-California stagecoach line until about 1872, and Brown later became a state senator.
74001697.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79002124.summary: The Gallon House Bridge, an 84-foot Howe truss covered bridge built about 1916 over Abiqua Creek northwest of Silverton, is described as the last covered bridge in Marion County. Local tradition says it got its name from an illegal liquor dispensary at its north end, in 'wet' Mount Angel territory, that sold whiskey while Silverton was 'dry'. After damage in the 1964-65 flood, county commissioners chose to repair it and keep it as a historical landmark. It was listed as part of the Oregon Covered Bridges Thematic Resource.
79002124.heading: Inventory narrative (no formal significance statement)

13000397.summary: The Peter and Bertha Soderberg House, built in 1921 in Silverton, is locally significant as a moderately expressed side-gabled Craftsman bungalow. It keeps the key features of that type identified in the Historic Architecture of Silverton, Oregon and its Environs multiple property study. Peter Soderberg, a Swedish immigrant of 1882, and his wife Bertha farmed in Nebraska before buying the Silverton property in December 1920.
13000397.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

04001066.summary: The Gordon House is Frank Lloyd Wright's only completed commission in Oregon. He designed it in 1957 for Conrad and Evelyn Gordon, and it was built in 1964 under supervising architect Burton Goodrich, a Taliesin apprentice. It is an excellent example of Wright's Usonian houses, his mature exploration of affordable middle-class housing. When a new owner planned to demolish it, the house was carefully moved about 26 miles from near Wilsonville to The Oregon Garden in Silverton, keeping its original orientation and materials.
04001066.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

15000052.summary: The Louise Adams House, built about 1923, is locally significant as one of Silverton's best examples of a jerkinhead side-gabled Craftsman bungalow, with an octagonal front porch, exposed rafters, a brick chimney, and casement windows. Its period interior keeps the open plan and built-in features typical of the style. The land has unusually stayed in one family since 1861, when pioneer banker Ai Coolidge bought part of the Price donation land claim; it later passed to his daughter May Barbara's family, the Adamses.
15000052.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

82003736.summary: The Queen of Angels Priory in Mount Angel is one of the few monastic building groups in Oregon to survive intact from the nineteenth century. Benedictine Sisters from the Convent of Maria Rickenbach in Switzerland, led by Mother Bernardine Wachter, arrived in 1882 and set up their motherhouse at Mount Angel in 1888, opening Mount Angel Academy the next year. The group includes the 1888 Second Empire Baroque convent designed by Otto Kleemann (with wings of 1902 and 1913) and the 1913 Georgian academy and normal school building later called Howard Hall.
82003736.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

11000078.summary: Built in 1904, this house is the last building tied to June D. Drake, a regionally prominent photographer, Silverton historian, and civic leader. He was the driving force behind the creation of Silver Falls State Park, the largest and best-known park in Oregon's state park system. The house is also a fine example of a moderately expressed Free Classic Queen Anne residence in the cross-wing form, and it was the first house in Silverton built with electricity.
11000078.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

85001182.summary: This Silverton church was begun in 1891 and finished in 1892 for the First Christian Church, a congregation organized near Bethany in 1851 that moved to Silverton in 1887. Lutherans bought it in 1906, enlarged it, and used it until 1974, reflecting the many Silverton families of Scandinavian descent. It is the oldest church building in Silverton and a fairly intact Gothic Revival building with Eastlake ornament and a fine jigsawn steeple. The 1926 bungalow parsonage beside it adds to the group.
85001182.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

11000077.summary: Built in 1906, the Murton E. and Lillian DeGuire House is a large, highly visible example of a moderately expressed Free Classic Queen Anne residence in Silverton. It has strong Colonial Revival influences, including a symmetrical block form, pedimented gables, and porch columns. Murton DeGuire, born in Silverton in 1875, was a dentist and dairy farmer who lived his whole life in the town.
11000077.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

13000032.summary: The Magnus and Emma Ek House, built in 1890 during a period of rapid industrial growth in Silverton, is one of the area's finest remaining Queen Anne residences. It began in the Stick Style and was soon remodeled with Queen Anne elements such as a wraparound porch. Its varied exterior siding and abundant interior woodwork show off the lumber available locally to its builder, Swedish-born carpenter, millwright, and sawmill owner Magnus Ek, who came to the United States in 1882.
13000032.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

13000396.summary: The Joseph Henry Moser Barn, built in 1910 behind 507 S. 3rd Street, is the only known barn standing within Silverton's city limits. It is an excellent example of a barn used to support a livery business in the early twentieth century, just before cars quickly replaced horses after about 1914. It is also a rare intact urban bank barn with an economical balloon frame and a truss-free roof that left open hay storage on the top level. Its German vernacular form may reflect the Moser family's German heritage.
13000396.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

15000053.summary: Built about 1907 in Silverton's Johnson's Addition, this house is among the city's best examples of a moderately expressed Colonial Revival house in the foursquare form. It has a wraparound corner porch with a Tuscan colonnade, symmetrical openings, and a side-hall foursquare plan that keeps its original doors and hardware. Businessman Charles F. DeGuire, an organizer of Silverton's People's Bank, built it, and German-born builder John Ludowitzki and his wife Mary bought it in 1910.
15000053.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

80003347.summary: Windischar's General Blacksmith Shop in Mount Angel was running by 1905 on a central lot John Windischar bought in 1902. Brothers Anton and Louis Weissenfels revived it in 1919, and Louis ran it for exactly sixty years until he retired in November 1979, as the work shifted from shoeing horses to repairing farm machinery and motor vehicles. With its equipment still in place and working, demonstrating forge, acetylene, and electric welding, it is a rare intact early twentieth-century industrial process together with its building. Only one other historic blacksmith shop with early equipment is known to survive in western Oregon.
80003347.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

76001583.summary: St. Mary's Church, finished in 1912, is a fine late Gothic Revival masonry church on a knoll at the center of the German Catholic town of Mount Angel, which surrounds it in the manner of a medieval European town. Designed by local parishioner Engelbert Gier and built largely by local craftsmen, it has a 185-foot tower, pointed stained glass windows with tracery, ribbed vaulting, and polychrome interior painting. When completed it was said to be the grandest church in the Northwest, and the nomination calls it unique in Oregon for its setting and strict High Victorian Gothic design.
76001583.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96001049.summary: The two-story brick Bank of Woodburn opened in 1890 at Front and Arthur Streets, beside the Southern Pacific main line. It is an outstanding local example of late Italianate commercial architecture and the older and better preserved of Woodburn's two historic bank buildings. From 1890 to 1906 especially, the bank helped foster the town's enterprise as Woodburn became the leading shipping center between Salem and Portland. Damaged in the 1993 Scotts Mills earthquake and threatened with demolition, it was rehabilitated by 1995 as a keystone of downtown revitalization.
96001049.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

79002125.summary: The Old Woodburn City Hall, a simple but imposing brick building of academic design, was the seat of Woodburn's city government for over sixty years, from October 1914 to January 1977. It was designed by Salem architect George M. Post, who used the same buff pressed brick as on his 1912 Carnegie Library in Salem. Its second-floor assembly hall was first used as a play area by the school across the street and later became the council chamber. Outside, the main change has been the conversion of the firehouse doors into a single overhead door.
79002125.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74001704.summary: Jesse H. Settlemier, son of a pioneer nurseryman, bought a donation land claim on the Portland-Sacramento route in French Prairie in 1863 and moved the family nursery business there. In 1869-1870 he helped bring the Oregon and California Railroad through the area, then platted four blocks and offered a free lot to anyone who would put up a building, starting the town of Woodburn. He became the town's first official mayor after its 1895 charter. His 1889 house, little altered since 1911 and later owned by the French Prairie Historical Society, is the centerpiece of a small neighborhood of houses from the same period.
74001704.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96001050.summary: The Victor Point School is a one-room schoolhouse built in 1889 for Victor Point School District No. 112, in the Cascade foothills between Silverton and Sublimity. It meets Criterion A as the focal point of the rural community of Victor Point from 1889 to 1946; after the store and gas station were removed around 1920, it was for a time the only building left marking the community's center. It also meets Criterion C as a well-preserved, well-documented example of a once-common vernacular type. It still stands on its original fieldstone foundation and one-acre school parcel.
96001050.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

78002304.summary: Built in 1882 in the pioneer Miller Cemetery, the Miller Cemetery Church is a rare Oregon example of a 'burying church' used mainly for funerals. It has a sloping floor, reverse entry, double doors for the casket, and a raised platform for the bier. It stands on land settled in 1847 by Richard Miller, an early politician and Marion County leader described as a member of Oregon's 'Constitutional Congress'. In 1860 he gave the cemetery to the community on condition that a church open to all denominations be built there. Pews from the 1853 Cumberland Church were installed, and the church was restored as a community Bicentennial project.
78002304.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88001156.summary: Briedwell School, a one-room rural schoolhouse built in 1895 a mile west of Amity, is one of only six school buildings in Yamhill County older than 1900. Along with Gibbs School it is one of the two best preserved, and it is the only one of the six to show a modest Queen Anne-Eastlake influence and to keep its belfry. It served grades 1-8 in District No. 7 until it was consolidated with Amity in 1957. It is also the last building left from the once-busy farm shipping point of Briedwell on the old Oregonian Railway narrow-gauge line.
88001156.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87000867.summary: The Kirk House on the eastern edge of St. Paul began as a vernacular Gothic farmhouse of about 1878 and grew through 1890, adding an 1880 main block with paired two-story polygonal bays and an 1890 windmill tower. It is locally significant as the headquarters of an outstanding historic farmstead and for brothers John W. and Thomas F. Kirk, who began farming part of their father's land here in 1878 and became very successful farmers in the railroad era. The unmarried brothers built the 1880 front section as two separate living areas. A large Ionic-columned porch added in 1971 is the main later change.
87000867.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

03000230.summary: The Birmingham Branch of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, finished in late 1926 to designs by Warren, Knight & Davis, marks the establishment and growth of the Federal Reserve system in the Sixth District. Its blend of twentieth-century classicism and Art Deco, sometimes called 'Greco-Deco', expressed the classical ideals of safe money and good government in a modern form. Unlike branches in other Atlanta District cities, the original building was kept when the bank expanded, and a set-back modernist addition was built beside it in 1958.
03000230.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

76000332.summary: Birmingham's U.S. Post Office and Federal Building was planned by 1916, delayed by World War I (its cornerstone was laid in 1918), and finished in September 1921. Congressman, later Senator, Oscar W. Underwood gets much of the credit for winning its appropriations. Its huge size and sleek, lightly ornamented classicism mark the shift from pre-war Beaux Arts design to the more austere federal classicism of the 1920s-1940s. It fills a full downtown block and remains a local landmark.
76000332.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002972.summary: The Cathedral Church of the Advent (1893), built of gray sandstone, is an early Birmingham interpretation of the English Gothic style, with a crenellated square bell tower and lancet windows. It is one of the few major buildings left from the young city's Victorian period, and it is usually credited to Charles Wheelock, one of the city's first architects. Its congregation was formally organized in 1872, months after the city was incorporated, and included leaders such as developers Robert Jemison Sr. and Jr. and coal operator Edward M. Tutwiler.
83002972.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

80000694.summary: The three-story brick Fox Building (1895) is one of the most intact late nineteenth-century commercial buildings in downtown Birmingham, a city founded in 1871 that keeps only a handful of its early commercial buildings. It was named for the Fox family, longtime grocers, and housed the city's largest grocery store and meat market, built the year after David Fox served a term as mayor. Its classical pressed-metal cornice and fine brickwork make it a good example of the Victorian commercial architecture that followed the city's first boom.
80000694.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

84000634.summary: The Ridgely (1914) was the first luxury apartment hotel built in downtown Birmingham and stayed its finest and most prestigious. Distinguished local architect William Leslie Welton worked with New York architect J. E. R. Carpenter on the eight-story red brick and terra cotta building, known for its two-story arch motif. It offered private porches with self-watering flower boxes, a roof garden with a children's playground, a cafe, and ground-floor shops. Coal and iron entrepreneur Edward M. Tutwiler financed it for his friend Robert Jemison Jr., probably the city's most influential developer.
84000634.heading: Significance and History

98000709.summary: This 1998 boundary increase adds the remaining eligible buildings around the Downtown Birmingham Retail and Theatre Historic District, found in a new survey: a small group of early twentieth-century commercial blocks on 4th Avenue North. The largest is the two-story Clark Building (1908) at 20th Street, once an important corner of the old business and hotel district, home to specialty shops and one of Birmingham's oldest bookstores, Smith & Hardwick. Most of these buildings were slated for restoration using historic tax credits.
98000709.heading: Boundary Increase narrative (no separate significance statement)

82002044.summary: Prominent Birmingham architect D. O. Whilldin designed this building at 513-517 21st Street North in 1923-1924 as his own office, at the height of a career that ran from 1905 to 1962. He designed some of the city's most important buildings in the 1920s and 1930s, founded and was an early president of the Alabama Chapter of the American Institute of Architects, and trained many of the next generation of Birmingham architects. Its eclectic exterior, including a terra cotta entrance lunette he designed, and its richly detailed reception and consultation rooms survive largely intact.
82002044.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

81000126.summary: The Crittenden Building was built in 1924 to designs by Harry Wheelock and remodeled in 1933 as the Burger-Phillips store, one of the finest women's apparel stores in Alabama. The locally owned company began in 1894 as a railroad salvage dry goods firm. Its 1933 store was one of the first in the South with electric-eye doors, air conditioning, and high-speed elevators. Architecturally it stands out for its high-style Art Deco storefront and its galleria, the larger and more elegant of only two in Birmingham.
81000126.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

82002042.summary: The S. H. Kress & Company Building (1936-1937), designed by Kress corporate architect Edward F. Sibbert, is high-style 1930s architecture bridging Moderne/Art Deco and the International Style. Glazed terra cotta wraps its curved corner, and its banded windows mark the warehouse floors above the store that Kress's high-volume, direct-from-manufacturer retailing required. With the nearby Loveman's and Woolworth buildings, it forms a unified group of Art Deco buildings at Birmingham's main retail intersection. Kress had opened its first Southeastern store in Birmingham in 1889.
82002042.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

83002974.summary: The 13-story Hotel Redmont (1925), named for Red Mountain, the source of Birmingham's mineral wealth, is one of only two hotels left from 'Hotel Row', the six blocks of Fifth Avenue that linked Terminal Station to the heart of the city. It reflects the rise of big-city hotels in the prosperous, train-travel era of the 1920s and was the first Birmingham hotel to offer a private bath in every room. Designed by Atlanta's prominent 'hotel architect' G. Lloyd Preacher, it is a good local example of the Chicago style, and its exterior is largely intact.
83002974.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

80004471.summary: The Alabama Penny Savings Bank building (1913) housed the first Black-owned bank in Alabama, founded in 1890. By 1907 it was the second-largest Black bank in the country, financing homes and churches for thousands of Black residents. A local Black construction company built it, possibly to designs by Black architect Wallace A. Rayfield, and it gave offices to the Black press and professionals. After the bank failed in 1915, the Grand Lodge Knights of Pythias owned the building for some 65 years.
80004471.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

80000692.summary: The First Christian Church Education Building (1924) is one of only a handful of distinguished 1920s Neo-Classical buildings in downtown Birmingham, with smooth ashlar walls and marble columns. It was designed by William Leslie Welton, a major local architect trained at MIT and the Ecole des Beaux-Arts. The congregation, organized in 1874 just three years after the city's founding, is one of Birmingham's pioneer churches. The Depression delayed its planned sanctuary, so this education wing served as the church until 1954.
80000692.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

84000620.summary: The Age-Herald Building (1909-1910), designed by William Weston, the city's leading turn-of-the-century architect, is one of Birmingham's best Beaux Arts buildings. It was built to house The Age-Herald, formed in 1909 by merging The Iron Age and The Elyton Herald, and the paper's line later led to The Birmingham News. It was the paper's office and printing plant until 1920, then housed the Exchange Club and later Rust Engineering.
84000620.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

85002718.summary: The 1908 Wimberly-Thomas Warehouse is an excellent example of the large, open, well-lit storage and distribution buildings built near the rail lines in Birmingham's early warehouse district. Wimberly-Thomas Hardware was the city's largest combined wholesale and retail hardware house, supplying the construction, mining, textile, and railroad industries vital to the city's growth. Its records also shed light on local labor history, including sales of firearms to security agents patrolling area mines.
85002718.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

83002971.summary: Loveman, Joseph & Loeb, founded in 1887, became one of the premier department stores in Alabama and the Southeast. When a 1934 fire destroyed its 1890 and 1899 buildings on this corner, the company built the present Art Deco store, which opened in 1935 along with the rehabilitated 1916 annex. Designed by William Lehman of Newark with Birmingham associates Miller, Martin & Lewis, it is the largest and most refined of Birmingham's Art Deco commercial buildings, combining stainless steel, aluminum, and Carrara glass with limestone, marble, and granite. The nomination ranks it with the finest department stores in any American city.
83002971.heading: 8. Significance

82002041.summary: The Carver Theatre (about 1941), at 4th Avenue and 17th Street North, is one of Birmingham's best Art Moderne buildings, with Carrara glass, glass block, marble, and a neon marquee. It was one of two movie theaters built for Black audiences in the Fourth Avenue district, the only surviving remnant of the heart of Black Birmingham's social and cultural life under segregation (1908-1941). The source PDF is the Fourth Avenue Historic District nomination, so details on the theater itself are brief.
82002041.heading: Statement of Significance (Fourth Avenue Historic District nomination)

82001604.summary: Built in 1888 of red pressed brick, First Presbyterian Church is the most refined Victorian Gothic church in Birmingham and the oldest church building standing downtown. Its dominant bell tower, with spire, pinnacles, and stone tracery, has held a 25-bell carillon since 1924, and its original corrugated-iron vaulted ceiling on Tuscan columns is believed to be unique in Birmingham. The congregation, organized in 1872 about five months after the city was incorporated, is one of Birmingham's pioneer churches. A 1957 east wing carefully matches the original.
82001604.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

79000389.summary: The Watts Building (1927), designed by Warren, Knight & Davis, is one of the most distinctive buildings on Birmingham's skyline and of more than local architectural importance. Its imaginative take on the 1920s skyscraper setback, its stylized ornament, and its colored vertical stripes make it a significant expression of evolving Art Deco design, and its elevator lobby shows the rich decoration given to 1920s office building lobbies. It replaced an 1881 building of the same name and honors a pioneer Birmingham family.
79000389.heading: 8. Significance

06000940.summary: This listing's source is the Birmingham Civil Rights Historic District nomination; the parsonage of Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, a two-story buff brick house matching Wallace Rayfield's 1911 church, is one of the district's contributing buildings. The nationally significant district covers the downtown streets, churches, and Kelly Ingram Park where the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights, founded in 1956 by Rev. Fred L. Shuttlesworth, and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s SCLC waged the 1963 Birmingham campaign. Marchers, many of them children, faced fire hoses and police dogs, and the campaign helped bring about the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
06000940.heading: Statement of Significance (Birmingham Civil Rights Historic District nomination)

82001605.summary: First United Methodist Church (1891), designed by Weary & Kramer of Akron, Ohio, and built of Ohio brownstone, is the finest Richardsonian Romanesque building in downtown Birmingham and a notable Southeastern example of the style. Its repeated arches, deep voussoirs on truncated columns, and textured stone give it both massiveness and vitality, and the craftsmanship came from a local firm (Gilreath-Decker) in a city only about 20 years old. The congregation was organized in February 1872, two months after Birmingham was incorporated, and this third sanctuary reflects the iron and real estate boom of the late 1880s.
82001605.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

80000696.summary: Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, built in 1911 to designs by Black architect Wallace A. Rayfield by the Black-owned Windham Brothers Construction Company, has long been a center of Black community life in Birmingham. Its congregation was organized in 1873 and is one of the downtown pioneer congregations given land by the Elyton Land Company. On September 15, 1963, a bomb exploded at the church and killed four children, a major turning point in the Birmingham civil rights struggle. A stained glass window given by the people of Wales commemorates the bombing.
80000696.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

00001028.summary: The A. G. Gaston Building, built over the winter of 1959-1960 across from Kelly Ingram Park, is significant for its link to A. G. Gaston, Birmingham's pioneering Black entrepreneur and civic leader. It housed the head offices of his Booker T. Washington Insurance Company, Citizens Federal Savings and Loan (founded 1957, later the South's largest Black-owned financial institution), Vulcan Realty, and his Booker T. Washington Business College. It is also a remarkably intact Modernist office building with an auditorium, designed by Perry C. Langston of St. Louis's Bank Building and Equipment Corporation.
00001028.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

82001607.summary: St. Paul's Cathedral (1893), designed by the Druding Company of Chicago, is Birmingham's most highly developed Victorian Gothic church and one of the most elaborate in the South, with steep spires and gables, contrasting materials, and limestone-capped buttresses. Its congregation, begun as a mission of St. John's in Tuscaloosa soon after the city was founded, was the first Roman Catholic church in Jefferson County and the mother church of Catholicism in north Alabama. Built during the iron and real estate boom of the late 1880s, it is also an important survivor of the city's first public square around the Jefferson County Courthouse.
82001607.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

85000918.summary: The Ideal Department Store Building (1928-1929), with its ornamental terra cotta facade, typifies one of Birmingham's most popular early twentieth-century commercial styles, which peaked in the prosperous 1920s with Renaissance Revival cartouches, arabesques, and dentil cornices. It represents the most notable period in the career of prominent Birmingham architect D. O. Whilldin, who also designed the Florentine Building and the Thomas Jefferson Hotel. It shows his love of fine surface decoration and a mannerist contrast between a heavy base and slender upper floors.
85000918.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

80000695.summary: The Nabers, Morrow & Sinnige Building (1898) is one of the few virtually intact late nineteenth-century buildings left in Birmingham. It is notable for its unified, finely ornamented facade by Charles R. and Harry B. Wheelock, which blends Renaissance Revival motifs with tall Chicago-style arches. It is also tied to two leading families who settled Jefferson County long before the city's founding in 1871; one partner built a drug business that grew into Doster-Northington, the state's largest. The building reflects the growth sparked by the turn-of-the-century steel boom.
80000695.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

85000305.summary: This boundary increase adds two buildings on the edge of the Downtown Birmingham Historic District. One is a c. 1908 one-story brick commercial building at 312-322 21st Street North with a lighted corner marquee, built by prominent industrialist and developer William A. Walker. The other is the 1916 Rialto Theatre on Third Avenue, a three-story brick building with intricate brickwork that opened as the Bonita moving picture house and ran as the Rialto until the Depression. The larger district preserves Birmingham's commercial core, from Victorian blocks to the early skyscrapers of the 'Heaviest Corner on Earth'.
85000305.heading: Boundary increase narrative (district inventory)

82002040.summary: The Empire Building (1909) was the third of four early twentieth-century skyscrapers at the intersection known as the 'Heaviest Corner on Earth', possibly the only such grouping in the nation. It is the most elaborate Neo-classical skyscraper in Birmingham and perhaps the Southeast, and the most distinctive work of MIT- and Beaux-Arts-trained architect William Leslie Welton. Robert Jemison Jr.'s Empire Improvement Company developed it with a Metropolitan Life mortgage, the first major development loan for a local project from outside the Birmingham area.
82002040.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

83002977.summary: The Woodward Building (1902) is significant as the first steel-frame building in Alabama and an excellent local example of the Chicago-style skyscraper. It has a bold two-story commercial base, a plain gridded office shaft, and a projecting classical cornice. Its engineers, Purdy & Henderson, and contractor, John Griffiths & Son, both of Chicago, worked with architect William C. Weston, linking it directly to the early development of steel-frame construction in Chicago.
83002977.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

80000698.summary: Peter Zinszer's Mammoth Furniture House (1888) is a rare, excellent local example of cast-iron-front architecture and the larger of only two such buildings in Birmingham, with intricate molded classical ornament and broad glazing. It was one of the most elaborate buildings of the 1886-1887 iron and real estate boom. For almost three decades it housed the city's largest furniture store, perhaps its largest credit business. Through Dutch immigrant Peter Zinszer and his wife Rosa, who ran the store in its most prosperous years and was one of the first women to run a large Birmingham business, it reflects immigrants' and women's roles in the city's growth.
80000698.heading: Statement of Significance (in one paragraph)

83002976.summary: The First National-John A. Hand Building (1912, with a 1940 two-story addition) is an exceptionally fine local Neo-Classical skyscraper with marble pilasters and Corinthian capitals, designed by William Leslie Welton with Uffinger and Mowbray. It is one of the four skyscrapers built between 1903 and 1913 at 20th Street and First Avenue North, the 'Heaviest Corner on Earth'. Together with the Empire, Woodward, and Brown-Marx buildings, it is the city's best visible record of the rapid growth that made Birmingham the largest city in Alabama.
83002976.heading: 8. Significance

80000697.summary: The Waters Building (1888) is the finest remaining example of the combined store-and-residence buildings that sprang up during Birmingham's first major boom in the late 1880s. It was built to sell 'Queen's ware' (English earthenware) on the ground floor and house boarders above. Its Italianate hood molds and decorative cornices give style to a modest building and hint at the growing sophistication of the industrial city founded in 1871. Its changing uses show how such buildings adapted in an active downtown.
80000697.heading: 8. Significance

100004626.summary: The 30-story South Central Bell Building, finished in 1971 as the tallest building in downtown Birmingham, was designed by New York's Kahn & Jacobs with associate architect Der Scutt. It housed the headquarters of South Central Bell, the company's new five-state operating region, which chose to consolidate in Birmingham. It is a notable Modernist skyscraper and a forward-looking design meant to rebrand Birmingham as part of the New South after the steel industry's decline and the conflicts of the civil rights era. Its lobby holds 'Momentum', a large metal mobile by Lin Emery.
100004626.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

80000688.summary: This seven-story building, faced with white terra cotta, housed the main offices of the Birmingham Railway, Light and Power Company, the private utility that ran the city's streetcars and electric power and continued as the Birmingham Electric Company until the 1950s. Built in 1915 and rebuilt after a 1926 fire, it is an excellent example of the rich materials and classical details of prosperous 1920s Birmingham architecture, with wreath-and-shield friezes and anthemion cresting. Its brilliant white facade stands out among the brick buildings at a major entrance to downtown.
80000688.heading: 8. Significance

90001555.summary: Fire Station No. 6, a brick fire house built about 1906, is locally significant as the oldest remaining fire station in Birmingham. It is also one of the only urban, utilitarian-style stations left from the early 1900s. Decorative bands of brickwork outline its windows and arched engine-bay openings, and despite later alterations it keeps much of its original character.
90001555.heading: Statement of Significance

100009643.summary: The Seaboard Air Line Railway Freight Depot (1904) is a tangible link to Birmingham's Railroad Reservation, the wide rail corridor the founders laid through the center of the city in 1871 as the key to its future. Birmingham grew up at the crossing of two railroads amid the coal, iron ore, and limestone of the Birmingham District, earning the nicknames 'Magic City' and 'Pittsburgh of the South'. The Seaboard Air Line was one of the trunk railroads that served the city, and the depot reflects rail's central role in its industrial growth.
100009643.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

14001002.summary: Built in 1895 and enlarged before 1901, the Powell Avenue Steam Plant generated the electricity for the Birmingham District's extensive streetcar network. That network supported the area's industrial growth, its streetcar suburbs, and its downtown businesses. The plant is also a good example of restrained, eclectic Late Victorian industrial architecture, with segmental-arched windows, corbelled brick, and recessed panels that echo the downtown buildings of the era. Its period of significance runs from 1895 to 1952.
14001002.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

100010966.summary: The American Laundry Company Building, designed by Birmingham architect Harry B. Wheelock and built in 1923 for about $240,000, represents the once-important commercial laundry industry in Birmingham. Thirteen commercial laundries were listed in the city in 1924. This building and the Family Service Laundry are the only survivors, and this is the larger and the only freestanding one built specifically as a laundry. It operated as a laundry until 1955.
100010966.heading: Statement of Significance Summary Paragraph

79000386.summary: When the Alabama Theatre opened on December 26, 1927, it was the state's largest and most ornate movie palace. Chicago architects Graven and Mayger, veterans of the famous Rapp and Rapp firm, designed it for the Publix Theatres chain, blending Spanish Renaissance and Baroque details with a Sullivanesque facade; the foyer reportedly echoed Rapp and Rapp's Paramount Theatre in New York. It is one of the finest extravagant pre-Depression theaters in the Southeast and among the few Graven and Mayger theaters still standing.
79000386.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000331.summary: Powell School, completed in 1888, stands on the site of Birmingham's first public school and is the oldest school building in the city. The original 'Free School' of 1874 was started by working people who could not afford private schools, with help from Col. John Terry and city founder Col. James R. Powell of the Elyton Land Company, who donated the lots. It opened in March 1874 with about 150 pupils, a year after a cholera epidemic. The 1888 building became the center of the fast-growing city's school system and was its most up-to-date school facility.
76000331.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

79000388.summary: The McAdory Building is architecturally significant for the quality of its Victorian Renaissance Revival design in a city not yet 20 years old, with a richly varied facade, foliated consoles, and anthemion ornament. It is one of the finest survivors of Birmingham's first period of building sophistication during the 1886-1887 boom, standing beside the similar Caldwell-Milner Building (1887). It is named for prominent attorney and businessman C. L. McAdory, who built it during the city's first commercial expansion.
79000388.heading: 8. Significance

11000374.summary: This boundary increase adds one building, a one-story brick commercial building at 2208 Sixth Avenue South, to the Southside Historic District. It contributes under Criterion A for commerce as a typical early twentieth-century commercial building that housed a series of businesses serving the Southside community, from an auto painting shop in 1922 to car dealers and, by 1938, a carpet cleaner. It reflects the shift of this once largely residential, working-class area to commercial use, which sped up after the city's first zoning in 1926.
11000374.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

90001317.summary: The Dr Pepper Syrup Plant, opened in 1931, was a major step for the Dallas-based Dr Pepper Company. It gave the company a southeastern headquarters and distribution center and was its only syrup plant outside Dallas, which boosted sales in the eastern United States. For Birmingham it was a success of the young Birmingham Industrial Board's push to diversify the economy during the Depression. Designed by D. O. Whilldin, it is an intact example of an industrial building located to take advantage of the city's geographic and economic strengths.
90001317.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85001502.summary: The 'Heaviest Corner on Earth' is a rare, possibly unique group of four steel-frame skyscrapers built between 1902 and 1913 on the four corners of the city's first major intersection, First Avenue North and 20th Street. Together they are considered of regional or possibly national significance. They are the Woodward (1902-03), Brown-Marx (1906-08), Empire (1909), and John A. Hand-First National Bank (1912) buildings, designed mainly by local architects William C. Weston and William L. Welton, often with out-of-state firms. As a group they document Birmingham's major growth period, when local steel production changed the scale of the Victorian city and made it the largest city in the state.
85001502.heading: Statement of Significance

79000387.summary: Built in 1887, at the height of Birmingham's first boom, by Elyton Land Company officers Henry M. Caldwell and Willis J. Milner, the Caldwell-Milner Building is the city's finest surviving example of the Victorian Renaissance Revival style. Their initials appear in the facade ornament. Built by London-born contractor Henry M. Allen, it was a premier office building and the first in Birmingham with elevators and steam heat. Along with the McAdory Building next door, it shows the rapid growth in wealth and sophistication of the industrial city before it was 20 years old.
79000387.heading: 8. Significance

74000414.summary: The Steiner Bank Building, completed in 1890, housed the Banking House of Steiner Brothers, chartered in 1888 by Bohemian-born brothers Burghard and Sigfried Steiner. The bank financed much of Birmingham's early growth. As investment bankers they financed municipal projects, dealt in foreign money and mortgages, and sold steamship and train tickets that brought many European miners to the Birmingham district. It was the first commercial building in Alabama with an elevator, and the L&N Railroad ran a special excursion train to bring visitors to see it.
74000414.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90001557.summary: Fire Station No. 11, built around 1910, is locally significant as one of only two one-story, pre-1920 utilitarian commercial-style fire stations left in Birmingham. It was built as a single-use station in an urban brick commercial style rather than the more suburban style of other fire houses of the period, and it sits beside an alley, which was typical of the type. Despite later changes, it is the only remaining early commercial-type fire station in an early twentieth-century working-class Birmingham neighborhood.
90001557.heading: Statement of Significance

05000292.summary: East End Baptist Church, organized in 1917 by Rev. G. G. Austin, built its present church in 1947. It is significant as one of the leading churches of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights during the civil rights era. From 1958 to 1974 its pastor was Rev. Calvin W. Woods, a Miles College graduate whom historian Glenn T. Eskew called one of Rev. Fred Shuttlesworth's 'stalwart lieutenants' and a leading figure in the movement from the 1950s through the 1960s. It is listed under the Birmingham Civil Rights Movement multiple property listing.
05000292.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

05000299.summary: First Ebenezer Baptist Church, a congregation founded in 1941 by Rev. W. H. Perry, is locally significant for its role as a strategy center during Birmingham's civil rights movement. In the late 1950s it became one of several north Birmingham congregations that supported the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights and helped lay the groundwork for the mass protests of the early 1960s. Its members took part in the Project C demonstrations of April and May 1963, and the church held voter registration workshops in 1965. It also reflects African American community identity in the Smithfield neighborhood.
05000299.heading: Statement of Significance

72000162.summary: The Sloss No. 1 Furnace, first fired on April 12, 1882 and in continuous use until 1970, is the oldest surviving blast furnace in the Birmingham area and the only one left from the city's early days. A second furnace was added in 1883. It was founded by Col. James Withers Sloss, a railroad builder and industrialist involved in nearly every part of early Birmingham's growth, who had earlier helped form the Pratt Coal and Coke Company, Alabama's first large coal company. The furnace is linked with many of the most important figures in the district's industrial history, including Joseph F. Johnston, president of the later Sloss Iron and Steel Company and Governor of Alabama from 1896 to 1900.
72000162.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

05000293.summary: Peace Baptist Church, begun in 1948 under Rev. J. H. Stenson, is significant as one of the leading churches of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights (ACMHR) and a civil rights strategy center. Because it was close to downtown, had a large meeting space, and had an activist pastor, it was one of the early congregations to host ACMHR meetings, supporting the movement in 1956-58. As designed, it was the last major gable-front, twin-tower Black church built in Birmingham. The historic building is now the J. H. Stenson Fellowship Hall of the Sixth Street Peace Baptist Church.
05000293.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

05000306.summary: New Pilgrim Baptist Church, built in stages in 1946 and 1959, was home to the largest congregation in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights in its early years and hosted many mass meetings. Its pastor of 52 years, Rev. Nelson Smith Jr., was especially important to the movement in 1961-62 for drawing in student activists. He helped found the Progressive National Baptist Convention in 1961. On April 7, 1963, Smith, Rev. John T. Porter, and Rev. A. D. King led the 'preachers' march' toward City Hall, where they knelt in prayer at Kelly Ingram Park before being arrested.
05000306.heading: Statement of Significance

05000298.summary: The historic Sardis Baptist Church on Enon Ridge, a congregation dating to 1884, is significant as the place where the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights was founded on June 5, 1956, and as a civil rights strategy center in Birmingham. The church was built in phases: a frame Gothic Revival building around 1907, brick veneer by 1925, and a two-story education wing in 1962-63. It served a stable working-class community and was a center of community life. Its pastor, Rev. Robert Alford, was a key early ACMHR officer.
05000298.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84000638.summary: The Windham Brothers Building, built in 1912, was the home office for about fifty years, until the late 1960s, of Windham Brothers Construction Company. Founded in 1895, it was the oldest Black construction company in Birmingham and a major Black builder in Alabama. The company built many of the most important buildings in Birmingham's Black community as well as several prominent buildings in the white business district, and it ran branches in Nashville, Chicago, Indianapolis, and Detroit from here. An early example of the firm's work, the building originally housed a drugstore and other small Black businesses, along with apartments, including the home of founder Thomas Windham, and is significant in the growth of Black commerce in the city.
84000638.heading: 8. Significance

84000632.summary: Quinlan Castle, built around 1926-27 during Birmingham's mid-1920s building boom, is an exceptional example of 1920s Romantic Revival architecture. Its rough stone and stucco walls, battlements, and four octagonal turrets reflect a medieval castle at its most fanciful. It is also one of Alabama's best examples of the large, multi-level apartment complexes that first became widely popular in the late 1910s and 1920s, when the city's growing population created a strong demand for housing. The architect may have been William Leslie Welton, though the nomination marks this as uncertain.
84000632.heading: 8. Significance

74000413.summary: This house, built around 1908, was the home of Dr. Arthur McKinnon Brown, a Raleigh-born, University of Michigan-trained physician. He helped found Children's Home Hospital, for many years the only place in the area where Black doctors could treat their patients, and he started what became National Negro Health Week. The house was designed by Wallace A. Rayfield, a pioneering Black architect who came to Birmingham from Tuskegee Institute in 1907. In 1972 Brown's son leased it to the Birmingham Art Club, which uses it as a community arts center.
74000413.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89000163.summary: Manchester Terrace, built in 1927, is locally significant as the first project in Birmingham to combine two popular revival styles. A row of four Mediterranean-influenced shops on the street is split by a flight of steps leading up to the courtyard of a U-shaped, 12-unit English Tudor apartment building. It is also an early and successful mixed-use development. It reflects the period when Southside businesses were spreading south toward the Highland Park and Chestnut Hill residential areas, creating neighborhood commercial zones like the one at 7th Avenue and 29th Street South.
89000163.heading: Statement of Significance

86002616.summary: Second Presbyterian Church, built in 1901, is a good example of turn-of-the-century Romanesque Revival architecture. It has single-color brickwork, round-arched windows and doors, corner entry towers, and corbeled brick cornices, and inside it has three large rose windows and a groin-vaulted ceiling. It is believed to have been designed by local architect D. A. Helmich, who designed the 1892 South Highland Presbyterian Church and the 1891 post office, since features of both appear here.
86002616.heading: 8. Significance

07001027.summary: The Center Street Historic District is significant as a key battleground in the fight for Black civil rights in Birmingham. Center Street was zoned as a buffer between white and Black neighborhoods, and from 1946 until 1965, when the last bombs were found before they exploded, violence was used to keep Black families from crossing the line, which earned it the name 'Dynamite Hill.' The street is also the spine of a Black neighborhood whose residents, including NAACP attorney Arthur Shores, led the legal campaigns to desegregate Birmingham's neighborhoods, schools, and public facilities. Many of its houses and its two churches date from the late 1940s and 1950s, including homes designed and built by Leroy Gaillard Jr.
07001027.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86001959.summary: St. Andrew's Episcopal Church, built in 1913-15, is Birmingham's best example of Gothic Revival architecture in the English country parish tradition. It reflects a more academic approach than the earlier, more eclectic Victorian Gothic. Built of rusticated brownstone in a T-plan, it has typical features of the type: a single front bell tower with an enclosed entry porch, low overall massing, a square chancel, and an open timber ceiling. This English parish design was especially popular with Episcopal congregations in the early twentieth century; the interior furnishings were added in 1926-28.
86001959.heading: 8. Significance

84000630.summary: The Highland Plaza Apartments, an eight-story building from 1924, is one of the finest and most intact 1920s apartment hotels in Birmingham. It is distinguished by fine exterior detailing and a Beaux Arts plan and design, with arched windows on the first and top floors, a classically detailed entrance, and a simple classical cornice. It was built by the Smallman Brice Construction Company from plans by the architects Denham, Van Keuren & Denham.
84000630.heading: Significance and History

90001554.summary: Fire Station No. 3, built in 1927 and designed by architects Warren, Knight & Davis, is the only Beaux Arts-influenced fire station in Birmingham and one of the most ornate left. Its quality design reflects the affluent Highland Avenue suburbs it was built to serve, and like other suburban stations of the 1920s it hid its working use behind a refined, residential look. It also housed the captain and his family, as was typical. Set at the southern edge of the Five Points South and Highland Avenue neighborhoods, with Fire Station No. 22 at the northern edge, it is a good example of how the city planned services around neighborhoods.
90001554.heading: Statement of Significance

90001562.summary: Fire Station No. 22, a one-story Spanish Revival stucco building from about 1927-28, is one of the best examples of how Birmingham developed in the mid-to-late 1920s. During that time, fire stations became more stylish and were located to fit neighborhood planning. It marks the northern edge of the Highland Avenue neighborhood, a middle- and upper-middle-class suburb, while Fire Station No. 3 (1927) marks the southern edge. It is a typical example of the residential-style fire houses built in the city's suburbs in the 1920s, and its small lawn reflects the city's Progressive-era beautification campaign.
90001562.heading: Statement of Significance

84000626.summary: The Exclusive Furniture Shop, built in 1926-27, is an excellent early Birmingham example of Tudor-style commercial architecture by prominent architect Charles H. McCauley, whose Tudor designs are considered among the city's finest. It was probably McCauley's first Tudor commercial building, and it served as a model for later commercial designs such as Mountain Brook Village (1928) and English Village (c. 1928). It remains one of the only Tudor-style buildings in the Southside area.
84000626.heading: 8. Significance

86001962.summary: The Agee House, built around 1900, is the only existing example of fully developed Shingle style architecture in Birmingham. It has the style's main features: a free-form shape fully covered in textured shingles, a hipped roof with cross-hipped dormers, a two-story half-round bay blending into the main roof, banded windows, and wrap-around porches. The academic Shingle style was widely known but never very popular in America and is especially rare in Alabama. The architect is unknown, and the Birmingham Historical Society has suggested it may have been the only house of its type ever built in the city.
86001962.heading: 8. Significance

05000296.summary: St. Luke AME Church, built in 1926, is locally significant for its role in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights (ACMHR) and the Birmingham civil rights movement from 1956 to 1963. Rev. Andrew W. Thomas, pastor from 1956 to 1969, was an ACMHR activist who opened the church for many mass meetings, starting as early as 1957. The church, a restrained Gothic Revival design, and its 1926 parsonage are also significant as representative works of African American architect Wallace Rayfield.
05000296.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86001952.summary: The Bottega Favorita, built in 1926, is an excellent example of the early twentieth-century academic phase of the Italian Renaissance Revival, which combined historic forms with modern streamlined detail. It is a very rare commercial example of this style in Alabama, and it is unusual for combining shops and residences. Designed by Warren, Knight & Davis, one of Birmingham's most prestigious firms, it is among their best work. Its left-hand first-floor shop is the best-preserved early twentieth-century commercial interior left in Birmingham.
86001952.heading: 8. Significance

84000625.summary: The Claridge Manor Apartments, a ten-story Colonial Revival brick building from 1924, is one of four apartment hotels in Birmingham. It was developed by G. L. Miller and Company of Atlanta and is both an excellent example of the type and a reflection of the mid-1920s boom in such construction. It offered hotel-style services including a formal dining room, maid and valet service with servants' quarters in the basement, silent butlers, a lobby, and a landscaped lawn. Many original interior features remain, including marble lobby floors, French doors, and oak floors.
84000625.heading: Significance and History

07000838.summary: Graymont School, built in 1908 to a design by William Ernest Spink, with additions in 1929 and 1950, is significant as the first school in Birmingham to be desegregated. In 1960 James Armstrong and the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights applied for his sons Dwight and Floyd to attend Graymont, and the effort succeeded in September 1963 amid civil rights protests at the school. Historians agree that the desegregation of Birmingham's schools that fall led to the bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church, which in turn sped passage of the federal Civil Rights Act of 1964. The building is also one of the few early twentieth-century school buildings left in Birmingham and now serves as headquarters of the Jefferson County Committee for Economic Opportunity.
07000838.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

88000446.summary: The Hanover Court Apartments, built in 1915-16, is a well-preserved example of the apartment buildings that shaped the look of Birmingham's Five Points South and Highland Avenue districts. It reflects the popularity of the Tudor Revival style and the growing taste for roomy apartments in place of houses in fashionable neighborhoods. One of the most substantial mid-size apartment buildings in the area, it stands out for its castle-like look, limestone trim and quoins, quatrefoil-decorated parapet, and large apartments set around curved central corridors. It occupies a prominent corner where single-family houses and apartments of different ages and sizes stand side by side.
88000446.heading: Statement of Significance

75000314.summary: The Enslen House, completed in 1910, is one of Birmingham's finest Neoclassical Revival residences and is notable for its high-quality craftsmanship and lavish use of mahogany, fine woodwork, and art glass. It was the home of a member of the Enslen family, early citizens who helped drive the city's rapid growth through the Jefferson County Savings Bank, which they organized in 1885 and housed in a 22-story building in 1911. The house was among the largest and most elaborate on Highland Avenue, laid out by the Elyton Land Company in 1884, which by 1900 was the city's main upper-class residential street. Many of the avenue's other large homes have since been demolished.
75000314.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000690.summary: The Bradshaw House, built in 1892 and designed by George Torgeson, is one of only two surviving nineteenth-century Queen Anne residences in Birmingham, along with the Hassinger House. They are the last of the nineteenth-century mansions on Highland Avenue, the city's premier upper-class boulevard. It was built for Caldwell Bradshaw, longtime attorney for New York and English investment firms and co-founder of Consolidated By-Products, which installed Birmingham's gas mains. In 1905 it was bought by industrialist Erskine Ramsay, who lived there with four other bachelors and became locally famous for lavish entertaining.
80000690.heading: Statement of Significance

05000291.summary: First Baptist Church, East Thomas, organized on March 21, 1938, built this gable-front, twin-tower brick church in 1939. It is significant as one of the leading churches of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights (ACMHR) and hosted at least two documented ACMHR mass meetings, the first on June 23, 1958. It is also one of the best surviving examples of the twin-tower, Gothic Revival-influenced churches built by African Americans in Birmingham in the middle decades of the twentieth century. It is listed under the Birmingham Civil Rights Movement multiple property listing.
05000291.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

85000444.summary: The Avalon, two Tudor Revival apartment buildings from 1925 and 1927 designed by prolific Birmingham architect Charles H. McCauley, illustrates the 1920s apartment boom that set Birmingham apart from other Alabama cities. Apartment houses reflected rising land costs, the extensive streetcar system, and housing shortages from rapid growth, and they gave the middle class more privacy, space, and status than boarding houses, with less upkeep than a home. Located on a streetcar line and the city's premier residential boulevard, Highland Avenue, the Avalon served the comfortably well-off middle class. Its two buildings, one using half-timbering and the other limestone trim, show the range of the Tudor Revival style.
85000444.heading: Statement of Significance

76000333.summary: Vulcan, Birmingham's best-known landmark, was created in 1904 by Italian-born sculptor Giuseppe Moretti as Alabama's exhibit at the Louisiana Purchase Exposition in St. Louis. Cast from iron mined and smelted in the Birmingham district to represent the city's industry, it was the largest cast-iron statue ever made. After the fair it lay on Red Mountain for a time, then stood at the Alabama State Fairgrounds from 1906 for about thirty years. With Works Progress Administration help it was moved and reassembled in 1939 in a park on Red Mountain on land donated by U.S. Steel, and it was restored between 1967 and 1971.
76000333.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90000309.summary: The Orlando Apartments, a four-story, 20-unit building finished in 1928, was designed by William Leslie Welton and built by real estate developer Henry H. Hancock. It shows architecture in transition, from the decorative motifs and craftsmanship of the 1920s toward a more modern, angular, unadorned look with vertical emphasis, with patterned brickwork and distinctive projecting porches on its two fronts. Completed just before the Depression, the project ran into money trouble: the original owners were foreclosed on, and the City later bought the building in 1978.
90000309.heading: Statement of Significance
