90001556.summary: Fire Station No. 10, built around 1926-27, is a good example of Birmingham's 1920s suburban fire stations, with strong Spanish Colonial Revival influences and a homelike feel. The garage and meeting room are at the front and living quarters at the rear. Set half a block off Avondale's main commercial strip, it was designed to look residential rather than commercial. In 1928 it won first place in the city's annual fire house landscape contest for its lawns and Spanish flower boxes. It is one of the smallest historic fire stations in the city.
90001556.heading: Statement of Significance

05000455.summary: Bethel Baptist Church, its 1957 parsonage, and its guardhouse are significant in the origins of the church-led, nonviolent southern civil rights movement of the 1950s. From 1956 to 1961 the church was headquarters of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights (ACMHR), led by its pastor Rev. Fred L. Shuttlesworth, whose direct-action campaigns against segregation became a model for the 1963 Birmingham protests. The ACMHR was also the Alabama contact for the 1961 Freedom Ride and helped rescue stranded riders, aiding the push for federal action to desegregate interstate travel. After the Christmas 1956 bombing of the original parsonage and another bombing of the church in June 1958, volunteer 'Civil Rights Guards' kept watch from the purpose-built guardhouse.
05000455.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

05000295.summary: St. Luke AME Zion Church, an eclectic Gothic brick church facing Patton Park, is significant as one of the Birmingham churches active in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights and as a site of conflict during the civil rights era. Its minister from 1960 to 1963, Rev. John O. Hart, gave spiritual and financial support to the movement, and civil rights meetings were held at the church. In 1962 it was one of three churches bombed, the first church bombings in Birmingham since Bethel Baptist in 1958. The bombings were meant to discourage campaigns to desegregate parks and pools and the Selective Buying Campaign. The congregation stayed in the movement and repaired the damage.
05000295.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

00000133.summary: The John D. and Katherine Gleissner Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel prefabricated houses the Lustron Corporation built from 1946 to 1950 to meet the nationwide housing shortage after World War II. It is the only three-bedroom Westchester model in Alabama and one of just eleven surviving Lustrons in the state. It keeps its metal wall and ceiling panels and built-in cabinets, shelves, and vanity. It reflects postwar ideals of durability and easy upkeep, and it is linked to Realty Investment, Birmingham's Lustron dealer.
00000133.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

00000130.summary: The Bernice L. Wright Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel prefabricated houses the Lustron Corporation built from 1946 to 1950 in response to the post-World War II housing shortage. It is a two-bedroom Westchester model, one of nine in Alabama, and one of only eleven surviving Lustrons in the state. It has porcelain-enameled steel panels outside, metal wall and ceiling panels inside, and built-in cabinets, shelves, and a vanity, reflecting postwar ideals of durability and easy upkeep. It is linked to Realty Investment, Birmingham's Lustron dealer.
00000130.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

05000305.summary: New Rising Star Baptist Church is significant for its role in Birmingham's civil rights movement and for its ties to African American identity in the Collegeville neighborhood. It was founded in 1958 by Rev. George E. Pruitt Sr., its pastor until 1986. He was one of the five ministers who met in June 1956 to call for creating the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights (ACMHR) and later served on its advisory committee. The working-class congregation was a stalwart of the movement, holding many meetings at the church on issues such as police brutality, voting rights, and the Selective Buying Campaign.
05000305.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

05000300.summary: First Baptist Church, Kingston, is locally significant as one of the leading Birmingham churches in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights (ACMHR) during the civil rights activism of the 1950s and 1960s, and served as a strategy center. Rev. George W. Dickerson, pastor from 1941 to 1972, was an ACMHR officer and an active leader until his death, and the church was one of the movement's early activist congregations. The ACMHR's 1958 annual report listed it among the churches that had 'generously opened' their doors for mass meetings. The congregation used the building until 2000.
05000300.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

05000297.summary: Shady Grove Baptist Church, built in 1942, is locally significant as a strategy center for Birmingham's civil rights movement. Its mostly working-class congregation strongly supported the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights and met regularly at the church to plan their part in the Project C mass demonstrations of spring 1963. Its pastor, Rev. Lewis J. Rogers, was active in ACMHR leadership and helped raise money for the organization's legal fees. After the protests, the church hosted voter registration drives.
05000297.heading: Statement of Significance

03000232.summary: The Mountain Brook Estates Building, a one- and two-story Tudor Revival commercial building designed by architect Jesse W. Green, was built in 1928 as the village store building for Robert Jemison Jr.'s Mountain Brook Estates. It is significant as a key part of an early planned community that combined residential, commercial, recreational, and educational areas, reflecting the move of Birmingham's well-off residents away from the smoke and noise of the industrial city to automobile suburbs. Its English village style, built with clinker brick and local Red Mountain sandstone, was popular between the World Wars.
03000232.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

87001417.summary: The West End Masonic Temple, built in 1926 and designed by prominent Birmingham architect David Oliver Whilldin, is one of the city's finest examples of the Neoclassical style used for both commercial and civic purposes in a single building. Shops have always filled the first floor, while the upper floors hold the Masons' dining hall and lodge room. Its symmetrical facade has paired fluted Doric columns, a stone belt course, and an entablature decorated with Masonic symbols, and the upper floors and interior woodwork remain original. It is the largest and most ornate building in the West End commercial center on Tuscaloosa Avenue.
87001417.heading: Statement of Significance

15000430.summary: Blessed Sacrament Catholic Church, built in a cruciform plan from 1928 to 1930, is locally significant as an excellent Romanesque Revival example of American Roman Catholic architecture before the mid-twentieth century. Its architecture and decoration express Catholic theology and liturgy, with a campanile beside the facade and richly symbolic stained glass and altars. Art historian John M. Schnorrenberg, in his study of Birmingham's first century of religious buildings, called it 'one of the hidden glories of Birmingham church architecture.'
15000430.heading: Significance Summary

88000990.summary: Woodlawn City Hall, built in 1908 under Mayor W. E. Perryman, recalls the independent town of Woodlawn. The town grew from a Wood family settlement of the 1820s, was renamed Woodlawn in 1886, incorporated in 1891, and annexed by Birmingham in 1910. The imposing building, with classical terra cotta detailing around its central entrance, reflected the mayor's wish that the town's funds be 'memorialized in concrete.' It housed most of the town's public functions, including city offices, the court and jail, the fire department, an auditorium, and the first branch of the Birmingham library system, which started with 890 books.
88000990.heading: Statement of Significance

00000131.summary: This Lustron House on Columbiana Road, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel prefabricated houses the Lustron Corporation built from 1946 to 1950 in response to the post-World War II housing shortage. It is a two-bedroom Newport model, the only one in Alabama, and one of only eleven surviving Lustrons in the state. Its porcelain-enameled steel panels, metal interior walls, and built-in furnishings reflect postwar ideals of durability and easy upkeep. It is linked to Realty Investment, Birmingham's Lustron dealer.
00000131.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

08000428.summary: This house, built in 1960 as the parsonage of the First Baptist Church of Ensley, a strong supporter of the Birmingham movement, is significant for events of May 1963. It was the home of Rev. A. D. King, brother of Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., and it was bombed on May 11, 1963, just after the negotiated agreement that ended the marches and demonstrations. That night's bombings set off rioting in downtown Birmingham that historian Glenn Eskew called 'the first urban riot of the 1960s.' It is listed under the Birmingham Civil Rights Movement multiple property listing.
08000428.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

90001559.summary: Fire Station No. 15, built around 1928-29, is architecturally significant for its unusual blend of the utilitarian downtown fire station with a suburban residential setting. Unlike Birmingham's other suburban stations, with their homelike Spanish or Tudor Revival styles and lawns, it is a two-story brick building with a flat facade set close to the street, like the city's urban stations. It also has Renaissance Revival elements, a style used on one other station, Fire Station No. 4 downtown.
90001559.heading: Statement of Significance

80000689.summary: Blessed Sacrament Academy, built as the Convent of the Perpetual Adoration (cornerstone laid 1912, dedicated October 8, 1913), is a rare local example of the French Renaissance Revival style. It was designed by Washington, D.C. architect A. O. von Herbulis, a fitting choice of style for an order of French origin, and it has fine classical detailing, a portico, and a striking two-story chapel lined with giant Ionic pilasters. It was the only combined convent and school in the city and possibly the state. Run by the Sisters of the Most Holy Sacrament from 1913 until 1974, it was Birmingham's earliest Catholic high school, one of its first Catholic elementary schools, and a cultural center for the Catholic community.
80000689.heading: Statement of Significance

90001558.summary: Fire Station No. 12, built around 1926-27, is the best surviving Birmingham fire station with Tudor Revival influences and one of the best examples of the city's late-1920s suburban stations. It has a strong residential character, is one of only two stations faced with quarried stone, and is one of five with a tower. Unusually, it sits beside an alley rather than on a corner. It is also a good example of Woodlawn's community development, which planned commercial areas, public buildings, and residential enclaves as a whole.
90001558.heading: Statement of Significance

09000603.summary: The Belcher-Nixon Building, built around 1922, housed Black dentists and physicians, mainly Dr. Andrew F. Belcher (c. 1922-1951) and Dr. John W. Nixon (1951-1988). It is the only surviving historic commercial building at Tuxedo Junction, the African American business center in Ensley made famous by the 1939 song 'Tuxedo Junction' by Erskine Hawkins' band, which became a national hit after Glenn Miller's orchestra recorded it. Dr. Nixon, a prominent dentist and civil rights leader, used the building as his main base for civil rights work and helped organize an NAACP-sponsored 1968 rally against police brutality.
09000603.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

90001560.summary: Fire Station No. 16, a large U-shaped Spanish Revival brick and stucco building from about 1925-26, is a fine example of Birmingham's 1920s suburban fire houses. It is the best surviving example in the city of the multi-use station, serving as the Ensley community's fire station, police station, and jail. Its Spanish Revival style, popular for suburban homes in the 1920s, gave the municipal complex a residential scale, and it sits just off the busy commercial strip along 19th Street.
90001560.heading: Statement of Significance

70000103.summary: Arlington, sometimes called the 'Birthplace of Birmingham,' is the oldest structure in Birmingham and Jefferson County. It began as a modest four-room timber house built around 1822 by planter Stephen Hall near Elyton, the early county seat. Later owner William S. Mudd enlarged it in 1842 into an impressive Greek Revival mansion with large square pillars and a full upstairs veranda, a design almost unique in Alabama. It is the only Greek Revival mansion in the area to survive the Civil War, Union raids, and the city's explosive industrial growth. The City of Birmingham later bought it and opened it as a museum, restored and furnished by the Arlington Historical Association.
70000103.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

05000303.summary: West End Hills Missionary Baptist Church, built in stages between 1959 and 1965, is an outstanding example of the smaller working-class congregations that supported the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights (ACMHR) from 1959 to 1965. Under Rev. Coleman M. Smith, the congregation finished a basement sanctuary in 1959 and held services and civil rights events there while raising money for the Colonial Revival sanctuary above, dedicated on May 31, 1965. Many members regularly attended and took part in ACMHR meetings. It is listed under the Birmingham Civil Rights Movement multiple property listing.
05000303.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

93001591.summary: Pratt School, a red-brick building with simple Neoclassical details built around 1910 and enlarged in 1918, 1925, and about 1948, is significant as an early work of prominent Birmingham architect D. O. Whilldin. It is probably the first, and perhaps the simplest, of the many schools he designed for the city between 1910 and 1927, and it was begun before Pratt City became part of Birmingham in 1910. It is also a good example of the early development of education in the Birmingham area.
93001591.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

08001273.summary: The Ramsay-McCormack Building, built in 1929-30, was the only major office tower in the suburban community of Ensley, then home to the largest steel mill complex in the Birmingham District. Designed by noted Birmingham architect Brooke B. Burnham, it is Ensley's only skyscraper and its only major Art Deco building. Ensley itself was developed from the 1880s by Enoch Ensley and the Ensley Land Company, with the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company as majority owner, to exploit the nearby Pratt coal seam.
08001273.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

01001290.summary: Stonecroft, built between 1921 and 1924 by builder W. E. Sparks, is a fine, essentially original example of Tudor Revival residential architecture. It is notable for its extraordinary use of local stone and its intact landscaped grounds, including stone walls, arched gateways, and a large rear terrace. Its 'landmark' scale reflects the post-World War I taste among the well-to-do for English manor houses and country living, a style that suggested achievement and status. The kitchen and butler's pantry remain close to original.
01001290.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84000623.summary: The Bank of Ensley, a two-story Neoclassical building from 1918 designed by local architect H. D. Breeding, stands on Ensley's most important commercial corner and is significant for its role in the commercial growth of the town, later a Birmingham suburb. Organized in 1899, it was the first bank in what is now western Birmingham and was backed by the powerful Ramsay and McCormack interests. Erskine Ramsay and George B. McCormack served as president and vice president until 1921, when they sold it to Robert E. Chadwick and Sam C. King. The bank thrived through the 1920s but closed for good on January 10, 1930 because of frozen assets.
84000623.heading: 8. Significance

05000307.summary: Mount Ararat Baptist Church, founded around 1915 in the Sherman Heights section of Ensley, is significant as a civil rights strategy center tied to the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights between 1956 and 1963. After a lightning fire destroyed the first church in 1929, the congregation hired African American architect Wallace Rayfield to design a larger Gothic-style frame sanctuary, which was brick-veneered and enlarged in the early 1950s. Under Rev. John H. Glover, pastor from 1936 to 1973, adult and teenage members met at the church to plan their part in the movement, and several were jailed during the April 1963 Project C demonstrations.
05000307.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

90001561.summary: Fire Station No. 19, built around 1925, is one of the best Romanesque Revival fire stations in Birmingham and a good example of the city's 1920s effort to build fire houses as protected residential oases, their style and landscaping hiding a dangerous mission. It was built in the East Lake community after a devastating fire there, when the city moved the old company at Highland Avenue and Linden Street to meet the area's growing needs. It stands next to the almost identically designed East Lake Library, showing the city's interest in planning its new suburban communities.
90001561.heading: Statement of Significance

93001031.summary: Brown Hall (1927), the administration building, is part of the old Miles College campus, nominated as the Miles Memorial College Historic District for its importance in education and African American heritage. Miles College was founded by the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church and opened on this site in January 1908, when Williams Hall was finished. It is one of seven private Black colleges in Alabama, and for the first half of the twentieth century it was the only college open to Black students in the Birmingham area. The historic district also includes the Erskine Ramsay Library (1920, 1943) and the W. A. Bell Library (1961).
93001031.heading: Statement of Significance

87001778.summary: The story-and-a-half log core of the William Reed House (Spring Lake Farm), built around 1816-20, is the oldest structure in the city of Birmingham and one of the earliest surviving buildings in north central Alabama. It predates the city by more than fifty years. Later frame additions and Victorian and Craftsman changes make it an excellent example of a prosperous upland farmhouse that shows a century and a half of changing building methods and taste. It is linked to the pioneer William Reed family, who settled here in territorial days, and to the Jemison family, leaders of modern Birmingham, who used it as their country home for twenty years. It also links the area's early small-farm economy with the later industrial city.
87001778.heading: Statement of Significance

90001563.summary: The Wylam Fire Station, built around 1908-10, is one of the best surviving buildings from Wylam's brief period of growth as an independent industrial town, incorporated in 1900 and annexed by Birmingham around 1910. It is the second-oldest fire station in Birmingham and the oldest in the city's western industrial suburbs. It is also the best-preserved example in the city of the plain brick, single-use, utilitarian fire station typical before the 1920s, when the city turned to more residential-style stations.
90001563.heading: Statement of Significance

10001051.summary: Dunbar High School, opened in 1923, was Bessemer's only African American high school until 1960 and a key institution in the city's Black community. The two-story brick school was designed by acclaimed Birmingham architect David Oliver Whilldin. Its first principal was Professor J. B. Bickerstaff, and a gymnasium wing was added by 1939. Originally Bessemer Colored High School, it was renamed in 1928 for poet Paul Laurence Dunbar. After 1960 it served as Dunbar Primary School, and it was renovated beginning in 1989 as the Dunbar-Abrams Community Center.
10001051.heading: Significance Summary

82002038.summary: This house, built in 1890-92 by the Natchez Land and Improvement Company as speculative housing in industrial Bessemer, is significant mainly as the first home of Thomas McAdory Owen and Marie Bankhead Owen. Thomas Owen, then a Bessemer lawyer and city solicitor, bought it in 1893 and lived there with his wife until 1894. He went on to found the Alabama Department of Archives and History and serve as its first director, and Marie Bankhead Owen, a playwright and author, succeeded him as director. It is the only known surviving house in Alabama tied to their life together. From 1904 into the 1930s it was the home of Bessemer merchant Sam Kartus, founder of 'Kartus Korner.'
82002038.heading: Statement of Significance

08000456.summary: The Jonathan W. Bass House, built around 1865 for Jonathan Washington Bass (1837-1897), is the best surviving example in Jefferson County of a house type common along the upper Cahaba River and in Jones Valley from the late 1850s to the 1870s. The type has a gabled, symmetrical main block with two rooms on each side of a central hall, a rear ell, and a narrow front porch. It is also notable for its trompe l'oeil painted ceilings in the main parlor and hall. The Bass family were among Jefferson County's first settlers, arriving around 1816, and Jonathan Bass served in the Confederate cavalry.
08000456.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96000595.summary: The Parham Apothecary Building, built in 1947, was a landmark of Fairfield's African American commercial district in Interurban Heights. Besides Dr. Glover Patrick Parham's pharmacy, it housed medical offices, a library, a post office, a restaurant, and a gas station, many of them services Black residents could not get anywhere else in segregated Fairfield. It shows how African Americans met Jim Crow segregation by building their own community institutions. It is also significant for Dr. Parham (career 1937-1978), a prominent businessman, civic leader, philanthropist, and educator who built and leased nearby buildings to Black entrepreneurs and was named Fairfield's Most Outstanding Citizen in 1955.
96000595.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

73000348.summary: The Southern Railway Terminal Station in Bessemer, completed in 1916 at a cost of $30,000 and opened on March 2 of that year, is an excellent example of a small-city railroad terminal of the early 1900s. It stands as a monument to the importance of Bessemer, founded in 1887 by Henry DeBardeleben during Jefferson County's iron and steel boom, which grew rapidly thanks to nearby coal and iron deposits. The town's leading citizens worked through the state Railroad Commission to get the new station built. When the nomination was written, the Bessemer Hall of History hoped to acquire it as a museum.
73000348.heading: 8. Significance

72000161.summary: The Thomas McAdory Jr. House, built around 1840-41 by people enslaved by McAdory, is a typical example of early Alabama plantation house architecture. McAdory, whose family came to Alabama in 1818 and developed a large plantation, built it for his bride, Emily Owen, whom he married in 1836. Their son Isaac became a noted educator, founded Pleasant Hill Academy, and served in the Alabama Legislature. Their grandson Thomas M. Owen, founder and first director of the Alabama Department of Archives and History, was born in the house.
72000161.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000330.summary: The Owen Plantation House, built in the late 1830s by Thomas H. Owen, is a fine example of an important nineteenth-century Alabama folk house type: a two-story frame 'I' house with an open central hall, or dogtrot, a form that showed high economic and social status. Its elegance shows in wainscoting painted to look like marble, shiplapped walls and paneled columns on the front porch, and finely made mantels. The Owens were among Jefferson County's pioneer families, arriving from South Carolina in 1816, and Thomas Owen was active in his community and Methodist church. It was one of three western Jefferson County houses being restored to depict early nineteenth-century plantation life.
76000330.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002975.summary: The Southern Railroad Depot at Leeds, built in 1883-84 as the Georgia Pacific Railway depot, is a representative small-town depot of the late nineteenth century, combining freight and passenger rooms in one board-and-batten frame building with deep eaves on large curved brackets. It is closely tied to the founding of Leeds, which began as a stop on the Georgia Pacific line linking Birmingham and Atlanta in the early 1880s. The town was laid out by railroad construction engineer E. M. Tutwiler, and the town's first store opened nearby soon after the depot was built.
83002975.heading: 8. Significance

82001606.summary: The Jefferson County Courthouse, built in 1929-32, has been the seat of county government since the early 1930s and is a major public building by Holabird and Root, a leading Chicago firm of national reputation. Its exterior bas-relief panels, probably the finest in Birmingham, were designed by Chicago sculptor Leo Friedlander after Holabird and Root architect Jack Smith, a Birmingham native, studied the county's history. They reflect the Art Deco blending of sculpture, painting, and architecture. Their themes of local history and industry, including smokestacks, blast furnaces, and power lines chosen at the county commission's request, express the city's image as the industrial leader of the South.
82001606.heading: Statement of Significance

05000290.summary: Canaan Baptist Church, founded in 1865 and one of the oldest African American Baptist congregations in Bessemer, was a key civil rights strategy center in Bessemer in the early to mid-1960s. The present church was built in 1961 under Rev. Dr. J. H. Browder, pastor from 1948 to 1964, who was active in the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights and made the church known locally as a strong voice for voting rights and desegregation. The congregation met here to plan its part in the 1962 Selective Buying Campaign and the 1963 Project C demonstrations. Under Rev. A. L. Bratcher, it went on to help carry out civil rights and War on Poverty programs in Bessemer.
05000290.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

73000350.summary: The Five Mile Creek Bridge is one of the few early reinforced concrete arch bridges left in Alabama, with a 35-foot arch span. It carries one of the few surviving pieces of the original Huntsville Road, one of the first roads into the rugged interior of north Alabama when the land opened for settlement in 1816. It is a good example of early reinforced concrete engineering from a time when the technique was still new; the first such bridge in the United States was built in 1889. All of its materials were made locally from the district's own resources for steel and concrete. Its 20-foot width matched the state road commission's 1911 standard.
73000350.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000315.summary: The Sadler House has statewide significance as a very intact example of an extended I-house with an open dogtrot, a once-common antebellum Alabama house type of which only about fifty examples were known in 1988. It is the only documented extended I-house in the state that still has its open dogtrot. It likely began as a log cabin built by John Loveless in the late 1820s. Isaac Wellington Sadler bought the property in 1836 and expanded it into an I-house in the late 1830s, perhaps with lumber from the sawmill of his father, surveyor and builder William Rose Sadler, who built the area's first sawmill.
75000315.heading: Statement of Significance

83002982.summary: The Presley Store, built in 1902 for R. Porter Presley and his brother John to house their general store, is one of Alabama's best examples of ornamental pressed metal on a small commercial building. It is the most ornate and elaborate commercial building in Springville, with an elaborate pressed-metal entablature and the town's only intact cast-iron storefront with ornamental detail. It served the small community as a general store during the first decades of the twentieth century.
83002982.heading: 8. Significance

74000437.summary: The Columbiana City Hall, formerly the Shelby County Courthouse, is one of the few surviving historic buildings in Columbiana and one of Alabama's oldest standing courthouses. Columbiana won the county seat from Montevallo in the 1820s because it was closer to the center of the county. In 1854 Judge John M. McClanahan ordered a new courthouse, built by contractors McCan and Williamson for $2,500, and it was enlarged and bricked over in 1881. After a new courthouse opened in 1908, the old building served as a hotel, boarding house, and apartments until the town bought it in 1955 for $5,000 to use as City Hall.
74000437.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

100011941.summary: The Wallace House in Harpersville, built in 1841, is locally significant for its ties to the development and change of plantation society in the Coosa River Valley from 1841 to 1922, when the last Wallace family member lived there. The well-documented history of the Wallace family and of the African Americans who were enslaved on the property, and who later worked the land as free people after the Civil War, shows how social relations on plantations changed before and after Emancipation. No other house linked to a large slaveholding plantation has been identified in the area, making it a rare property. Ground-penetrating radar in 2023 suggested the remains of at least five more structures on the site.
100011941.heading: Significance Summary

06000182.summary: The Old Rock House near Harpersville, also called the Condon-Cohill-Norris-Eastis-Newman House, is a rare, intact early stone house, possibly the only surviving example of its type in Alabama. Architectural historian Robert Gamble called it 'the oldest rock structure of its kind between West Point, Georgia and Fredericksburg, Texas.' Its strictly symmetrical facade, transomed doorways, and simple mantels reflect late Georgian and early Republic taste and suggest it was built around 1835. Its stone construction and refined design resemble eighteenth- and nineteenth-century stone houses of New England and the mid-Atlantic more than typical antebellum Alabama homes.
06000182.heading: Statement of Significance

15000434.summary: Farrington Hall, built from 1905 to 1908, is a locally significant example of early twentieth-century American eclecticism, blending elements of popular styles of the day into a well-crafted whole. It was built with steel framing and concrete walls to be fireproof and served as the library, office, and clubhouse of mine owner William Aldrich in the coal mining town of Aldrich, with a basement garage for his son Farrington, who loved working on automobiles. Farrington died of typhoid at eighteen just as the building was being finished, and the family named it in his memory. Along with the 1928 company store, it is one of the only buildings left from the Aldrich mining town and estate.
15000434.heading: Statement of Significance Summary

78000509.summary: Peterson Hall (1913), a two-story Georgian Revival brick building with a central two-story portico, is part of the historic core of the University of Montevallo, nominated as the Alabama Girls' Industrial School district. The school was founded in 1896 as the Alabama Girls' Industrial School, reflecting a late nineteenth-century push to give young women vocational and technical education, and it later grew into a coeducational university. The district's 16 structures include the 1823 King House and 1851 Reynolds Hall, both recorded by the Historic American Buildings Survey, nine Georgian and Classical buildings from 1897 to 1940, and a 'medieval' 1911 water tower that became a campus landmark.
78000509.heading: 8. Significance

72000179.summary: The King House, or Mansion House, built in 1823 by Edmund King, is one of the earliest masonry buildings still standing in Alabama, and its crisp design and refined detail were uncommon in central Alabama in the 1820s. King, a Virginia-born merchant and planter who came to Alabama in 1817, gave land for churches, roads, and schools, and his home sheltered orphaned boys and, during the Civil War, the sick and wounded of both sides. After his death in 1863 it passed to his son-in-law, Judge George B. Shortridge. In 1865 it briefly served as headquarters for Union General James H. Wilson during his raid through Alabama.
72000179.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90001529.summary: The Peterson-Hall Home (1900), an elaborate two-story Eastlake-style frame house on Middle Street, is part of the University of Montevallo Historic District Expansion. Built by Mrs. Lucy Cary, it was bought around 1908 by Dr. Peterson, the second president of the college, and his daughter Charlotte Peterson, longtime principal of the elementary school, lived there until 1970. The district shows Montevallo's long history as a center of higher learning since the school was founded in 1896 as the Alabama Girls' Industrial School, later Alabama College (1923), coeducational from 1956, and the University of Montevallo from 1969. It also takes in campus support buildings and nearby homes linked to the college.
90001529.heading: Statement of Significance

01001408.summary: The McKibbon House, built around 1900, is a substantial and intact example of the Queen Anne style, which peaked in Alabama in the last two decades of the nineteenth century. Despite later asbestos siding, it keeps its tower, porches and balconies, turned posts, balusters and spindles, curved brackets, jigsawn woodwork, and irregular massing. Its eclectic exterior and interior details reflect the broad tastes of Alabama's middle and upper classes at the turn of the twentieth century. It is Montevallo's finest surviving example of Victorian-era architecture.
01001408.heading: Statement of Significance

96000054.summary: The Charles Butler House, built around 1890, is a locally significant example of the Queen Anne style in Childersburg and keeps a high degree of integrity. The large two-story, 12-room frame house has gingerbread-trimmed gables, Eastlake-style geometric ornament probably ordered by mail, bay windows, and a two-tier wraparound porch, with side additions made around 1920. Set on a small hill overlooking downtown Childersburg, it is a prominent landmark and the first thing visitors see when they come into town.
96000054.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

81000124.summary: The Nectar Covered Bridge is a four-span Town truss covered bridge, 385 feet long and 14 feet wide, standing 38 feet above the water on rubble masonry piers, with timbers of local oak and pine and its original corrugated metal covering. In June 1934 the county commissioners ordered it built as a high-water bridge to replace the old low-water crossing over the river. Builder Zelma Tidwell was paid $3 a day, his carpenters $2, and laborers $1.25, and some workers were supplied through the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which provided labor for county projects at the time.
81000124.heading: History and Additional Data

76000356.summary: The Kymulga Mill and Covered Bridge complex is the only place in Alabama with a grist mill and covered bridge close together on their original sites. The covered bridge, which carried the Old Georgia Road (originally an Indian trading path) over Talladega Creek, is one of three remaining nineteenth-century covered bridges in the state, though its exact date is unknown. The mill, begun in 1864 by Confederate Captain Forney and completed in 1867 by millwright G. E. Morris under the direction of Forney's widow, is unusually large at three and a half stories, with rare bracketed eaves, five runs of stones, and one of the few surviving original wooden mill dams. The site also includes a stand of some of the largest and oldest white oaks in the state.
76000356.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000188.summary: The Gilchrist House, a farmhouse built in 1812 in what is now Walker County, is one of Alabama's oldest buildings and is believed to be the oldest farmhouse in the state and the oldest structure in central and west Alabama. It was built by Edmon Gilchrist, who moved from Edgefield, South Carolina, first to Lowndes County in the Mississippi Territory and then to this area. Like many early settlers, he lived here as a squatter until he homesteaded the land, and his family still keeps the original sheepskin land patent.
72000188.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

91001480.summary: The Rev. Thomas Newton House near Ashville is a fine, intact example of an early one-story log dogtrot, built of hand-hewn, dovetailed logs with a sandstone chimney and two rooms flanking an open breezeway. Thomas Newton and his son-in-law John Ash built it after 1817, when their families settled in the Beaver Valley area later called 'Newton's Spring,' and both families lived in it until a separate house was built for Ash. It is reputed to be the oldest recorded building in St. Clair County. The site may also hold archaeological remains of early outbuildings.
91001480.heading: Statement of Significance

99000464.summary: The Blocton Italian Catholic Cemetery, established in 1896 and mostly developed in the 1910s and 1920s, is the site most closely tied to the Italian immigrants who came to Bibb County beginning in the mid-1880s to work in the coal mines around Blocton, a Tennessee Coal and Iron Company town. The immigrants lived in their own community, 'Little Italy,' near the Klondike and TCI mines, and worshiped at St. Francis Catholic Church, now demolished. The cemetery is now the main surviving place associated with this ethnic community.
99000464.heading: Statement of Significance

73000331.summary: Montebrier is an excellent example of early Gothic Revival architecture in Alabama, with a design that could have come from A. J. Downing's The Architecture of Country Houses. S. W. Mahan began building it in the early 1850s, with Archimedes Mahan as carpenter, near the prosperous Brierfield Iron Works; it was occupied by 1855 but not finished until after the Civil War. In 1866 Mahan sold it to General Josiah Gorgas, former Confederate Chief of Ordnance, making it the childhood home of William Crawford Gorgas, who later played a key role in conquering yellow fever. It later served as a country club in the 1920s.
73000331.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

91001479.summary: The John Ash House near Ashville, built around 1817, is one of the oldest log houses in Alabama and a good, intact example of an early settler's house in St. Clair County. The two-story log building, now covered in frame siding, may have begun as a one-story dogtrot, and its interior still shows wide hand-planed boards and the original log construction. John Ash was a county judge from 1819 to 1821 and a state senator in the 1820s, 1830s, and 1840s, and the town of Ashville was named for him.
91001479.heading: Statement of Significance

85000257.summary: The First United Methodist Church of Jasper, built in 1921, is among Alabama's most outstanding examples of Beaux Arts Neoclassicism in a church. It is smaller than contemporaries such as Birmingham's Southside Baptist and Temple Beth-El but equally sophisticated in design and second to none in finish, and it has kept its early twentieth-century character inside and out. Its interior is crowned by an artificially lit stained-glass dome of 109 sections and more than 30,000 pieces of glass. It is also an architectural symbol of Jasper's boom years as a mining center in western Alabama.
85000257.heading: 8. Significance

73000375.summary: This was the longtime home of U.S. Senator John Hollis Bankhead, who lived here from 1906 until his death in 1920 and founded one of Alabama's most powerful political families. Born in 1842, he was a Confederate soldier, state legislator, congressman for 20 years, and senator for 13. He pushed for the first federal survey of Muscle Shoals for hydroelectric power and helped make the Warrior River a canalized waterway and Mobile a deep-water port. He is best remembered as the 'Father of Good Roads' for starting federal aid to highways, and the Bankhead Highway was named for him. His son, Senator John H. Bankhead Jr., lived here from 1922 to 1946, and his son William B. Bankhead also stayed here at times.
73000375.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85001160.summary: The Walker County Hospital, built in 1923, was the first hospital built in Walker County and the only one there until 1936, and it served until 1980. Paid for by selling stock to local citizens, it brought modern health care to Walker, Winston, Lamar, and Fayette counties, which had previously sent patients to Birmingham. Its development was started by at least three Birmingham-based coal companies working with local businessmen and the Walker County Medical Society, and it specialized in industrial injuries among the region's growing workforce. It is also a typical example of early twentieth-century hospital construction.
85001160.heading: Statement of Significance

81000123.summary: The Swann Covered Bridge is a three-span Town truss covered bridge, 320 feet long with a 12.5-foot roadway, built of local pine and oak on rubble masonry piers and abutments, standing 28 feet above the Locust Fork. On September 11, 1933, the county commissioners ordered this high-water bridge built by the county bridge crew under foreman Zelma Tidwell, who was paid $2.75 a day, his carpenters $1.75, and laborers $1.25. When it was dedicated on November 7, the local community held a supper for the workers.
81000123.heading: History and Additional Data

100007850.summary: The William Brockman Bankhead House, a high-style Colonial Revival house built in 1924, is nationally significant as the main home of William B. Bankhead from 1924 until his death in office in 1940. As Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives from 1936 to 1940, he guided passage of some of the most important and lasting New Deal laws and helped broker compromise legislation that let the country prepare for war and supply its allies in World War II. A member of one of Alabama's most prominent political families, he remains the highest-ranking elected U.S. official from the state. The house, the only property in its neighborhood to fill an entire city block, is also locally significant for its architecture.
100007850.heading: Significance Summary

81000125.summary: The Easley Covered Bridge is a single-span, 83-foot Town truss covered bridge of pine and oak on rubble masonry abutments, standing 18 feet above Dub Branch. It is the oldest of Blount County's four covered bridges and was built under foreman Forrest Tidwell, assisted by his nephew and successor Zelma Tidwell. County records give no construction date. The commonly cited date of about 1927 is undocumented, but county minutes show repair materials ordered for the bridge in 1929.
81000125.heading: Significance

78000510.summary: The Stephenson House, built in 1887 from plans bought from a New Orleans architect, is one of Oakman's oldest landmarks and one of the area's finest Victorian homes. Its Queen Anne and Eastlake details appeared on local postcards around 1900, and it remains virtually unaltered and still in the family. It was the home of Dr. Hugh Watson Stephenson, one of Walker County's most noted physicians and civic leaders, who served three generations of patients in south Walker County. He was the area's only general physician until the 1940s and was at one time reported to be the oldest practicing physician in Alabama, working until shortly before his death at 88 after a 62-year career.
78000510.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

05000651.summary: The Winterboro Stagecoach Inn, also known as the John Gano Winters House, is a locally significant example of vernacular architecture. Built around 1850 as a dogtrot and enlarged around 1867 into a two-story, central-hall I-house with a rear ell, it represents the homes of middle- and upper-class planters and farmers in Talladega County. It is one of the few I-houses left in the county, a type that is fast disappearing. It keeps its original weatherboards, interior boards, doors, windows, and hardware.
05000651.heading: Statement of Significance

73002127.summary: The Inzer House, a fine small Greek Revival home, was built in 1852 by master brickmaker and mason Jefferson Campbell for Moses Dean, one of Ashville's earliest landowners and merchants, who helped oversee construction of the 1844 St. Clair County Courthouse. In 1866 it became the home of Judge John Washington Inzer, a noted Alabama politician known as St. Clair County's 'Grand Old Man.' Inzer studied law under John Tyler Morgan, opened a law practice in Ashville in 1856, served as probate judge, and was a delegate to the 1860 Democratic convention in Montgomery.
73002127.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82004612.summary: The Dr. James J. Bothwell House, built in 1835 as a single-pile Plantation Plain house with Federal-period refinements, is one of the finest early houses left in Ashville. It was enlarged in 1852, 1882, and 1917, with each phase keeping its period character; the 1852 kitchen and dining wing was built by master builder Richard A. Crow. It is noted for its portico and robust Adam-style parlor mantel. Dr. Bothwell, who came to Ashville in 1834 as the town's second physician, also served as clerk of the circuit court and was a charter member of the local Masonic lodge; attorney James A. Embry bought the house in 1882.
82004612.heading: Statement of Significance

05000972.summary: The B. B. Comer Memorial Library, built in 1939, is a representative Works Progress Administration project and a largely intact WPA Moderne library, one of only five libraries the WPA built in Alabama. Unlike most WPA buildings of brick and concrete, it uses local Alabama marble from the Sylacauga quarries along with brick. The project employed both construction workers and white-collar workers, including women, under the New Deal. In 1962 the library was rededicated as the Isabel Anderson Comer library.
05000972.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

97000650.summary: The Hightower Brothers Livery Stable is significant as an example of a twentieth-century small-town livery stable. From 1914 to 1952 the business in this building supplied horses, mules, buggies, wagons, and later automobiles, along with other services, to people and businesses in Sylacauga, providing the muscle power behind the town's daily life for over half a century. It stands in New Town, the business district laid out in 1890 by the Marble City Land and Furnace Company near the junction of two railroads.
97000650.heading: Statement of Significance

74002223.summary: Swayne Hall, completed in 1857 as a Baptist men's college, is the oldest building at Talladega College and was built with the labor of enslaved people. After the Civil War, the American Missionary Association bought it with help from the Freedmen's Bureau and founded Talladega College in 1867, and the children of the enslaved people who built the hall became its first pupils. Starting with four teachers and 140 elementary pupils, the college grew into a full institution of higher learning, graduating its first bachelor's degree class in 1895. Talladega is significant in Black education as one of the few Black colleges that pursued a strong liberal arts program when vocational training dominated.
74002223.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90001316.summary: Foster Hall (1869, enlarged 1901) is part of the Talladega College Historic District, which shows how the college grew from a single building in 1867 into a multi-building liberal arts campus serving mainly Black students. The campus was bought in 1868 after the 1865 freedmen's convention in Mobile declared the education of their children vital to their freedom. Campus building culminated under President Sumner (1916-1932) with Colonial Revival buildings by Joseph Fletcher, the last being Derricotte House in 1941. Despite limited funds and social burdens, the college became a major institution and a symbol of the struggle for education long denied to Black Alabamians.
90001316.heading: Statement of Significance

74002179.summary: The Looney House is possibly the oldest standing two-story log dogtrot house in Alabama. The two-pen, open-breezeway dogtrot was the most popular rural house type in nineteenth-century Alabama, but few two-story versions survive. Henry Looney, a veteran of Andrew Jackson's Creek War campaigns, and his father John built it in 1818 about a mile away, then took it apart and moved it to this higher, healthier site in 1820. In 1838 Henry married Jane Rutherford Ash, eldest daughter of Ashville founder John Ash.
74002179.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000181.summary: The Talladega Courthouse Square Historic District is architecturally significant as an example of industrial 'boom town' construction, with brick storefronts showing classical revival and Victorian influences and many unusual design features. Most buildings on the square went up between the 1870s and early 1900s, a period of growth for Talladega. The oldest, the Leverette Hardware building, dates to about 1835. The square was the city's most important business center, and the courthouse has been the seat of county government since the county was created.
72000181.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

77000207.summary: Lakeview School, which opened on January 17, 1902, was Birmingham's seventh public school and is now the second-oldest school building standing and in continuous use in the city. Designed by Birmingham architects Charles Wheelock and Son, the well-detailed brick building with Renaissance Revival touches shows the twentieth-century move away from the ornate Victorian style of schools like Powell School (1888). It was one of three four-room schools planned for the fast-growing Southside as early as 1890 but delayed until 1901 by the Panic of 1893. It took its name from the Elyton Land Company's Lakeview park and resort, whose lakeside hotel operated from 1886 to 1891.
77000207.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83003489.summary: The First Presbyterian Church of Talladega, dedicated on October 18, 1868, is the most fully developed of Alabama's mid-nineteenth-century Neo-Romanesque churches. It has many features of the style as popularized by architect Samuel Sloan and may be based on a plate from Sloan's The Model Architect. Of several similar Alabama churches, including those in Jacksonville, Montgomery, and Oxford, it is the most orthodox example and the only one with a monumental spire. The congregation was organized on November 29, 1834, and began the present church after raising $10,000 to $11,000 by subscription in 1859.
83003489.heading: Statement of Significance

83002983.summary: Boxwood, the Dowdell house, built in the mid-1850s, is a rare example of the Gothic Revival in antebellum Alabama houses and one of the state's oldest examples of 'carpenter's Gothic,' which used wood boldly to create a picturesque Gothic feel. Alabama has only a score or so of clear-cut Gothic Revival houses, perhaps half a dozen of them from before the Civil War, and Boxwood is among the best, earliest, and least altered. No house in the state more faithfully follows the principles of Andrew Jackson Downing's influential 1851 book The Architecture of Country Houses, as seen in its board-and-batten walls.
83002983.heading: Statement of Significance

01001294.summary: The Crane Hill Masonic Lodge, built in 1904 by Philip Aquilla Cooper, has served since then as both a Masonic lodge and a multipurpose community building for social, religious, educational, and government uses. It is a reminder of the influence of the Masonic order in rural Alabama. The two-story, gable-front building is the only historic community building left in Crane Hill and still dominates the old village center. It is the oldest surviving Masonic lodge building in Cullman County, and the Crane Hill Masons still use it, having celebrated their centennial in 1999.
01001294.heading: Statement of Significance

75000329.summary: Boshell's Mill, a small rural complex of a sawmill, gristmill, and mill dam from the late nineteenth century, is the only known combined saw and grist mill in northern Alabama. W. R. Boshell brought the sawmill here in 1885 to cut railroad trestle timbers for the Frisco Railroad, rebuilt it after a fire in the 1890s, and switched it from steam to water power in 1901. The gristmill was added in 1903 to keep sawmill workers busy in slack times and was run by Boshell's son George until 1938. The mill closed in 1963.
75000329.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87001552.summary: The Davidson-Smitherman House, built in 1837, is one of two outstanding pre-Civil War houses left in Bibb County. With the Henry-Kennedy House, it is one of the two earliest and least altered houses by Centreville's leading builders, George Howard and Enoch Carson, and reflects the town's first wave of substantial home building. The two-and-a-half-story house has abundant Federal-period detail, including tall multi-pane windows, a center hall, end chimneys, a continuous reverse-flight stair, and original wainscoting and mantels. Once the center of a 2,000-acre plantation, it is the only surviving building of the antebellum Davidson estate and is tied to prominent local families of public officials and soldiers.
87001552.heading: Statement of Significance

90001507.summary: The Jemison House, built around 1840, is significant for its unusual plan and its exceptionally fine, intact Federal-period interiors, which appear to keep their original paint. The raised cottage has two front rooms of equal size, each with its own entrance and no central hall, plus a split-level rear wing offset to one side and once flanked by open galleries. Only one other house with this plan is known to survive, the McMillan House, also built for a Jemison. It was probably built by Robert Jemison (1788-1870), a Georgia migrant from one of Talladega County's largest landowning families, or his son Samuel, who farmed the Chocolocco and Cheaha creek bottoms and ran a gristmill.
90001507.heading: Statement of Significance

02001067.summary: Shady Grove Methodist Church, built in 1892-93, is an intact example of a rural frame church with late nineteenth-century Gothic Revival detailing, and its exterior, interior, and ornament remain remarkably unchanged. It is one of the few wood-frame rural churches of its era left in Cullman County. Its simple Gothic Revival design carries on a tradition introduced to Alabama in the 1850s through economical frame churches based on Richard Upjohn's pattern book Rural Architecture. The nomination includes the adjoining cemetery.
02001067.heading: Significance

84000610.summary: Ave Maria Grotto, on the grounds of St. Bernard Abbey, is an unusually sophisticated, extensive, and well-preserved folk art environment of about 150 miniature buildings, shrines, and sculptures handbuilt in concrete by Brother Joseph Zoetl. Born Michael Zoetl in Landshut, Bavaria, in 1878, he was sent to Cullman at 14 to study for the priesthood and spent his life at the abbey, where he tended the boilers. Many miniatures are modeled on real buildings, especially the Franciscan missions of the Southwest. The abandoned rock quarry that holds them was turned into a park for the display from 1932 to 1934, centered on the large Ave Maria Grotto itself.
84000610.heading: Statement of Significance

83003444.summary: Stiefelmeyer's, built in 1892 and enlarged around 1896, is the only commercial building left in downtown Cullman that shows the wood-frame construction and Italianate styling of the town's first generation of business buildings. Most Alabama towns built Italianate storefronts in brick, often required by fire codes, but early Cullman, with fewer than 2,000 people in 1890, had mostly wooden buildings. Cullman was founded in 1873 by Bavarian immigrant John G. Cullmann, who bought thousands of acres from the Louisville & Nashville Railroad and brought German settlers.
83003444.heading: Statement of Significance

92001828.summary: The Ernest Edward Greene House, built in 1913, is a fine, intact example of the Neoclassical style that prevailed from 1900 to 1940. It has a two-story portico on fluted Ionic columns, multi-pane windows, a symmetrical facade and central hall, and leaded and beveled glass around the entrance. Greene was a prominent figure in Cullman through his position with the oil mill, then the community's most important employer, and he and his wife were active in the First Methodist Church. The house has seen few changes despite many owners.
92001828.heading: Statement of Significance

76000357.summary: The Elston House, or Elston-Barta House, is the oldest brick house in Talladega County and a simple, well-proportioned example of the earliest form of Georgian architecture in Alabama. Its design follows the mid-eighteenth-century Georgian houses of the Carolina seaboard, a style rarely seen on the Alabama frontier nearly a century later, and it is the only known surviving brick example in the state. It was built by Allen Elston, a New Jersey native who had prospered in South Carolina's Pendleton District and moved to the new Talladega County in 1833, on land still formally held by the Creek Indians. It was later carefully restored.
76000357.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80004238.summary: The Jacob Green House, built in the early nineteenth century, is significant as a survival of the hall-and-parlor plan, a seventeenth-century form that had nearly gone out of use by 1800 and is rarely recorded in Alabama. It is unusual in carrying the plan, a large 'hall' beside a smaller 'parlor' behind a symmetrical front, through two full stories. Its massive north chimney is one of only two known Alabama examples of diapered brickwork, with glazed headers set in a diamond pattern, and its mantels and paneled dado are fine rural cabinetwork. Jacob Green, born in 1767, came from York District, South Carolina, around 1819 and entered this land the next year.
80004238.heading: Statement of Significance

05000457.summary: Foster Auditorium, built in 1939 and designed by Miller, Martin and Lewis, is nationally significant as the site of Governor George Wallace's 'stand in the schoolhouse door' on June 11, 1963. There he defied a federal order to admit two African American students, Vivian Malone and James Hood, to the University of Alabama, then stepped aside. That evening President John F. Kennedy gave a nationwide address on civil rights, and a week later he sent Congress the bill that became the foundation of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The building is a symbol of southern 'massive resistance' to school desegregation after Brown v. Board of Education, and its lobby and corridors remain much as they were in 1963.
05000457.heading: Statement of Significance

72000186.summary: The President's Mansion at the University of Alabama is a Greek Revival house built in 1841, ten years after the university began classes, for its first occupant, President Basil Manly. It was designed by William Nichols, the architect of the earlier campus buildings, who returned after gaining national fame for the Mississippi State Capitol. In 1865, when Union troops under General John T. Croxton burned the campus, Mrs. Garland, the president's wife, is credited with saving the house: a fire had already been lit in the hall when she insisted only public buildings were to be burned, and the soldiers put it out.
72000186.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000187.summary: The Old Observatory at the University of Alabama, built in 1844, was one of only four campus buildings to survive the 1865 raid by Union General John T. Croxton's troops. It was built under the supervision of Frederick A. P. Barnard, the university's professor of chemistry and mathematics from 1837 to 1854 and later president of Columbia University. The observatory's instruments were wrecked in the raid, but some valuable university papers and library books hidden there under a pile of rubbish survived.
72000187.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

04000557.summary: The Gragg Field Historic District is significant for its role in Chilton County's aviation history and its ties to the Works Progress Administration's work in the county and state. Its beacon tower and generator building date from 1940, and its two hangars, from 1937 and 1942, are representative of the few pre-World War II hangars left in Alabama. The larger hangar, moved here in 1948 from Tuskegee Army Airfield, where the Tuskegee Airmen did their secondary flight training, is one of only three documented surviving buildings from that field.
04000557.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100005356.summary: The Alabama Book Store, a third-generation family business, has been part of University of Alabama student life since it opened in 1938 and moved into this building in 1942. The building, built in 1939 with a 1957 addition, is a locally significant example of Depression Modern architecture, combining simplified Beaux-Arts Classicism with Modernism. It is also one of the select Tuscaloosa commissions of architect David O. Whilldin (1881-1970). It stands on the 'Strip' along University Boulevard and keeps much of its historic exterior and interior.
100005356.heading: Statement of Significance Summary

70000099.summary: The Horton Mill Covered Bridge, built in the 1930s, is described in its nomination as the covered bridge standing highest above water in the United States. It is one of only sixteen covered bridges left in Alabama, out of 46 standing in 1958 and several hundred in the 1930s. It replaced a bridge built about three-quarters of a mile downstream in 1895 by T. M. Horton to reach his mill complex, which included corn and flour mills, a cotton gin, a sawmill, a blacksmith shop, and a store. Like other covered bridges, it was roofed mainly to protect its wooden floor, and it also served as a community gathering place.
70000099.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000320.summary: The Louisville and Nashville Railroad Depot in Cullman, completed in 1913 at a cost of $22,200, is unusual among the railroad's Alabama depots for its Spanish Colonial Revival style; most followed a simple standard design. It was designed by the L&N's Office of Chief Engineer. The railroad was vital to Cullman, founded in 1873 by German refugee Col. John Cullman on land optioned from the L&N for a colony of German immigrants. Cullman left $15,000 to lower the tracks through town, which was finally done in 1911 when the L&N double-tracked its line, moving the tracks and requiring this new depot.
76000320.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

00000126.summary: The Margaret Quayle Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel prefabricated houses the Lustron Corporation built from 1946 to 1950 in response to the post-World War II housing shortage. Its porcelain-enameled steel panels, metal interior walls and ceilings, and built-in cabinets, shelves, and vanity reflect postwar ideals of durability and easy upkeep. It is linked to Southern Sash, the Lustron dealer for northern Alabama and southern Tennessee, and is one of only eleven surviving Lustrons in Alabama.
00000126.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

01001170.summary: This boundary increase adds ten houses on the northeastern edge of Tuscaloosa's Druid City Historic District that were left out of the original 1975 nomination: eight on the College Park cul-de-sac and two on Queen City Avenue. Built between about 1915 and 1941, they are mostly Tudor and Colonial Revival houses, the two most popular revival styles of the early to mid-twentieth century, with the oldest being a more vernacular pyramidal cottage. They share features such as brick, stucco, and faux half-timbered walls, side porches, and decorated entrances.
01001170.heading: Statement of Significance

73000374.summary: The Guild-Verner House, completed in 1822 by Dr. James Guild a year after he arrived in Tuscaloosa, is the oldest brick house still standing in Tuscaloosa County. Guild was a prominent west Alabama doctor who became nationally known as a surgeon, and his son Lafayette Guild, who grew up here, served as chief medical officer on Robert E. Lee's staff. Later residents included druggist and legislator Dr. W. G. B. Pearson and, from 1911, C. B. Verner, a lawyer, legislator, University of Alabama land commissioner, and bank president.
73000374.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85000449.summary: The City National Bank, built in 1922, is Tuscaloosa's best example of privately funded Neoclassical Revival architecture and shows the wide influence of McKim, Mead & White on American civic buildings. It was designed by William L. Welton, who worked as a draftsman for that firm from 1902 to 1905, with strict Doric order and marble finishes. With the 1910 Federal Building, it is one of downtown's important monumental classical buildings. It was the third of four main offices of the bank, which began as J. H. Fitts and Company and became City National Bank in 1902.
85000449.heading: 8. Significance

84000748.summary: The Searcy House, built in 1904, is one of only two remaining Tuscaloosa examples of a southern version of the Colonial Revival style, with a giant-columned portico and projecting balcony, a two-story rear gallery, and a hipped roof that once had a widow's walk. Unlike the Georgian- or Federal-inspired Colonial Revival common elsewhere, its large-scale, Greek Revival-like design reflects the romantic glorification of the Old South popular at the time. It keeps its major exterior features, original floor plan, and much of its interior trim.
84000748.heading: Statement of Significance

90001808.summary: The Robert Jemison Servants' House, built from 1860 to 1862, is a representative modified Italianate building that echoes the ornate main house, now the Friedman Library, in its shape, central gable, full-length porch, and brackets. Both were designed by John Stewart, formerly of the Philadelphia firm of Sloan and Stewart, which also designed Bryce Hospital and is credited with bringing the 'Italian style' to the South. Robert Jemison Jr., who owned six plantations and more than 500 enslaved people, invested in stagecoach lines, mills, coal mining, plank roads, and bridges and amassed one of Alabama's largest fortunes. The quarters building shows how that wealth extended even to housing for the enslaved household staff.
90001808.heading: Statement of Significance

84000746.summary: The Bama Theatre-City Hall Building, built in 1937-38 to a design by D. O. Whilldin, is Tuscaloosa's best example of 1930s WPA Art Moderne architecture and the finest and best known New Deal building in Tuscaloosa County. It combines streamlined classicism in stone with Art Moderne touches such as rounded corners, low-relief sculpture, and polished interior surfaces. Unusually, it joined a commercial movie theater and a government building in one structure, a pairing well suited to the style. It reflects the growing role of the federal government in American communities during the 1930s.
84000746.heading: 8. Significance

14000357.summary: The Jemison School-Drish House was built in 1837 as the home of prominent physician, builder, and planter John R. Drish. It is significant for its use as Jemison School, an elementary school, from 1906 to 1925, and much of its present appearance, including an auditorium and classrooms, dates from that period. Tuscaloosa was slow to start a public school system, not doing so until 1885, and the system was underfunded and in debt by the 1890s. Opening Jemison School in the former Drish mansion was an important step in the city's early twentieth-century push to improve and expand public education.
14000357.heading: Statement of Significance Summary

96001029.summary: This second boundary increase adds the buildings on both sides of 7th Street between Greensboro Avenue and 25th Avenue to the Downtown Tuscaloosa Historic District. The district holds the commercial, government, civic, religious, and recreational buildings of the city's historic business center, laid out in the 1821 federal survey beside the Black Warrior River at the intersection of the city's two widest streets, Greensboro Avenue and University Boulevard. Tuscaloosa's growth was shaped by river trade and later the Louisville and Nashville Railroad. None of the district's early nineteenth-century buildings survive, and most date from the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
96001029.heading: Statement of Significance

100002717.summary: The Kennedy-Foster House, built in 1887, is a locally significant example of Late Victorian eclectic architecture that combines the Italianate and Second Empire styles. Italianate design was popular elsewhere but appears in only about a dozen Tuscaloosa houses, and this is one of only two asymmetrical Italianate villas ever built in the city and the only one left. It is also a rare local example of the Second Empire style. Its tower lost its third floor in a 1955 remodeling, but the house keeps one of the finest porches in Tuscaloosa.
100002717.heading: Significance Summary

76000315.summary: Janney Furnace, a 25-foot sandstone stack, was one of two Calhoun County furnaces built to supply pig iron to the Confederacy during the Civil War, when Alabama iron ore was first used in large quantities. It was built by Alfred A. Janney, founder in 1845 of Janney and Company Iron-works in Montgomery, one of Alabama's earliest foundries, and his partner Ned Lewis, drawn by rich brown ore deposits nearby. The site was ideal, with ore within wheelbarrow distance and limestone for flux just to the north. The furnace was abandoned after a Union raid on July 14, 1864.
76000315.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87001027.summary: The Fitch House, begun around 1830, is one of the few early nineteenth-century buildings left in Tuscaloosa and an excellent example of Federal-period interior woodwork. Its finely crafted cantilevered stairway is unusual for a house of this modest size and period. It was built and lived in by John S. Fitch, a Connecticut-born master carpenter hired by architect William Nichols to do the carpentry for Alabama's state capitol in Tuscaloosa (1827-1831). Its later enlargement with Greek Revival details shows the changing architectural tastes of the area.
87001027.heading: 8. Significance

74000408.summary: The Clarkson Covered Bridge, built in 1904, is one of the longest two-span covered bridges standing in the Deep South, one of only 13 covered bridges left in Alabama, and the last of eleven in Cullman County. It is one of nine Town truss bridges in the state, a lattice truss of crisscrossed planks patented by New England promoter Ithiel Town in 1820 and known for its strength. The bridge stands on land donated to the county by the father of W. H. Legg. After storm damage in 1923, it was repaired by Cullman contractor Bill Slosler's crew in 1923-24 for $1,000 to $1,500.
74000408.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92001824.summary: The Murphy-Collins House, a two-story stuccoed brick bungalow built around 1923, is significant for its ties to the rise of a Black middle class in the early twentieth century and to the segregation that shaped Southern life until the 1960s. It was the home of Will Murphy, the first licensed Black embalmer in west Alabama, whose funeral business from 1906 gave Tuscaloosa's Black community an alternative to white undertakers, and his wife Laura, a teacher and school principal. Its bricks came from the old Alabama State Capitol in Tuscaloosa, made by freedmen and enslaved craftsmen. Its waffle-pattern ceiling echoes that of nearby First African Baptist Church.
92001824.heading: Statement of Significance

88001580.summary: First African Baptist Church, built in 1907 by church members George Clopton, contractor, and William Medlock, brickmason, is one of the best surviving and least altered early twentieth-century churches in Tuscaloosa. It is the earliest of the city's five pre-World War I churches to keep its original site and essentially its original interior and exterior. It is also the only known building in Alabama outside the Tuskegee campus that shows the design ideas of Robert Robinson Taylor, the first Black architect to graduate from MIT and Tuskegee Institute's main architect, and it is widely seen as patterned on his Tuskegee Institute Chapel (1898).
88001580.heading: Statement of Significance

85000448.summary: The Carson Place shows the freedom architects took in the 1850s with the strict classical forms of the 1830s and 1840s. On a standard house plan it uses exaggerated classical door and window hoods and eclectic details such as octagonal columns with alternating flutes, scalloped door moldings, scroll-sawn balustrades, and unusual mantels, and its interior is intact. The house may have begun in the 1820s on lots bought by George Cox, a U.S. Navy commander in the Tripoli war and the War of 1812, in the Newtown section, and his widow Mary Cox enlarged it in 1827 and 1835.
85000448.heading: 8. Significance

100004680.summary: The 1956 Sheppard Library stands at the center of the original quadrangle of the Stillman College Historic District, on the site of the Cochrane Mansion. The district shows broad patterns in African American higher education, as Stillman grew from a white-led ministerial training school into an African American-led four-year liberal arts college. It is also significant as a civil rights strategy and planning site whose faculty and students took part in civil rights activities in Tuscaloosa. Its period of significance runs from 1898 to 1972, when the Harold N. Stinson building, named for the college's first African American president, was built.
100004680.heading: Significance Summary

75000331.summary: The Houston Jail is the only known surviving log jail in Alabama and the only public building left in Houston, the old seat of Winston County. The county, first called Hancock, was renamed in 1858 for Governor John Anthony Winston, and Houston served as county seat until 1884, when it moved to Double Springs. The jail's exact date is unknown, but an 1867 grand jury called for a new courthouse and jail, and since the courthouse (now gone) was built in 1868, the jail was probably built soon after.
75000331.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87001416.summary: The Winston County Courthouse in Double Springs grew around an 1894 sandstone courthouse, enlarged in 1929-30 with matching stone from the same quarry. The addition, associated with the prominent Birmingham firm of Warren, Knight & Davis, is a good local example of the Neoclassical Revival style, with a pedimented, columned portico and clock tower. The building is significant as a small rural courthouse that grew over time to handle the expanding role of county government. It is the largest and most prominent building in town.
87001416.heading: Statement of Significance

71000107.summary: The Collier-Overby House, built in the 1820s by James Walker, is one of Tuscaloosa's older homes and was from 1826 the longtime residence of Henry Watkins Collier. Collier served 18 years on the Alabama Supreme Court, 12 as chief justice, was governor from 1849 to 1853, and was the first president of the Alabama Historical Society. During his second term, reformer Dorothea Dix, whom he had met at this house, addressed the legislature, leading to the state mental hospital in Tuscaloosa, whose first superintendent, Dr. Peter Bryce, made it a national model of non-restraint treatment. After the Civil War the house was home to Confederate Brigadier General Philip Dale Roddey, the 'Defender of North Alabama.'
71000107.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85000737.summary: The Wilson-Clements House in Northport, built around 1835, is an excellent example of a one-story Federal-style brick cottage with a simple four-room central-hall plan and Federal woodwork. Small houses like it were once common in northern Alabama, but this is one of the few surviving brick examples of this early house type in the state.
85000737.heading: 8. Significance

73000333.summary: The Coldwater Creek Covered Bridge, built before 1850 and possibly as early as 1839, is one of the few covered bridges left in Alabama, which had about 200 in 1930 and only 46 by 1958. It is one of three surviving bridges in the state built in the modified kingpost style. After a hunter's dropped torch partly burned it in 1920, local men Frank Morris, E. A. Walker, and Eli Bynum quickly rebuilt it, since it was the only crossing over Coldwater Creek. Like other covered bridges, it was roofed to protect its floor and served as a community gathering place.
73000333.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

02001069.summary: The Samuel Johnson House near Buhl is a locally significant example of a second-generation dogtrot house and one of the few left in Tuscaloosa County, where most have been lost to neglect, demolition, or vandalism or changed beyond recognition. It keeps its historic hand-hewn and mill-cut framing and mill-cut weatherboards. The house and its land represent the plantation and tenant farming eras of Alabama's history. A granddaughter born in the house recalled a detached kitchen, smokehouse, barn, corncrib, and slave and tenant dwellings, none of which survive, so the site may hold archaeological remains.
02001069.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100011947.summary: The Oxford Railway Depot, a one-story Italianate building built in 1884 by the East Tennessee, Virginia and Georgia Railroad, is locally significant for its role in the growth of Oxford and the surrounding area. Serving as both passenger station and freight warehouse, it supported transportation and commerce until Southern Railway closed it in 1962. It is one of only two documented train stations of this Italianate type left in Alabama and west Georgia.
100011947.heading: Statement of Significance Summary

72000184.summary: The Battle-Friedman House was built in 1835 by Alfred Battle, a North Carolina native who came to Tuscaloosa in 1821 as a merchant and planter, held extensive plantations, and helped bring the first railroad to Tuscaloosa. Hungarian-born merchant Bernhard Friedman bought it in 1875. He managed a cotton mill and in the boom year of 1887 became vice president of the Tennessee Coal, Iron, and Land Company. His son Hugo, an industrialist and philanthropist, left the house to the City of Tuscaloosa in 1965 for public use. Battle's niece Virginia Tunstall Clay, who lived here as a child, later personally appealed to President Andrew Johnson for the release of her husband, Confederate Senator Clement C. Clay.
72000184.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE
