72000183.summary: The James Shirley House, also called the Christian Home, built in the early 1830s, is one of the older Federal-style houses in west Alabama and the oldest surviving building in Northport, across the Black Warrior River from Tuscaloosa. It was the first brick building in Northport and stands on the site of the town's first industrial plant, a horse-drawn cotton gin. James Shirley, a South Carolina native, also built Northport's first brick commercial buildings in 1850 after a fire destroyed an entire district. The house later passed to his brother-in-law William Lewis Christian, whose family still owned it.
72000183.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000407.summary: The Coosa County Jail, completed in August 1842, is the oldest remaining stone jail in Alabama and one of the few buildings left from the county's early years. Coosa County was created on December 18, 1832 from lands ceded in the Creek Treaty of Cusseta, and its seat moved from Lexington to Rockford in 1835. After a first contract was forfeited, the county hired Miller and Heard in 1841 to build the jail for $2,745.
74000407.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000737.summary: The Wheeler House, built in 1890 as the home of prominent brick manufacturer M. J. Wheeler, is one of the finest houses in Tuscaloosa's Capitol Park area and one of the first buildings put up in the city after a long economic depression. With its multi-gabled projecting bays and wraparound Tuscan-columned porch, it is typical of the houses built in this middle-class neighborhood between 1890 and 1920. It was nominated individually after a proposed Capitol Park historic district was withdrawn in 1976 because of local opposition.
80000737.heading: 8. Significance

75000328.summary: The Searcy House, built around 1830, is one of Tuscaloosa's older buildings and was home to two prominent Alabamians. It was built as a town house for Henry Minor, a member of Alabama's first constitutional convention in 1819, who served as a Supreme Court justice from 1823 to 1825 and then as clerk of the court until his death in 1839. From 1868 it was home to Dr. James T. Searcy, a close friend and follower of Dr. Peter Bryce, the pioneer of non-restraint treatment of mental illness. Searcy succeeded Bryce as superintendent of the Alabama Insane Hospital in 1892 and served until 1919. The house's six square paneled portico columns match those on two other 1830s Tuscaloosa houses.
75000328.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002968.summary: The U.S. Post Office in Attalla, built in 1931-32 by the Adams Construction Company of Washington, D.C., is significant for its architecture. Its Federal-style design is typical of the period, but its detail and workmanship are well above those of most Depression-era post offices, and its $93,839 cost was well above average for a building of its size. In 1968 it received a citation of merit from President Lyndon B. Johnson, given to a few attractive postal buildings across the country.
83002968.heading: 8. Significance

85002886.summary: The Lansing T. Smith House, or Smith-Mallory-Cater House, a two-story Victorian frame house designed by architect John Henry Norris, is significant as the home of Lansing T. Smith, Anniston's 'Father of Golf' and a leader of the sport's early growth in the South. Smith laid out the town's first golf course in a cow pasture in 1890, owned its first golf clubs, and brought in a pro for the new Highland Country Club, which became the Anniston Country Club with the state's second golf course. He also laid out the Municipal Golf Course with WPA help in 1936 and helped found the Southern Golf Association. In 1920 he sold the house to John William Mallory, president of the Polar Ice and Coal Company.
85002886.heading: 8. Significance

72000185.summary: The Jemison-Van de Graaff House, completed in 1862, is one of the finest antebellum Italianate mansions in Alabama, and many architects rank it with Fendall Hall in Eufaula as the state's best examples of the style. It reflects the shift away from Greek Revival. It was built of materials from the vast holdings of Robert Jemison Jr., a wealthy businessman who served in the Alabama House and Senate and the Confederate Senate and led the strong but unsuccessful opposition to secession at the 1861 State Convention, making him Alabama's most influential opponent of secession. He also helped bring the State Hospital for the Insane to Tuscaloosa. Begun by architect William Robertson, the house was finished by a Philadelphia architect named Lewis.
72000185.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000410.summary: The Alabama City Library, the Nichols Memorial Library, completed in 1902, was one of the earliest free public library buildings in Alabama. The J. Howard Nichols family of Massachusetts built and supported it as a memorial to their son Howard Gardner Nichols, who was killed in 1896 while supervising construction of the family's Dwight Manufacturing Company mill and mill town. Almost all of its materials, including the brick, were shipped from New England, and its eclectic design is attributed to an unidentified Boston architect. It faces the Dwight mill across a triangular lot surrounded by workers' houses.
74000410.heading: 8. Significance

92001069.summary: The Forrest Cemetery Chapel, formally the Ruth Cross Memorial Chapel, built in 1935-36 by Works Progress Administration workers, is a unique local example of Gothic Revival architecture in native stone. WPA workers quarried and hand-cut the sandstone from nearby Lookout Mountain, gaining both income and skills, and the Gadsden Times praised it as 'an architectural gem' and one of the top WPA projects. It was built as the funeral chapel for Forrest Cemetery, Gadsden's earliest burial ground, dating to the mid-nineteenth century. The nomination also includes the cemetery's comfort station.
92001069.heading: Statement of Significance

05000835.summary: The Davis C. Cooper House, built in 1911 and remodeled around 1925, is the only large Colonial Revival house in Oxford. It was the home of Davis C. Cooper, who in 1888 became the first president of the Bank of Oxford, then the youngest bank president in Alabama, and led it and its successor, the First National Bank of Oxford, for forty-five years. He was also mayor of Oxford for twenty years from 1910, a leader in the Alabama Baptist Association, and a Howard College trustee. When the bank was forced to close in the Depression, he and his family mortgaged their personal property.
05000835.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

85002738.summary: The Glen Addie Volunteer Hose Company Fire Hall, built in 1885, is significant as the first fire house built in Anniston and for its ties to Glen Addie, the Woodstock Iron Company's village for furnace workers and Anniston's first workers' neighborhood. It provided fire protection for the town's largest workers' neighborhood and was a center of village life, hosting the annual Firemen's Ball and Fireman's Day. The two-story brick building keeps its pressed-metal roof and Victorian corbeled brickwork, though its arched openings have been altered.
85002738.heading: Statement of Significance

85002875.summary: Mount Zion Baptist Church, the second Black church organized in the Anniston area and the oldest still in existence, is an important local example of late nineteenth-century vernacular Black church design. Its stone basement was built in 1890 and the brick sanctuary with its corner tower added in 1894, designed and built by members of the congregation using native materials and Romanesque and Victorian influences. It stands on Zion Hill, once part of the speculative town of Oxanna. When the nomination was written, it was about to become the last surviving nineteenth-century church building of Anniston's Black community.
85002875.heading: Statement of Significance

79000404.summary: The Old Tuscaloosa County Jail, built in 1856 by William B. Robertson for $8,029.40, was one of the finest antebellum jails built in Alabama and one of the few that survive. Unlike the plain masonry or log jails of the time, it looked like one of Tuscaloosa's fine homes and had many interior refinements, and its thick brick walls and solid log decking made it one of the most secure jails in the state. It is remembered for one of Alabama's most remarkable jailbreaks: on July 7, 1884, notorious outlaw and former Sumter County sheriff Stephen S. Renfroe escaped by burning through the log decking of his cell. After 1890 the building became a residence and boarding house.
79000404.heading: Statement of Significance

78000483.summary: St. Michael and All Angels Episcopal Church, begun in 1888 and consecrated on St. Michael's Day, September 29, 1890, is acclaimed as one of Alabama's most beautiful churches and one of its finest late nineteenth-century churches. It is believed to be the only Alabama work of noted architect William Halsey Wood, and its interior has an exceptional double hammer-beam ceiling, a large rose window, and an elaborate reredos. John Ward Noble built it for the English stone masons, brick masons, and furnace men, mostly Episcopalians, whom the Woodstock Iron Company brought in to build and run its furnaces. It reflects the Noble and Tyler families' aim to make Anniston a model industrial city.
78000483.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85002889.summary: The Union Depot, built in 1885, was the first depot in Anniston to serve all incoming railroad lines during the city's greatest growth in the late 1880s, and it is the only depot left from that period. It is a good local example of Richardsonian Romanesque depot design, built of the vermiculated native sandstone used in many of Anniston's nineteenth-century churches. Its stonework and arched entry show the craftsmanship of master stonemason Simon Jewell. A late-1950s fire damaged the roof, which was rebuilt to its original lines. The nomination also includes the freight house.
85002889.heading: Statement of Significance

10000270.summary: The Greyhound Bus Station (about 1957-60) is part of the expanded Downtown Anniston Historic District, nominated for its planning as a New South 'model city,' its commerce, and its Black heritage. On Mother's Day, May 14, 1961, Ku Klux Klan members attacked a CORE Freedom Riders bus here while police a block and a half away did not respond, and the bus was burned after fleeing into the countryside. The attack drew international attention and led local Black and white leaders to form a biracial Human Relations Council that guided the city's desegregation. The district also includes the Trailways station, where the second bus was attacked, and sites such as the Dr. Charles E. Thomas Drug Store and the Alabama Penny Savings Bank.
10000270.heading: Statement of Significance

85002878.summary: The Nonnenmacher Bakery Building, built around 1890, is significant for its role in Anniston's early commercial development as the first building in the city built specifically as a bakery. It is a good example of a late Victorian commercial building, a two-story pressed-brick structure with Eastlake-style cast-iron storefront supports, segmental-arched upper windows, and a galvanized-iron pseudo-Italianate cornice. It is one of the least altered of Anniston's remaining nineteenth-century commercial buildings.
85002878.heading: Statement of Significance

91000611.summary: The Old Anniston Electric and Gas Company Plant consists of two surviving buildings from a complex built in 1888 and 1915 to produce gas and electricity for the early town. Anniston was a model company town, and the Woodstock Company began producing electricity on a small scale in 1882, making it the first town in Alabama where electricity was put to practical use. As demand grew, the newly formed Anniston Electric and Gas Company built the Electric Light and Power Plant, which still stands, along with a gas works, coal shed, and gas holding tank on this low-lying site in 1888. The second surviving building was built in 1915 as an electrical transformer station.
91000611.heading: Statement of Significance

85002866.summary: The Calhoun County Courthouse, built in 1900, has been the seat of county government since that year, when the county seat moved to Anniston from Jacksonville, where it had been since the county's founding in 1832. It symbolizes the bitter political fight between the two cities and the economic and political dominance Anniston had gained by the turn of the century. Designed by J. W. Golucke, it is one of the earliest surviving Neoclassical courthouses in Alabama, preceded only by the Lee and Chambers County courthouses, and one of the earliest uses of the Neoclassical revival for public buildings in the state.
85002866.heading: Statement of Significance

85002882.summary: The Peerless Saloon building, built in 1899, is associated with one of the first elaborate saloons in Anniston after the city opened to liquor sales in 1890. It symbolizes the bitter wet-dry fight of the late 1880s, which ended when a State Supreme Court decision overturned a local referendum banning liquor in the city. Architecturally, it is a highly developed, almost mannerist example of Victorian Neoclassical motifs applied to a small two-story brick commercial building, with fluted galvanized-iron pilasters, egg-and-dart moldings, and a bold entablature and balustrade.
85002882.heading: Statement of Significance

93000052.summary: The Charles Gunn House, built in 1886, is a good representative of the late Victorian homes popular in Gadsden in the 1880s, one of the few survivors of a building boom that followed a large public land sale in the city. It keeps its mansard roof with iron cresting, eave brackets, latticed front porch with turned posts, and much of its original interior, including mantels, staircase, stained glass, and woodwork. It was built for Edward Tracy Hollingsworth, of a pioneer Gadsden family, who became a prominent merchant and banker. It is better known for its later owner Charles Gunn, an early Gadsden dentist, and at nomination it was being restored as a house museum.
93000052.heading: Statement of Significance

85002879.summary: The Nonnenmacher House, built in 1902 by baker Charles Nonnenmacher, is the best and most intact example in Anniston of the turn-of-the-century shift from asymmetrical, highly textured Victorian styles to symmetrical, restrained designs that drew on classicism and the nation's colonial heritage. The two-and-a-half-story pressed-brick house keeps some Victorian touches, and its hall has an elevator, the first built into a home in the city. The family lived there until the city acquired it in 1983. His daughter Louisa Nonnenmacher, who died in 1981 at 94, was Anniston's unofficial historian, recording city events in a newspaper column.
85002879.heading: Statement of Significance

85002890.summary: The Wikle Drugstore building, built in 1883, is associated with Anniston's first building boom (1883-1886), after the company town opened to the public. It was the first drugstore building in Anniston and the first brick commercial building on Noble Street, and it is the only downtown building still housing the business it was built for. Although its first floor has been altered, its three-story facade is the city's best surviving example of late nineteenth-century Victorian Neoclassical commercial design, with an egg-and-dart and dentiled cornice, cartouches, scrolled keystones, and bas-relief swags.
85002890.heading: Statement of Significance

85002873.summary: The Kress Building is an excellent, intact local example of the Art Deco style, with a glazed-tile facade from about 1930 featuring stylized terra cotta fleur-de-lis capitals and a polychrome geometric band above the second-floor windows. The facade was the only one of its kind in Anniston, though it was typical of the S. H. Kress & Co. chain at the time. The two-story-plus-mezzanine building on Noble Street still carries its 'S. H. Kress & Co. 5-10-15 Cent Store' lettering, and its interior has had few major alterations.
85002873.heading: Statement of Significance

73000332.summary: The Anniston Inn Kitchen and main dining hall are the only remains of the Anniston Inn, a hotel known for its outstanding architectural design, its importance in local history, and its place in Anniston's original city plan. Woodstock Company founder Samuel Noble had long wanted a fine hotel for his 'Model City,' and the $260,000 inn was built in the mid-1880s building boom; local sources credit both Stanford White and Philadelphia architect George T. Pearson with the design. When fire destroyed the main hotel in January 1922, a dividing wall saved the kitchen. Later that year the Woman's Civic Club, then the Axis Club, began leasing it from the city.
73000332.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002000.summary: The Dudley Snow House, whose hewn-log core dates from the early 1830s, is quite possibly the oldest building in Calhoun County and one of the earliest surviving dwellings in the Coosa River basin. It marks the first spread of settlement onto the northeastern Alabama lands the Creeks ceded in 1832, when Dudley Snow chose land at the mouth of the Choccolocco Valley and built a log dogtrot. It shows a common pattern in rural Alabama architecture: a log house transformed into a roomier weatherboarded house with simple stylistic touches. As the home of a small slaveholder, it represents a class, neither planter nor small farmer, often overlooked in studies of the Old South. Tradition holds that the area's first post office, before Oxford existed, was at the house.
82002000.heading: Statement of Significance

85002885.summary: The Security Bank Building, built in 1890, is associated with Anniston's major development boom of the late 1880s and early 1890s. The bank was one of the city's first financial institutions and was closely tied to the Southwestern Land Company, one of the major real estate companies behind the city's growth. Architecturally, the three-story brick building on the corner of Noble and Eleventh Streets is a very good local example of a late nineteenth-century Victorian commercial building, with one of the most elaborate decorative parapets surviving from the period in Anniston.
85002885.heading: Statement of Significance

85002865.summary: The Bank of Anniston building, built in 1888, is associated with the city's early commercial development. It housed one of Anniston's first banks, which failed in 1898, and later held various businesses. It is a notable local example of a small Victorian Neoclassical commercial building, distinguished by its stone facade with arched second-floor windows, oversized keystones, and rough-cut pilasters, the only original stone facade on Noble Street, where all the others are brick. It is one of the few Noble Street commercial buildings to survive the downtown modernization that began in the late 1940s, though its first floor was remodeled in 1967.
85002865.heading: Statement of Significance

85002874.summary: The Montgomery Ward-Alabama Power Company Building, built in 1927, is significant for its highly developed 1920s ornament and as one of only two Noble Street buildings showing Art Deco influence; the other is the Kress Building. Its terra cotta front is the only surviving local example combining geometric designs with classically inspired pilasters, swags, and urn finials. The two-story commercial building stands at the corner of Noble and Twelfth Streets in Anniston's central business district.
85002874.heading: Statement of Significance

86001000.summary: The Col. O. R. Hood House, built in 1902-04 by local builder and architect James Crisman, is associated with Oliver Roland Hood (1867-1957), a Gadsden attorney and industrial promoter. He was one of the three original organizers of the Alabama Power Company, wrote its charter, and served as its first vice president (1906-1911) and its legal advisor until 1941. He later helped bring the southern branch of the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company to Gadsden in 1926. The house is an exceptionally fine local example of an eclectic, Neoclassically inspired home with Victorian embellishments.
86001000.heading: Statement of Significance

85002740.summary: The Anniston Transfer Company building, built in 1889, is a good local example of the style, rich detailing, and craftsmanship of commercial buildings from Anniston's building boom of the late 1880s. Its features include a Victorian Neoclassical metal cornice with modillions and paired brackets, lozenge-pattern brickwork, blind arches on corbels, and segmental-arched lintels with stone keystones. Business leader Luther Glenn Jones ran it as the Anniston Transfer Company, a combination funeral parlor and livery stable whose bricked-in stall openings remain. It later housed an outdoor advertising business serving northeast Alabama and Georgia.
85002740.heading: Statement of Significance

85002876.summary: The Samuel Noble Monument, erected in June 1895, is a good local example of late nineteenth-century commemorative sculpture and reflects the national movement to honor important people and events with publicly commissioned sculpture. Designed by Durham & Company of Charlotte, North Carolina, and carved in Italy by an unnamed sculptor, the statue of Anniston's founder was paid for by contributions from the city's residents during an economic depression. It still stands in its original place in the median of Quintard Avenue at Eleventh Street, on a three-tiered North Carolina granite base.
85002876.heading: Statement of Significance

85002871.summary: The Richard P. Huger House, built in 1888 and also known as the Huger-Brazelton House, is associated with Dr. Richard P. Huger, the first physician to practice in Anniston, who served two terms as mayor from 1887 to 1891 and was the first president of the Alabama Medical Society. John Ward Noble built the house on his estate as a wedding gift for his daughter Alwera and her husband, Dr. Huger. It is one of the few surviving quality houses from Anniston's late-1880s building boom and a local example of Shingle Style influence mixed with classicism, with a sandstone foundation, red-brick first story, and cedar-shingled upper story.
85002871.heading: Statement of Significance

84000616.summary: The Eleventh Street School, built in 1907, is the oldest surviving public school in Gadsden and reflects the growth of public education and the city's steady population growth driven by rapid industrial development. It was built to relieve crowding at the College Street School and served as an elementary school until its students moved to the new Queen City Elementary School in January 1963. Its architect, Scottish-born A. D. Simpson, designed about nine of the thirteen Gadsden city schools built between 1901 and 1930, as well as the building's 1926 addition. The otherwise unchanged building survives as a major landmark of turn-of-the-century Gadsden.
84000616.heading: Statement of Significance

82001997.summary: The Caldwell Building, built in 1889 at the main business intersection of nineteenth-century Anniston, is one of the few early commercial buildings in the city that have survived with only ground-floor changes. It is one of the city's best examples of the Victorian Italianate style, with russet stone trim and an elaborate cornice against red brick, and it stands on the first lot sold to the public after the town opened in 1883. It was built by John Caldwell, city attorney and a state representative. From the early 1900s to 1925 it held the offices of corporation lawyer John B. Knox, president of the 1901 Constitutional Convention and a major proponent of disfranchising Black voters, and in the 1910s it was known as the Knox Building.
82001997.heading: Statement of Significance

80000681.summary: The Lyric Theatre, built in 1918 for the Anniston Theatre Company, is a very good example of early twentieth-century entertainment buildings in smaller Alabama cities and is noted for its flyloft, an unusual feature in the state. Until 1928 it hosted the main Keith Vaudeville circuit and a summer Chautauqua circuit, and it was the main entertainment for the 27,753 men training at Camp McClellan in World War I. It was adapted for motion pictures in the late 1920s, opening with 'The Jazz Singer' in October 1928. With the city's opera house gone, it is the oldest building in Anniston associated with popular entertainment.
80000681.heading: Statement of Significance

76000314.summary: The U.S. Post Office (Federal Building) in Anniston, built in 1904-06 under Supervising Architect James Knox Taylor, is one of the city's most distinguished buildings and an unusual example of the classical style. Its materials, massing, and rich ornament make a powerful statement of the federal government's presence in Anniston, and it is a visual anchor on one of the city's main streets. Plans for an entirely different Colonial-style building were completed in 1902 and foundations begun before the building was redesigned. It was enlarged in 1934 and served as a site of federal activity for more than sixty years.
76000314.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000597.summary: The McKleroy-Wilson-Kirby House, built in 1888 and attributed by tradition to John Moser, is the last surviving mansion on Quintard Avenue, Anniston's premier residential boulevard of the late-1880s boom. A good example of Queen Anne architecture with fine interior detailing, it keeps its carriage house and guest house. It was the home of John Martin McKleroy, a powerful politician who chaired the State Democratic Executive Committee in 1886 and was involved in major Anniston industries. His son William Henry McKleroy, also a resident, was mayor of the city and president of the Anniston National Bank and the Oxford National Bank.
84000597.heading: Statement of Significance

76000325.summary: The U.S. Post Office (Federal Building) in Gadsden was completed in 1910 as a one-story building with a central portico and enlarged to three stories in 1913, both under Supervising Architect James Knox Taylor. It shows Taylor's mannered use of classical forms to make an imposing statement of the federal government's presence and his skill at building in stages to meet Congressional budget limits. Its two-story central courtroom, expressed on the facade, departs from classical form. Its mass, ornament, and rich materials made it the most distinctive building in town, and despite a 1959 fire it remained essentially unaltered.
76000325.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000313.summary: The Noble Cottage (Noble-Roberts-Morris Cottage), built in 1887 for Anniston founder Samuel Noble, is a mature expression of the style of Henry Hobson Richardson and one of only two examples of that style in Alabama. It is nearly identical to the nearby Crowan Cottage, though smaller and more compact, which heightens its sculptural quality. Local tradition credited both cottages to Stanford White, but research found that L. B. Wheeler of Atlanta designed the Noble Cottage, and he may have designed the Crowan Cottage too. Its custom-designed doors, brass hinges, and windows have been restored.
76000313.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88001581.summary: The Legion Park Bowl (Gadsden Amphitheater), built in the mid-1930s of native sandstone quarried on nearby Lookout Mountain, is the most ambitious of three rustic stone projects built in Gadsden by the Works Progress Administration; the others are the Forrest Cemetery Chapel and the Gadsden High School Stadium. Designed by local architect Paul W. Hofferbert, it shows the rustic vernacular character of WPA architecture. The original complex includes a 1,500-seat tiered stone arena, a hexagonal gatehouse, a proscenium stage, dressing rooms, and a club room. Except for a 1960s brick clubhouse addition built by the American Legion, it looks as it did when first built.
88001581.heading: Statement of Significance

82001998.summary: The Parker-Reynolds House, built in 1888-89, is the finest surviving mansion from the late nineteenth-century boom that made Anniston one of Alabama's largest cities, second only to Birmingham in industrial importance. It is a rare early Alabama example of the Chateauesque style popularized in the Northeast by Richard Morris Hunt, and its opulence reflects the wealth and power of the entrepreneurs drawn to the new industrial town. It was built for Duncan T. Parker, a Mobile businessman who became a select partner of the founding Noble and Tyler families. Parker headed the Anniston Land and Improvement Company and the First National Bank and helped organize the gasworks, the water company, and the Anniston and Cincinnati Railroad Company.
82001998.heading: Statement of Significance

85002881.summary: Parker Memorial Baptist Church, built in 1888-89 to a design by George Kennerly, is a fine local example of Victorian Gothic church architecture. Master stonemason Simon Jewell cut and laid its native pink sandstone, trimmed with Kentucky bluestone. It has a dominant three-stage entrance tower with a broach spire and Gothic pointed-arch entrances. It is one of three large sandstone Victorian Gothic churches Jewell built during Anniston's rapid growth of the late 1880s, and it has been enlarged over the years.
85002881.heading: Statement of Significance

85002869.summary: Grace Episcopal Church, built in 1882-85, is associated with the 'welfare capitalism' many nineteenth-century industrialists practiced. Woodstock Iron Company owners Samuel Noble and Daniel Tyler built it on company land to meet the spiritual as well as physical needs of their workers and families. It is a fine local example of Gothic Revival church architecture in finely cut native sandstone and one of three Anniston churches built by English master stonemason Simon Jewell. The nave was lengthened and a narthex added in the 1950s, and additions matching the original were built in 1958 and 1967.
85002869.heading: Statement of Significance

100008433.summary: The Noojin House, built in 1926 and remodeled and expanded in 1941, is the best local example of the French Eclectic style popular from 1920 to 1945 and the only known example in Gadsden or Etowah County. North Alabama architect Paul W. Hofferbert designed both the original house and its 1941 redesign in consultation with Billie Noojin, using the finest materials of the day. The house sits on the brow of Lookout Mountain overlooking Gadsden and the Coosa valley. The property also holds the ruins of an 1889 building, designed by architect Norrman, that housed the Bellevue Hotel, Jones Female College, and the Mineral Springs Hotel until it burned in 1912.
100008433.heading: Summary Paragraph

85002887.summary: Temple Beth-El, built in 1891, is a good local example of a vernacular Neo-Romanesque religious building with Byzantine influences, seen in the rounded lintels over its arched windows, circular moldings, an unusually high dome, and Eastern-style finials. The small brick, stucco, and wood temple at Quintard Avenue and Thirteenth Street houses Anniston's only Jewish congregation. Its square entrance tower has art-glass transoms, and a menorah facing Quintard Avenue was dedicated during Brotherhood Week in 1974.
85002887.heading: Statement of Significance

83002967.summary: The Gadsden Times-News Building, built in 1904, is significant for its twenty-four-year association with Gadsden's main newspaper and as one of the few early commercial buildings left in the city. Founded in 1867 by Confederate veterans Leonidas Grant and T. J. Cox as a Democratic paper opposed to Reconstruction, the Times became a major civic and business booster. In the early twentieth century it was the main source of news for the city and much of the county, and by 1926 it had one of the largest circulations of any daily outside the major cities.
83002967.heading: Statement of Significance

85002868.summary: The Henry Burt Glover House, built in 1906, is associated with Henry Burt Glover, county treasurer and a leader in Calhoun County government at the turn of the century, who built it a few years after the county seat moved from Jacksonville to Anniston. It represents the Leighton Avenue area developed by county officials after the move and is one of the few survivors of the house-building boom that followed Anniston's victory in the fight for the county seat. Architecturally, it is one of Anniston's best examples of the transition from asymmetrical Victorian styles to more symmetrical forms, pairing Victorian wall and roof treatments with a symmetrical facade.
85002868.heading: Statement of Significance

85002884.summary: Saint Paul's Methodist Episcopal Church, built in 1888-89, reflects the founders' view that Northerners were welcome in Anniston, both to help heal the wounds of the Civil War and to boost the productivity of the town's industry. It was built by the Methodist Episcopal Church, the northern branch of the denomination that had split over slavery before the war. It is one of three large Victorian Gothic sandstone churches built in Anniston's late-1880s boom under English master stonemason Simon Jewell. The congregation did not outlast its first generation, and by 1920 the First Christian congregation had acquired the building.
85002884.heading: Statement of Significance

91000594.summary: The Pines, built in 1896, is one of the oldest documented Colonial Revival houses in Alabama and reflects the shift in residential taste from Victorian styles to classicism. It keeps its original character and setting despite its deteriorated condition. It was built by Captain Edmund Leighton Tyler, a railroad man and son of General Daniel Tyler, co-founder of Anniston. Edmund Tyler fought beside his father at Bull Run, joined him and Samuel Noble on the original board of the Woodstock Iron Company in 1872, and in 1883 formed and managed the Anniston and Atlantic Railroad for the company.
91000594.heading: Statement of Significance

85002872.summary: The Kilby House, built in 1914, was the home of Thomas E. Kilby, the only Anniston resident ever to become governor of Alabama. He was lieutenant governor from 1914 to 1918 and governor from 1919 to 1923, when he pushed highway improvements, financial and prison reforms, the creation of the State Board of Education and the Child Welfare Department, and a stronger Public Service Commission. The large two-and-a-half-story brick house has perhaps the finest Georgian Revival facade left in Anniston, with symmetrical massing and elaborate moldings. It represents the building boom that ran from the turn of the century to World War I.
85002872.heading: Statement of Significance

85002877.summary: The Noble-McCaa-Butler House, built in Anniston's boom year of 1887, is closely associated with the family of founder Samuel Noble and is the only house in the city continuously occupied by Noble descendants. It is one of Anniston's best surviving examples of the eclectic Queen Anne style, with a clapboard first story and a second story of alternating fishscale and coursed shingles. It originally stood on a large tract between the estates of Samuel Noble and Daniel Tyler. Lowndes McCaa, husband of Noble's daughter, was brought from Mobile in 1883 by Duncan Parker to be cashier of the town's first bank.
85002877.heading: Statement of Significance

85002880.summary: Oak Tree Cottage, built in 1922, is one of the best examples in Anniston of the Craftsman-rooted Bungalow style popular across the country in the early twentieth century, with a broad low gable roof, central dormer, deep front porch, and exposed rafter ends. It was built by Frederick O. Tyler, then head of the Anniston Manufacturing Company, and his wife Christine. Their family is the only example of a marriage between Anniston's two founding families, the Tylers and the Nobles, and their descendants still live there. The house is named for one of the largest oak trees in town, which stands in its yard.
85002880.heading: Statement of Significance

75000307.summary: Crowan Cottage, built around 1886 for $6,307.14 for James and Jennifer Noble, parents of Anniston founder Samuel Noble, is one of the city's most important landmarks for its architecture, craftsmanship, and ties to Anniston's early history. With the nearby Noble-Roberts Cottage, it is a mature expression of the architecture of H. H. Richardson, and the two are the only known examples of the style in Alabama. Family tradition credits the design to Stanford White. James Noble, born in England, had been in the iron business in Georgia before the family founded the planned industrial city of Anniston.
75000307.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85002870.summary: Hillside Cemetery, the city's first cemetery, whose site the town council chose in 1876, illustrates the 'welfare capitalism' many nineteenth-century industrialists practiced. It was laid out for the workers of the Woodstock Iron Company by noted landscape architect N. F. Barrett, who helped design the company town of Pullman, Illinois. It reflects founders Samuel Noble and Daniel Tyler's view that their workers should be provided all the necessities of life, including burial. Its funerary art, including elaborate obelisks, statuary, pedestal urns, and crosses, contrasts with the traditional folk memorials common in Alabama at the time.
85002870.heading: Statement of Significance

85002864.summary: The Bagley-Cater Building, built in 1908, is a well-developed local example of early twentieth-century Neoclassical commercial architecture. The three-story brick building on Tenth Street has very ornate upper floors with Ionic pilasters, quoined end pavilions, and a breakfront entablature with swags, dentils, and egg-and-dart molding. Apart from larger plate glass in the street-level storefront, it is unaltered.
85002864.heading: Statement of Significance

76000316.summary: The Clay County Courthouse, completed in 1906 to plans by C. W. Carlton, who also designed the Cleburne County Courthouse, is one of the few surviving historic buildings in Ashland and Clay County. It is a good example of the Neoclassical Revival style with Italian Renaissance motifs, such as banded brickwork recalling the rusticated base of an Italian palazzo and a curving interior staircase. Ashland has been the county seat since soon after the county was created in 1866. The first courthouse burned in 1875 with all county records. The present building was the most imposing in the county when completed and still is.
76000316.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73000334.summary: The Hugo Black House, typical of late-1880s homes in rural eastern Alabama, was the boyhood home of Supreme Court Justice Hugo Black, described in the nomination as one of the most influential Justices ever to serve and one of the Court's finest legal authorities. Born in 1886 in the Harlan community of Clay County, Black moved to Ashland with his parents, William LaFayette and Martha Black, in 1889. He lived in this house from 1893 to 1903 and again in 1906-07. Though he kept other residences during his long career, he always considered this house his home, and he spent his formative years here.
73000334.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

86003661.summary: The Driskell-Martin House, built in 1850, is a very fine example of a mid-nineteenth-century Greek Revival house and Plantersville's oldest surviving high-style residence. It reflects the antebellum affluence of Alabama's Black Belt and of its owner, planter and merchant Thomas Sanford Driskell. The two-story frame house has a giant-order pedimented portico and a second-story balcony. As the finest residence in Plantersville, it was taken over as Federal headquarters in April 1865, when Union Major General Wilson occupied it as his cavalry fought from Ebenezer Church to Selma, which may have saved it from destruction.
86003661.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

16000834.summary: The John Clifford Grimsley House, built around 1916 according to family tradition, is an excellent example of high-style Neoclassical architecture and the only such residence in Fayette County. It was designed by architect John David Gullett (1873-1935) for Cliff Grimsley, a prominent businessman involved in successful Fayette enterprises in the first half of the twentieth century and a local philanthropist, as a house befitting his standing. The Neoclassical style was especially popular in the post-Reconstruction South, where its classical forms evoked an idealized antebellum past.
16000834.heading: Summary Paragraph

85000451.summary: The Robert Savidge Foster House at Sylvan Plantation, believed to have been built in the 1820s, was probably as advanced a house as could be found anywhere in the plantation region of west Alabama at the time. It is a rare example of pure Federal design in Alabama south of the Tennessee Valley. Its two-tiered Tuscan portico, diminishing window openings, and massive corbeled chimneys reflect the building traditions of the older seaboard South. Such superimposed porticos were popular around Tuscaloosa before the Greek Revival, but of several that stood into the 1920s only this one survives. It and the Elizabeth Savidge Foster House are the last of the Foster family homes on the large Sylvan cotton plantation.
85000451.heading: Statement of Significance

86003662.summary: The Antique Store, built around 1870, is the oldest surviving commercial building from Plantersville's nineteenth-century role as a small mercantile center serving the surrounding farm community, and it is still used as a store. It is a representative example of vernacular commercial buildings in rural Alabama towns, with a pedimented front gable, recessed porch, symmetrical three-bay facade, and board-and-batten siding. It keeps its original six-over-six windows and paneled double doors, though it has a turn-of-the-century wing and replacement porch columns.
86003662.heading: Statement of Significance

99000468.summary: The Snead Junior College Historic District documents the development of secondary and higher education in Boaz and Marshall County and how the town offered schooling to the white boys and girls of the remote, impoverished Sand Mountain area. Founded in the late 1890s as Boaz Seminary and later named the John H. Snead Seminary, the private Methodist-supported school worked within the state public education system and at times provided Boaz's only grammar, junior high, or high school education. It became a junior college in the mid-1930s, and the State of Alabama bought it for its junior college system in 1967. The district includes the Neoclassical Administration Building and buildings from 1920 to 1949.
99000468.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86003663.summary: The Doctor's Office, built around 1850, is a very fine and rare example of a small vernacular Greek Revival professional office, a type once common in south central Alabama but now rarely seen. It shows a conscious effort to bring high-style architecture to the workplace, and it reflects Plantersville's era as a service center for the surrounding countryside. Local historian Todd considered it the oldest building in Plantersville. The one-room frame building with a pedimented portico is basically unaltered apart from a metal roof, keeping its original flooring and wide pine paneling.
86003663.heading: Statement of Significance

86003664.summary: The Christian Church, built in 1898, is a good example of turn-of-the-century vernacular church architecture, with a gable-roofed main block, a two-story corner bell tower, and mottled stained-glass windows. It is Plantersville's only surviving nineteenth-century church and the only symbol left of religion's importance in the community's life. The 1898 parsonage is the town's best example of late nineteenth-century two-room vernacular housing, with a center chimney and double front entry.
86003664.heading: Statement of Significance

96000167.summary: The Thomas A. Snellgrove Homestead preserves every remaining building of the Snellgrove family homestead, built between 1900 and 1938, making it the earliest intact homestead in Boaz and the only surviving residential reminder of the Snellgrove family. The main house, built in 1900, is believed to be the oldest house in Boaz. It is a rare local example of the vernacular Greek Revival style common in the Georgia Piedmont in the mid-nineteenth century, with a two-tiered full-width porch and a largely intact interior. The district also includes a tenant house, garage, warehouse, and the Tomie Snellgrove Gaines House, now surrounded by outlet-mall development.
96000167.heading: Statement of Significance

86003665.summary: The Todd House (Todd-Briscoe House), built in 1867-68, is an excellent example of pattern-book Gothic Revival, or Carpenter Gothic, domestic architecture, a rare style scattered across Alabama. It reflects the house designs spread nationally by noted architects Richard Upjohn and A. J. Davis and shows how a national style reached remote rural areas. The two-story board-and-batten house has steep gables with ornamental bargeboards. Its original owner, Dr. Samuel G. Todd, was Plantersville's first dentist, and two upstairs bedrooms were reserved for travelers and one for visiting preachers.
86003665.heading: Statement of Significance

97001163.summary: The Edward Fenns Whitman House, built in 1924, is the finest example of Craftsman architecture in Boaz. It has a massive front-gabled roof, tile roofing, prominent porch piers, exposed rafters, and knee braces outside, and simple Craftsman living spaces with brick fireplaces and glazed tile inside. It represents the tail end of the Craftsman movement's height. It is also an example of the work of prominent Birmingham architect William Leslie Welton, one of Alabama's most significant Craftsman designers of the early twentieth century.
97001163.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

99000855.summary: Julia Street Memorial United Methodist Church, built in 1917, is the only church in Boaz and perhaps one of the best in Alabama built on the Akron Plan, popular with evangelical Methodists in Britain and the United States. The plan reflected the Progressive Era belief that churches should be multi-purpose, accessible, and geared toward social action. It has a narthex flanked by Sunday school rooms, a central pulpit, curved pews, and more classroom space in the balcony, rear, and basement. It is also a well-executed example of the Neoclassical Revival style and stands in one of Boaz's oldest neighborhoods.
99000855.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

95001020.summary: The Edward Rose House, built in 1898, is a good local example of a Queen Anne cottage and a landmark in Fayette, with a wraparound porch, a hexagonal tower with a bell-shaped roof, and patterned shingles. Though Fayette was founded in 1821, the house is one of the few buildings that predate the disastrous 1911 fire that destroyed much of downtown, and it was recently sensitively rehabilitated. Edward Rose, its owner for about fifty-five years, ran one of the area's leading mercantile houses and served as school trustee, postmaster, town councilman, and mayor from 1918 to 1920.
95001020.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

83002980.summary: The U.S. Post Office in Albertville, built in 1931, is a two-story brick building with a mansard-type roof and a portico that the nomination calls more attractive than those of most post offices of its era, built with excellent materials and workmanship. Because urban renewal had removed many of Albertville's older buildings, it was one of the few remaining structures still essentially as built. The nomination is brief and gives little further history.
83002980.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000320.summary: The Albertville Depot, also called the L & N Railroad Depot, was built in 1892, the year the Nashville, Chattanooga and St. Louis Railroad completed a long-sought rail link between the Tennessee and Coosa rivers and made its first official run from Guntersville to Gadsden with a stop in Albertville. The railroad gave the young town, incorporated in 1891, a tremendous economic boost; by 1897 it had two newspapers and at least 33 businesses. Two fires in 1905 and a tornado in 1908 left the depot as Albertville's only surviving business building from the 1890s. Its simple dignity stands out in an area of modern buildings.
75000320.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82001999.summary: The First Presbyterian Church of Jacksonville, begun in 1859 and completed in April 1865, is one of Alabama's earliest examples of the mid-nineteenth-century Romanesque Revival, with many features popularized by architect Samuel Sloan and possibly based on a plate in his 'Model Architect.' Strong similarities to Kahl Montgomery (1862) and churches in Oxford and Talladega suggest that Sloan's partner John S. Stewart may have provided plans for all of them. The church is also notable for its unusual segmental vaulted ceiling and locally crafted woodwork, said to have been carved largely by elder Gilliam Southers, with pews made by enslaved workers under cabinetmaker John H. Crawford. The congregation was organized in 1834.
82001999.heading: Statement of Significance

97001168.summary: The Charles B. Henry Barn, built around 1915, is an excellent example of a Progressive Era dairy barn and is notable for being built of concrete. With its milk house and silos, the complex embodied the latest Progressive agricultural ideals, such as those set out in U.S. Department of Agriculture farmers' bulletins, in its layout, building design, equipment, and materials. It is one of the best and most intact such dairy complexes identified in Alabama. All of its parts keep a high degree of integrity and help explain early twentieth-century dairy farming in the state.
97001168.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

01001298.summary: Ten Oaks, completed around 1856, is an outstanding example of the Italian villa style as built in mid-nineteenth-century Alabama, part of the Picturesque movement away from plain Federal lines toward romantic, ornamented designs. James Madison Crook, one of many who came to Jacksonville while it was the county seat, hired builder Elbert Green Morris to construct the sixteen-room Italianate house. It was the largest house in the area when finished and stands as a vivid image of the romantic strain in American thought before the Civil War. A well house is its only surviving original outbuilding.
01001298.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

90002109.summary: The A. J. and Emma E. Thomas Coley House, built in 1895 as the home and occasional office of a prominent local physician and his wife, is a representative, relatively unaltered late example of the Queen Anne style in Alexander City. It shows the style's typical irregular massing, steep hip roof with lower cross gables, wraparound veranda, and classically inspired ornament. It also shows how Alabama builders applied the mass-produced Queen Anne style, spread by pattern books and catalogs, to a traditional central-hall plan.
90002109.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

95001023.summary: The Reuben Herzfeld House, built in 1890-95 and believed to have been designed by an Auburn architect, is a three-story frame house in the Free Classical Queen Anne style, set unusually high on a hill on Hillabee Street in Alexander City. It retains a high degree of integrity, and it stayed in the Herzfeld family until 1993. Reuben Herzfeld was a prominent citizen who helped organize the town's first cotton mill and founded and led its first bank. He also served as president of the Bank of West Point and chairman of the Swift Manufacturing Company of Columbus, Georgia.
95001023.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84000659.summary: The Saratoga Victory Mill (Guntersville Mill), begun in 1928 by Saratoga Victory Mills of New York to make cotton linings, represents the 1920s movement of northern textile mills to the South. That shift was driven by postwar profits, rising demands from northern workers, and declining southern agriculture, which created a large pool of low-wage labor. The mill illustrates every part of the pattern: a rural small-town site, company housing, no unions, very low wages and long hours, and northern ownership. It is also architecturally significant for the typical features of 1920s southern mills: a rectangular multistory brick building with daylight walls, a roof monitor, and timber framing.
84000659.heading: Statement of Significance

70000100.summary: The Dr. J. C. Francis Office, built in the early 1850s, is a typical doctor's office of the period and the only remaining building of its type in northeast Alabama. The small frame building has a fanlit entrance, pilasters, and a pediment on fluted columns. Dr. Francis, who interned with the Army Engineers in 1832, moved to Jacksonville in 1837, soon after the Cherokee lands were ceded, and practiced medicine there for more than fifty years, running an apothecary in the same building. The office was moved from the Court Square back to the Francis family property and was being restored by the Alabama Historical Commission.
70000100.heading: Statement of Significance

87001651.summary: The Alexander Woods House (Woods-Crook-Tredaway House), built around 1853 by contractors John Hubbard and Elbert Morris, is a fine local example of a Greek Revival house with transitional Italianate detailing. It is associated with Judge Alexander Woods, a probate judge and early government leader during Jacksonville's years as county seat (1833-1899), and it is the only surviving house associated with him. It is one of several surviving Jacksonville homes of the county's early political leaders. Woods sold the house to Samuel W. Crook in 1866.
87001651.heading: Statement of Significance

05000842.summary: The Company E, 167th Infantry, Alabama National Guard Armory in Guntersville was built in the 1930s by the Works Progress Administration. It is significant both as a WPA project and for its architecture, and it is an intact WPA armory that is unique in Alabama for its use of materials native to the northeast part of the state, including limestone walls and a striking limestone fireplace. Few armories existed in Alabama before the 1930s, and its form follows a statewide prototype, Earl G. Lutz's 1935 Dixie Bibb Graves Armory in Montgomery.
05000842.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

03001135.summary: The Guntersville City School, built in 1926 in the Craftsman style, reflects Progressive Era school philosophy and design and may be the most intact and highly developed example of a Progressive Era public school in Alabama. Reformers of the 1910s and 1920s set detailed standards for site orientation, classroom size, lighting, and materials to create ideal learning environments, and the school's form, spaces, and features show those ideals. It is also notable for its stone construction using materials native to northeast Alabama, and it keeps original transomed doors, hopper windows, and built-in blackboards.
03001135.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

74000434.summary: The Old Jail in Gordo was completed on June 9, 1914, at a total cost of $1,169.79 to serve as both the town jail and the mayor's office, during the term of Mayor Ben Garrison. It served as jail and town hall until about 1930, when the town office moved to Main Street, and as a jail until 1955. It later housed a youth center, a draft board, and other community services. The plain two-story brick building's only ornament is its arched window heads, and residents long used the 'Old Jail' as a landmark when giving directions.
74000434.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

10000558.summary: The Guntersville Post Office Building, built in 1940-41, is an excellent example of a restrained Colonial Revival New Deal-era post office. It was designed under the direction of Louis A. Simon, Supervising Architect of the Treasury, whose office designed federal buildings during the Depression. Simon broke from the more elaborate federal designs of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries in favor of simpler, restrained buildings. Alterations have been minimal and mostly limited to interior partitions and dropped ceilings.
10000558.heading: Summary Paragraph

89000291.summary: The Albert G. Henry Jr. House, built around 1895 for a wealthy Guntersville merchant, is a fine example of Queen Anne architecture in Guntersville. It has a large wraparound porch, a tower room, spindle work, and steep intersecting gables over a rambling plan. Though in poor condition at nomination, its coved plaster cornice, ornate mantels, heavy door and window casings, and beadboard wainscoting show it was once a Victorian showplace. It stands across the street from the Henry-Jordan House, built by Albert's brother Pat Henry.
89000291.heading: Statement of Significance

79003351.summary: The Henry-Jordan House, built between 1875 and 1877 for Pat Henry, is one of the oldest buildings in Guntersville, an early Tennessee River town almost entirely destroyed in the Civil War, and is associated with two of the county's most prominent families. Its traditional central-hall plan with a rear ell and its use of older construction methods reflect stylistic conservatism and the economic and technological limits of the postwar period. Pat Henry, born near Guntersville in 1835 and educated at Cumberland Law School, was the son of one of the county's most successful merchants, who had married a daughter of the town's founder. The Jordan family, one of the county's oldest, owned the house until 1974.
79003351.heading: Statement of Significance

72000177.summary: The Somerville Courthouse, built in 1837, is the oldest standing courthouse in Alabama and one of the state's outstanding landmarks. Its Federal style follows Virginia buildings of the late 1700s and early 1800s, a type rare in Alabama. Somerville became the seat of Cotaco County, created in 1818 and renamed Morgan County in 1821, and the legislature levied special taxes in 1836 to replace the first courthouse. After several failed attempts, the county seat moved to the growing river town of Decatur in 1891, and the records were taken from Somerville at night under armed guard. The building later served as a school and as a meeting place for the town council.
72000177.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

10000523.summary: The Bryand Brand House, built around 1845 and moved in 1978 to save it, represents a distinctive type of upper-end antebellum planter house in cotton-rich Perry County: a two-story, five-bay main block with a projecting central four-column portico. It is one of two such plantation houses left in the county and the only one two rooms deep. Though modified and enlarged in recent decades, it keeps novel adaptations of style to function, including a wide central hall treated almost like a dogtrot for Alabama's long, hot summers. Its interior door surrounds appear to be inspired by Asher Benjamin's 'The Practical House Carpenter' (1830).
10000523.heading: Summary Paragraph

09000607.summary: The building housing Feldman's Department Store, built in 1911 for John Dodd, is a locally significant example of an early twentieth-century department store in Haleyville. It reflects a common pattern in small Alabama towns: railroads reached isolated areas rich in resources, in Winston County's case timber and coal, and the newcomers who came to exploit them needed merchants and professionals. The Feldman family bought the building in 1914, ran their department store on the first floor while renting out the second-floor offices, and operated it until the late twentieth century.
09000607.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

73000346.summary: Tanglewood, built in 1859 by Page Harris as his permanent home, represents the smaller plantation houses of its period and area, which have survived in Alabama far less often than the large plantation homes. Harris and his family homesteaded the land after a year in Tennessee and prospered, adding neighboring land to the plantation. The house passed to his daughter Louincy Harris Bishop and then to her three children. One of them, J. Nicholene Bishop (born 1863), was a noted educator, author of 'Our Settlement' and 'Roadside Flowers,' and the first woman to receive a Bachelor of Science from the University of Nashville.
73000346.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96000111.summary: The Perry County Jail, a two-story brick Colonial Revival building from about 1910, contributes to the Marion Courthouse Square Historic District. It stands on the site where Michael Muckle built the cabin that began the town once called Muckle's Ridge, later renamed Marion. The district is significant for its architecture, education, commerce, government, and social history. It includes the c. 1855 Greek Revival Perry County Courthouse, the historic business district, and the Marion Female Seminary, one of the region's earliest institutions of higher education for women.
96000111.heading: Statement of Significance

73000372.summary: Marion Female Seminary is one of the oldest educational landmarks in West Alabama. Marion residents founded it in 1836 as a nondenominational academy for girls through a joint stock company. When the first building, completed in 1837, was declared unsafe in 1850, the present building replaced it in 1852. The school is also notable as the place where Nicola Marschall, an art instructor at the Seminary in 1861, is credited with designing the first flag of the Confederacy and the Confederate uniforms.
73000372.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82001615.summary: Siloam Baptist Church, built in 1848-49, housed Alabama's most influential Baptist congregation of the mid-nineteenth century, in Marion, then described as 'the strongest denominational center in Alabama and one of the strongest in the South.' The Alabama Baptist Convention met there often, and its secretary had offices in the church from the 1840s until the Convention moved to Montgomery in 1892. From 1845 to 1882 the Home Mission Board of the Southern Baptist Convention was based in Marion, with offices in the church. The building is the third used by the congregation, which was founded in 1822.
82001615.heading: Statement of Significance

79000401.summary: The President's House at Marion Military Institute, built in 1912, dates from one of the school's major growth periods, when its military training program gained national recognition. It is a typical example of the Neoclassical Revival style popular in the early twentieth century. Together with the Classical Revival Chapel and Lovelace Hall, it set a precedent for keeping the classical character of the original campus buildings. Apart from added closets, an enclosed back porch, and central heating, it remains in its original condition.
79000401.heading: Statement of Significance

82001614.summary: The First Congregational Church of Marion, built in 1871 by the skills and labor of its members, is significant mainly for its close ties to Lincoln Normal School, an important Black educational institution for much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It is the only surviving nineteenth-century building tied to the efforts of Marion's Black community and the American Missionary Association to provide academic education to Black citizens, and it shows the role of Black churches in higher education after the Civil War. Freedmen founded the Lincoln School in 1867, and the church was organized in 1870. It is the only Reconstruction-era Black church in Marion without major changes.
82001614.heading: Statement of Significance

78000508.summary: The Chapel and Lovelace Hall at Marion Military Institute are two of West Alabama's most noted antebellum educational landmarks and the last surviving buildings of the 1854-58 Howard College campus. They show the quadrangle plan and Classical style popular on nineteenth-century campuses. Howard College, founded in Marion in 1841 by the Alabama Baptist Convention, helped make the Black Belt town one of the state's leading educational centers. Lovelace Hall (1854) is the oldest building on campus. The Chapel was built in 1857 to a plan by faculty member Dr. Noah K. Davis. When Howard College moved away, its longtime president James Thomas Murfee stayed to become the first president of Marion Military Institute.
78000508.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88003243.summary: The Phillips Memorial Auditorium, built in 1937-38, is the last remaining building of Lincoln Normal School in Marion. Founded in 1867, the school was the last normal school established by the American Missionary Association, which founded schools across the South to give Black students a liberal academic education beyond industrial and vocational training. The AMA oversaw the school for 76 years, though local contributions provided most of its funding. The auditorium was the school's last large project before it became part of the Perry County public school system in 1943, and it is a good local example of the Classical Revival style.
88003243.heading: Statement of Significance

01001296.summary: The Mount Sinai School, built in 1919 north of Prattville, is significant as a school funded by the Julius Rosenwald School Building Fund, the most important philanthropic force aiding African American education in the first half of the twentieth century. From 1913 to 1937 the fund helped build some 5,358 school buildings for Black students in fifteen southern states, so that more Black children attended school longer, with better-trained teachers and better buildings. The frame T-shaped school follows a plan by Tuskegee architect W. A. Hazel, oriented to take advantage of natural light. It is among the last surviving of Autauga County's six original Rosenwald schools.
01001296.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

76000317.summary: The Cleburne County Courthouse, built in Heflin in 1907, is an excellent example of Neoclassical architecture and the center of political life in this mostly rural, agricultural county. In 1905 residents of Heflin and the lower county petitioned Governor William Jelks for an election to move the county seat from Edwardsville, and Heflin won by 88 votes. The Edwardsville faction challenged the law and sought a recount without success, and the courthouse was built while some court orders were still pending. Its central pavilion has a triple-arched base supporting a temple front with Ionic columns and a shallow pediment.
76000317.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

93000762.summary: The John Morgan House, built around 1880 and expanded around 1900 and 1930, is one of the oldest surviving homes in Heflin and a good, intact example of a typical late nineteenth-century Victorian residence. It was the home of John Morgan, elected Heflin's first mayor in January 1893 after the town was incorporated in 1892. The house grew from a two-room central-hall plan into a sixteen-room house with pedimented gables and patterned shingles. Later family members included Esther Elizabeth Morgan, the first music teacher in Cleburne County, and Lucile Morgan, who founded the county's first library.
93000762.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100002763.summary: Cleburne County High School, built in 1936 with help from a Public Works Administration grant, represents the federal government's efforts to restore the nation's economic and social life after the Great Depression. The PWA sought to modernize education by replacing scattered, often pre-1900 one-room schools with consolidated schools offering better conditions and education beyond the elementary grades. As the county's largest town and railroad business center, Heflin got the consolidated school, which was the county's only combined junior and senior high school until Ranburne High School opened in 1941. The one-and-a-half-story brick building shows the restrained, modernized interpretation of popular styles typical of federally funded projects that employed local architects and builders.
100002763.heading: Summary Paragraph

100012394.summary: The Dr. Robert Price Irwin House, a two-and-a-half-story Free Classic Queen Anne house built in 1907 with Colonial Revival porticos, is significant as an important example of a rural home health clinic in the small town of Moulton. Physician Robert Price Irwin moved there in 1919 and saw patients in the house, first informally and later full time, until his death in 1967, making it a key part of Moulton's early healthcare network. Dr. Irwin also co-founded the Irwin-Dyar Clinic, Lawrence County's first hospital, and helped secure funding for the present Lawrence Medical Center.
100012394.heading: Summary Paragraph

00000712.summary: The Ice House in Moulton, a concrete-block building with an associated house, built just after World War II, represents Moulton's postwar boom. Fueled by a revived cotton economy and wartime savings, the town saw one of its busiest building periods, with about thirty-two commercial buildings erected on and near the courthouse square between 1945 and 1950. The Ice House made crushed and block ice for restaurants, cafes, entertainment venues, and other businesses, as well as residents of Moulton and the surrounding area.
00000712.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

98001026.summary: The Moulton Courthouse Square Historic District is significant for its collection of early to mid-twentieth-century commercial buildings dating from about 1911 to 1948. It is unusual among Alabama county-seat squares because most of its buildings date from the 1930s and 1940s, so despite the town's nineteenth-century origins the square reflects its twentieth-century history. Its buildings show the influence of the New Deal, the county's slow recovery from the Depression, and the postwar consumer boom. Landmarks include the 1936 Classical Moderne courthouse, the 1926 Gibson Building, and the 1947 Star Theatre.
98001026.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100006665.summary: Magnolia Hall, built in 1857 just outside downtown Greensboro, is an exceptional example of Greek Revival domestic architecture in the rare amphiprostyle form, with porticos at both front and rear, and is recognized as nationally significant. Its form is unusually pure, and the original contract between its New England builder, Benjamin F. Parsons, and owner David McCrary survives. Parsons built a number of significant buildings in the region, but only a few remain. The two-story house has a cast-iron balcony over the front door.
100006665.heading: Summary Paragraph

97000651.summary: The Lassiter House (Lassiter Homeplace), built around 1825 in the Mulberry community near old Statesville, is a good and particularly intact example of an I-house with front and rear shed extensions, a distinctive southern variant of the I-house. The type came to Alabama with migrants from the South Atlantic states, especially the Carolinas and Georgia, and few examples survive this far south. Local tradition says it was built in 1821 by Dr. William Smith or by merchant Major Thomas Stone. Records show Stone sold the 1,074-acre property to Jeremiah and Nancy Lassiter in 1846. The farm keeps five outbuildings.
97000651.heading: Statement of Significance

94000690.summary: The Payne House, historically Atkins' Ridge, built around 1840 by John Atkins and his wife, is a significant example of an early Canebrake plantation house and one of the last raised cottages in the region. It shows the styles, forms, construction methods, and craftsmanship used by Canebrake residents and keeps a high degree of integrity. John Atkins owned about 480 acres, and the house stood at the northeast edge of the plantation.
94000690.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

80000686.summary: The McGehee-Stringfellow House, built for Abraham McGehee between 1824 and 1831, is an outstanding example of early nineteenth-century brick construction in an area where rural builders overwhelmingly preferred wood. Though built in the Federal period, it carries archaic late eighteenth-century Georgian forms to frontier Alabama, reflecting the conservatism of the rural South and the cultural lag between the seaboard and the new western lands. The McGehee family came from Prince Edward County, Virginia, and Micajah McGehee reportedly built the first substantial house in the Broad River area.
80000686.heading: Statement of Significance

76000323.summary: Valley Creek Presbyterian Church, built in 1857-58 for $15,000, is unequaled in Dallas County as a simple, elegant example of Greek Revival architecture and is noted for its unusual curving staircases. Its congregation is one of the oldest Presbyterian churches in Alabama, organized by eight Scotch-Irish families who came from Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, around 1816, and it hosted the second annual meeting of the Synod of Alabama in 1836. Its architect and builder are unknown because Wilson's Raiders burned the manse and church records in the Civil War. It is the mother church of Presbyterianism in northern Dallas County and helped found four churches near Selma.
76000323.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78000488.summary: The John Erwin House, called Glencairn, begun in the mid-1830s and completed in 1837, is one of the finer antebellum homes in Hale County, noted for its especially fine front-entrance woodwork. It reflects the growing popularity of Greek Revival in Alabama's Black Belt, and family tradition says Erwin hired Philadelphia craftsmen for the portico and interior ceilings. Erwin, a Virginia native who opened a law office in Greensboro around 1820, became one of the town's wealthiest men, owning extensive land and enslaved people. He served as president of the state Senate and later as Speaker of the state House. The house has stayed in the Erwin family with few alterations.
78000488.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

10000258.summary: The Warden's Residence near Triana, built with a stone outbuilding as part of the Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge, became in 1950 Madison County's only public health clinic for rural African Americans during the post-World War II segregation era. Dr. Harold Fanning Drake and nurse Johnnie LouJean Dent, both African Americans from Alabama, provided obstetric, gynecological, and pediatric care there, illustrating the work of Black public health workers across the mid-twentieth-century South. The house and stone shed are also locally important for their architecture, and the stone building later served as Triana's city hall beginning in 1967.
10000258.heading: Summary Paragraph

82002010.summary: Marshall's Grove, built in 1840-42 by Dr. Hugh Marshall, is a good example of the early plantation houses of Dallas County. Its Federal styling, largely unaltered design, and continuous ties to the original owner's descendants make it an important county landmark, and much of the original furniture is still in use. Marshall, a Charleston-born physician and planter, came to Alabama by 1830 and built on high ground because his plantation near the Beech Creek swamp was thought unhealthy. The first section was built of logs floated down from Wetumpka and hand-hewn on site, and a great-granddaughter later restored the house.
82002010.heading: Statement of Significance

82002012.summary: Robinson Springs United Methodist Church, built in the late 1840s, is one of Alabama's most noted rural churches and a fine local interpretation of the Greek Revival style. The temple-form frame church, with two columns set between end walls, resembles Town and Davis's West Presbyterian Church in New York (1831), though its local model was more likely Dakin and Gallier's Government Street Presbyterian Church in Mobile (1836-37). It was the center of nineteenth-century Methodist worship for the small communities of Rocky Mount, Millbrook, Coosada, Elmore, Deatsville, Robinson Springs, and others. The congregation dates to about 1828-30, and its first church was built of logs.
82002012.heading: Statement of Significance

74000404.summary: Shoal Creek Baptist Church, built between 1885 and 1890, is one of the few hand-split, hand-hewn pine log church buildings left in Alabama. As one of only two community buildings in the area, it also served as a public school and meeting place and played a central role in the social, educational, and religious life of this rural area. Most of the community helped build it, with local men notching the corners. In summers between harvest and cotton picking it hosted a singing school where young people got their formal music lessons. An earlier building from about 1845 burned around 1935.
74000404.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92001089.summary: The Butlers' Store in New Hope, built in 1909 by James Edward Butler, with a connected building added in 1939, is a good and intact example of early twentieth-century commercial architecture in rural Alabama. Its brick buildings have corbelling and a facade with cast-iron columns made by G. L. Mesker and Co. of Evansville, Indiana. The main building served as a general merchandise, hardware, and dry goods store, and the north building housed a bank. Inside it keeps an 18-foot ceiling with a mezzanine, a rope-hung freight elevator, rolling ladders, and most of its dry-goods shelving. The Butler family had been in business in Madison County since the 1850s.
92001089.heading: Statement of Significance

99000150.summary: The Bell House, built in 1893 for merchant Joseph Bennett Bell, son-in-law of prominent industrialist Merrill Pratt, is an outstanding example of the Queen Anne style and the most intact, high-style Queen Anne house left in Prattville. Its design is attributed to prominent architect Frank Lockwood (1869-1936). The two-and-a-half-story frame house has a round shingled tower with a conical roof and its original copper finial, a wraparound porch, and a gabled entry on paired Ionic columns. Its interior shows high craftsmanship and eclectic sophistication.
99000150.heading: Statement of Significance

79000384.summary: Riverdale, built around 1829 as the plantation home of Virgil H. Gardner, is the most elegant and refined house of its period in Dallas County and perhaps in the entire Alabama Black Belt. It is one of the few early Alabama houses to keep its original graining and finishes. Gardner, who was schooled in Vermont, built the house on his father's 7,000-acre tract on the Alabama River after his father's death and his marriage to Margaret Louise Aylette. It was the scene of one of the county's most lavish celebrations, the 1854 wedding of Mary Gardner to Henry Quitman, son of the governor of Mississippi.
79000384.heading: Statement of Significance

86000914.summary: The Cotaco Opera House, built in 1890, is associated with Decatur's late nineteenth-century boom, sparked by the arrival of two important railroad lines in 1886. It is the only surviving building from that period designed to strengthen the city's economy by giving its growing population a social and entertainment center, and it was Decatur's only such center. It housed shops on the ground floor and became a Masonic Hall in the 1920s, remaining the city's main venue for meetings, dances, and receptions. Although the interior has been heavily altered, the exterior is one of Decatur's best late nineteenth-century facades.
86000914.heading: Statement of Significance

95000810.summary: The Princess Theater, part of the New Decatur/Albany Historic District, was built in 1887 as the opulent stables of the Casa Grande Hotel.
