It became a vaudeville theater in 1921 and later a 960-seat movie house. Its 1941 Art Deco renovation, with an intact glass facade and a marquee the nomination calls a masterpiece of glass and neon, is a highlight of the district. The district preserves the commercial core of New Decatur, a planned new town laid out in 1887 by the Decatur Land Improvement and Furnace Company under Major E. C. Gordon. Its planners laid out broad streets named for both Union and Confederate generals to appeal to Northerners and Southerners alike.
95000810.heading: Statement of Significance

99000148.summary: This boundary increase added one building to the New Decatur-Albany Historic District: the Decatur Light, Power, and Fuel Company Building, which shares the development history of the rest of the district. The expansion followed a 1998 survey requested by the owner, the City of Decatur, as part of a grant project with the Alabama Historical Commission to restore the building and return it to use. The building keeps most of its original architectural integrity. The district preserves the commercial center of New Decatur, a planned town laid out in 1887.
99000148.heading: Explanation of Expansion

73000342.summary: The Alabama State Penitentiary in Wetumpka, built in 1840-41, was the first brick state prison in Alabama's history and one of the older surviving prison landmarks in the Lower South. A law of 1839 called for a penitentiary within fifty miles of the center of the state and appropriated $30,000 for land and buildings. The cornerstone was laid on March 14, 1840, builder W. H. Thomas constructed the buildings, and the keys were handed to the State Prison Commissioners on October 27, 1841. The buildings were unusually attractive and, but for the barred windows, could have been mistaken for any other public building.
73000342.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000324.summary: The First Presbyterian Church of Wetumpka, built in 1856, was listed in 1976 as a fine local builder's interpretation of the Gothic Revival style, a board-and-batten church with Greek Revival interior elements. It was a center of community gatherings, the Wetumpka Light Guard departed from its grounds for Confederate service in 1861, and future senator John H. Bankhead was married there. Its distinctive triangular battens were later removed and the exterior covered with aluminum siding. In 1996 the Alabama State Review Board voted to recommend removing it from the National Register for loss of architectural integrity.
76000324.heading: Statement of Significance

06001101.summary: The First Baptist Church of Wetumpka, on West Bridge Street near the Coosa River, is significant for its Neoclassical and Eastlake architecture and the integrity of its original church, begun in 1846 and completed in 1852, which was substantially remodeled in 1909 by architect Frank Lockwood. It also includes a 1929 educational building. Later additions from 1959-60, 1967, and 1991 greatly enlarged the complex but connect only at the rear and use matching materials, so they do not overwhelm the older buildings. The original church is now known as the historic chapel.
06001101.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

73000343.summary: The First United Methodist Church of Wetumpka, completed in 1854, is architecturally unique for its period, with a heavily pilastered Greek Revival exterior that suggests Italianate influence. The original two-story building had the sanctuary on the second floor and a fellowship hall below. The congregation was organized in 1837 and used two earlier buildings. Following early Methodist custom, men and women sat on opposite sides, and a place was set aside in the sanctuary for enslaved people in the early years.
73000343.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000312.summary: The Wetumpka L & N Depot, built in 1906, is typical of the turn-of-the-century depots the Louisville and Nashville Railroad built in smaller towns, a small one-story frame building on the T-shaped plan the line used widely. Built during a financial panic, it helped stimulate the town's growth after a long decline. Settled in 1820 at the head of navigation on the Alabama River system, Wetumpka had grown to 3,000 or more by the 1840s and competed to become the state capital. After Montgomery won in 1846 it declined to fewer than 200 people by 1870. The L & N line connecting Montgomery and Decatur reached the town in 1872.
75000312.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

94000441.summary: The Pickens County Courthouse in Carrollton, an Italianate brick building constructed in 1877 by builder F. M. Rousseau, is significant for its architecture and as the center of county government and civic life. Carrollton became the county seat on 80 acres granted by the federal government in 1831. The first courthouse, built in 1840, was burned by Union troops under General John T. Croxton in April 1865. Its 1872 replacement burned on November 16, 1876, during a time of great tension when federal troops were stationed in Carrollton to oversee elections. The present courthouse was built on the old foundation and its interior remains much as built, apart from a 1949 restoration.
94000441.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84000599.summary: The Southern Railway Depot at Piedmont, built in 1868 for the Selma, Rome and Dalton Railroad, is an excellent example of a small mid-nineteenth-century board-and-batten train station, with Italianate influences in its bracketed cornice and segmental-arched windows. The railroad, whose final link between Jacksonville, Alabama, and Dalton, Georgia, was completed in 1870, brought modern transportation and new prosperity to the small community of Cross Plains, later renamed Piedmont. New businesses and homes sprang up around the depot, which became the center of the growing town and for many years its main link to distant places.
84000599.heading: Statement of Significance

89000292.summary: The Hugh Wilson Hill House, built around 1835, is a fine local example of a common vernacular house type, the hipped-roof central-hall cottage with an interior chimney, with pattern-book Greek Revival details. This type appeared across Alabama from the mid-1830s to 1870, especially in the southern half of the state. It stands on a lot in the original plat of Carrollton, laid out as the county seat, and was one of the first houses built on the town's planned streets. It is one of two Greek Revival cottages in town, keeping its original sash, doors, pilasters, portico, and mantels. Dr. Hugh Wilson Hill, the third generation of a family of Carrollton doctors, was the first Hill to live there.
89000292.heading: Statement of Significance

80004470.summary: The Southern Railway Depot in Decatur, built in the early twentieth century, is associated with the development of Alabama's railroads. It succeeded the first depot at the terminus of Alabama's first railroad, the Tuscumbia, Courtland and Decatur, which reached Decatur in 1834, bypassing the Muscle Shoals and giving Tennessee Valley cotton planters a clear route to New Orleans markets. Southern Railway built the station as part of a series of new depots shortly after becoming one of Alabama's two principal railroad systems. There is some indication it was designed by noted southern architect Frank Milburn, possibly his only depot in Alabama.
80004470.heading: Statement of Significance

99000884.summary: This boundary increase added one building to the East Wetumpka Commercial Historic District: the former post office at 206 South East Main Street, used from 1937 to 1988. It was designed by the Office of the Supervising Architect of the Treasury, and the construction contract was awarded to Upchurch Construction Company of Montgomery in December 1936 for $55,286. The City of Wetumpka bought the building and requested the listing, planning to restore its wood sash windows and find a suitable new use. The building fully keeps its original integrity.
99000884.heading: Statement of Significance

80000732.summary: The Col. Francis Dancy House (Dancy-Polk House), built in 1829 for Colonel Francis Dancy, an early and wealthy settler, is the oldest remaining building in Decatur and one of two early homes in the town to survive the Civil War. It represents the earlier and finer houses of North Alabama and reflects the South Carolina Georgian architecture brought into the Tennessee Valley. Enough detailed evidence survives for an almost exact restoration.
80000732.heading: Statement of Significance

72000176.summary: The State Bank Building in Decatur is a two-story brick Greek Revival building with Federal ornament, built for the Tennessee Valley branch of the State Bank, which Decatur won over Courtland, Huntsville, Florence, and Tuscumbia in 1832. The branch thrived during the land and credit boom of the 1830s. After the bank became a political issue, Governor Benjamin Fitzpatrick's reforms led to the liquidation of the Decatur branch from 1843 and the expiration of the State Bank charter in 1845. The building later became a residence, a Civil War hospital and site of skirmishes, and from 1881 to 1902 the First National Bank of Decatur, before passing to the American Legion.
72000176.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000165.summary: Mooresville, incorporated in November 1818, is one of the older incorporated towns in Alabama and the only village in North Alabama that keeps a majority of antebellum buildings, little changed since the mid-1850s. Settlers on the Old Winchester Road were drawn by its spring and high ground away from the swamps, and the town became an important stop on Tennessee Valley travel routes, with a popular stagecoach tavern. In the late 1820s or early 1830s future president Andrew Johnson spent several weeks there learning refinements of tailoring from Joseph Sloss. Thomas Bibb, Alabama's second governor, also lived there.
72000165.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000715.summary: The Rhea-McEntire House, built in 1836 by prominent merchant John S. Rhea, preserves one of the more significant Federal-period interiors in northern Alabama, with door surrounds of unusual richness and variety. One of them, an Adamesque Ionic architrave with strapwork, may be unique in the state. As one of three buildings that survived the Civil War destruction of Decatur, it is a major link to the town's earliest development, and its quality represents the highest architectural achievement of an area still near the frontier in the 1830s. Known in Civil War records as 'the Burleson house,' it served more than once as a command post.
84000715.heading: Statement of Significance

100007813.summary: Northern Heights Presbyterian Church, whose central section was built in 1943 as Northside Baptist Church, is significant for its role in Selma's African American Civil Rights Movement after the March 1965 voting rights protests. Under its pastor, Reverend Ernest G. Bradford, the church hosted a Southern Christian Leadership Conference citizenship school in 1965-66 and meetings in the local Black community's campaign for an equal voice in federal anti-poverty funds. Bradford was a leader of Self-Help Against Poverty for Everyone (SHAPE), which fought for rural and working-class Black residents' role in anti-poverty programs and supported Black candidates for office.
100007813.heading: Summary Paragraph

13000469.summary: Tabernacle Baptist Church, built in 1922, is nationally significant for its many associations with the Civil Rights Movement in Selma from 1922 to 1968, serving as both a strategy center and a conflict center. It is also significant statewide for African American Baptist history through the ministry of Rev. D. V. Jemison, who led the expansion of the Black Baptist church until 1954, and locally as an African American community landmark. Designed by African American architect and congregation member David T. West, it is the most imposing Classical Revival building of any Black institution in Jim Crow-era Selma.
13000469.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

80000733.summary: Forest Home is Morgan County's best remaining example of mid-nineteenth-century plantation architecture, in an area where most significant rural buildings have been lost. Its one-room-deep, two-story gabled main block with end chimneys and a one-story ell reflects a house type once common on the larger local landholdings. It is the lone survivor of that type and one of only three antebellum plantation houses left in the county. It has the county's most notable Greek Revival interior. It is also associated with Absalom L. Davis, a leader of the Grange Movement, who received the land in 1856 with his wife Ann from her mother, Mary Fennel of neighboring Walnut Grove.
80000733.heading: Statement of Significance

85002804.summary: The Propulsion and Structural Test Facility, built by the U.S. Army in 1957 at Redstone Arsenal, is one of the oldest rocket motor test facilities at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center. It was built to test the Redstone and other rockets of the Army Ballistic Missile Agency and passed to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, which under Dr. Wernher von Braun developed the Saturn family of launch vehicles in the 1960s. The stand supported testing of the Redstone, Saturn components, and the F-1 engine used in the Apollo program. It was later modified for static tests of the Space Shuttle's solid rocket boosters.
85002804.heading: Statement of Significance

13001033.summary: The Sullivan and Richie Jean Jackson House, built in 1906 by educator Dr. Richard B. Hudson as a wedding present for his daughter, was a strategy center for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference during the Selma Civil Rights Movement. In early 1965, after the shooting death of Jimmie Lee Jackson, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Rev. Ralph Abernathy, and SCLC staff met there repeatedly to plan the march from Selma to Montgomery. The most significant meeting may have been with Assistant Attorney General John Doar on March 9, 1965, two days after Bloody Sunday, which led to 'Turnaround Tuesday.' The house has long been associated with Selma's Black professionals and has been home to three African American dentists and their families.
13001033.heading: Statement of Significance

11000428.summary: The Wadley Railroad Depot, built in 1907 by the Atlanta, Birmingham, and Atlantic Railroad, served the new town of Wadley, planned as a model industrial community by the Callaway Development Company of LaGrange, Georgia. The company abandoned its plans in 1910 and the town's hoped-for growth never came, but Wadley became a small regional trade center. The depot was central to the community's economic and social life as its main train station until it closed around 1964. It is also architecturally significant at the state level.
11000428.heading: Summary Paragraph

100007801.summary: The Burwell-Dinkins-Anderson House in Selma, first built around 1889 and later rebuilt as a two-story Craftsman-style house, is associated with some of the most important leaders of Selma's African American community from the late nineteenth century through the Civil Rights Movement. It was the home of Dr. Lincoln L. Burwell, one of Alabama's earliest and most influential Black pharmacists and physicians; Dr. William H. Dinkins, president of Selma University; and Rev. L. L. Anderson, a local leader of the Selma Civil Rights Movement, whose home served as a strategy center and safe place for visiting leaders. It was designed by nationally significant African American architect Wallace Rayfield and was featured by W. E. B. Du Bois in The Crisis as one of the most stylish homes owned by African Americans.
100007801.heading: Summary Paragraph

79000383.summary: First Baptist Church, built in 1894, is most noted as a major landmark of the mass meetings and demonstrations in Selma in the mid-1960s that led to the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Hailed on completion as 'the finest colored church edifice in Alabama,' it is one of the finer late nineteenth-century Black churches in the state, influenced by the Gothic Revival and designed by local Black contractor and architect Dave Benjamin West. The congregation was organized in the early 1840s by Samuel Phillips, a freed slave. During Reconstruction it helped establish Selma University, an early Black college and theological school.
79000383.heading: Statement of Significance

72000159.summary: The John Tyler Morgan House, built in 1859 by Thomas Badger Wetmore, later Confederate provost marshal of Selma, was bought in 1865 by John Tyler Morgan, who lived in Selma until his death. Morgan, largely self-educated, was admitted to the bar in 1845 and was a leader of the Secession Convention, second only to William Yancey in influence. He enlisted in the Confederate Army as a private and rose to brigadier general. After the war he practiced law in Selma, opposed Radical Reconstruction, and in 1876 was elected to the U.S. Senate, where he served for thirty years.
72000159.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92001827.summary: The Wesley Plattenburg House, built around 1855 on what was then the northern edge of Selma, is significant for its style, a raised cottage of a type that hardly exists in central Alabama. Its L-shaped brick main story rests on an aboveground stuccoed brick basement under a low hip roof. A two-story recessed gallery wraps the south and east sides, with ten massive piers below and slender square columns supporting a bracketed cornice above. Frame additions were made around 1930.
92001827.heading: Statement of Significance

85002806.summary: The Saturn V Dynamic Test Stand (Dynamic Structural Test Facility), built in 1964 at the Marshall Space Flight Center, is significant for its role in testing and developing the Saturn V rocket, on which the Apollo and Skylab programs depended. A launched Saturn V could never be recovered for testing, and any flaw could cost the vehicle and the astronauts' lives, so as much as half of the program's effort and money went into ground testing. The 360-foot tower was built to conduct mechanical and vibration tests on the fully assembled Saturn V, supported so it could move freely as in flight.
85002806.heading: Statement of Significance

82002009.summary: Brown Chapel African Methodist Episcopal Church, built in 1908, is the landmark most closely tied to the Southern Christian Leadership Conference's 1965 Selma campaign for equal voting rights for Black citizens. In the first three months of 1965 it was SCLC headquarters, the site of rallies led by Martin Luther King Jr. and others, and the staging point for demonstrations, including the attempted march to Montgomery on March 7. The campaign directly spurred passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, considered by many historians the most important civil rights law of the 1960s. The church is also a very fine example of AME church architecture and the work of Black builder A. J. Farley.
82002009.heading: Statement of Significance

76000341.summary: The Redstone Test Stand, built in 1953 by the U.S. Army and known originally as the Interim Test Stand, is where the launch vehicles for Explorer 1 (1958), America's first satellite, and Alan Shepard's 1961 first American spaceflight were tested and checked out. Later transferred to NASA, it was the first static firing facility in what became the Marshall Space Flight Center test area, making it the birthplace of modern liquid rocket propulsion and testing at the center. Its greatest importance lies in the early development of rocket engines and propulsion systems capable of spaceflight.
76000341.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73000340.summary: Sturdivant Hall is one of Alabama's best known examples of Greek Revival architecture, resembling several Natchez mansions and especially Stanton Hall. It was built on land bought by Edward T. Watts to designs by Selma architect Thomas Helm Lee, a cousin of General Robert E. Lee. In 1864 Watts sold it to John Parkman, president of the First National Bank of Selma, who lost the bank to the Federal commander through cotton speculation and drowned trying to escape from prison at Cahaba. The Gillman family owned the house from 1870 until the City of Selma bought it in 1957.
73000340.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000311.summary: St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Selma is one of four Alabama churches attributed to Richard Upjohn and his son Richard M. Upjohn, and the only large one, drawn in the last years of their partnership. Its brick Gothic Revival design has English overtones and a cruciform plan. The parish was founded in 1838, and its first church was burned by Union soldiers during the Battle of Selma on April 1, 1865. Plans from R. and R. M. Upjohn arrived in 1871, and the church, built under John K. Snediker, held its first service on Easter Day 1875.
75000311.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002033.summary: The Asa White House, built around 1838, is a well-developed version of one of the early house types early settlers brought to Eutaw from the South Atlantic states, with a gable roof covering both the house and its open gallery. It is the only house in Eutaw with an original two-tiered gallery. Its chimneys have stepped brickwork at the base, a feature seen in earlier Georgia houses that became a hallmark of the Eutaw area. It mixes Federal details such as complex chimneys and chair rails with Greek Revival elements such as a volute newel post and pilastered mantels.
82002033.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

76000322.summary: The U.S. Post Office Building (Federal Building) in Selma was completed in 1909 to plans by James Knox Taylor, Supervising Architect of the Treasury, whose mannered use of classical forms made it an imposing statement of the federal presence. In front stands a monumental arch erected at the same time as a memorial to Alabama senators John Tyler Morgan and Edmund Winston Pettus, who both worked to win federal appropriations for the state. The building served as Selma's post office for more than fifty years and still serves as the federal courthouse, on a prominent site across from the county courthouse.
76000322.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002035.summary: The Daniel R. Wright House, built in 1847, is the best example in Eutaw of the house form established by the Vaughn House and survives very near its original form. It is essentially an enlarged version of that house, with higher piers, taller posts, a raised entablature, and two doorways. It is unique for its basement kitchen under the north wing. Its studied symmetry and heavy Greek Revival detail show a more self-conscious attention to style.
82002035.heading: Significance

82002027.summary: The Littleberry Pippen House, built in the early 1840s, is one of three similar Eutaw houses inspired by the Creole cottage, with strong Greek Revival modifications. It resembles the Vaughn House in shape, porch arrangement, and roof form. In place of slender colonnettes it has square Greek Revival piers, along with a pilastered doorway centered on a seven-post porch.
82002027.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002018.summary: The John W. Elliott House, built around 1850 by builder Jessee Gibson with a rear addition in 1857, is a good example of the typical story-and-a-half house with a cut-under porch that is locally called a 'Creole Cottage.' It is a typical home of a well-to-do storekeeper in this rich plantation town. The frame house's roof extends over a full-width front porch, which has a paneled dado and plastered upper wall like other Eutaw cottages. It has a standard central-hall plan with a staircase rising around an open well.
82002018.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

70000102.summary: The Coleman-Banks House, built about 1845, is one of the Black Belt's prime examples of Greek Revival architecture, called the 'Queen of Eutaw's Ante-Bellum Mansions' in Ralph Hammond's 1951 'Ante-Bellum Mansions of Alabama.' It was built by George W. Shauver, a Virginian who came to the county in 1839 and later ran the Parapet Hotel. After several sales, Mrs. John Coleman of Grassdale Plantation acquired the house in 1855, and her children, including Judge Wiley Coleman, lived there after her death in 1863.
70000102.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002016.summary: The Gustave Braune House, built in the mid-1850s and early 1860s, is a unique variant of Eutaw house types that shows the growing influence of Victorian picturesque taste at the end of the antebellum period. Braune, a Dresden native who opened a watch and jewelry store in Eutaw in 1853, bought Judge William C. Oliver's former one-room law office in 1859. He made it the stem of a T-shaped house whose central pavilion is octagonal on the second story, a form tradition says was inspired by buildings he knew in Saxony. The nearly flat-roofed house has a balustraded cornice and hexagonal porch piers. The source scan is partly illegible.
82002016.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

72000164.summary: Belle Mina, built in 1826, was the home of Thomas Bibb, Alabama's second governor. A Virginia native and son of a Revolutionary War captain, Bibb bought 2,500 acres in Limestone County after a trip through Alabama in 1808. He represented the county at the 1819 Constitutional Convention in Huntsville and served on the fifteen-man committee that drafted the state constitution. Elected to the first state Senate and chosen its president, he became governor in July 1820 when his brother, Governor William Wyatt Bibb, died after a riding accident. He served until December 1821 and later sat in the state legislature.
72000164.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000098.summary: The Greene County Courthouse in Eutaw, erected in 1869, was 'perhaps the last Greek Revival public building in Alabama,' according to architect Clay Lancaster. It is important mainly for showing the fading vitality of Greek Revival architecture after 1865, with pilasters reduced to frames around the windows and a thin cornice. The brick and stucco building stands on the foundation and nearly the same plan as the 1838 frame courthouse, built after the county seat moved from Erie to Eutaw. That courthouse burned after the Civil War, almost certainly by arson to destroy indictments brought against local citizens by the Reconstruction government.
71000098.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002030.summary: The Phillip Schoppert House, built around 1856 by Phillip Schoppert, is one of two hipped-roof variants of the I-house in Eutaw and reflects a lingering Georgian influence. Its rear lean-to and hipped roof give it a profile recalling one of the earliest seaboard prototypes, the Ludwell Paradise House in Williamsburg. Its chimneys have three setbacks on each side in a strictly medieval manner, surely a treatment the builder brought from South Carolina. Its unusually narrow windows and very wide double doorway are also unusual for western Alabama.
82002030.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002015.summary: The David Rinehart Anthony House, built around 1860 by Anthony himself, is a good example of the two-story house with a cut-under porch first seen in Eutaw at the Asa White House (1838). It is one of the few Eutaw houses attributed to a known builder. Anthony came from North Carolina in the late 1840s to build Rose Hill in Forkland, of which this house is a reduced version, and he built Eutaw's First Presbyterian Church in 1851. Its octagonal piers and gable ornament reflect the early Victorian taste seen in Eutaw only at the very end of the antebellum period.
82002015.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002031.summary: The Iredell P. Vaughan House, built in 1841, is the first and stylistically oldest of three Eutaw L-shaped cottages with L-shaped verandas; the others are the Littleberry Pippen and Daniel Wright houses. Its form set the pattern for the later houses. Listed in April 1982, it was moved about fifty yards toward the rear of its original lot that March to save it from demolition by the Presbyterian Church, and reoriented to face Mesopotamia Street. Because it stayed on the listed parcel, the state pursued a boundary revision rather than removing it from the Register.
82002031.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002017.summary: The Attoway R. Davis Home has a rear section, said to date from around 1817, which according to tradition was moved across the Warrior River from Erie, the vanished first county seat of Greene County. In the early 1840s a low front section was added, matching the old part exactly in width as a screen for it. The front resembles the Iredell P. Vaughan House across the street. The addition is significant as another variation on a common Eutaw house form, with a five-bay facade, paneled dado, and flush-board upper walls.
82002017.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

83002969.summary: The William B. Wills House, built around 1835, is a very good example of an early Greek Revival cottage in Eutaw with exceptionally fine woodwork. Its exterior features carved Greek key designs in the panels under the sidelights, guttae and regulae on an encircling cornice, and paneled ceilings on the front and side porticos. Inside, the woodwork shows lingering Federal-period influences, including chair rails in the original rooms.
83002969.heading: Statement of Significance

82002024.summary: The Dr. Willis Meriwether House, rebuilt in Eutaw in 1856, may be the only surviving trace of the early Greene County community of Springfield, from which it was transplanted, giving it value as a link to that vanished settlement. More importantly, it is one of three two-story Eutaw houses with a colossal portico of square piers, here six across a five-bay facade. Its hand-adzed roof beams predate the 1856 rebuilding, and its six-panel doors and flush-board dado reflect Federal-period practice. It also has an unusually wide main staircase.
82002024.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

74000411.summary: The First Presbyterian Church of Eutaw, built in 1851 for $5,500, is a two-story frame Greek Revival church with pedimented gables and a square bell tower with coupled corner pilasters topped by an octagonal spire. Sunday school rooms fill the first floor, and the second-floor sanctuary has not been significantly changed since construction. The congregation grew from the ministry of evangelist Andrew Brown, sent by the Synod of South Carolina and Georgia, who settled near Mesopotamia in 1822. It was organized in 1824 as the Mesopotamia Presbyterian Church.
74000411.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002021.summary: The Benjamin D. Gullett House, built around 1841 by Gullett himself, shortly after the Asa White House, is basically the same house type but is noted for its unusual floor plan. It has two single rooms, each with its own entrance and its own stair to the room above, a holdover from earlier forms brought from the Atlantic coastal states. The original four rooms, each about 16 feet square, were arranged two over two with external end chimneys. The original full-height veranda was converted to double galleries in the early twentieth century.
82002021.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002034.summary: The Catlin Wilson House, built in the mid-1840s for a Eutaw dry goods merchant who also sold groceries, spices, and wines, was a large and stylish home that has been kept in good repair. It survives in almost pristine original condition with many of its old dependencies, including a brick double storehouse connected by a dogtrot and a kitchen-laundry building. With the Hale House, it is one of Eutaw's prime examples of the story-and-a-half house. It keeps its original Doric columns, and its upper chambers have remarkably large floor-to-ceiling triple windows.
82002034.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

76000327.summary: Kirkwood, begun in 1857 by planter Foster M. Kirksey on 97 acres on the west side of Eutaw, is a modified temple-form Greek Revival mansion that by 1859 had become a town landmark and a symbol of planter prosperity. Kirksey insisted on the finest materials, importing Carrara marble mantels from Italy, and topped the house with an observatory cupola ringed by Ionic columns matching the veranda. The Union naval blockade kept the iron balcony grilles, mirrors, and chandeliers he ordered from Europe from ever arriving. After the war he kept the house but could never finish it as planned. It stayed in the family until 1961 and has since been restored.
76000327.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002032.summary: The William Peter Webb House, built around 1840 for lawyer William Peter Webb and possibly by builder Benjamin D. Gullett, shows how the traditional I-house was 'formalized' with a Greek Revival pediment, entablature, and doorway. That house form first appeared nearby at Mesopotamia and came from the South Atlantic states. It was built as a typical two-story, center-hall, four-room Mesopotamia-type house with eighteen-pane windows, colonnette newels, and pilastered mantels like those in the Gullett House across the street. Its portico was enlarged in 1914.
82002032.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002028.summary: The Edwin Reese House, built in the late 1850s by a prosperous carriage manufacturer, is one of four surviving mansion-style houses in Eutaw and an excellent example of the home of an upper-class businessman during the town's wealthy antebellum years. It derives from the same house type as the Asa White House, but with full-height Ionic columns in place of a double gallery. It keeps more of its original features than other similar houses in town. It is slightly larger than the earlier Coleman-Banks House and has a balcony with a cutout design over the doorway.
82002028.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002026.summary: The William Perkins House, built in the late 1850s, is, like its sister houses the Coleman-Banks and Edwin Reese houses, an elegant adaptation of an earlier Eutaw house form into a Greek Revival mansion. Its extraordinarily high first-floor platform and tall fluted Ionic columns give it an especially elegant air. A wooden balustrade surrounds the raised portico, and a cast-iron railing guards the balcony over the front door.
82002026.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002023.summary: The William C. Jones House, built between 1840 and 1845, is the more intact of only two fully raised cottages in Eutaw, with a ground floor largely above grade and subordinate to the main floor above. Each level has a center hall and two rooms about 21 feet square. A two-piered portico leads to a doorway with transom and sidelights, flanked by triple windows. There was no interior connection between the levels. Minor facade changes such as paired windows could easily be reversed.
82002023.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002022.summary: The Stephen Fowler Hale House, built around 1842, is a sophisticated story-and-a-half cottage whose two rear wings form a U-shape. It is one of four Eutaw houses with a three-bay pedimented four-column portico on a one- to one-and-a-half-story house, and one of two that originally used the Doric order. It has a full entablature and pilasters across the front, and its portico ends are finished like interior rooms. It is one of the few Eutaw houses that keeps an outbuilding, a two-room structure of unknown use.
82002022.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82001618.summary: The Samuel W. Cockrell House, built around 1859, is a nearly unaltered example of a small central-hall cottage with Greek Revival trim. As the small, stylish home of a practicing lawyer in the 1850s, it shows the typical residence of a Eutaw professional man of that period. It is the smallest of four one- to one-and-a-half-story, two-room-deep Eutaw houses with a characteristic one-bay pedimented portico of two columns.
82001618.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002020.summary: The Rev. John H. Gray House, built in the early 1830s with possible modifications around 1839, is the oldest surviving house within Eutaw's town limits still on its original site. Though slightly altered, it is a very good example of the I-house type with Federal-period refinements. It had a balanced facade and a handsome entrance with a large semicircular fanlight spanning the double doors and sidelights. Its details closely resemble those of a nearby house built about the same time for John Coleman.
82002020.heading: Significance

82002029.summary: The William A. Rogers House is a good example of a stylish mid-century Greek Revival house in its one-story version. Its front section, with a portico of four octagonal piers, was built in the mid-1850s for William A. Rogers and grafted onto an earlier two-room house at the rear, which has low ceilings, chair rails, and six-panel doors. It is one of four Eutaw houses with a pedimented three-bay, four-column portico on a one- to one-and-a-half-story house.
82002029.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

83003446.summary: The William F. Pierce House is one of two Eutaw raised cottages developed from Carolina seaboard prototypes and transplanted into Alabama's Black Belt, reflecting the original owner's strong wish to reproduce the houses of the area he came from. Pierce bought the lot from Asa White in 1839. The house is also a rare Greene County example of applied Italianate detailing of very high quality; such updates were common in larger towns just before the Civil War but few exist in the county. It has one of the best collections of nineteenth-century outbuildings in Eutaw, including a two-room servants' house.
83003446.heading: Statement of Significance

74000396.summary: The Montgomery-Janes-Whittaker House, built about 1822 by William Montgomery, is Federal in design and one of the very earliest elegant plantation homes in central Alabama, blending European fashions and materials with a pioneer way of life. Its most notable features are delicately crafted fanlights over the front entrances and in the gables, along with elaborate plaster medallions and cornices. Montgomery was a friend of industrialist Daniel Pratt and, by family tradition, of Andrew Jackson, both of whom visited. Family tradition says Jackson admired the staircase so much that he had it copied for the Hermitage, whose nearly identical staircase dates from 1834.
74000396.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002025.summary: The Samuel R. Murphy House, built between 1850 and 1859, is a very good example of the story-and-a-half Greek Revival cottage with a four-column portico, here with octagonal piers. Outside it resembles the Catlin Wilson House and the main block of the Stephen F. Hale House, but its chimneys stand between the rooms rather than on the flanks. Inside it has a developed front hall leading to a stair room. A square-piered rear gallery survives, and the house had a basement kitchen.
82002025.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

85002807.summary: The Neutral Buoyancy Space Simulator, built by the Army at Redstone Arsenal and later used by NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, provided a simulated zero-gravity environment where engineers, designers, and astronauts could work for long periods to solve the design and operational problems of working in space. By supporting research and testing of techniques and materials for crewed missions, it contributed significantly to Projects Gemini, Apollo, and Skylab and to the Space Shuttle. It was unique among NASA training facilities until a second facility was built at the Johnson Space Center in the mid-1970s.
85002807.heading: Statement of Significance

82001617.summary: The John Coleman House, called Grassdale, probably built in the 1830s, stands at the northwest edge of the almost vanished village of Mesopotamia, outside Eutaw's town limits. It is older than the other Eutaw houses nominated with it and is an important local prototype for the I-house form that early settlers brought from the Carolinas and Georgia. It has nine-over-nine and nine-over-six windows and an entrance with six-panel double doors, transom, and sidelights, with molded facings and corner blocks repeated inside.
82001617.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

82002019.summary: Glenville, built in the mid-1840s and enlarged in the 1850s and 1862, shows the traditional I-house transformed into a gable-front house with an inset porch, like the Herndon-Webb and Gullett houses. It is unique among them in using the Doric order for its colossal portico rather than piers or the Ionic order. It began as a two-story, four-room Mesopotamia-type house. Its second-floor overhang, like a seventeenth-century New England house, is highly unusual, with only one known southern predecessor, the Cupola House in Edenton, North Carolina.
82002019.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

13000470.summary: The Boxwood Plantation Slave Quarter, built around 1854, is significant statewide as one of the very few slave quarters left in Alabama and the only surviving building of Boxwood Plantation. It is also a rare Alabama example of raised plate construction, an architectural tradition from the Chesapeake region. Its period of significance runs to 1865, when slavery ended with the Union victory. The surrounding ground has high archaeological potential, as testing at a contemporary slave house at nearby Pond Spring plantation has shown.
13000470.heading: Summary Paragraph

99000793.summary: The Captain Nathan Carpenter House, built around 1853 in the rural Clinton community near Eutaw, is a fine and intact Greek Revival house whose design is attributed to builder David Rinehart Anthony. The imposing two-and-a-half-story house, now called Twin Oaks Plantation for the two large oaks framing its facade, sits on a slight knoll on brick piers. It has paneled corner pilasters matching those at its front doors. Tradition holds that a first-floor room was Carpenter's plantation office, and the attic held a 'seasonal room' or ballroom.
99000793.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

85001130.summary: The Stewart-Blanton House is a good example of a vernacular Greek Revival rural house and the only building left from a large, thriving nineteenth-century planter community near the Big Creek River in Pickens County. A pedimented Greek Revival portico was added to its traditional I-house form with a shed-roofed lean-to. It is also associated with Rev. Charles Stewart (1794-1856), founding pastor of two of the county's earliest Baptist churches, Enon and Big Creek. He also built a political career beginning with his election as county tax collector in 1830.
85001130.heading: Statement of Significance

75000316.summary: The James Greer Bankhead House, built by 1850, is an excellent example of the once numerous but fast-disappearing two-story frame pioneer house. It is associated with the Bankheads, early settlers of Lamar County who came from South Carolina by way of Tennessee and became prominent in Alabama history. James Greer Bankhead was a planter and a soldier in the Creek and Mexican wars. His son John Hollis Bankhead grew up in the house and became a Confederate officer, legislator, U.S. Representative, and U.S. Senator, founding one of Alabama's most prominent political dynasties.
75000316.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98000109.summary: The Emory School in Hale County is significant as a school built with help from the Julius Rosenwald School Building Fund, which from 1913 to 1937 helped finance more than 5,358 schools, teachers' homes, and shops for African American education in fifteen southern states. The fund was the most important philanthropic force aiding Black education in the first half of the twentieth century. The one-teacher school was built to Design #11 by W. A. Hazel and the Tuskegee Institute Department of Architecture. Though deteriorated, it keeps its original design, plan, and materials.
98000109.heading: Statements of Significance

84000651.summary: The James H. Bibb House, built in 1867, is the oldest known house in Madison and its only remaining Greek Revival house. Its uncommon pyramidal roof and late date show how long the Greek Revival remained a favored style for homes. Bibb, an early settler who owned more than 300 acres west of the depot at Madison Station, was instrumental in incorporating the town of Madison and was elected to its first town council in 1869.
84000651.heading: Statement of Significance

01001411.summary: The Stone Plantation house, built in the mid-nineteenth century, is an excellent and intact example of Greek Revival plantation architecture with hints of Italianate influence. With its surviving smokehouse, it is the domestic core of a once-thriving plantation complex. It is one of the few two-story brick antebellum Greek Revival rural plantation houses left in Montgomery County. It compares with urban 1850s Black Belt houses such as Sturdivant Hall in Selma and the Knox Mansion and Murphy House in Montgomery, and very few high-style houses of its scale and materials were built in rural Alabama. It was documented by the Historic American Buildings Survey in the 1930s.
01001411.heading: Statement of Significance

82002001.summary: County Line Baptist Church, built in 1889, is a good example of a simple country church of the late nineteenth century, with surprisingly sophisticated refinements for its time and rural setting. It has nicely detailed windows, a floor that slopes from the rear down to the pulpit, and walls angled inward beside the altar to form a truncated triangle. The first two acres were given by William C. Morgan, who bought them from the Creek Nation. The church's women were the first to form a woman's missionary society.
82002001.heading: Statement of Significance

87002178.summary: Building 800, Austin Hall, completed in 1931 and doubled in size in 1934, was the headquarters and classroom building of the Army Air Corps Tactical School at Maxwell Field, near the site where the Wright brothers opened the world's first civilian flying school in 1910. The school taught officers the strategy, tactics, and techniques of air power, and 916 officers had graduated by December 7, 1941. The tactics and strategy the U.S. Army Air Forces used in Europe and the Pacific in World War II were largely developed there in the 1930s. At the war's end, 320 of the Army Air Forces' general officers were graduates. The building is named for Lt. Charles B. Austin, an influential early instructor.
87002178.heading: Statement of Significance

75000310.summary: The old Dallas County Courthouse, now the Selma Historic and Civic Building, is one of Selma's most historic buildings. It was built in the late 1840s by Selma Fraternal Lodge No. 27 of the Free and Accepted Masons for the Central Masonic Institute, a school run with the Ladies Educational Society that opened in 1848. It served as a Confederate hospital during the Civil War. After the war, the city bought it and gave it to the county as a courthouse to help win the county seat from Cahaba. It housed county government from 1866 to 1902, then the Selma Military Institute, and from 1911 to 1960 the Vaughn Memorial Hospital.
75000310.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000734.summary: The Aliceville Elementary and High School, built in 1913, is the oldest brick building in Aliceville and the town's second school building, serving as a school until 1954. After the town's incorporation in 1907, a new school was the first major project of its leaders, and this building soon replaced a 1910 frame school. Its second-floor auditorium was long the town's social center, and Aliceville's first library began in the building. Its present appearance comes from a 1934 WPA remodeling and is a very good example of that era's interpretation of classical design.
80000734.heading: Statement of Significance

73000368.summary: Montgomery's Union Station and Trainshed, built in 1898 for $200,000, is one of the largest and most elaborate railway stations still standing in Alabama and an excellent example of late nineteenth-century commercial architecture. Designed for the Louisville and Nashville Railroad by local architect Benjamin Bosworth Smith, it replaced a small 1860 frame station after traffic grew to forty-four passenger trains a day by 1894. Near the Alabama River and the city wharf, it was the focal point of travel into Montgomery until the coming of commercial air travel. Its size, ambitious design, and rich materials make it a monument to the importance of rail transportation.
73000368.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

16000445.summary: The Wharton-Chappell House, built around 1854 for wealthy landowner and brickworks part-owner William G. Wharton, is significant for its role in Montgomery's mid-nineteenth-century development and was associated with the Chappell family for seven decades after 1859. The federal government acquired it in 1935 and rehabilitated it as offices for the Montgomery Housing Authority at the corner of Riverside Heights, one of the authority's first two Depression-era Public Works Administration housing projects, now gone. The rehabilitation is a rare example, and the earliest documented, of federally funded adaptive reuse of a historic building within a federal housing project.
16000445.heading: Summary Paragraph

78000500.summary: The Saturn V Space Vehicle at the Alabama Space and Rocket Center is made of full operational test stages of the rocket that carried Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins toward the first moon landing on July 16, 1969, and later launched the first U.S. space station. Because Saturn V stages were not recovered after flight, no flown Saturn V could ever be displayed, and these test units give a realistic view of the vehicle. It was the first large U.S. launch vehicle conceived and developed for a single purpose, the lunar landing. NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, under Dr. Wernher von Braun, led its design, development, and manufacture. The stages have been on display since 1969.
78000500.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73000370.summary: The Montgomery Powder Magazine is one of only two surviving Confederate storage facilities in Alabama; the other is in Eufaula. It stands at the end of Eugene Street on the Alabama River waterfront, near the river for easy water transport. It may have been copied from a magazine built as early as 1840 by Montgomery merchants after the city required gunpowder to be stored outside town limits. The State of Alabama bought the one-acre site from William P. Ashley on March 7, 1861, and powder for the Confederate Army was stored there throughout the Civil War.
73000370.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000433.summary: Westwood, built by James Lewis Price between 1836 and 1840, is a unique example of antebellum architecture whose classic simplicity shows Italian influence. It stands on a hill along the divide between the Alabama and Tombigbee river watersheds. Built for elegant plantation entertaining, it was famed at its height for its receptions and called 'the mecca of Canebrake society.' The Canebrake was the favored part of the Black Belt, the region that dominated Alabama politically, socially, and economically from 1819 to 1859.
74000433.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98000108.summary: The Oak Grove School in Prairieville, built in 1925 for $3,000, is significant as a school funded through the Julius Rosenwald School Building Fund, the most important philanthropic force aiding African American education in the first half of the twentieth century. The fund helped build thousands of schools for Black children across the South between 1913 and 1937, giving them longer schooling with better-trained teachers in better buildings. The school was built to designs and specifications supplied by Samuel Smith, director of the Rosenwald School Building Fund.
98000108.heading: Statements of Significance

100010460.summary: First Baptist Church in Montgomery, built in 1911-15, was a local strategy center for the Black community from 1915 to 1952 and a nationally significant strategy and conflict center of the Montgomery Civil Rights Movement from 1952 to 1980. It is the only surviving historic building closely tied to the Montgomery career of its pastor, Rev. Ralph Abernathy, a leader of the Montgomery Improvement Association from 1952 to 1961. The church was designed by Walter T. Bailey, one of the more important African American architects of the early twentieth century. Its French Romanesque style is unique among churches of its period.
100010460.heading: Summary Paragraph

78000498.summary: The Leech-Hauer House, built around 1830, appears to be a very early example of Greek Revival domestic architecture in Huntsville. William Leech bought 29 acres southwest of the city in 1825 and was living on the property by 1833. The two-story brick house combines Federal features, such as a five-bay facade, gable-end chimneys, and twenty-foot-square rooms around a central stair hall, with Greek Revival elements in its rear ell, mantels, doors, and entrance lights. A bungalow-style front porch was added in the early twentieth century.
78000498.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000324.summary: The Jefferson Davis Hotel, ten stories tall and built in 1927-29, was Montgomery's fourth major hotel and one of the earliest reinforced-concrete buildings in the city. Designed by architect Frederick Ausfeld and built by the Hugger Brothers Construction Company for the Capital City Hotel Company, it combines early twentieth-century commercial form with Classical and Sullivanesque details reflecting the decade's taste for modernity and luxury. A few blocks from the State Capitol, it became an important social and political gathering place.
75000324.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

86001106.summary: The Shepherd Building, built in 1922-23 by Hugger Brothers Construction, was designed by Frederick Ausfeld, Montgomery's most significant architect of early skyscrapers, who designed four of the city's seven early twentieth-century multistory commercial buildings. It was the only surviving Ausfeld building in Montgomery not already on the National Register. It shows his place at the forefront of mechanical innovation, keeping its original heating and electrical equipment, and the materials typical of 1920s Montgomery commercial construction. It was already 75 percent occupied when it opened, less than ten months after construction began.
86001106.heading: Statement of Significance

73000371.summary: The William Lowndes Yancey Law Office is where Yancey practiced law with partner John A. Elmore from 1846 until his death in 1863. Yancey was one of the greatest orators of his day and the leader of the states' rights and disunion movement in Alabama and the South. His 'Alabama Platform' of 1848, opposing the Wilmot Proviso and squatter sovereignty, foreshadowed the radical sectionalism that split the nation. The stuccoed brick building has a crenelated parapet. Its National Historic Landmark designation was withdrawn in 1986, after unavoidable structural problems affected the building.
73000371.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92000627.summary: The William Burritt Mansion, on Round Top Mountain a thousand feet above Huntsville, is a highly eccentric mountaintop house and an unusual example of twentieth-century Neoclassical architecture. It was apparently designed by its owner, Dr. William Burritt, with technical help from an architect, possibly Edgar Love. Begun in 1935, it burned on June 6, 1936, just as it was finished, and was rebuilt with changes by 1938. It is full of Burritt's inventive details, most notably insulation made of 2,200 bales of wheat straw, an idea he got from the cool shade of a Missouri haystack.
92000627.heading: Statement of Significance

87002182.summary: Building 836, now the Community College of the Air Force Building, was the first permanent building constructed at Maxwell Field. It is significant as an enlisted men's barracks built under the Army Air Corps Five Year Expansion Program authorized by Congress in 1927, which chose Maxwell as one of the fields to receive permanent facilities. The base site has a long aviation history: the Wright brothers ran the world's first civilian flying school there in 1910, and an Army Air Repair Depot opened in 1918. The building was designed by architects of the U.S. Army Office of the Constructing Quartermaster.
87002182.heading: Statement of Significance

100010582.summary: The Moore Building, a three-story brick and stucco office building designed by Montgomery architect Richard J. Adams and completed by 1941, is significant at the state level for its role in the Civil Rights Movement from 1954 to 1956. During those years it housed the state headquarters of the Alabama Council on Human Relations, which served as a 'reconciliation center' seeking solutions to civil rights strife. From these offices the council planned a grassroots network of local chapters, programs, publications, education, and research. The building stands near the Greyhound Bus Station and the U.S. Courthouse, both also tied to the movement.
100010582.heading: Summary Paragraph

06000439.summary: Winter Place, also known as the Winter-Thorington Houses, is a notable Alabama example of the Italianate and Second Empire styles. Its two stucco-over-brick houses, joined by a one-story passageway, were built shortly before the Civil War, when the Italianate was so popular that an 1861 visitor wrote that almost every house in the Confederate capital seemed built 'in the style of the Italian villa.' Few of those buildings survive, making Winter Place a rare example. It was finished in the Second Empire style some years after the war and is one of only several surviving examples of that style. Three brick dependencies behind the houses were originally slave dwellings.
06000439.heading: Statement of Significance

87001454.summary: The John McMahon House, built around 1828, is one of the oldest surviving brick houses in North Alabama and one of only six two-story brick houses south of the Tennessee River believed to predate 1830. It is a surviving example of early Alabama Federal-style architecture, carrying over Atlantic seaboard forms introduced by Virginia settlers, and has remarkably good integrity. It is associated with John McMahon of Harrisonburg, Virginia, part of the first wave of Virginians to settle Courtland, who came in the 1820s to open a branch of a Huntsville mercantile firm, and his wife Harriet Shackelford McMahon.
87001454.heading: Statement of Significance

80000730.summary: The McBryde-Screws-Tyson House, built in the 1850s by Ann McBryde, widow of Dr. Andrew McBryde, is one of the five remaining large Greek Revival mansions in Montgomery. It is elegantly detailed, with a projecting front pavilion and an uncommon paneled parapet. Ann McBryde was the daughter of Wade Allen, a South Carolinian who came to Alabama in 1817 and ran mail, stagecoach, and steamboat services between Mobile and Montgomery. The house is also associated with William Wallace Screws, editor and publisher of the Montgomery Advertiser, and local politician John Caius Tyson.
80000730.heading: Statement of Significance

90002177.summary: Old Ship African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church began as the 1835 frame church of Montgomery's Court Street Methodists. When the Methodists decided in the early 1850s to build a larger masonry church, they offered the old building to Black worshippers on condition that it be moved. In 1852 free Black contractor Thomas Wilson supervised rolling it to its present site at Holcombe and Mildred Streets. Local lore says the name came from a worker's reply that it was 'the Old Ship of Zion moving on.' The building was brick-veneered and remodeled in Classical Revival style in 1888, but parts of the original frame church remain at the rear.
90002177.heading: Statement of Significance

02001066.summary: Mt. Zion AME Zion Church, built in 1899 and remodeled in 1921 with twin towers, a Classical Revival portico, and brick veneer, is significant for its role in the Montgomery Civil Rights Movement. On December 5, 1955, after Rosa Parks's trial and conviction, its pastor Rev. L. Roy Bennett, head of the Interdenominational Ministerial Alliance, called church leaders together here. That afternoon sixteen men met in the pastor's study and organized the Montgomery Improvement Association to guide the bus boycott that had begun that morning, electing Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. as president and Bennett as vice president.
02001066.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84000655.summary: The White-Turner-Sanford House, built in 1827 by Virginia merchant James White on a lot bought from LeRoy Pope, is an excellent, well-preserved example of the Federal and Greek Revival architecture once common in Huntsville. White fell into debt and fled to Decatur in 1829, and the house was sold at auction in 1830. It is significant for its many residents who played important roles in Huntsville's history. Changes have been limited, including altered front windows around 1858 and a 1940s bathroom.
84000655.heading: Statement of Significance

82002066.summary: The Sayre Street School, built in 1891 by J. B. Worthington, is the oldest remaining public school building in Montgomery and is associated with the growth of public education in the city in the late nineteenth century, which accelerated after the state legislature passed an 1870 act on public schools. It was built after the school committee declared the existing buildings 'totally inadequate' in 1890. It is also a very good local example of a Victorian Romanesque school and one of the few surviving examples in the city of late nineteenth-century polychrome brickwork.
82002066.heading: Statement of Significance

82002065.summary: The Pepperman House (Pepperman-Ludlow House), built in 1887-88 by pawnbroker M. E. Pepperman and his wife Mary, represents the larger middle-class frame houses built in Montgomery's prosperous post-Reconstruction years. It is one of the few two-story 1880s Victorian houses left in its neighborhood and one of only two in the Eastlake style. Mildred Street, three blocks from downtown, was one of three neighborhoods that grew with the city's booming economy after Reconstruction. The house changed hands several times soon after it was built, and it is now the only building left on its block.
82002065.heading: Statement of Significance

84000717.summary: Pitts' Folly, built in 1852-53 under an 1851 agreement between P. H. Pitts and builder B. F. Parsons, is an unusual vernacular interpretation of Greek Revival design, with a colonnade of severely plain Doric pillars wrapping three sides of the house. Parsons was a Massachusetts-born architect and builder who worked in Perry County and the surrounding area. The two-story house had large rooms with twelve-foot first-floor ceilings and nine-over-nine windows, with jib doors in the parlor opening onto the porch. In 1860 a cooler was carved out of limestone twenty feet underground.
84000717.heading: Statement of Significance

13000894.summary: The Grove Court Apartments, built in 1947 to designs by architects Clyde C. Pearson and Farrow L. Tittle, are the only documented example of an International Style apartment complex in Montgomery and one of the most prominent examples of the style in Alabama. The complex displays all the typical elements of the style. Only a few other International Style buildings, including several office buildings and a hospital, have been identified in the city.
13000894.heading: Summary Paragraph

77000211.summary: The David C. Humphreys House (Humphreys-Rodgers House), built in 1848 as a two-story Federal-style townhouse, enlarged in the late 1850s, and remodeled around 1900, is the only surviving antebellum building from the North Huntsville area. It is most noted as the home of David C. Humphreys, a lawyer and legislator who backed Douglas at the 1860 Democratic Convention and opposed secession. He rose to regimental commander in the Confederate Army, then left as his Unionist sympathies grew and became, with Jeremiah Clemens, one of the most outspoken advocates of peace late in the war. After the war he joined the Republican Party. The front part of the house was later moved intact.
77000211.heading: Statement of Significance

78000497.summary: The Hundley House, built in 1900 by Oscar Hundley as his own residence, represents fashionable domestic architecture in a small southern town at the turn of the century. It blends Queen Anne massing and vertical emphasis, Shingle Style surfaces and living-hall plan, and Colonial Revival trim and gambrel gables without being a unified statement of any one style. Its mix shows how slowly rural areas adopted new styles from the Northeast. Hundley also built three other houses in the neighborhood.
78000497.heading: Statement of Significance

100005355.summary: The Bricklayers Hall, built in 1954 by Montgomery's African American bricklayers' union in the historically Black Centennial Hill neighborhood, is nationally significant for its association with the Montgomery Improvement Association. The MIA, which led the 381-day Montgomery Bus Boycott that began in December 1955 and played an important role in the national Civil Rights Movement, set up its headquarters in the newly finished hall in February 1956. It stayed there until 1960.
100005355.heading: Summary Paragraph

80000714.summary: The Hundley Rental Houses at 400 Franklin Street and 108 Gates Street were built by Oscar Hundley as rental properties behind the large house he built for himself in 1900, which is also on the National Register. He bought the adjoining land in 1902 and built the houses, which were assessed for taxes by 1905, after tearing down a stable and a two-story building reputedly dating from 1818. No architect has been identified, but the houses were likely designed by the same person as Hundley's other buildings. 400 Franklin was repaired after a 1909 fire and has a later rear addition and garage.
80000714.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

74000419.summary: The Clemens House was the home of Jeremiah Clemens, a leader of the opponents of secession at the Alabama Convention of 1861 and later an outspoken advocate of peace in the last months of the Civil War. His father James Clemens, who came from Kentucky in 1812, bought the property in 1838, and the house may date from the 1830s with a major remodeling between 1850 and 1875. Jeremiah Clemens, a lawyer, served against the Cherokees and as a colonel in the Mexican War, was U.S. Attorney for northern Alabama, served several terms in the legislature, and was a U.S. Senator from 1849 to 1853.
74000419.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000704.summary: The Big Spring was the principal reason Huntsville developed where it did, as early settlers valued its constant supply of fresh water over better transportation on the Tennessee River ten miles south. It also shaped the town's layout: the streets were laid out at an angle along the bluff so the spring would fall within a single 'Spring Block,' and all other streets followed that angle. By 1823 a water system with a reservoir on the Square and hollow cedar-log pipes was carrying spring water to houses. Huntsville probably had the earliest public water system west of the Alleghenies.
80000704.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

74000421.summary: The First National Bank building in Huntsville was built for the Huntsville branch of the State Bank of Alabama, established in 1835, and is the oldest building in the state in continuous use as a bank. It is also one of the finest examples of Greek Revival architecture in northern Alabama. It was designed by George Steele, the most competent architect-builder in the region. After the state banking system failed, the Northern Bank of Alabama used it until Federal troops occupied Huntsville in April 1862. The National Bank of Huntsville opened there in 1865, and its successor, the First National Bank of Huntsville, has occupied the building continuously since 1889. The purity of its design and materials stands out among later surrounding buildings.
74000421.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80004472.summary: The buildings at 104-128 South Side Square have been Huntsville's prime commercial property since the 1810s, a block called 'Commercial Row' until the twentieth century. Built up with small commercial buildings before the Civil War, it has kept the same size and number of buildings because party walls and foundations were reused in rebuilding. It is the only downtown block that survives as a complete unit. Numbers 108 and 110, from 1835-40, are the oldest and keep the tall, narrow proportions of antebellum commercial buildings. The block includes the only surviving commercial building by George Steele other than the First National Bank.
80004472.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000724.summary: The Schiffman Building is one of the few surviving antebellum commercial buildings in Huntsville and the city's only Richardsonian Romanesque building. The brick building, built sometime between 1835 and 1861, was remodeled inside and out in the Romanesque Revival style in 1895 by the Southern Building and Loan Association, to designs by Nashville architect George W. Thompson, and has not been altered since. Isaac Schiffman, a German immigrant merchant, bought it in 1905 and opened a loan office there, and it stayed in his family. Actress Tallulah Bankhead was born in the second-floor apartment in 1902.
80000724.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000712.summary: The Henderson National Bank, built in 1948 to designs by Birmingham architects Warren, Knight and Davis, is a fine example of the Art Moderne style and the only one in downtown Huntsville. Its exterior shows the style's smooth, streamlined design, vertical reeding, stylized low reliefs, and polychrome effects. It was nominated while still less than fifty years old to help protect Huntsville's few intact Art Deco and Art Moderne buildings.
80000712.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

74000420.summary: The Episcopal Church of the Nativity is the most elaborate and least altered of the three Gothic Revival churches in Alabama designed by Frank Wills of New York with the help of Henry Dudley. These churches were Alabama's closest approximations of the Gothic principles promoted by Pugin, Ruskin, and Upjohn, and all closely follow Wills' published ideas on English church architecture. Construction was under way in 1857 and 1858, and the church was completed in 1859 at a cost of $30,000. It was consecrated on January 29, 1860.
74000420.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000713.summary: The Hotel Russel Erskine, a twelve-story concrete and steel hotel built in 1928-30 to designs by Nashville architect Joe Holman of Marr and Holman, was the tallest hotel with the most rooms in the Tennessee Valley. It was 'the' place to stay for business in North Alabama, and for thirty years most civic clubs met there and important social functions took place there. It was financed by a group of Huntsville businessmen who incorporated in 1928, and many local firms had subcontracts. It opened with a formal ball in January 1930.
80000713.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000706.summary: The Donegan Block, built in 1870, is one of Huntsville's finest surviving examples of the Italianate style, which was the main style for the town's commercial buildings in the late nineteenth century. Huntsville then had fewer than 5,000 people and no trained architects, so local builders simplified the high styles. Unlike most two-story Italianate stores, the Donegan Block is two and a half stories tall, likely reflecting a lingering taste for the very tall, narrow proportions of antebellum buildings, since it was one of the first buildings erected after the Civil War.
80000706.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000722.summary: The Rand Building, a two-story brick Italianate commercial building built in 1883 by Huntsville contractors Mastin and Winston, is one of Huntsville's finest surviving examples of the period when the Italianate was the main style for commercial buildings. Huntsville then had fewer than 5,000 people and no trained architects, so local builders produced simplified versions of the high styles. Remodeling and rebuilding have destroyed most similar buildings, and the Rand Building and the nearby Donegan Block are the best survivors.
80000722.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

83004374.summary: The W. T. Hutchens Building illustrates the small-scale commercial buildings of small towns in the first quarter of the twentieth century, built for individual shop owners. The corner section was built in 1916 for the Hutchens hardware firm, and a two-bay addition followed in 1921; the addition's first floor long housed the Alabama Cafe. Terra cotta courses give the otherwise basic design a distinctive identity, and the building keeps good integrity of location, setting, materials, design, and associations.
83004374.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000720.summary: The May and Cooney Dry Goods Company building is one of the few surviving glazed terra cotta commercial buildings in Huntsville, notable for its ornate polychrome terra cotta cornice and arched front, and for its decorative exposed steel trusses supporting each floor. The locally owned dry goods firm lost its building to fire in 1911 and leased this new building on East Side Square in 1913. The firm went bankrupt during the Depression in 1931. J. C. Penney occupied the building from 1934 to 1965, and Madison County bought and renovated it in 1973.
80000720.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000721.summary: The Milligan Block, a two-story brick commercial building built in 1900 on the Huntsville Courthouse Square, illustrates the shift from the vertical complexity of nineteenth-century architecture to the horizontal restraint of early twentieth-century buildings. In Huntsville the Italianate remained the main style for small, locally owned businesses through the late nineteenth century, and the Milligan Block shows its basic form turning into the Commercial Brick style. Shallow pilasters still divide the facade into bays, but the building has become a static grid. It was remodeled in 1930.
80000721.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000715.summary: The Terry Hutchens Building, originally called the Tennessee Valley Bank Building after its main tenant, was the first of three 'skyscrapers' built in downtown Huntsville in the 1920s. Completed in 1925, the seven-story building is the first tall office building in Huntsville, the city's only late Gothic Revival commercial building, and the first built without load-bearing walls, which amazed local onlookers. It was designed by R. H. Hunt and Company of Chattanooga and built by a Birmingham contractor. The first floor has since been modernized.
80000715.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000723.summary: The Randolph Street Church of Christ, built in 1887 as the Christian Church, is a late example of early Gothic Revival design, with simple wood tracery in pointed-arch windows, a central entrance tower, buttresses, and a small spire. It was built half a block off the Public Square when the center of town was Huntsville's religious, cultural, and governmental as well as commercial hub. Mr. and Mrs. O. M. Hundley, parents of the builder of the Hundley House, were instrumental in erecting it: Mrs. Hundley donated the land and Mr. Hundley supervised construction. It is a brick version of the box-like towered church popular in rural areas across the country.
80000723.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

76000351.summary: The Opp Cottage is one of Montgomery's few remaining raised cottages. Modest but well crafted, it reflects the taste and means of a middle-class merchant who settled in Montgomery after the Civil War. Construction was likely begun in 1860 by T. J. Wilson and his wife Eliza, and Valentine and Catherine Opp bought the unfinished cottage in 1866. Valentine Opp, an Austrian immigrant who had married Irish immigrant Catherine Hart in Lowndes County, ran a successful tailoring business on Court Square.
76000351.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000703.summary: Beckers Block, a one-story row of five brick commercial bays built in 1925, is a fully developed example of the Commercial Brick style in Huntsville. It shows the style's strong horizontal lines, stepped parapet, and mix of brown brick and cream-colored stone. The block illustrates most of the ways the style created decoration from the building materials themselves rather than applied ornament, with brick laid vertically and as headers to form panels, channels, and edgings. The upper walls are intact, and the southern two units are nearly unchanged.
80000703.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

01001167.summary: Cleveland Court Apartments 620-638, part of a public housing complex completed in 1941, are significant as the home of Rosa Parks when she was arrested for violating Montgomery's bus segregation laws and throughout her trial and appeals. Her refusal to give up her seat sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott, which marked the start of the modern civil rights movement and brought Rev. Ralph Abernathy and Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. to national attention. Her arrest led to a test case in which the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that segregation on city buses was unconstitutional.
01001167.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84000653.summary: The building at 105 North Washington Street, built in 1931 after a fire destroyed an earlier building on the site, is an excellent example of early twentieth-century small-town commercial architecture. Its two-story brick facade has Art Deco detailing in light tan terra cotta, including a large frieze, cornice, and window surrounds, with a faint French Renaissance flavor. The upper facade is apparently original, though the storefront was replaced around 1975. It was listed as part of the Downtown Huntsville Multiple Resource nomination.
84000653.heading: Significance

80000717.summary: The Kress Building, built in 1931, is the second Art Deco building in Huntsville. It was designed by Edward Sibbert of New York, who also designed the Kress Company's Art Deco main office and store on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. It is a fine Art Deco design, showing the style's vertical emphasis, polychrome low-relief patterns, angular composition, and terra cotta. The street level has been greatly changed, but the upper wall is original.
80000717.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000725.summary: The Struve-Hay Building, erected in 1900, combines Victorian and Commercial Brick features from a transitional period in Huntsville commercial architecture. Its most obvious Victorian feature is its corner tower, and it is the only surviving one of several towered commercial buildings once in Huntsville. It also has an applied metal cornice and a Romanesque-style side entrance. At the same time, its regular composition, strong horizontals, and restrained walls point to the direction local commercial architecture would take in the early twentieth century.
80000725.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000719.summary: The Mason Building, built in 1927, is one of the few terra cotta commercial buildings in Huntsville and was designed by local architect Edgar Love. It was built for Mason's, a furniture store founded in 1908 by James Mason that grew from 300 square feet to 42,000 square feet of leased space by 1926. The building was designed as a five-story structure with cascading polychrome terra cotta floral ornament at the top, but only the first two-story phase was built, on a foundation strong enough for five stories.
80000719.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

96000597.summary: Fowler's Department Store (later Belk-Hudson's) consists of two joined Commercial-style buildings built in 1930 and 1936 at Washington and Holmes Streets in downtown Huntsville. They are significant for their association with Huntsville's early twentieth-century commercial history and as examples of Depression-era department store design.
