They were two of the last major buildings built downtown until after World War II, and they survived the 1950s downtown building boom and 1970s urban renewal. They are an extremely rare and intact example of commercial buildings built during the Depression.
96000597.heading: Statement of Significance

80000708.summary: The Dunnavant's Building was erected in 1905 by Terry Brothers and Rogers, a local dry goods company, from a design by Huntsville architect Edgar Love. It was built of brick with heavy timber floors. A 1927 remodeling by contractor Charles E. Baxter was reported as building an entire new front, but drawings and photographs show the only exterior changes were to the entrance and display windows. A 1940 fire damaged the third floor and roof, which were then repaired.
80000708.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000709.summary: The Everett Building, a two-story brick commercial block built in 1899, is an elegant example of the early Commercial Brick style before it lost all ornament. It drops Victorian applied decoration and relies instead on creative use of brick and the pattern of its windows, with corbelled pilasters, flush masonry lintels, and a stepped brick parapet. The ground-floor storefronts have been modernized, but the second floor remains intact. Its original street front of slender cast iron columns and plate glass would have made the design even lighter.
80000709.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

81000129.summary: The U.S. Courthouse and Post Office in Huntsville was built in 1932 to replace an earlier Romanesque Revival building. Congress approved $200,000, but it was built for $169,000, and its construction was the only major building work downtown during the Depression. It was probably built to a standard government design, with Huntsville architect Edgar Love and the Birmingham firm Miller, Martin and Lewis as associated architects. Love died just as it was completed. It is one of only two Neo-Classical Revival buildings in the central business district, with minimal detailing.
81000129.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000727.summary: The Yarbrough Hotel is significant as one of Huntsville's premier hotels of the 1920s and as a major building in the popular Commercial Brick style. Work on the foundation began in late 1922, and in 1923 the Yarbrough Brothers let the contract for a brick and reinforced concrete hotel with 75 rooms with baths. Architect D. Anderson Dickey then drew plans for an added fifth story with more guest rooms and a summer dining and banquet room.
80000727.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000707.summary: The Downtown Chevron station, built in 1919 and enlarged in 1929 and 1938, is the oldest filling station in downtown Huntsville and has been used as one since it was built. It was one of the first buildings there built to serve the automobile and is the only one of that early phase still standing. It predates standard oil company designs and was built of local dark red brick with bungalow-type windows to blend with the neighborhood, with a cottage's scale and roofline but an obvious function. It is important locally for its early role in defining drive-in buildings designed for cars rather than pedestrians.
80000707.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

03001134.summary: The brick warehouse at 305 Jefferson Street, built around 1925, is significant for commerce and architecture as part of a block of grocery, produce, and fruit wholesale warehouses in downtown Huntsville. Though not highly ornamented, it represents the Commercial Brick style and matches its neighbors in construction, materials, setback, and design. Three adjacent warehouses were listed in the 1980 Downtown Huntsville Multiple Resource nomination, and this one, the only warehouse on the block not then listed, adds to the integrity and continuity of the block.
03001134.heading: Statement of Significance

80000705.summary: The Church of the Visitation is the oldest Catholic church in Northeast Alabama and one of the state's earliest examples of the Romanesque Revival style. The parish was established in 1860 by Father Jeremiah Trecy, and work began in 1861, but the Civil War halted construction and the church was not finished until 1872 or dedicated until 1877. It is the only nineteenth-century church in the area with a barrel-vaulted nave ceiling or load-bearing limestone walls, and one of only two mid-nineteenth-century churches with columns inside the nave. Its architect is not known.
80000705.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000710.summary: The Halsey Grocery Warehouse, a one-story brick building built in 1923 for the Halsey Grocery Company, is typical of the many small commercial buildings erected in Huntsville during the expansion of the mid-1920s. It embodies the Commercial Brick style as interpreted locally, with a flat facade, stepped parapet, brick arches, corbels, and a broken cornice. Compared with the company's first building across the street from 1904, it shows how commercial styles changed over those two decades.
80000710.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000726.summary: The Times Building, built in 1926-28, was the second of three 'skyscrapers' built in Huntsville during the building boom that lasted from about 1900 until the Depression. It was designed by R. H. Hunt and Company of Chattanooga, which also designed the Terry Hutchens Building and Huntsville's synagogue. It is a subtle design whose unbroken piers end in an elegant Art Deco-inspired terra cotta cornice.
80000726.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000711.summary: The W. L. Halsey Warehouse, a two-story brick building erected in late 1904 by wholesale grocer W. L. Halsey, is one of the finest commercial buildings in Huntsville, with a subtle combination of cast iron, brick, and a metal cornice. It is one of only two downtown buildings that keep their cast iron intact, used to create an all-glass street-level front. The cast iron was made locally by the Huntsville Foundry and Machine Works. A brick addition on the north side has not affected the original facade.
80000711.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000716.summary: The Kelly Brothers and Rowe Building, a one-story brick warehouse built in 1928, is locally significant for showing how commercial architecture changed just before the Depression. It represents a late phase of the Commercial Brick style, refined to the point that function essentially replaced decoration: the facade is perfectly flat, with only a raised central section with a name plaque and darker brick outlining openings and edges. Together with three nearby warehouses, it illustrates the evolution of warehouse design in the first thirty years of the twentieth century.
80000716.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

80000718.summary: The Lombardo Building, a three-story brick warehouse built in 1922, is a fine example of the fully developed Commercial Brick style applied to a larger than average building. It has the style's regular, symmetrical brick facade, grouped windows, and stepped parapet, and relies on its windows and building materials rather than applied ornament for effect. The vertical pilasters are balanced by horizontal window groupings and an elaborate parapet. The ground floor has been slightly altered without obscuring the original design.
80000718.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

71000101.summary: The Southern Railway System Depot, built in 1860 as the Memphis and Charleston Railroad Depot, is the oldest railway terminal standing in Alabama and one of the last surviving reminders of the South's most important antebellum rail system. The Memphis and Charleston, chartered in Alabama in 1850, realized an early Southern dream of linking the Mississippi River at Memphis with the Atlantic at Charleston, and it was a major force in North Alabama's commercial development. Huntsville citizens raised money to bring the line through the city, which became headquarters of its Eastern Division. During the Civil War the depot served as a temporary Federal prison.
71000101.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

15000069.summary: This boundary increase and additional documentation updates the Old Town Historic District in Huntsville, first listed in 1978 and described then as the city's only predominantly Victorian neighborhood, with closely spaced, ornate Victorian homes, brick sidewalks, and Monte Sano as a backdrop. The update enlarges the district and extends the period of significance to about 1830-1962. A new survey found that the original description still holds, and also recorded many Bungalow variations and good examples of mid-twentieth-century houses. Because the end date was extended, most buildings once counted as intrusions are now contributing.
15000069.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

79000399.summary: The Tyson-Maner House, built in 1890, is one of Montgomery's rare large masonry Victorian Italian Villas, with a central tower, scroll brackets, and grouped windows, plus Victorian window framing and a projecting gabled bay. Its Neo-Classical porch dates from alterations around 1916. It was built by Archibald Pitt Tyson, a Lowndesboro native who came to Montgomery in 1877 and prospered in real estate and loans, building ten downtown stores in 1886. The house illustrates upper-middle-class taste and prosperity during the post-Reconstruction boom.
79000399.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000325.summary: The Gay House is one of Montgomery's most outstanding examples of late Queen Anne architecture, with an eclectic blend of Victorian and Classical motifs and detailed woodwork. It was designed by its owner, Charles Linn Gay, who was trained as a civil engineer, and built by the Hugger Brothers Construction Company in 1900 in the suburb of Burtonville. Gay was a partner in wholesale grocery and drug firms before opening the Farmer's Compress Warehouse Company, which included a gin, grist mill, and commissary. Kept very near its original condition, the house reflects the tastes and lifestyle of a prominent turn-of-the-century businessman.
75000325.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98001228.summary: G. W. Trenholm Hall is part of the Alabama State University Historic District, which has statewide significance in African American educational history from 1920 to 1948. Founded in 1866, ASU was the first state public institution of higher education for African Americans in Alabama and for many years the only state-supported normal school and university for them. The district's buildings, from Bibb Graves Hall in 1920 to Trenholm Hall, the North Dining Hall, and the bus garage in 1948, represent African Americans' efforts to provide education under segregation. Trenholm Hall, a Georgian Revival brick building, served as the library until 1978.
98001228.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

77000215.summary: The Dr. C. A. Thigpen House (Thigpen-Hill House) was the home of Dr. Charles A. Thigpen, an eye, ear, nose, and throat specialist and one of Alabama's most noted physicians. A native of Greenville, he was educated in New Orleans, New York, London, Vienna, and Heidelberg before practicing in Montgomery. The house was designed by Frank Lockwood, one of the best-known architects in the southern states in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, and reflects the period's preference for classical eclecticism. Much of the nomination text is badly garbled, so details are limited.
77000215.heading: Statement of Significance

94000692.summary: Bermuda Hill, built around 1845, is a significant example of a Canebrake plantation house based on the I-house form, and it shows the styles, construction methods, and craftsmanship used in the Canebrake region. The land once belonged to the Manning family, early settlers and prominent planters around Prairieville, within the original French grants of the Vine and Olive Colony. William W. Manning sold the tract in July 1845 to a buyer from Madison County, Alabama. The house retains its integrity of design, materials, workmanship, feeling, and setting.
94000692.heading: Statement of Significance

81000130.summary: The Vaught House, built in 1900, is a well-maintained example of late Victorian domestic architecture and a reminder of the East Huntsville Addition as Huntsville's first modern suburb. The addition was platted in 1892 next to the city's first large textile mill, begun in 1890, and the streetcar line made it a practical and fashionable neighborhood. The Vaught House was one of the earliest privately built homes there and is one of the few Victorian and large houses left in the area, where most homes are later bungalows.
81000130.heading: Statement of Significance

72000158.summary: Cornwall Furnace is a largely unaltered cold-blast iron furnace, one of the best preserved of its period in Alabama. In 1862 the Confederate government commissioned the Noble Brothers of Rome, Georgia, to build it near Cedar Bluff on the Chattooga River to produce pig iron for the war effort. Skilled workers came from Confederate Army personnel, and hundreds of enslaved people were hired from nearby plantations; an estimated thousand people built the furnace, a tunnel, and a half-mile canal. Its flammable parts were destroyed in 1864 and rebuilt in 1867, but only the massive stone stack remains.
72000158.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

01001295.summary: The Hain House, built in 1913 by Selma builders James C. Rutledge and Thomas Franklin Person, is an excellent example of a Neo-Classical Revival house in rural Alabama. Neo-Classical was a dominant style for American houses in the first half of the twentieth century, and this two-story frame house keeps a remarkably high degree of original detail. It is the only example of the style in Sardis and one of the best residential examples of Neo-Classical architecture in Alabama. Trees planted by its first residents still shape the surrounding landscape.
01001295.heading: Statement of Significance

82001608.summary: Lincoln School was built in 1929 by Lincoln Mills of Alabama, which became one of Huntsville's largest textile mills, and it is tied to both local industrial and educational history. Lincoln Village, just north of the city limits, was a self-contained company community with housing, stores, a community hall, churches, the school, and mill buildings, typical of the paternalistic mill system. The company school served the workers' children but was staffed through the Madison County Board of Education. It replaced an overcrowded first school and is the oldest school building in the city and the only mill school still operating.
82001608.heading: Statement of Significance

01001165.summary: The Lowry House is an early and important example of a gable-front, T-plan house in Huntsville. Its exact construction date is unknown, but its architecture suggests 1860-1870, with major renovations around 1890-1900 and about 1905. It reflects the trend away from neoclassicism toward more eclectic and irregular house forms, influenced by A. J. Downing's promotion of the picturesque country villa. Some original features survive, including Greek Revival mantelpieces and a heavily molded early door.
01001165.heading: Statement of Significance

74000422.summary: The Steele-Fowler House is a Greek Revival home that the noted architect George Steele designed for himself and built in 1840 on what was then the outskirts of Huntsville. Steele was one of the more outstanding architects of the antebellum South; his surviving Huntsville works include the State Bank branch building on the Courthouse Square and several notable homes, and he designed the Parthenon-inspired Madison County Courthouse of 1840, razed in 1914. The stone and stucco house is built on three levels, though it looks like two stories over a basement from the front.
74000422.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002014.summary: Myrtle Hall, originally called Boligee Hill, is a raised cottage begun in the late 1830s by Dr. John D. Means and his wife Charlotte Johnston Means, who came from Fairfield District, South Carolina, in 1831. It represents the formalizing of the vernacular raised cottage, a house type brought to west central Alabama by settlers from the South Atlantic seaboard, through academic symmetry, proportion, and fashionable detail. Once perhaps one of several such houses in an area dominated by South Carolina planters, it is now unique among surviving Greene County plantation houses. It was also the home of Charles Hays, a Reconstruction-era Congressman and a leader of Alabama's Radical Republicans.
82002014.heading: Statement of Significance

82002051.summary: Kildare (the McCormick House) was built in 1886-87 for Michael O'Shaughnessy, a northern capitalist who, with his brother James, sought investment opportunities in the South. They settled on Huntsville, then a town of about 5,000 that had not recovered from the Civil War, and bought large tracts of land and buildings. Through their influence, other wealthy outside investors and self-styled 'town builders' came to Huntsville and, with local businessmen, helped promote it as an industrial center. The house has seen few changes beyond a conservatory, an enclosed porch, and some redone interior trim.
82002051.heading: Statement of Significance

98001019.summary: The Monte Sano Railroad Workers' House, built in 1888, is the only surviving building connected with the nineteenth-century Hotel Monte Sano and the Monte Sano Railway. The 233-room hotel opened atop Monte Sano Mountain on June 1, 1887, and work on the railway, a private line linking the Southern and L&N lines to the hotel, began in February 1888. This house, originally a saddlebag plan of two identical rooms with a central chimney, is locally significant as an example of housing for the railway's workers.
98001019.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

75000313.summary: St. John's-in-the-Prairie is a well-proportioned small rural Gothic church built in 1859, traditionally attributed to architect Richard Upjohn, though documentary proof is lacking. Its curved roofline, found on no other Episcopal church in Alabama, gives it a more Gothic feeling, and its covered side entrance is also unique. It was originally built nine miles southwest of Greensboro to replace a dilapidated older church. In the 1870s it was moved and re-erected at Forkland.
75000313.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

94000697.summary: The Kerby House, also known as the Randolph plantation, is a small Greek Revival cottage built around 1850 and a significant example of a Canebrake plantation house. Although it has been covered with siding and has modern windows, it keeps its original form and detailing and shows the styles, construction methods, and craftsmanship used in the Canebrake from 1830 to 1942. It is also one of the few remaining plantation houses of a Canebrake planter whose main residence was there.
94000697.heading: Statement of Significance

73000367.summary: Edgewood is the oldest remaining house in the city of Montgomery. It was built in 1821 by Zachariah T. Watkins, then dismantled timber by timber in 1832 and rebuilt on its present site; the original land entry for its 300 acres dates from 1818. In 1855 it passed to Peachy Ridgeway Gilmer, brother of Georgia Governor George Gilmer, and later to John Gregory Thomas, who served in Semple's Battery and was twice wounded in the Battle of Atlanta. The house remained in the Thomas family.
73000367.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000099.summary: Rosemount is a grand wooden plantation house with a commanding cupola, described by architectural writers as one of the Deep South's finest Classical compositions in wood and 'the most grandly conceived mansion in Alabama.' It was begun in 1832 by Allen Glover, who had come from South Carolina to the Alabama Territory in 1818, and took seven years and the labor of dozens of enslaved people to complete. The house sits on a knoll overlooking a planned landscape of lake, formal garden, orchards, pastures, farm buildings, and slave quarters, all visible from the cupola. It stayed in the Glover family for more than a century.
71000099.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002054.summary: Quietdale, the Mrs. William Robinson House, built around 1854, is a clear example of the mid-nineteenth-century shift from strict neoclassicism to the freer forms of romantic eclecticism. Its symmetrical five-bay facade keeps neoclassical form and proportions, but an ornate porch of shallow Tudor-style arches with Italianate brackets shows the influence of A. J. Downing, Samuel Sloan, and other promoters of the new ideas. It is one of the earliest expressions of this trend in the Huntsville area. It was built for Caroline Moore Robinson, widow of Madison County sheriff and planter William Robinson, and may have been designed by George Steele or his son Matthew.
82002054.heading: Statement of Significance

73000347.summary: St. Andrew's Church at Prairieville is a country Gothic church believed to have been designed by Richard Upjohn. It was built in 1853 by enslaved people owned by church members, working under master carpenters Peter Lee and Joe Glasgow, who were enslaved by Captain Henry A. Tayloe. The congregation grew from Episcopal services that Rev. Caleb S. Ives began holding at Prairieville in 1834. Its story is closely tied to the growth of the Episcopal Church in Alabama.
73000347.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78000501.summary: The Withers-Chapman House, built around 1835, is one of the few known intact Madison County examples of a one-and-a-half-story frame cottage of the early nineteenth century, a once-common rural house type. It has restrained but well-crafted Federal and Greek Revival details and is one of the few houses in the area with corner fireplaces upstairs. Built as the center of a moderately prosperous farm, later a major dairy serving Huntsville, it keeps two nineteenth-century outbuildings and a semi-attached kitchen. Governor Reuben Chapman acquired the property in 1873.
78000501.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

77000212.summary: Oaklawn, the John Robinson House, is a two-story brick Greek Revival house completed in the 1840s as the center of one of the largest plantations in Madison County. It is a severe and well-proportioned example of a Greek Revival plantation house, with a central five-bay block and attached two-bay wings that project beyond the main house, a plan found in few Alabama houses. Its central portico has four fluted Doric columns. Much of the nomination text is badly garbled, so details are limited.
77000212.heading: Statement of Significance

86001239.summary: The Adams Grove Presbyterian Church, built around 1853, is one of the least altered of the seven antebellum Greek Revival rural churches surviving in Dallas County, which has one of Alabama's highest concentrations of early nineteenth-century religious buildings. It shows how builders adapted high-style features to the plain meetinghouses of evangelical Protestant worship, with a pedimented front, an in-antis portico, and molded pilasters giving it austere dignity. It also shows the local architectural flavor such buildings often took on. The site, five miles southeast of Cahaba, was sold to the congregation by Henry Adams in 1853.
86001239.heading: Statement of Significance

82002008.summary: St. Luke's Episcopal Church, built in 1854 after designs by Richard Upjohn, is one of three antebellum board-and-batten Gothic Revival churches in Alabama designed by Upjohn, the largest group of his country churches in any Deep South state. It was originally built at Cahaba, the state's first capital, and was moved in 1878 to Martin Station, about 20 miles west. The church reflects the influence of Bishop Nicholas Hamner Cobbs, who was sympathetic to the ecclesiological Gothic movement. Though in poor condition when nominated, it kept most of its original fabric.
82002008.heading: Statement of Significance

01001407.summary: The Carnegie Library, built around 1904, is part of the Alabama A&M University Historic District, significant for its collegiate Neoclassical Revival architecture and campus planning. Andrew Carnegie gave $12,000 to the Normal school for a library; when the first building burned the year it was built, Carnegie paid again to replace it. The two-story brick library, with its symmetry and pedimented portico, recalls Greek and Roman temples. The district's eleven Neoclassical buildings reflect a nationwide twentieth-century trend in campus design.
01001407.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

73000358.summary: The Domestic Science Building, erected in 1911, is one of the oldest buildings on the campus of Alabama Agricultural and Mechanical University, which began in 1875 as the Huntsville Normal School through the efforts of William Hooper Councill, a formerly enslaved man, to train Black teachers. It was funded by the Robert R. McCormick family of Chicago before the founding of the McCormick Foundation, and it is the only building on a predominantly Black college campus given directly by the family. The school invited North Alabama families to bring their produce and meat to the building to be canned under the supervision of teachers and students.
73000358.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002055.summary: The Steger-Nance House in Maysville, probably built around 1854 shortly after Dr. Francis Epps Harris Steger bought the lot in 1853, is associated with several prominent local citizens: doctors Steger and Isaac W. Howard, who provided the community's medical care, and Rev. Thomas Maddin, a prominent Methodist minister. It is also architecturally significant for its very intact simple Greek Revival interior trim. The house applies stylistic detail to the basic Federal-period house type of the area, three bays wide and one room deep with a rear ell.
82002055.heading: Statement of Significance

83003521.summary: The U.S. Snagboat Montgomery is a steam-powered, stern-wheel river work boat built in 1926 by the Charleston Drydock and Machine Company for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Snagboats kept Southern rivers open to commercial traffic by removing trees, sunken logs, and other debris and by helping maintain locks. The Montgomery worked on the Alabama and Coosa Rivers until 1933, then on the Black Warrior and Tombigbee until 1959, and then on the Apalachicola, Chattahoochee, and Flint Rivers until it retired in 1982. It is one of the last operational stern-wheel, steam-powered work boats in the United States, with its original boiler and engines.
83003521.heading: Statement of Significance

73000354.summary: The Donnell House was built in 1840 by Robert Donnell, an early religious leader in North Alabama who helped compile the Confession of Faith and Discipline of the Cumberland Presbyterian Church. Born in North Carolina in 1784, he was ordained by the Cumberland Presbytery in Tennessee in 1811 and later spent the rest of his life in Athens. After his death in 1855, the house served many educational uses: the Athens Male College opened there in 1869, it later became part of the city school campus, and in 1889 it was deeded to the North Alabama Experiment Station and Agricultural School. The city took it back in 1936 for use by the high school.
73000354.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73000344.summary: Overton Farm is one of the earliest surviving pioneer homesteads in Northwest Alabama and one of the few early sites that keeps many of its original outbuildings. Abner Overton of Raleigh, North Carolina, first came to Alabama in 1815 peddling tobacco and in 1817 claimed 160 acres on Bear Creek, registering the land in Mississippi Territory. After marrying Judy May in 1819, he began a one-room log cabin. The core of the surviving log house was built before 1838, and some sources say the 1819 cabin became the nucleus of a five-room log home, two rooms of which survive.
73000344.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

00000139.summary: The George Jude House, also called the David and Lucy Crutcher House, is a one-and-a-half-story log dogtrot built around 1812, among the earliest surviving log houses in Madison County. It is an excellent example of an early nineteenth-century vernacular house form; the dogtrot was a popular choice of Alabama's yeoman farmers. Its loft rooms and original L-plan staircase are almost pristine. The open dogtrot passage was enclosed in recent decades, and the Jude family cemetery stands nearby.
00000139.heading: Statement of Significance

84000643.summary: The Blackburn House is a fine and very well-preserved example of a story-and-a-half 'saltbox' house with a nicely proportioned Italianate portico. It was built around 1873 by Edward Alexander Blackburn (1840-1899), and the small community of Blackburn grew up around it. Its interior keeps original nineteenth-century details, including trim and built-in cupboards.
84000643.heading: Statement of Significance

82002047.summary: The old Athens Main Post Office, built in 1931-32 to designs by Britt Alderman of Atlanta, is a good example of twentieth-century Neo-Classical Revival architecture, with a well-articulated limestone colonnade. It makes good use of quality materials, including limestone, marble, and granite, in a well-proportioned and restrained design. Standing on a prominent site near the county courthouse, it reflects the importance and craftsmanship still given to post offices in moderate-sized towns early in the Depression.
82002047.heading: Statement of Significance

82002053.summary: The Phelps-Jones House, probably built around 1818-20, is one of the oldest buildings in Alabama with features of academic architectural style. It belongs to the Federal period and has much-modified Adamesque details, but its overall form has a solid Georgian character from the eighteenth century. It reflects a conservative building tradition carried west by country builders from the Atlantic states, seen in its heavy window muntins, Flemish-bond brickwork with gauged lintels, and provincial Federal woodwork inside. The land was bought by Virginian James Browning in 1818, and a rise in its tax value soon after suggests when the house was built.
82002053.heading: Statement of Significance

85000254.summary: Founders Hall is the main building of the Athens State College Historic District, which is significant for its role in the early development of advanced education for women in Alabama. The school was chartered in 1843 as the Female Institute of the Tennessee Annual Conference and is generally accepted as the oldest Methodist college for women in Alabama. Its curriculum included the natural sciences and mathematics, unusual at a time when women were rarely offered such scholarly studies. Founders Hall, completed around 1843, is one of the oldest surviving buildings built for women's higher education in the state.
85000254.heading: Statement of Significance

71001070.summary: The Alabama Great Southern Railroad Passenger Depot in Fort Payne, built in 1890-91 in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, is a fine example of boom-town architecture and one of the few surviving nineteenth-century railroad stations in Alabama. Fort Payne boomed after the Fort Payne Coal and Iron Company formed in 1889, with mainly New England investors pouring in, and the town grew from 500 people in 1888 to 2,698 in 1890. The first train stopped at the station on October 21, 1891. The boom ended when coal and iron proved scarce, but the depot remained in use until passenger service ended in 1970.
71001070.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

86001043.summary: The Governor George Smith Houston House, now the Houston Memorial Library, is significant as the home of George Smith Houston (1811-1879) from 1845 until his death. Houston served nine terms in Congress between 1841 and 1861, and his election as governor in 1874, as the first Democratic governor since the Civil War, marked the end of Reconstruction in Alabama. He was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1879 but died before completing his term. The house, probably built in the 1830s, is also a good local example of Federal-period architecture with Greek Revival and later Victorian features.
86001043.heading: Statement of Significance

74002262.summary: The Fort Payne Opera House is a boom-town theater from the years after the Fort Payne Coal and Iron Company was organized in 1889, when New England investors poured money into Fort Payne, promoted as the 'little Chicago of the South.' The town grew from 500 people in 1888 to 2,698 in 1890, then shrank to 1,078 by 1900 when the boom collapsed. Planned in 1888 among the company's boom buildings, the opera house hosted performers, lecturers, and musicians for its New England clientele. After it closed in 1893 it changed hands many times; one owner was Milford W. Howard, the only Populist ever elected to Congress from Alabama, who wrote, directed, and acted in plays there.
74002262.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92000637.summary: This boundary increase adds the 1927 Annex, or 'New Mill,' to the Alabama Builders' Hardware Manufacturing Company complex, better known as the W. B. Davis Hosiery Mill. The complex is significant for its role in the growth and revival of Fort Payne's industry in the early twentieth century. Chattanooga hosiery manufacturer W. B. Davis acquired the plant in the early 1900s, and it became the main workplace for many local people and a training ground for many local hosiery makers, helping Fort Payne earn the title 'Sock Capital of the World.' The Annex, designed by J. E. Sirrine and Company, housed Banner knitting machines.
92000637.heading: Statement of Significance

93000763.summary: Cedar Crest is a significant example of a Canebrake plantation house and a good local interpretation of the Greek Revival cottage. The one-and-a-half-story house was built in 1850 by enslaved people owned by Kimbrough Cassells Dubose, a wealthy planter who moved his family and enslaved workers that year from the Darlington District of South Carolina to northeast Marengo County. A log cabin on the property, believed to have been the overseer's house, is one of the few surviving examples of log construction in the Canebrake. The house keeps a high degree of integrity.
93000763.heading: Statement of Significance

82002067.summary: Grace Episcopal Church, built in 1892-93 near Mt. Meigs in eastern Montgomery County, is a good example of a small, late nineteenth-century rural Gothic Revival church and shows how long the style remained popular for churches. The area was once one of the richest cotton-producing sections in the region, and the church has long been the only Episcopal church there, with a congregation dating back to at least 1846. The designer is unknown, but the simple Carpenter Gothic building was probably built under the supervision of E. S. Armistead, its first senior warden. Apart from a 1970 parish hall, it is essentially unaltered.
82002067.heading: Statement of Significance

93000598.summary: Altwood, built in 1836 as a log dogtrot house and later modified to resemble the Tidewater cottages of the Atlantic seaboard, reflects the Virginia origins of its builders, Richard Henry and Anna Carter Harrison Adams of Charles City County. It shows how settlers carried architectural forms from the Atlantic seaboard to the Alabama frontier. Most Tidewater cottages in Alabama were built in the Tennessee Valley, and Altwood is one of the few in the Black Belt and the only one still standing in the Canebrake. It was moved to its present site in the late 1980s but keeps a high degree of integrity.
93000598.heading: Statement of Significance

74000402.summary: The Ernest McCarty Oliver House (Oliver-Allen-Tucker House) was built in 1895 by Ernest McCarty Oliver in a late Victorian style that had largely passed elsewhere but was then at its height in the South, where Reconstruction had slowed the economy. It is distinguished by a three-story square tower with a steep pyramidal roof. All of its bricks were made on the site from local clay and fired in a kiln Oliver set up. LaFayette merchant Moses Allen and his wife Minnie Stanley Allen bought it in 1904, and their descendants continued to live there.
74000402.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

77000214.summary: The Curtis House (Howze-Culpepper House), built in the 1830s or early 1840s, is a fine example of a house from the early years of the cotton plantation system in Alabama's Black Belt. It served as the town residence of Samuel Curtis, a Revolutionary War veteran from North Carolina who settled in Mississippi Territory in 1805 and had built up a large plantation at Old Spring Hill, about 12 miles southeast of Demopolis, by 1819. He acquired the property in 1836. Like many prosperous planters, he kept a house in town. Much of the nomination text is badly garbled.
77000214.heading: Statement of Significance

77000213.summary: The McCartney-Bone House is one of the finer examples of early brick houses in its area. It was built by James McCartney, one of the county's earliest settlers, and a date of 1826 is inscribed on the attic framing. It is noted for Flemish bond brickwork on all four sides, high-quality brick, an elaborate cornice, and fine woodwork, all unusual refinements for the 1820s there. The central entrance portico dates from 1960. Much of the nomination text is badly garbled, so details are limited.
77000213.heading: Statement of Significance

82002036.summary: The Brown-Proctor House, completed in 1881 for John A. Brown, is mainly significant for its association with John F. Proctor, a prominent attorney and politician who bought it in 1907 and gave it its current appearance. Proctor served in the Alabama House from 1892 to 1895 and the Alabama Senate from 1896 to 1899, was a member of the Alabama Constitutional Convention, and was a court-appointed attorney in the first trial of the Scottsboro Boys in 1931. His family lived in the house until the early 1980s.
82002036.heading: Statement of Significance

75000319.summary: Confederate Park, the public square of Demopolis, has existed since the town's commissioners laid out its street plan on June 10, 1819, setting aside a block of eight lots for public buildings. It is one of the oldest public squares in Alabama and an early example of town planning in the state. From the town's earliest years it has been a central meeting place for business, preaching, and politics, and it is now at the center of the business district. Features include a pond built in 1895, fed by a three-tiered cast iron fountain.
75000319.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000701.summary: The Robert Wilton Burton House, built in 1885, is significant as the home of Robert Wilton Burton (1848-1917), a locally noted poet and one of Auburn's most prominent and beloved citizens. A native of Camden County, Georgia, Burton published four poems between 1880 and 1885 and used the money to build this house, which he called 'The Four Story Cottage.' He lived there until his death and served Auburn in a variety of public roles. The house is also a good example of a late nineteenth-century vernacular cottage.
80000701.heading: Statement of Significance

78000502.summary: The Ashe Cottage, built in 1858 for Dr. William Cincinnatus Ashe, is a fine example of the early influence of the Gothic Revival style on Alabama houses and one of the few antebellum Gothic homes left in the Canebrake. Like many mid-nineteenth-century Alabama houses aiming for the new look, it is Gothic more in its details, such as twin peaked gables, pointed gable windows, and decorative bargeboards, than in its overall design. Dr. Ashe, born in 1815, was one of the leading physicians and surgeons of Demopolis from the 1840s to 1860. The house was moved a few blocks from its original site near the business district.
78000502.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

14000318.summary: The Hezekiah Ford House has statewide architectural significance as one of only a handful of brick I-houses in Alabama from the early settlement period, with a vernacular interpretation of the Federal style outside and in its interior woodwork. It shows how prosperous yeoman farmers on the Alabama frontier sought to emulate the taste of the planter elite. It was likely built around 1820, when Hezekiah Ford received a patent for the land. After his widow Nancy died in 1844, his brother John Ford inherited the house and probably enlarged the rear wing to two stories.
14000318.heading: Summary Paragraph

98000107.summary: The Scottsboro Memphis and Charleston Railroad Depot, begun in late 1860 and completed in 1861 for $2,000, is significant for its association with the transportation history of Scottsboro and Jackson County and with the Memphis and Charleston Railroad. Chartered in 1850, the line was the only east-west railroad running entirely across the Confederacy, making it a major Union target during the Civil War. On January 8, 1865, a brief but intense skirmish took place at the depot, where soldiers of the 101st and 110th U.S. Colored Infantry had been sent to guard the water tanks and depot against Confederate raiders.
98000107.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

74000425.summary: The Lyon-Lamar House (Lyon Hall), built in 1853, blends the massive columned portico of the Greek Revival with the delicate cast iron work popular on the Gulf Coast, and its plan shares features with Sturdivant Hall in Selma. It was built by George Gaines Lyon, a prominent lawyer and planter who advised governors, served as a Confederate sequestrator and commissioner and as a governor's aide for West Alabama, and became Commissioner of Immigration in 1875. He was a grandnephew of George S. Gaines and General Edmund Pendleton Gaines, and his wife Anne was a member of the prominent Glover family.
74000425.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

70000105.summary: Bluff Hall is one of Alabama's oldest, largest, and most impressive Greek Revival river mansions. It stands on White Bluff, the 1817 landing site of the Bonapartist exiles on the Tombigbee River, and was the home of F. S. Lyon, a prominent lawyer, planter, state bank manager, and Confederate congressman. The first part was built in 1832, and the columns and west wing were added in the late 1840s. Its six thick, massive columns give the front a fortress-like strength, softened by graceful doorways and wrought iron balcony railings.
70000105.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85002929.summary: The Park and Bandstand in Gainesville was the social center of the town in the mid-nineteenth century, used for concerts, political rallies, and celebrations. The pavilion is a rare surviving mid-nineteenth-century structure of its type and an example of Greek Revival design applied to a bandstand. It appears on the earliest Sanborn map of Gainesville, from November 1884, and may date from the 1840s or 1850s. The small triangular park lies just north of the town's commercial district, once faced by business buildings and the Gainesville branch of the State Bank.
85002929.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85002930.summary: The Coffin Shop is a small frame building significant as the only survivor of Gainesville's mid-nineteenth-century commercial district along McKee and State Streets. Long known locally as 'the Coffin Shop,' it was probably built around 1860-70 by Edward N. Kring as an adjunct to his carpenter shop, and coffins he built were displayed there. Its scalloped bargeboard trim was a feature of other early Gainesville commercial buildings now gone. It was moved about 12 feet back from the highway around 1970.
85002930.heading: Statement of Significance

85002928.summary: The Laura Watson House, built around the turn of the twentieth century if not earlier, is an unusually intact example of a house of a small Black landowner in Alabama at that time. It is a good example of a vanishing vernacular house type with a spreading roof, a full-width front porch, and a rear shed. The whitewashed house was built for the Watson family and occupied by Laura Watson and her son Booker. Its setting includes small outbuildings, such as a privy and corncrib, and a cedar fence.
85002928.heading: Statement of Significance

74000424.summary: The Glover Mausoleum, built around 1856, is one of the largest and most imposing mausoleums in Alabama, notable for its Greek Revival design and the rarity of above-ground burials in the Black Belt. It was built by Mary Ann Diven Glover, second wife of Allen Glover, after his death in 1840. Allen Glover, a pioneer merchant and planter from South Carolina, was one of the founders of Demopolis; he moved to Marengo County in 1819 with his family, brothers, enslaved people, and livestock, and traded with the Indians while building a large planting interest.
74000424.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000172.summary: The Governor's Mansion is one of the finer examples of Neoclassical Revival architecture in Alabama and has served as the official residence of Alabama's governors since the state bought it in 1950. It was built in 1907 by Robert F. Ligon Jr., a former mayor of Tuskegee and son of a lieutenant governor, who served as clerk of the state Supreme Court, adjutant general during the Spanish-American War, and later quartermaster general. The Ligon family sold it to the state for $100,000 after his death. Governor Gordon Persons was the first to live there, followed by governors including nationally known figures such as James E. Folsom.
72000172.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000657.summary: The U.S. Post Office in Demopolis was built in 1910-12 by A. Anderson and Company of St. Louis, at a time when the Treasury Department was responsible for designing and building federal post offices. The building continues a long postal history: the first post office serving any part of present Demopolis was at Aigleville, the village of French emigrants, and operated only from December 1817 to January 1818. Postal service reopened in December 1819 and has continued since.
84000657.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83003453.summary: The Demopolis Public School, built in 1913-14, was the first school in Demopolis built specifically for public education, and until a high school was built in 1937 it was the only public school for white residents of the town. It was designed by Frank Lockwood, a leading Alabama architect of the period. It is a good example of the neighborhood and small-town public schools built across Alabama in the early twentieth century, with a wide center-hall plan, restrained Beaux Arts form, classical portico, and a rear auditorium with an inclined floor and stage. Low stair risers were reportedly designed for the young pupils on the first floor.
83003453.heading: Statement of Significance

82002070.summary: The Col. Green G. Mobley House, built around 1845, is one of West Alabama's most sophisticated Greek Revival houses and the most imposing surviving antebellum mansion in Gainesville, a town noted for its antebellum homes. Its pedimented Ionic portico and interior and exterior trim are based on published designs by Asher Benjamin and Minard Lafever, leading promoters of the Greek Revival. It was built for Colonel Green G. Mobley (1806-1877) of Fairfield District, South Carolina, and his Vermont-born wife Henrietta. After their deaths it became a boarding house until it was bought and restored in 1935.
82002070.heading: Statement of Significance

08000434.summary: The Vines Funeral Home and Ambulance Service, built in 1952 by Julius Summers Vines, is significant as an example of a mid-twentieth-century rural African American-owned funeral home. Undertaking was one of the few professions open to African Americans under segregation, and Black funeral directors stood with doctors and lawyers at the top of many communities' economic and social hierarchy. Vines, a licensed mortician at a time when other local funeral homes were not licensed, played a leadership role in LaFayette and earned respect from Black and white residents alike. The business was later the only funeral home in Alabama still operating an ambulance service.
08000434.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

92000034.summary: The Urquhart House is a log house built in stages, beginning with a log pen probably built between about 1813 and 1830 on land transferred to Allen Urquhart in December 1813. It was later expanded with another pen, a center hall, a west room likely from the 1870s, a kitchen, and porches, and one room was improved with Federal-style trim comparable to more ambitious houses of the period. The land later passed to Robert Strong and then to his daughter Mary A. Strong. The site also includes a privy, garage, a 1926 barn, and a spring. The nomination's statement of significance is brief, so this summary relies mainly on its description.
92000034.heading: Statement of Significance

76000319.summary: The Oaks, or Abraham Ricks Plantation, is one of the finest remaining plantation homes in the Tennessee Valley. It combines an early weatherboarded log house, one of the finest and best preserved of its type from the area's first years of settlement, with a large frame house finished by 1832, whose fine trim and classical pediment reflect the planter class's prosperity in the late 1820s. Built within about ten years of each other, the two sections illustrate the rapid shift from frontier to plantation era. Abraham Ricks came from Halifax, North Carolina, in the early 1820s with his family and enslaved workers, bought this land in 1826, and hired a local builder named Dial to build the main house, which became a social center of the area.
76000319.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000167.summary: Gaineswood, a National Historic Landmark, is one of Alabama's most remarkable Greek Revival mansions. Its builder, planter Nathan Bryan Whitfield, served as his own architect, spending more than fifteen years on the house, which was completed in 1860; he drew on architectural handbooks including Vitruvius, Stuart and Revett, and Minard Lafever, and ordered relief ornament from Charles Frederick Bielefeld of London. As the work went on, Whitfield kept up with shifting national tastes, adding Italianate features such as balustrades to the Greek Revival design. The house grew around an earlier small wooden structure on land Whitfield bought in 1843 from George S. Gaines.
72000167.heading: Statement of Significance

71000100.summary: The Lowndes County Courthouse, built in 1856 in the Greek Revival style after the 1832 courthouse was condemned as unsafe, is one of only four antebellum courthouses still in use in Alabama. It was considerably altered around 1905, but its basic design remains. Hayneville, now a quiet Black Belt village, was reputed in antebellum days to be the greatest gambling town of its size in the country, with a racetrack, eight gambling houses, and cockpits on the square. The probate judge when the courthouse was built was Edward Hampton Cook, a second cousin of Confederate General Wade Hampton.
71000100.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000423.summary: The Foscue-Whitfield House, a Federal-style country house built in 1840 with a front addition in 1849, is an outstanding example of its type in the South and was occupied by the same family for generations. Augustus Foscue of North Carolina, who acquired land in Marengo County by 1831 and owned much of present-day Demopolis, built it as the residence for his large plantation. In 1842 he took in the family of General Nathan Bryan Whitfield, later the builder of Gaineswood, and in 1855 his daughter Mary Alice married Whitfield's son, Dr. Bryan Watkins Whitfield. She inherited the house when her father died in 1861.
74000423.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

15000433.summary: The Shiloh Missionary Baptist Church Cemetery has served as a burial ground for local African American residents since at least 1881, the earliest identified marker date, and probably since the church was founded around 1870. It is an intact remnant of an early post-Reconstruction African American community and the oldest known property associated with the Shiloh community of northern Macon County. It also has statewide significance for its association with victims of the U.S. Public Health Service Syphilis Study who are buried there. They include Charlie Pollard, who testified to Congress about the study's abuses in 1973 and was buried here in 2000.
15000433.heading: Summary Paragraph

82002056.summary: Greenlawn, the William Madison Otey House, built in 1849-50, is the lone survivor of several mid-nineteenth-century plantation houses of its scale that once stood in northern Madison County. As first built, its two-tiered Italianate porch in front of a Greek Revival core expressed the growing eclecticism of the late antebellum years. An early twentieth-century renovation remade it as a white-columned mansion, matching a later generation's romantic image of the plantation house, so it reflects both the past and the early 1900s view of the Southern past. The land, settled by Virginian Walter Otey, has been farmed by the same family for more than 150 years.
82002056.heading: Statement of Significance

99000465.summary: The Pleasant Hill Presbyterian Church, also known as Mt. Carmel Cumberland Presbyterian Church, built in 1851, is an outstanding example of the vernacular Greek Revival style adapted for a church. Its two-column in-antis temple front and austere classical details show how popular Greek Revival design was even in remote areas, and how it spread through this prosperous antebellum plantation community. It is one of several Greek Revival buildings that survive around the almost-vanished village of Pleasant Hill. The surrounding cemetery has more than 140 grave markers dating from the 1830s to the 1980s.
99000465.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

94000689.summary: Allen Grove, built in 1857 by Demopolis builder David Rudisill, is a significant example of a Canebrake plantation house with a double-pile plan and Greek Revival influence. The house and its outbuildings show the styles, construction methods, and craftsmanship used in the Canebrake from 1830 to 1942, and it retains a high degree of integrity. The Allen family's plantation began when John Gray Allen, a North Carolina native who came to Alabama in 1841, moved to Spring Hill in 1847 and bought about 300 acres from Edwin Glover.
94000689.heading: Statement of Significance

10000522.summary: The Shiloh Missionary Baptist Church, built around 1919, and the Shiloh Rosenwald School, built around 1922, form a historic district in Notasulga with local, state, and national significance. The school, built with help from the Julius Rosenwald School Building Fund on a standard Rosenwald plan, educated the community's African American children under Jim Crow segregation, and the church supported it financially and physically. The two buildings stand side by side because the landowner who donated the land required it. The district is also nationally significant for its association with the U.S. Public Health Service Syphilis Study in Macon County (1932-1975).
10000522.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

76000353.summary: McCosh Grist Mill was the only known stone grist mill still standing in Alabama and one of the oldest mills in the eastern part of the state, notable for using millstones as decoration. It is believed to have been built in the early 1870s by James Eichelburger McCosh after flooding destroyed an earlier mill, though some local traditions date it to the 1840s and his grandfather Jacob Eichelburger, a pioneer industrialist who built the cotton mills at nearby Rock Mills. A 1985 letter in the nomination file reports that the mill, then at West Point Lake, burned around February 7, 1985.
76000353.heading: Statement of Significance

88003078.summary: The Old Brick Presbyterian Church, probably built in the 1830s or 1840s, is among Alabama's oldest surviving church buildings. It is significant for its Federal design, with pilasters and an arched doorway, built by local labor of locally made brick. Inside, the original slave gallery and hand-hewn pews preserve the separation of men from women and of Black and white members. After the Civil War another church was built for Black members, but many chose to remain. The church also served a judicial role in the rural community of Bricksville, disciplining members for drinking, cursing, slander, and other offenses.
88003078.heading: Statement of Significance

04000232.summary: The Vance C. Larmore House, a two-story frame I-house built around 1845 with Victorian influences, is one of the earliest and most intact houses of its type in the region. It is the first permanent home and only surviving resource associated with Vance C. Larmore, who married in Washington County, Virginia, in January 1838 and came with his wife Margaret to the Big Wills Valley around that year, during the county's earliest settlement. Local historians credit Larmore with important contributions to the county's architecture, agriculture, and transportation.
04000232.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100011916.summary: WZZA Radio Station in Tuscumbia, built in 1960 and expanded in 1980 with its distinctive concrete-block facade, is significant as the first and only locally owned and federally licensed African American radio station in northwest Alabama. It is also associated with Robert Carl Bailey, the entrepreneur, community activist, and concert promoter who became the station's general manager in 1972 and part-owner in 1977, and who worked throughout his life to advance civil rights and empower the Black community. The station is still on the air.
100011916.heading: Summary Paragraph

73000355.summary: The Sulphur Trestle Fort Site in Limestone County was the scene of a major military action in September 1864 between Confederate General Nathan Bedford Forrest and the Union garrison guarding the railroad trestle over Sulphur Creek. The Nashville-to-Decatur railroad was an important supply line for General Sherman in Atlanta. Forrest's raid began by bluffing the Union commander at Athens into surrendering, then moved north against the trestle fort. A nearby antebellum brick house served as a hospital after the battle.
73000355.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

01001297.summary: The New Hope Rosenwald School, built in 1915, is significant as a school built with help from the Julius Rosenwald School Building Fund, which from 1913 to 1937 helped finance more than 5,000 schools, teachers' homes, and shops for African American education in fifteen Southern states. The fund was the most important philanthropic force aiding African Americans in the first half of the twentieth century, helping more Black children attend school longer, with better-trained teachers in better buildings. The school follows Design No. 11-A, drawn by W. A. Hazel while teaching architecture at Tuskegee Institute, and was once the focal point of its community.
01001297.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

82002004.summary: The John and Archibald Christian House, built in the 1830s, still reflects in its form, proportions, and materials the strong Jeffersonian influence seen in a number of early Tennessee Valley buildings, despite later additions and the loss of its two-tiered Roman Doric portico. Its surviving wooden Roman Doric entablature shows that the influence extended to exterior details. Its unusual two-room first-floor plan, rare in a house of this size and refinement, supports the tradition that it was built as a joint home for the brothers John and Archibald Christian. The site was among lands the U.S. government granted to the University of Alabama in 1824 for resale.
82002004.heading: Statement of Significance

13000365.summary: The Skyline Commissary, built in 1935 of locally quarried sandstone in the Colonial Revival style, was the cooperative store of Skyline Farms, a New Deal resettlement community originally called the Cumberland Mountain Farms Project. Run by the Skyline Farms Cooperative Association, it supplied the colonists' goods and served as a gathering place at the heart of the community. It is perhaps the most intact stone building built at Skyline Farms. A rear addition was built in 1937.
13000365.heading: Statement of Significance

82001603.summary: Locust Hill, the John Daniel Rather House, built in 1823 for William and Catherine Winter of Prince William County, Virginia, is one of the earliest remaining houses in Tuscumbia. It is noted for Flemish bond brick on two sides and fine Adamesque mantels reputedly made by local cabinetmaker Andrew Braden; an Eastlake veranda was added later. It served as headquarters for a Union general in 1863. In 1865 it was acquired by Capt. John Taylor Rather, an early Alabama settler and politician, and it was later also the home of a local author and artist.
82001603.heading: Statement of Significance

72000166.summary: The Half-Chance Bridge, an iron bridge built before 1880 by the King Iron Bridge Manufacturing Company of Cleveland, Ohio, is one of the South's few remaining examples of a bridge design common from 1860 to 1890. After 1880 most bridges were built of steel and later concrete, and most iron bridges were replaced or bypassed. It stands in the Marengo County Black Belt, the heart of the antebellum Cotton Kingdom, on the Half-Chance Road leading to Linden, a town settled by French Napoleonic exiles from the short-lived Vine and Olive Colony.
72000166.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

00001029.summary: The C. S. Golden House is an outstanding vernacular Queen Anne cottage and the only building in Thomaston that fully represents the Queen Anne style, though several others have Victorian details. It shows the style's romantic verticality, irregular form, and layered detail. Its interior is largely intact, with a 12-foot-wide central hall, 14-foot ceilings, heart pine floors, and original mantels, and its original bathroom is said to have been the first in Thomaston. Mr. Golden was the son of a wealthy Columbus, Georgia, foundry owner who married Mary Louise Buck of Marengo County.
00001029.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

00001026.summary: The Patrick Farrish House is an outstanding example of vernacular Craftsman architecture and the most intact of Thomaston's Craftsman and bungalow houses, which date from a later building wave between 1910 and 1949. It was nominated individually because it lies outside the original city limits. Its probable builder, farmer Patrick Farrish, came to Thomaston from the Camden area and followed the town founder's plan for a first-quality modern town by building a modern-style home. Notable interior features include Craftsman built-in bookcases and cabinetry.
00001026.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100001876.summary: St. John's Episcopal Church in Tuscumbia, built in 1852, altered in 1876, and consecrated in 1879, is the oldest surviving Carpenter Gothic church in Alabama. It represents the shift in Southern churches from Greek Revival to Gothic Revival architecture, part of a broader movement that began with the Ecclesiological movement in England and spread to the American frontier. It is an early version of a form that became extremely popular in Episcopal church architecture for the next hundred years, making it important for understanding later developments in the state.
100001876.heading: Summary Paragraph

01000284.summary: The Tuskegee Airmen National Historic Site preserves Moton Field, built by Tuskegee Institute between 1940 and 1942 with financing from the Julius Rosenwald Fund as the primary flight school for the Tuskegee Airmen, the first African American military pilots. Designed largely by architect Edward C. Miller and engineer G. L. Washington and built by engineer and contractor Archie A. Alexander, the field had hangars, a control tower, and support buildings. The National Park Service found that the Tuskegee airfields commemorate the birth of Black participation in U.S. military aviation. This summary is based on the 1998 NPS Special Resource Study filed for the site, as no nomination form was available.
01000284.heading: Moton Field/Tuskegee Airmen Special Resource Study

00001024.summary: The Thomaston Colored Institute opened in 1910, two years after Thomaston built its segregated white Marengo County High School. Privately owned by the West Alabama Primitive Baptist Association, its unusually substantial two-story brick building reflects the efforts of African American churches to secure education for their children after Reconstruction, the 'New South' outlook of Thomaston's founder, and the statewide push to improve rural schools. Its common bond brick construction was widely used by Tuskegee-trained builders, and it may have been designed by someone with Tuskegee training. It held five classrooms downstairs and two classrooms and an auditorium upstairs.
00001024.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

88000511.summary: Johnson's Woods, built around 1835-37, is one of the best early Classical Revival houses surviving in the Tennessee Valley with regional characteristics, including an L-shaped plan with two interior passages and two formal entrance porticoes. Its main staircase is exceptional for the period, and its Federal mantels were copied from popular pattern books. It also has statewide significance as one of the best-preserved collections of mid-nineteenth-century agricultural buildings in Alabama, with a plantation house, eight outbuildings, and an early cedar-lined path from a Tennessee Valley cotton plantation.
88000511.heading: Statement of Significance

84000749.summary: The Felix Grundy Norman House, probably built around 1851, is one of the finest, if not the finest, surviving one-story Greek Revival cottages in Tuscumbia, where many once stood. It is the only one with porticoes on two street sides and the only one with three-part windows flanking each portico, and it keeps most of its original interior woodwork. Felix Grundy Norman practiced law in Tuscumbia from 1841 until his death in 1885, served many years as mayor, sat in the state legislature, and was Master of the Grand Lodge of Freemasons in Alabama from 1845 to 1847.
84000749.heading: Statement of Significance

90000919.summary: The New Market United Methodist Church is architecturally significant for combining two major influences: pattern-book church design of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and the 'Akron Plan' developed by Methodists in Ohio. Its design follows Andrea Palladio's sixteenth-century Villa Rotonda in Italy, modified for the Akron Plan, with three-column Ionic porticoes on two sides and a quarter-circle auditorium and Sunday school alcoves on the others. The church keeps most of its original features, including its octagonal segmented dome.
90000919.heading: Statement of Significance

82002005.summary: The William Winston House is one of the few remaining antebellum brick houses in Tuscumbia, a large, well-detailed house whose bullseye-incised stone lintels reflect Middle Tennessee traditions. It keeps a continuous spiral staircase and finely fluted door and window facings. Begun by a local merchant, it was bought and completed around 1840 by planter William Winston and his second wife, Judith. Their daughter married Robert Lindsay, governor of Alabama from 1870 to 1872, and Winston's son John Anthony Winston became the first Alabama-born governor of the state (1854-1857).
82002005.heading: Statement of Significance

88001348.summary: The New Market Presbyterian Church, built in 1888 by church member Lem Teague, is an excellent and little-altered example of the small clapboard rural Gothic Revival church, a rapidly vanishing type in north Alabama. It is the oldest essentially intact religious building in northeast Madison County. Its lancet openings and high, steep roof reflect the solid, unpretentious dignity of a rural Presbyterian congregation. Inside, a high barrel-vaulted ceiling with patterned varnished woodwork gives the nave a feeling of spare good quality.
88001348.heading: Statement of Significance

05000838.summary: The Townsend Farmhouse is significant for its association with the settlement of Jackson County and as a good example of a modest mid-nineteenth-century farmhouse in northern Alabama. A log dwelling on the property was built around 1860, about when the land, previously reserved by the state as school land, passed into private hands, marking the close of the county's main settlement period that began in the 1820s. The main farmhouse was built for Daniel Townsend soon after he acquired the property in 1866.
05000838.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

72000163.summary: Noble Hall is a Greek Revival plantation house built in 1854 for Addison Frazier, a wealthy cotton planter, as the center of a 2,000-acre plantation. Frazier hired Henry Foster of Kentucky, who brought his own carpenters, plasterers, and stonemasons. The house has few frills, but its symmetry and solid construction give it an air of elegance, with a two-story veranda on four Doric columns. It reflects the prosperous cotton-growing years before the Civil War.
72000163.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

66000151.summary: Tuskegee Institute National Historic Site commemorates Tuskegee Institute, a pioneering school for African Americans chartered by the State of Alabama in 1881. As its first president, Booker T. Washington put into practice a program of industrial and vocational education designed to improve the economic conditions of Black Southerners, and in the early twentieth century he was regarded as the leading figure of his race. The institute had far-reaching effects and became one of the outstanding Black schools in the United States. The campus was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1966.
66000151.heading: National Historic Landmark documentation

80000364.summary: Grey Columns, built from 1854 to 1857 as the center of a 5,000-acre cotton plantation, is an excellent example of a late Greek Revival plantation house with some Italianate details. It is by far the most magnificent of the many antebellum mansions in Tuskegee and ranks among the finest surviving plantation houses in the South. Despite later additions, it keeps much of its original appearance, though its outbuildings and farmland are gone. The property was owned by the Varner family for about 120 years.
80000364.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002979.summary: The U.S. Post Office in Auburn was built in 1933 by the Charles H. Barnes Construction Company of Logansport, Indiana, and opened on October 1, 1933. The nomination calls it one of the most impressive postal buildings in Alabama. The red brick building, laid in Flemish bond, has an arched loggia and arched windows in a Georgian Revival style with strong Federal influence. A large 1968 addition matches the original so closely it is hard to detect. The nomination offers little discussion of significance beyond these facts.
83002979.heading: Statement of Significance

06000437.summary: The Muscle Shoals Sound Studio at 3614 Jackson Highway is significant in American music history, ranking alongside Sun and Stax in Memphis, Chess in Chicago, and Motown in Detroit. From 1969 to 1978 the modest concrete block building housed the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section, which produced more than 50 gold and platinum hits and hundreds of albums. Artists who recorded there spanned pop, rock, blues, funk, soul, reggae, and country, including Cher, the Rolling Stones, Paul Simon, Willie Nelson, Joe Cocker, Rod Stewart, and Bob Seger. The building keeps a high degree of integrity.
06000437.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

03000423.summary: The Old President's Mansion, now Katharine Cooper Cater Hall, was built in 1915 at Alabama Polytechnic Institute (now Auburn University) and symbolizes the school's growth in the early twentieth century. The Neoclassical house, with a two-story Ionic portico and symmetrical wings, was designed by Joseph Hudnut, a professor of architecture at API, and cost $17,000. President Charles Coleman Thach oversaw its construction and was the first president to live there. After a new president's home opened in 1938, it became the campus Social Center, home to the Dean of Women and a hub for women students and campus social life.
03000423.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

08001332.summary: The Tankersley Rosenwald School, built around 1922, is a statewide significant illustration of African Americans' struggle for quality education in segregated rural Alabama, where poverty and racism kept Black children from good, safe schools. Of almost 400 Rosenwald schools built in Alabama between 1913 and 1932, thirteen were in Montgomery County, and Tankersley and Cecil are the only two still standing. Before it was built, the community used the old Pythian Masonic Hall as a school. It served as a segregated elementary school for Black children until it closed with integration in 1967.
08001332.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

73000351.summary: The Auburn Players Theater, originally the Presbyterian Church, is the last remaining church from Auburn's early period and one of the three oldest buildings in the city. It was designed and built in 1850 by Edwin Reese, a planter, architect, and ruling elder of the new Presbyterian congregation, on a lot donated by Auburn founder John Harper, with bricks and labor supplied by people enslaved on Reese's plantation. The first church meeting was held in September 1851. Like many Alabama buildings, it served as a Confederate hospital during the Civil War, and it later became the Auburn University Little Theatre.
73000351.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

95001022.summary: Butler Chapel AME Zion Church is significant for its role in Tuskegee's grassroots civil rights movement, a reflection of the Black church's role in the national movement of the 1950s and 1960s. After Black voters were gerrymandered out of Tuskegee's city limits, Macon County Black residents gathered here on June 25, 1957, to launch the 'Crusade for Citizenship,' which held mass meetings until 1964 with Butler Chapel as its flagship church. The Tuskegee Civic Association had sought mass Black voter registration for almost two decades. A marker beside the church notes the site of the shanty where Tuskegee Institute was first established.
95001022.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

78000495.summary: The Macon County Courthouse, designed in 1905 by J. W. Golucke and Company and built for $42,000, is an unusually impressive building for this rural county and one of the finest turn-of-the-century courthouses in Alabama. Its central tower, flanking octagonal turrets, and twin west towers give it a strong Richardsonian Romanesque character. Overlooking the town square, it has been the center of county political and social life. It is the fourth courthouse on the square, following a log courthouse of 1833, a brick one of 1841, and a Greek Revival courthouse of 1855.
78000495.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

00000134.summary: The E. L. Newman Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel prefabricated houses made by the Lustron Corporation from 1946 to 1950 in response to the nationwide housing shortage after World War II. Its porcelain-enameled steel panels, metal roof, and built-in cabinets and shelves reflect Lustron's acclaimed factory production line, distribution, and marketing system. The interior looks much as it did when it was built, with its original metal wall and ceiling panels uncovered.
00000134.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

87002390.summary: The Old Rotation at Auburn University, started in 1896 by J. F. Duggar, is the oldest continuous cotton experiment in the United States, possibly in the world, and the third oldest continuous field crop experiment in the country. It was the first experiment to demonstrate the benefits of rotating cotton with other crops and to measure the contribution of nitrogen-restoring winter legumes to cotton production. It continues to document the long-term effects of these systems after nearly a century of cotton growing in the same soil.
87002390.heading: Statement of Significance

75000318.summary: The Scott-Yarbrough House, which Colonel Nathaniel J. Scott built in 1847 and called Pebble Hill, is one of the oldest houses in Auburn. Scott was one of four commissioners named when Auburn was incorporated in 1839 and served in the state legislature and senate; secessionist William Lowndes Yancey and his family spent several summers at the house. It was later the home of Dr. Yarbrough, who acquired it in 1912 and served in the state legislature, another important figure in the history of the town and Auburn University. With its pyramidal roof, square columns, and fireside closets, it is typical of the smaller cottages built in Auburn in that period.
75000318.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000317.summary: The Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church, completed in 1870 by its own members, was one of the early Black churches organized after the Civil War and shows a high degree of craftsmanship. During Reconstruction, freedpeople steadily withdrew from white-controlled churches, and the number of Black congregations grew rapidly. Ebenezer was organized before 1868 under Rev. Thomas Glenn, a noted preacher from Columbus, Georgia, and in December 1868 it was one of twenty-seven churches that sent delegates to organize the Colored Baptist Convention of Alabama. Member Mary Glower donated the land.
75000317.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

93000419.summary: The Chambers-Robinson House, built in 1890 for Judson G. and Mary F. Chambers, is a good and intact example of the Queen Anne style popular in the late nineteenth century. The two-story frame house has a steep hipped roof with corbelled chimneys, wall dormers, a wraparound porch with elaborate sawnwork, and a bay window. Inside it keeps an Eastlake stairway, pocket doors, and decorative mantels. Its decorative details show the skill of its craftsmanship.
93000419.heading: Statement of Significance

100010428.summary: This additional documentation covers the Memphis and Charleston Railroad Bridge, which research suggests is Alabama's oldest surviving river bridge and the only one with a double-decked design carrying both rail and pedestrian traffic. Built in its present form in the 1890s, it was the main crossing for all traffic over the Tennessee River in the Florence-Sheffield area in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It connected Florence, Sheffield, and nearby towns with regional trade centers on the railroad such as Memphis and Nashville. The span from Patton Island to Florence, including a 1962 lift section, has been removed, but the remaining spans keep their original design.
100010428.heading: Summary Paragraph

03000231.summary: The Cullars Rotation at Auburn University has studied soil fertility continuously on the same plots since 1911. The cotton-corn-soybean rotation on 42 research plots is the oldest continuous soil fertility study in the South, the second oldest cotton experiment in the world after the nearby Old Rotation, and one of the oldest continuous field research plots in North America. It has served as a teaching tool for Auburn students and researchers from across the country, and it is the only site in the South where students can study plant nutrient deficiencies on five different crops in a single year.
03000231.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance
