08001116.summary: Sunny Slope is one of Auburn's six surviving examples of the single-story, hipped-roof Greek Revival cottage typical of east central Alabama in the late antebellum period. Such houses had lofty, spacious rooms with spare detailing, and just before the Civil War their exteriors took on Greco-Italianate touches such as scrolled brackets. Sunny Slope is one of four of the six with a full-length colonnade recessed beneath the front slope of the main roof, here a six-columned veranda. A dormer added around 1910 is the only significant change to the original facade.
08001116.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96000045.summary: The Dr. J. A. Gorman House, also called the Hanging Cottage, is an excellent example of the bungalow style in Mentone, built of wood and stone in a wooded setting on the brow of a mountain. Its wide veranda with log columns, many windows, stone chimney, and exposed rafters reflect the bungalow movement's aim of blurring indoor and outdoor space. Dr. Gorman, a New Orleans dentist reputed to be the first in the country to use X-rays in treating cavities, came to the area in 1917 and chose the site for its view. The house took five years to build, and locals predicted it would fall over the edge.
96000045.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

78000492.summary: The Rosenbaum House, built in 1940 with a 1948 addition, is an outstanding example of Frank Lloyd Wright's Usonian houses, the only Usonian house Wright enlarged with a major addition, and the only Wright building in Alabama. It is a mature statement of his Usonian work on low-cost housing, with a concrete slab floor with underfloor heating, cypress sandwich walls, brick chimneys supporting flat roofs, a brick service core, and a modular grid. Its strong horizontal lines are emphasized by deep eaves and raked brick joints. Its first owners, Stanley and Mildred Rosenbaum, maintained it in original condition.
78000492.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

100001877.summary: The Maud Lindsay Free Kindergarten, built in 1913, is significant for its role in the development of early childhood education in Alabama during the Progressive Era and for its association with Maud McKnight Lindsay, an important figure in the state's educational history and the progressive movement. The school opened in 1898 as the Florence Free Kindergarten and used several temporary spaces before this Neoclassical cottage was built on Ironside Street. Lindsay's teaching career spanned 1893 to 1941. Although the building has been moved and covered with vinyl siding, it is the most significant property associated with her.
100001877.heading: Summary Paragraph

00000127.summary: The E. H. Darby Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel prefabricated houses made by the Lustron Corporation from 1946 to 1950 to help meet the housing shortage after World War II. It is a fine example of the two-bedroom Westchester model, one of nine in Alabama. Its porcelain-enameled steel panels and built-in cabinets, shelves, and vanity reflect Lustron's acclaimed factory production, distribution, and marketing system.
00000127.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

82002046.summary: The George Coulter House, later known as Mapleton, is probably unexcelled in Alabama as an example of Federal-period craftsmanship and architecture, and its delicate Adamesque interior woodwork, especially in the double drawing rooms, is the most elaborate of its era surviving in the state. Its form and details show the close link between the early architecture of far northern Alabama and that of Middle Tennessee and Kentucky. It was built, presumably in the 1820s, for George Coulter, a planter, lawyer, and military officer who came to Florence from Middle Tennessee and Kentucky.
82002046.heading: Statement of Significance

74000426.summary: The Old Courthouse in Linden, built about 1848 to replace the first Marengo County courthouse, a log building of 1827 that burned, is a two-story building similar in plan to a New York church designed by the firm of Town and Davis. Linden was chosen as county seat in 1821; first called Marengo, it was renamed Hohenlinden after one of Napoleon's victories and later shortened to Linden. The building served as the courthouse until 1902 and was later used as a skating rink, stable, dance hall, and National Guard armory before being sold by the county. It has since been used for Masonic lodge meetings.
74000426.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83003445.summary: The Mentone Springs Hotel, built in 1884-87, is Alabama's only remaining example of the large resort hotels that flourished in the last three decades of the nineteenth century. Of about two dozen resort hotels built in the state in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, only it and the smaller, simpler 1909 Clairmont Springs Hotel are known to survive. It has lost its original wraparound veranda, some interior detail, and a rear wing, but keeps its basic massing, setting, and much of its original design, and enough documentation exists to restore it.
83003445.heading: Statement of Significance

00000135.summary: The William Bowen Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel prefabricated houses the Lustron Corporation made from 1946 to 1950 in response to the nationwide housing shortage after World War II. Its porcelain-enameled steel panels, metal roof, and built-in cabinets, shelves, and closets reflect Lustron's acclaimed factory production, distribution, and marketing system. It also shows features of postwar housing that combined contemporary and traditional design with durability, easy maintenance, and built-in comforts.
00000135.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

95001021.summary: The Downtown Florence Historic District is significant for its late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century commercial buildings, which reflect sixty years of commercial growth, and for its late Victorian and Classical Revival architecture. Though many storefronts have been altered, the buildings keep a high degree of integrity not found elsewhere downtown, where many comparable buildings have been demolished or heavily modified. Florence's history began with the Cypress Land Company in 1818, whose trustees included John Coffee and LeRoy Pope; Italian-born surveyor Ferdinand Sannoner helped lay out the town's grid of about four hundred lots.
95001021.heading: SIGNIFICANCE

98001025.summary: Rogers Department Store has been owned and run by the same family at the same location for more than a century, with roots going back to 1894, and has always been the largest department store in the Muscle Shoals area. It is significant for its role in Florence's twentieth-century commercial history and as the city's best example of Art Deco architecture. Built in 1910 as a two-story brick store, it was extensively rebuilt in 1944-48 and is the most prominent historic commercial building downtown.
98001025.heading: Statement of Significance

80000699.summary: The Southall Building, home of Southall Drugs, represents late nineteenth-century commercial Italianate architecture as built in Alabama's smaller cities. It was built of the finest materials available to house the wholesale and retail drug business of Charles M. Southall. Its corner site on the main business street, its distinctive curved band of second-story windows, its continuous use as a drugstore, and its ownership by one family have made it a noted downtown landmark.
80000699.heading: Statement of Significance

70000104.summary: The Karsner-Carroll House, also called the Oscar Kennedy House, is one of the few remaining small Federal-style houses of the early nineteenth century in the Tennessee Valley, where many large mansions survive but few modest homes do. It is a cottage of modest size with surprisingly refined detail and precise workmanship. Its construction date is unknown, but a December 1831 mortgage by B. F. Karsner described a brick dwelling on the lot. The house was later owned for many years by the family of Dr. Carroll and his son-in-law Oscar Kennedy.
70000104.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

01001171.summary: Prairie Mission was built in 1895 by the United Presbyterian Church of North America to educate African American children in rural Wilcox County, and many considered it the finest school building for Black students in the county at the time. The complex includes the three most important public institutions of rural Black communities: a school, a church, and a cemetery. Its history reflects the humanitarian work of a small northern religious group. The school was named for Jennie Hastings Gillespie, the first Junior Secretary of the denomination's Women's General Missionary Society.
01001171.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

79000390.summary: The Wilson Park Houses are three upper-middle-class homes built between about 1890 and 1918 at the north end of Wilson Park in Florence, fine examples of the Victorian and Georgian Revival styles popular during one of the city's most prosperous periods. The oldest, the Southall House of about 1890, is a two-story frame house with patterned shingles. The 1918 Kennedy-Douglass House, a handsome symmetrical Georgian Revival home designed by a Birmingham architect, dominates the group.
79000390.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

95000092.summary: The Seminary-O'Neal Historic District is a small, cohesive Florence neighborhood of 13 houses with good examples of residential architecture from 1908 to 1943, including vernacular cottages, bungalows, and two Sears, Roebuck 'American Foursquare' houses. Its growth followed national and local economic booms and declines, and the arrival of TVA in 1933 and Reynolds Metals in 1941 revived Florence after World War I and the Depression. Its tree-lined streets lead toward the 1930 president's home of the University of North Alabama, and the neighborhood has changed little in fifty years.
95000092.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96000021.summary: This second boundary increase to the Walnut Street Historic District in Florence adds more houses and extends the district's period of significance to 1870-c. 1930, so the 1870 Alonzo D. Lewis House at 414 North Poplar Street can be included. The district features three main house types: large frame houses with Victorian or Classical details from its earliest years, smaller frame and brick cottages, and two-story brick Georgian Revival houses from about 1918 to 1930. The added buildings contribute to the district in location, design, materials, workmanship, feeling, and association.
96000021.heading: Statement of Significance

74000415.summary: Courtview, probably begun in 1854 or 1855, was the town house of George Washington Foster, a wealthy planter with plantations in Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi. He built it on the highest point in downtown Florence at the head of Court Street, getting a special act of the legislature to close the street; a board signed by carpenter and builder John Ballinger is dated August 24, 1855. During the Civil War, Union officers stayed there in 1863, and Generals Beauregard, Forrest, and Stephen D. Lee visited in 1864. In 1900 it was sold to lawyer Emmet O'Neal, who was elected governor of Alabama in 1910.
74000415.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002045.summary: Coffee High School, later F. T. Appleby Junior High School, was the first secondary school building in Florence and reflects the growing movement to provide high school education in Alabama in the early twentieth century. Before it was built, Florence's school system had only four elementary schools. Designed by Richard G. Deacon of Chattanooga, it was built in 1916-17 on land donated by Camilla M. Coffee, during a period of rapid population growth. It cost $95,000, and the mayor was sharply criticized for the expense and size. It served as Coffee High until a new building opened in 1951.
82002045.heading: Statement of Significance

76000340.summary: The Calhoun School Principal's House, known as Hampton Cottage, is the only building left from the founding period of the Calhoun Colored School. The school was established in 1892 in Lowndes County, in the heart of Alabama's Black Belt, by Charlotte R. Thom and Mabel Dillingham, who had taught together at Hampton Institute and came at the urging of Booker T. Washington and General Samuel C. Armstrong. Thom built Calhoun into one of the most influential schools for Black students in the South before her death in 1932. It offered elementary and trade training and also bought land for resale to Black farmers in 40- to 60-acre tracts.
76000340.heading: Statement of Significance

74000417.summary: Wesleyan Hall, built in 1855 as the main and only building of Wesleyan University on what became the Florence State University campus, is one of the few surviving examples of the Gothic Revival style in the Tennessee Valley and perhaps the only one that is not a house. It was built by Zebulon Pike Morrison, a Virginia-born cabinetmaker who became a funeral director, alderman, mayor, and architect in Florence and built bridges and other buildings in the area. The university's first president, Dr. R. H. Rivers, came from the faculty of LaGrange College. Enrollment grew until students left to enlist in the Confederate army.
74000417.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98001030.summary: This boundary increase adds eleven contiguous buildings to the College Place Historic District in Florence. They share the district's development history and architectural styles, and most keep their original integrity. The expansion followed additional survey work in 1997 requested by the property owners. Residents of the added houses included Helen Chandler, a beloved longtime educator.
98001030.heading: Statement of Significance

73000353.summary: The Lee County Courthouse, built in 1896, was an unusually fine courthouse for a small rural county. It was designed by Andrew J. Bryan and Company of Atlanta and built with a separate jail for a total of $35,000, replacing an earlier two-story brick courthouse. Lee County was created in 1866 and named for General Robert E. Lee; Opelika, incorporated in 1854, became its seat. Judge Dickinson, the first Republican to represent the Second Congressional District since Reconstruction, held court here as both county and circuit judge.
73000353.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000339.summary: The U.S. Post Office in Opelika, now the George W. Andrews Federal Building, was built in 1913 as a federal office building and post office. The three-story building has rusticated arches on the ground floor, a balustraded stone parapet, and brick pilasters. The nomination notes it as an early example of reinforced concrete construction. Much of the nomination text is badly garbled, so details are limited.
76000339.heading: Statement of Significance

09000605.summary: The Dr. John W. Darden House, built in 1906, is significant for its association with Dr. John W. Darden, Opelika's first African American doctor and its most prominent Black citizen, who was a pivotal civic and business leader. It is also an excellent example of an early twentieth-century house designed and built by African American builders. It is largely unchanged except for a balcony added over the front porch in 1925 and a porch bay enclosed as a waiting room in 1944.
09000605.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

72000180.summary: The Sumter County Courthouse, built in 1902, is mainly influenced by Beaux-Arts Classicism with some Romanesque elements. It is the fourth courthouse in county history: a log courthouse of 1833 hosted many early county activities, including the founding of several churches, and its 1838 brick successor collapsed while everyone was out to lunch. A frame courthouse followed before the present building. The courthouse square was also home to a once widely known mineral well, struck while drilling for the town's water supply, whose saline water was believed to have curative properties.
72000180.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

81000128.summary: The Martin-Bounds House, built around 1843 and enlarged around 1860, is significant for its association with James Martin, a leading industrialist of early Florence who helped develop its textile industry. Martin was the major partner in Martin, Weakley and Company, the largest industrial business in antebellum Florence. The story-and-a-half frame cottage, with two rooms on each side of a central hall and end chimneys, is also a good example of a house type especially popular around Muscle Shoals before the Civil War.
81000128.heading: Statement of Significance

80000700.summary: The Florence Water Tower, built in 1889-91, is a large, well-executed example of a masonry water tower with a central masonry pier, a type popular in the 1870s and 1880s of which few are believed to survive. Its design reflects the technology of the time, before self-supporting curved-bottom tanks were introduced in the United States. It is also tied to the growth of Florence and the expansion of American waterworks in the late nineteenth century. Built by a private water company and later transferred to the city, it reflects the national shift to public ownership of waterworks in the 1890s. It was retired after a new tank was built in 1935.
80000700.heading: Statement of Significance

03000228.summary: The Ackerville Baptist Church, built in 1848 in the community of Oak Hill, is a simple one-story frame church in the Greek Revival style with vernacular influences. It is a rectangular block with a temple-form front and portico, smooth white walls, and a symmetrical plan, and it shows construction methods typical of rural Alabama in the mid to late nineteenth century. It also played an important social role in the community.
03000228.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

74000416.summary: The Larimore House was built in 1870 by Theophilus Brown Larimore as a combined home and school. It shows only slight Romantic influence in its window sash, chimneys, and baseboards, otherwise following traditional framing, floor plan, and hand-made trim, reflecting its builder's conservative taste. Larimore's school opened on January 1, 1871, and ran six months a year until 1887; the house was one of about 20 buildings that once made up the school. Larimore, born in Tennessee in 1843, had served in the Confederate army at Shiloh. The property later belonged to Mars Hill Bible School.
74000416.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

00000140.summary: The Forks of Cypress Cemetery, the burial ground of the Jackson family of the Forks of Cypress plantation, contains many fine grave markers representing the high end of antebellum funerary art in Alabama's western Tennessee Valley. Its obelisks and tombstones show the work of both local stonecarvers and workshops from Nashville, Boston, Philadelphia, and St. Louis, in Federal, Greek Revival, Gothic Revival, and other styles. The oldest burial is William Augustus Jackson's in 1819. Two uninscribed slabs traditionally mark the graves of enslaved jockeys, the only enslaved people allowed burial inside the wall, and the cemetery is traditionally linked to Queen Ester, great-grandmother of author Alex Haley.
00000140.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

100001875.summary: Bethlehem Baptist Church, built in 1870-72 near two textile mills founded in the mid-1860s, embodies the distinctive characteristics of frame churches built in east Alabama between 1840 and 1875. Its front-gable form with two front doors, high ceilings, large windows, and undivided interior were typical of rural Baptist and Methodist churches of the period. Its pediment, columned porch, and box cornice are characteristic Greek Revival elements. The church and its cemetery now lie within the city of Valley.
100001875.heading: Summary Paragraph

100003107.summary: The Easterwood House, built in 1912, is an excellent example of Colonial Revival architecture combining Dutch Colonial and Greek Revival elements, and it was the most significant Colonial Revival house in Cherokee. Its massive Greek Revival portico recalls antebellum houses of Middle Tennessee, while its side-gabled gambrel roof adds a Dutch Colonial touch. Built before the style's peak, it appears to have been influenced by houses in Memphis rather than the nearby Shoals cities. Its craftsmanship and size express early twentieth-century middle-class wealth and status in the town.
100003107.heading: Summary Paragraph

78000494.summary: Spring Villa is one of the more noted examples of the early Gothic Revival style in Alabama houses. It was built, probably in the 1850s, by William Penn Younge, a Virginian who married Mary Ann Godwin of Girard in 1848, as the centerpiece of his 455-acre plantation with elaborate landscaping, a 30-acre lake, and a racetrack. It was the scene of many lavish entertainments before and after the Civil War. In the early twentieth century it became a public recreation area, and the house was restored as a Civil Works Administration project.
78000494.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000329.summary: The Stevenson Railroad Depot and Hotel, both built about 1872 between the tracks of two rail lines, reflect a town that owed its existence to the railroads. Stevenson was named for Vernon King Stevenson, president of the Nashville and Chattanooga Railroad, which came through in 1851-52, and it became a junction when the Memphis and Charleston Railroad was completed in 1856. In the Civil War it was a strategic point occupied by Union forces from 1862, and in 1863 it became a major base of the Department of the Cumberland, supplying the campaign for Chattanooga. The depot replaced an earlier one believed to have burned.
76000329.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78000490.summary: The General's Headquarters, a brick house built around 1855 in Stevenson, is significant as the personal headquarters of Major General William S. Rosecrans, commander of the Union Army of the Cumberland, from August 18 to September 4, 1863. During that time Stevenson was the staging area for the campaign that ended in the Battle of Chickamauga, the bloodiest battle of the Civil War in the West. Visitors likely included his chief of staff, future President James Garfield, along with Sheridan, Thomas, and Assistant Secretary of War C. A. Dana.
78000490.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000330.summary: The Wilcox Female Institute is the oldest educational landmark in this part of Alabama and one of the better-known early schools for women in the state. It reflects the desire of prosperous Black Belt planters to give their daughters a proper education. Local citizens began raising subscriptions for a girls' school in 1848, and by 1850 the institute was incorporated, a faculty hired, a catalog published, and the building finished. Camden had become the Wilcox County seat in 1833 on land donated by W. T. Dunn.
75000330.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73000337.summary: Barton Hall, a National Historic Landmark, is built in a form of Greek Revival architecture unusual for Alabama, with late Georgian and Federal trim showing Carolina rather than Kentucky influence. Its most unusual feature is its stairway, similar to one in the Magnolias at Aberdeen, Mississippi. Armstead Barton, born in Tennessee in 1800, came to Tuscumbia around 1825, acquired about 40,000 acres, and began the house in 1840. When he died in 1847 it was unfinished, and his widow Amanda completed it in 1849.
73000337.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89000309.summary: The Franklin Yarbrough Jr. Store is significant for its role in the commercial diversification of the Lee County economy during Reconstruction, when new transportation networks brought consumer goods from the wider national market to the rural South. It also served as a gathering place in Beaulah where farmers exchanged news with neighbors and travelers, and it housed the local Masonic lodge. Built of local limestone, it is the only nineteenth-century stone commercial building in Beaulah and a significant example of late nineteenth-century vernacular commercial architecture in the county.
89000309.heading: Statement of Significance

76000157.summary: Buzzard Roost was the second stand, or inn, on the Old Natchez Trace in Alabama, about 8.5 miles south of Colbert's Ferry on Buzzard Roost Creek, and was run by Levi Colbert. A circuit rider noted that Colbert, though of mixed ancestry, was considered a clever man by travelers and kept a good house. Sometime between 1815 and 1818 Colbert moved to a farm in Mississippi and left the stand to his son-in-law, Kilpatrick Carter. Colbert, a frequent spokesman for the Chickasaw Nation who grew wealthy through frontier enterprises, died at Buzzard Roost in 1834 while traveling to Washington on tribal business. It was one of about 50 stands that served Trace travelers.
76000157.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83002978.summary: The Dr. Andrew D. McLain Office and Drug Store, built in the late nineteenth century, is a representative example of small-town commercial and professional architecture of the period. It is associated with Dr. Andrew Demetrius McLain, a 1901 graduate of the University of Alabama Medical School, who was the main source of medical care for rural communities in southeastern Lee County from 1903 until his death in 1954, when most of the county's doctors practiced in the larger towns. He was known locally for promoting screened windows and doors to prevent insect-borne disease. The building also served as the town post office from 1922 to 1955.
83002978.heading: Statement of Significance

07001390.summary: The Jenkins Farmhouse is a good and intact example of a modest early twentieth-century Lee County farmhouse. It was built around 1912 for Richard Horace and Hattie Jenkins as the centerpiece of a 184-acre farm that has remained in the Jenkins family. Part of the land had been acquired by Mary Elizabeth Green through a federal land grant in 1904.
07001390.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

75000309.summary: The Kirkpatrick House (Kirkpatrick-Bradley House), built sometime before 1870, is the oldest building in Highland Home and one of two remaining structures associated with Highland Home College, a coeducational post-Civil War school and the only institution of higher learning ever located in Crenshaw County. It was built by Col. M. L. Kirkpatrick, who founded the school with his brothers-in-law, Professors J. M. Barnes and Samuel Jordan. Chartered in 1889 as the Highland Home Male and Female College, the school offered four-year degrees, though most students came to qualify for teaching certificates.
75000309.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000156.summary: This section of the Old Natchez Trace near Florence is part of the historic route between Nashville and Natchez, which grew from a network of Native American trails following watershed ridges and appears on French maps of the 1730s and British maps of the 1770s. After the 1780s, boatmen who floated western goods down the Mississippi to Natchez and New Orleans walked home along it, and it became a vital trade route for the West. Traffic grew after the Mississippi Territory was formed in 1798, and in 1801 President Thomas Jefferson authorized improvements to the road. By 1810 about 8,000 to 10,000 people were using it.
76000156.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

98001021.summary: The Foster House is perhaps Alabama's finest surviving example of the Moorish Revival style, applied here to a symmetrical, columned, two-story Greek Revival frame house with striking ogee arches in its portico. It also features rabbeted shiplap siding typical of antebellum houses on Chunnenuggee Ridge, making it unique for combining two styles with a local vernacular feature. It is attributed to Dr. Sterling J. Foster, who married Virginia Heard in 1850 and moved to Union Springs by 1854. Bathrooms were added around 1896 and 1912.
98001021.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

85000452.summary: The Hawthorn House, built in 1854 by Connecticut-born builder Ezra Plumb, is perhaps the finest remaining example of his domestic work in southern Alabama and an excellent adaptation of a traditional house form to the region's climate. It was built for Joseph Richard Hawthorn (1805-ca. 1870), a wealthy planter who moved to Pine Apple from Conecuh County and later served in the legislature from 1865 to 1867. It was also the boyhood home of John Herbert Kelly, who attended West Point, became one of the youngest Confederate brigadier generals at 24, and was killed in 1864 leading a charge in Tennessee.
85000452.heading: Statement of Significance

76000312.summary: The Bullock County Courthouse is the centerpiece of the Bullock County Courthouse Historic District, three blocks along Prairie Street in Union Springs with a concentration of late nineteenth-century commercial buildings and one of the finest post-Civil War courthouses in Alabama, a two-story brick Second Empire building of 1871. Most buildings date from the late 1860s to 1910, when Union Springs became the political and commercial center of the county thanks to its status as county seat and its location on the Mobile and Girard Railroad. The district housed the county's most important businesses and newspapers and keeps the character of a late nineteenth-century county seat.
76000312.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89000310.summary: Creekwood, built around 1850, is an example of the classic plantation house of east central Alabama, with a full-length columned portico, symmetrical facade, hipped roof, and central-hall plan. Its interior keeps original mantels, trim, and staircase. It is the last Greek Revival building on the historic Old Federal Road in Macon and Russell Counties since the Old Key mansion was demolished in the 1950s. The road began as a horse path through the Creek Nation secured by a treaty negotiated by Secretary of War Henry Dearborn. Wing additions from 1929 and 1983 do not detract from its historic appearance.
89000310.heading: Statement of Significance

15000432.summary: The Creek Stand A.M.E. Zion Church Cemetery, established around 1895 on land sold to church trustees in 1893 and 1894, reflects the creation and growth of rural African American churches and cemeteries in Macon County during the Jim Crow era. Most of its more than 160 identified burials date before 1965 and trace the growth and decline of Creek Stand, considered one of the oldest African American rural communities in southern Macon County. It is also significant as a "Roundup Center" where, from around 1950, U.S. Public Health Service officials and Nurse Eunice Rivers gathered participants in the Public Health Service syphilis study, which continued until victims testified before Congress in 1973.
15000432.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

01001299.summary: Sardis Baptist Church, a one-story Greek Revival frame building constructed in the 1850s, is one of the oldest Baptist church buildings still standing in Alabama and has seen few changes since it was built. The congregation was organized in 1837 and received four and a half acres for a church and cemetery in 1841, when a log church was built. The contributing cemetery holds more than 150 grave markers, the earliest dated 1848.
01001299.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86001861.summary: The Little-Stabler House, built around 1850, is one of Greenville's best local examples of a one-story frame bracketed Greek Revival cottage, a type commonly built in central and southern Alabama between 1850 and 1885 that shows the influence of the Italianate style. Its notable features include its original T-shaped form and a hipped roof with a recessed porch wrapping around three sides. A 100-foot alley of cedar trees leads from the porch toward the street.
86001861.heading: Statement of Significance

00001025.summary: The Dr. James Alvis Beavers House, built in 1854, is significant as an intact example of a vernacular double-pile house with Greek and Gothic Revival detailing. The one-and-a-half-story frame house with a truncated pyramidal roof keeps a remarkably high degree of integrity in its exterior, interior spaces, and ornament, including a T-shaped first-floor hallway. It is one of several intact nineteenth-century houses in the Cuba area that combine popular styles with vernacular building forms.
00001025.heading: Statement of Significance

86001799.summary: The First Missionary Baptist Church, historically known as First Baptist Church (Colored), was one of three Black-controlled institutions in Greenville in the early twentieth century and is locally significant as the social and cultural center for most of the city's Black residents. Built in 1908 atop a hill on the western edge of the Baptist Hill neighborhood, it is a one-story stucco-over-brick building with a steep gable roof, side bell tower and steeple, and a three-part arched portico.
86001799.heading: Statement of Significance

86001751.summary: The W. S. Blackwell House, built around 1930, is Greenville's best example of a Tudor-style building and a very good example of the work of Montgomery architect Frank Lockwood Jr. (1888-1954), one of Alabama's leading architects of Tudor-style buildings, who practiced widely across the southern part of the state. The two-story brick and half-timbered house has a cross-gabled entry bay and a catslide roof over one end.
86001751.heading: Statement of Significance

86001854.summary: The Hinson House, built around 1875, is a good local Greenville example of a vernacular house form found all over Alabama between about 1840 and 1890. It has a one-story, ell-shaped frame main block with a gable roof and extended boxed eaves, stuccoed exterior chimneys at each end, and a low hipped-roof porch across the full facade.
86001854.heading: Statement of Significance

86001752.summary: The Buell-Stallings-Stewart House, built in 1874, is one of the best examples in Alabama of the rarely seen Carpenter Gothic style, with a very steep multi-gabled roof, vertical wood siding, scalloped bargeboards, and Gothic arched spandrels between slender porch posts. It is also significant for its association with Jesse Francis Stallings, a delegate to the 1888 Democratic National Convention who served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1893 to 1901. Later it was home to A. Graham Stewart, a prominent Greenville druggist and merchant in the early twentieth century.
86001752.heading: Statement of Significance

86001865.summary: The McMullan-Skinner House, built around 1890, is a good local Greenville example of a vernacular house form built in south central Alabama between about 1840 and 1890 and related to a house type brought from the Carolinas and Georgia. The one-and-a-half-story frame house has a gable roof with exterior chimneys at each end and a full-width front porch set beneath the roof slope. Its interior is unaltered, with an original double-pen plan and very simple original woodwork.
86001865.heading: Statement of Significance

86001803.summary: The Gaston-Perdue House, built in 1895, is Greenville's finest surviving Queen Anne cottage, with projecting octagonal bays, a wraparound porch with turned columns and spindlework, sunburst-patterned gable ends, and outstanding interior woodwork. It is also significant for its association with Judge Zell Gaston, Butler County Probate Judge from 1896 to 1903, and with Dr. J. L. Perdue, who served as Butler County Health Officer for more than twenty years in the early twentieth century.
86001803.heading: Statement of Significance

86001858.summary: The Lane-Kendrick-Sherling House, built around 1850, is Greenville's best local example of a one-story raised frame Greek Revival cottage with a truncated pyramidal roof topped by a flat platform. Houses of this type were built in Alabama from the 1840s to the 1870s, mostly along the rail lines between Columbus, Georgia, and Mobile. The house keeps its exterior form, original floor plan, and wide heart pine floors, though some interior detailing has been replaced with elements from other houses.
86001858.heading: Statement of Significance

86001856.summary: The house at 308 South Street, built around 1890, is a good local example of a vernacular house form with a narrow, single-pile rectangular block, a gable roof with stuccoed exterior chimneys at each end, and a full-width shed-roofed front porch. This house type, built between about 1850 and 1900, is found mainly in south central Alabama. The interior keeps its center-hall plan and original floors, baseboards, and doors.
86001856.heading: Statement of Significance

86001805.summary: The Graydon House, built around 1909, is an excellent local example of a South Alabama vernacular house type with a square, symmetrical form, a high hipped roof, and a wraparound porch. The form appeared around 1880 and was built until about 1915 throughout southern Alabama, especially in the southeast. The Graydon House has very fine slender Victorian turned porch columns with scroll-sawn brackets.
86001805.heading: Statement of Significance

86001807.summary: Greenville City Hall, built in 1937, is a very fine example of Colonial Revival civic architecture and the city's best example of the style. It was designed by Montgomery architect Moreland Griffith Smith. It is also significant for its association with the federal Works Progress Administration; it was built at a federal cost of about $30,000 and was one of several federally funded construction projects in Greenville in the mid to late 1930s.
86001807.heading: Statement of Significance

86001801.summary: The First Presbyterian Church, built in 1886, is one of Greenville's oldest church buildings and one of only two Romanesque Revival-influenced buildings in the city. It shows the style in its single-color brickwork, round-arched windows, square side bell tower with corbeled brick belt courses, and steep gable roof with exposed timber eaves. The congregation was organized in June 1825 and is considered the oldest continuously meeting congregation in Greenville.
86001801.heading: Statement of Significance

86001873.summary: The Wright-Kilgore House, built around 1850, is a good local example of a one-story vernacular Greek Revival cottage with a rectangular form, hipped roof, and recessed front porch; of particular note is the full entablature that runs along the roofline of the original house. Houses of this type were built in Alabama between 1840 and 1870. The house is also significant for its association with Robert R. Wright, who served in the Alabama House of Representatives in the 1855 session.
86001873.heading: Statement of Significance

86001797.summary: The Evens-McMullan House, built around 1870, is Greenville's best local example of an uncommon house type that adds early Victorian elements, including a central peaked gable, extended boxed eaves, and a trellis-work porch, to the basic I-house plan. It also contains a fine curved center-hall stair, the only one remaining in the town. It was built for Evens, a lumberman from West Florida who moved to Greenville around 1860 and selected the timber for its construction.
86001797.heading: Statement of Significance

86001853.summary: The Hawthorne-Cowart House, believed to have been built as early as the 1850s, is Greenville's best local example of a vernacular house type with a raised rectangular main block, a gable roof with exterior chimneys at each end, and a full-length front porch set beneath the front slope of the roof. Houses of this type, brought to Alabama from the Carolinas and Georgia, were built mainly between 1840 and 1875. Major A. J. Hawthorne bought the house in the early 1870s.
86001853.heading: Statement of Significance

86001870.summary: Ward's Corner Store is the earliest remaining evidence of Black commerce in Greenville and the city's best remaining example of a late nineteenth- to early twentieth-century neighborhood business. It was opened around 1885 by Rev. Frank W. Ward (1857-1925), a prominent A.M.E. Zion minister and merchant who helped build the denomination in the East Alabama Conference between 1881 and 1892, when it grew to more than 11,000 members and became the largest conference in the state. The store reflects the late nineteenth-century movement for Black economic independence and served as a social gathering place for the surrounding neighborhood.
86001870.heading: Statement of Significance

86001755.summary: Butler Chapel A.M.E. Zion Church, completed in 1913 to replace the congregation's original 1867 building after it burned in 1911, is the most imposing and highly detailed early twentieth-century Black-built building remaining in Greenville. Its rebuilding was aided by the A.M.E. Zion Church Extension Program, which provided financial help to struggling local congregations. As one of three Black-controlled institutions in Greenville in the early twentieth century, it was a social and cultural center for most of the city's Black residents. The building is an eclectic late Victorian design with Medieval and American Colonial elements.
86001755.heading: Statement of Significance

97000654.summary: Uchee Methodist Church, built around 1859, is a very good and intact example of the Greek Revival style in perhaps its purest form, the temple-front house of worship, with classical proportions and austere details. It reflects the popularity of the style even in rural settings and its spread through Russell County, opened to white settlement in 1832, before the Civil War. Its original floor plan let the church's small number of Black members enter separately at the rear and sit apart from white members, an arrangement changed in 1980. The congregation met there through the mid-1980s.
97000654.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86001794.summary: The Dickenson House, built around 1890, is a good local example of a South Alabama vernacular house type with a square, symmetrical main block, a truncated pyramidal roof with gable extensions, and a wraparound front porch. The form was built between about 1880 and 1915, and its flat-topped pyramidal roof is typical of houses along the rail lines between Columbus, Georgia, and Mobile. The Dickenson House has Ionic porch columns and Queen Anne interior features.
86001794.heading: Statement of Significance

98001020.summary: The Dr. H. B. Ward House, built in 1880, is an excellent example of a two-story frame I-house with Greek Revival and Victorian detailing, and its exterior, interior spaces, and ornament keep a remarkably high degree of integrity. The I-house form came to frontier Alabama from the eastern seaboard in the early nineteenth century and became a common house type for the upper-middle and upper classes. It is one of several significant houses in Cuba that mix classical details with other stylistic elements.
98001020.heading: Statement of Significance

00000142.summary: The Airmount Grave Shelter, built in 1853 by planter John Hope, apparently as the start of a family cemetery, is an unusually early and substantial example of the grave shelter building type. Its roof uses a distinctive framing method, with splayed eaves that brace the main truss and support a barrel-vaulted "compass" ceiling, a technique traced to eighteenth-century rural churches in Delaware and Virginia. It is the only known use of this framing technique in the southern half of Alabama.
00000142.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

86001867.summary: The Theological Building of Lomax-Hannon Junior College, built in 1911 as a boys' dormitory with classrooms below, is the earliest remaining building associated with Black education in Butler County. It is the only known building tied to the A.M.E. Zion Church's efforts to develop church-supported schools for Black students in Alabama in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a period from 1875 to 1915 when churches led efforts to improve higher education in the state. Lomax-Hannon, the second of the denomination's three school ventures in Alabama, is the only one that survives.
86001867.heading: Statement of Significance

09000001.summary: The Hurtsboro Historic District is significant for its main street commercial buildings and surrounding residential streets, which represent the town from its founding in the late 1850s through the first half of the twentieth century. Its houses range from Greek Revival to early ranch styles, and its commercial core dates from the 1890s to the mid-twentieth century. The town, then called Hurtsville, was incorporated in 1878, becoming the second of only two incorporated towns in Russell County, which gave it the framework for many years of well-run municipal government.
09000001.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

05000834.summary: The Joel Hurt House, built in 1857, is a typical and intact Alabama plantation house of the Greek Revival period, with an interesting departure from the pure form and Edwardian enhancements added in 1906. It was built by Joel Hurt Sr., founder of Hurtsboro and at one time among the most prominent landowners in Russell County. It was also the childhood home of Joel Hurt Jr., who became a leading citizen and urban developer of Atlanta.
05000834.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

93000986.summary: The Samuel Lowther House, built around 1853, is a fine and intact example of a one-story Greek Revival house with a central-hall plan, a style common in East Alabama and West Georgia. It was the seat of the Lowther plantation, which once covered more than 700 acres, and it is still owned by descendants of the builder. The property is also significant for its surviving nineteenth-century outbuildings, including a smokehouse, a one-room cook's house, a split barn, a privy, and early sheds.
93000986.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

92001090.summary: The John W. Howard House, built around 1859-60 by builders Wright and Rouse, is one of the few surviving examples of Greek Revival architecture in the Greenville area. The one-story frame house has a symmetrical facade, central-hall plan, and a full-length front porch with four fluted Doric columns, and it was built of hand-hewn heart pine timbers. According to a family descendant, its doors and windows were made by inmates of the state penitentiary at Wetumpka.
92001090.heading: Statement of Significance

98000110.summary: The Merritt School, built around 1922, is significant as a school for African American children built with help from the Julius Rosenwald School Building Fund, which from 1913 to 1937 helped finance more than 5,000 school buildings across fifteen Southern states and was the most important philanthropic force aiding African Americans in the first half of the twentieth century. It is a two-teacher school built according to standard plans from Samuel Smith and the Rosenwald Fund's Southern Office in Nashville. Wings were added later, including one in 1946.
98000110.heading: Statement of Significance

76000354.summary: Fort No. 5 is one of a series of eight earthen forts built in 1863 to guard the western approach to Columbus, Georgia, a major producer of war materials for the Confederacy, and it is the better preserved of the two that remain. The forts were designed by Major General Jeremy F. Gilmer, described as perhaps the South's outstanding military engineer. During the Battle of Columbus on April 16, 1865, fought mostly in Girard (now Phenix City) against Union cavalry under General James H. Wilson, Confederate forces abandoned the outer line to defend the river bridges, so the fort was never manned. It is almost completely intact and is the only accessible relic of the battle.
76000354.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87000858.summary: The Robbins Hotel is locally significant as an excellent surviving example of a small, privately owned Southern hotel that opened because of the 1899 completion of the railroad linking west Alabama and the Gulf Coast. The core of the building was a dogtrot farmhouse built about 1840 for the Daniel Robbins family; when the railroad passed about 200 feet away, the house became a haven for railroad workers, salesmen, sportsmen, and other travelers and was enlarged around 1905 into a hotel. For about 50 years it served rail and then automobile travelers, until mid-twentieth-century changes in transportation altered travel patterns.
87000858.heading: Statement of Significance

86000995.summary: Mount Sterling Methodist Church, built around 1859, is a little-altered example of simple, rural mid-nineteenth-century Greek Revival church architecture in Alabama. Its roof is supported by a large truss running down the center of the building, the only known example of this type of roof structure in West Central Alabama. It was the first building in Mount Sterling built specifically as a church. The churchyard includes the grave of David Gregg, who died in 1814.
86000995.heading: Statement of Significance

05000646.summary: New Hope Baptist Church is a relic of the old settlement of Natchez in Monroe County, about three miles west of Beatrice, and is significant for its role in the life of this early community, which has since dispersed. The congregation was founded in 1855, and while the building is traditionally dated to that time, an architectural historian has noted features that suggest construction around 1870. The church served the community as long as it remained self-reliant and is still used occasionally, cared for by descendants of its early members.
05000646.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

76000355.summary: The Bass-Perry House, built between 1840 and 1844, is one of the two finest plantation houses in Russell County and was home to three of the county's most prominent families. Built soon after the end of Creek hostilities and removal in the area, it was the center of a large cotton plantation, and its style and craftsmanship reflect the taste and prosperity of its builder, Hartwell Bass. Bass, who had come from Virginia by way of North Carolina and Georgia, bought the land from an aide at the Creek Agency at Fort Mitchell.
76000355.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

83003484.summary: The Morgan-Curtis House is locally significant as the first home used as a medical clinic in Phenix City. Dr. David Elias Morgan, a native of Monmouthshire, Wales, and one of the area's leading doctors, built the house in 1904 using materials from a partly burned house. In 1914 he converted the second floor into a sanatorium for out-of-town patients, the first facility for in-patient care on the Alabama side of the river. The house is also architecturally significant as an earlier house remodeled into an eclectic building unmatched in style in Phenix City.
83003484.heading: Statement of Significance

83004373.summary: The Floyd-Newsome House is significant as an example of the few large houses built by prominent citizens of the Phenix City area around the turn of the century: a Victorian cottage built in 1898 that was raised and enlarged into a classical-style mansion in 1908 as its owner's prosperity grew. It was the home of Dr. Franklin Ashby Floyd, a Tulane-educated physician, druggist, mayor, and judge who was long important in Phenix City politics and promoted medical services and education.
83004373.heading: Statement of Significance

74000436.summary: The Russell County Courthouse at Seale is one of the oldest standing courthouses in Alabama and one of the oldest public buildings in the eastern half of the state. After part of Russell County was given to the new Lee County in 1866, leaving the old seat at Crawford near the new boundary, voters chose the more central Silver Run (later Seale) as county seat. Built by Simeon O'Neal for $6,500, the courthouse was first used in 1869, and wings were added in 1908. The county seat moved to Phenix City in 1935.
74000436.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

100007192.summary: The Phenix City Post Office Building, built in 1938, is locally significant for its association with New Deal-era federal efforts to improve public infrastructure and with post-World War II civic improvements. It is an excellent example of a restrained Colonial Revival New Deal post office designed under Louis A. Simon, Supervising Architect of the Treasury. It also contains the mural "Cotton" by the important Alabama artist John Kelly Fitzpatrick. In 1964 the building was converted into a public library.
100007192.heading: Summary Paragraph

83003477.summary: The Brooks-Hughes House is architecturally significant as the finest example of a Victorian cottage in Phenix City, with a gazebo-like porch, lyre-patterned trim, and chamfered posts with applied trim. It was built shortly after 1897 by the construction division of the Columbus Iron Works, and in 1904 it was bought by R. E. Brooks, a machinist at the Iron Works. It represents the type of housing popular among skilled craftsmen who worked in Columbus industries while living in Phenix City.
83003477.heading: Statement of Significance

83003480.summary: Girard High School, originally Girard Elementary School, is significant in the educational history of Phenix City as the first brick public school in Girard; unusually for the area at the turn of the century, it provided classes for both Black and white students. It was built on the site of Girard's first public school of 1867, after the school board's treasurer persuaded Gunby Jordan, president of the Eagle and Phenix Mills, to help fund a new building in 1909. It became an accredited high school in 1923 and closed in 1970. The building is also the only example of Neoclassical architecture in Phenix City, with some Italianate features.
83003480.heading: Statement of Significance

100011023.summary: The Troy Masonic Temple, built in 1893, was the meeting place of the local Freemasons until 1975 and a center of the community's social and political life. Its second floor also served as Troy City Hall until 1910, and its first floor housed the U.S. Post Office from 1894 to 1912 and then a movie theater until 1937; from 1944 to 1959 the second floor was the Teenage Canteen. Designed by architect Enos Crites, it is one of three grand Masonic lodges surviving in Alabama and the only one in the Romanesque Revival style.
100011023.heading: Summary Paragraph

83003485.summary: The Sharpe-Monte House, built around 1890 by the Sharpe brothers, is one of Phenix City's few remaining examples of outstanding large-scale Victorian residential architecture, with an exceptional front porch displaying woodwork patterns found throughout the city. Its elaborate millwork and large scale reflect the rapid residential growth and prosperity of the 1890s. It later became the home and place of business of Jacob G. Monte, a Dutch tailor, and stayed in the Monte family until 1968.
83003485.heading: Statement of Significance

84000721.summary: Troy High School, built from 1917 to 1919, was the first school in Troy built specifically for secondary education and served as the city's only high school for white students until 1960. Designed by prominent Montgomery architect Frank Lockwood and built by Thomas Purvis, it is one of only three school buildings constructed in Alabama during the World War I years, along with schools in Sheffield and Opelika. It represents a major community investment at a time when wartime conditions stalled school construction in many small Alabama towns.
84000721.heading: Statement of Significance

99000885.summary: The Bush House, built in 1912 by prosperous farmer Preston Randolph Bush as a town house in the county seat, is one of the most substantial houses in Grove Hill from the first two decades of the twentieth century. While most houses of the period in the area were modest folk forms, the Bush House shows the options available for a larger home: a traditional two-story double-pile central-passage form finished with manufactured, stylish details. It is largely representative of building techniques in Clarke County at the time.
99000885.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

80000680.summary: Oakey Streak Methodist Episcopal Church is an example of the vernacular Gothic style in a rural Alabama church, with lancet windows typical of the simple one-room frame churches built across the Southeast after the Civil War. The congregation was organized by 1831, received its ten-acre site in 1850, and replaced its log church with the present building in the second half of the nineteenth century; the square tower was added in 1903. The church and the nearby Masonic lodge were the center of social life in this rural community, and the cemetery's earliest marked graves date from the 1860s.
80000680.heading: Statement of Significance

78000485.summary: The Dickinson House, built around 1845, is a typical antebellum country house made unusual by its Italianate ornament, including an elaborate fanlight, paired windows, finely carved brackets, an octagonal parlor, and a circular stairway. It was built for Colonel James Shelton Dickinson (1818-1882), one of Clarke County's leading mid-nineteenth-century citizens, and has remained in his family. The builder is believed to have been James Newman, an English-born carpenter who came to Grove Hill from Virginia to build it.
78000485.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

99000887.summary: The John A. Coate House, dating from about 1855 to 1865, is a good example of the spraddle roof cottage, a house type prominent in nineteenth-century Clarke County that spread from the Chesapeake, Albemarle Sound, and Charleston areas across the coastal South. It keeps the type's distinctive broken roof pitch on both the front and rear. It is one of only two spraddle roof houses left in Grove Hill.
99000887.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

79000382.summary: The Alston-Cobb House, built around 1854, is a notable example of a simple but handsome two-story plantation plain-style house and one of the few of its kind remaining in Clarke County. Its symmetrical facade and finely crafted double veranda, a feature common in the Gulf Coast region, give it a refined character. It was the home of physician Lemuel L. Alston, who opened a medical office in Grove Hill around 1852 and was one of only two doctors in the area during that decade.
79000382.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

99000888.summary: The Cobb House (Cobb-Waite House), built around 1865-1870, is the only remaining example of a rural extended I-house in Clarke County, keeping the front shed porch and rear shed rooms that give the form its "extended" character, typical of the Deep South. It is also one of the few examples of Reconstruction-era architecture in the county and one of two houses that define rural building of that period there. Its plain, simple interior finishes reflect the scarcity of skilled joiners in the area at the time.
99000888.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

74000400.summary: The Petty-Roberts-Beatty House, an octagonal house built by B. F. Petty in 1861, is significant mainly for its architectural rarity: it is one of only two known surviving octagon houses in Alabama. Petty is believed to have modeled it on a similar house he had seen in New York, and most American octagon houses were built between 1848 and 1860. Union forces used the house as their headquarters after capturing Clayton during the Civil War. The Petty family lived there until 1901, when it was sold to Judge B. T. Roberts.
74000400.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

95001116.summary: Grace Episcopal Church, consecrated in 1876, is a significant example of Gothic Revival architecture, reflecting the style's popularity for Episcopal churches throughout Alabama and the nation, and it keeps a high degree of integrity. Its building fund was helped by proceeds from an 1875 banquet celebrating the arrival of the first railroad in Barbour County. Grace Church grew out of an Episcopal mission in Clayton, and Rev. DeBerniere Waddell, who served from 1876 to 1885, was the only minister of the church to live permanently in the town.
95001116.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

70000097.summary: Fendall Hall, completed in 1854 for Edward B. Young, is a two-story frame Italianate house with a cupola, built during an era of wealth and statewide influence for Eufaula, when the region shipped thousands of bales of cotton down the Chattahoochee River each year. Its timber was cut at Young's own sawmill and seasoned for two years before construction. Young, a native of New York, settled in Eufaula, where he built the first toll bridge across the Chattahoochee. The house remained in his family for generations.
70000097.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000399.summary: The Miller-Martin Town House, built in 1859 by John H. Miller as a town house, is one of about ten pre-Civil War houses still standing in Clayton and an early example of Gothic Revival influence in Alabama. Miller had come to Barbour County from Orangeburg, South Carolina, in the early 1830s and established a large plantation west of Clayton. Ceiling murals in three rooms are thought to be the work of an artist named Massillon. After the Civil War the Millers sold the house in 1871 to Judge Henry Clinton Russell, Barbour County's probate judge.
74000399.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000403.summary: Fort Sinquefield was one of a number of crude defenses hastily built by settlers in southwestern Alabama in the summer of 1813 amid rumors of advancing Creek war parties. The Creek attack here, part of the same first major offensive as the attack on Fort Mims on August 30, signaled the start of the Creek War, which changed relations between Native Americans and settlers and led to the Creeks losing more than half their land and, within 20 years, removal west of the Mississippi. A party of warriors led by the prophet Josiah Francis killed 12 settlers nearby and then attacked the fort on September 3 while the dead were being buried.
74000403.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000683.summary: Woodlands, built around 1840 as the seat of a 2,000-acre plantation, is one of the finest of the few remaining antebellum houses in rural Clarke County. A story-and-a-half Creole cottage enriched with Greek Revival details, it is a surprisingly sophisticated example of the type, equaled only by a few Mobile houses. Its most noted feature, a small elliptical vault in the porch ceiling that makes room for an oval bull's-eye window above the entrance, is unique in Alabama. It was built for Frederick S. Blount (1806-1885), a North Carolina lawyer who practiced in Mobile before moving to Clarke County around 1840.
80000683.heading: Statement of Significance

73000366.summary: The Old Monroe County Courthouse, built in 1903, is a prominent Alabama literary landmark because of its association with Harper Lee and Truman Capote, who were next-door neighbors in Monroeville as children, and it served as the seat of Monroe County government from 1903 to 1967. Both writers mentioned the building in their work; Lee made the courthouse a central setting of her Pulitzer Prize-winning novel To Kill a Mockingbird, and it was used extensively in the making of the film. After a new courthouse opened in 1967, the old building became the Monroe County Museum.
73000366.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

100012399.summary: The Lee Family Home is significant for its association with Nelle Harper Lee, who wrote much of To Kill a Mockingbird there starting in 1958. The novel, which explored themes of racial injustice and tolerance, won the Pulitzer Prize and was made into an Academy Award-winning film. The house remained Lee's Alabama residence, to which she returned every year after the book's success, until she moved into an assisted living home in Monroeville in 2007.
100012399.heading: Summary Paragraph

99000886.summary: The Stephen Beech Cleveland House, built around 1860, embodies many characteristics of planter-class houses built in South Alabama on the eve of the Civil War, including a blend of mass-produced and handmade details and a mix of classical and picturesque motifs. Its jigsaw-work railings, cornice brackets, and sashes came from factories that mass-produced architectural elements, while its mantels, closets, and door surrounds show the hand of local craftsmen. It illustrates the gradual mid-nineteenth-century shift from reliance on craftsmen to manufactured ornament.
99000886.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

16000398.summary: Evergreen School is locally significant as the city's only elementary school from its construction in 1923 until it closed in 2002; it served only white students until it was integrated in the 1960s. Its auditorium also served as a community theater and meeting place. The building is representative of a small community school of its period and is the only historic school building remaining in Evergreen. An addition was built in 1948.
16000398.heading: Summary Paragraph

71000094.summary: The Cato House, built by enslaved labor in 1858, was the setting for some of the most influential secessionist meetings held in Alabama in the late 1850s and the scene of a great celebration when Alabama left the Union. Its builder, attorney Lewis Llewellen Cato, was known as "the great secessionist"; a friend of William L. Yancey, he was a member of the Eufaula Regency, the group of Southeast Alabama fire-eaters credited with the most advanced steps toward secession. The one-story frame house has a T-plan with a square-piered gallery across the front.
71000094.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000154.summary: The Drewry-Mitchell-Moorer House, an exceptionally fine Italianate house for its period, was built in 1867 for Dr. John Drewry. A Georgia native and graduate of Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia, Drewry moved to Eufaula in 1848, ran his own apothecary shop, and became known as one of the most successful typhoid fever doctors in the area; during one fever outbreak his office and home served as a temporary hospital. The house passed down through his descendants.
72000154.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000155.summary: Kendall Manor, completed in 1867, is a fine example of Italianate architecture and an excellent reflection of the rare merchant-planter whose prosperity continued after the Civil War. It was built for James Turner Kendall, a merchant and planter from Virginia. Work began shortly before the war under local contractor-architect H. George Whipple, who likely supplied the plans, as he designed many of Eufaula's fine houses; construction stopped during the war and was then completed at great expense.
72000155.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000156.summary: The Shorter Mansion, built in 1906 by Eli Shorter Jr. to replace an earlier house that burned in 1900, is a notable example of Neoclassical (Greco-Roman Classical Revival) architecture in the South. Shorter belonged to the politically powerful Shorter family; he served four terms in the Alabama House of Representatives in the 1880s, including one as Speaker, and his uncle John Gill Shorter was governor of Alabama from 1861 to 1863. Restored by the Eufaula Heritage Association, the house serves as a memorial to the six Alabama governors who were born in or lived in Barbour County.
72000156.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000093.summary: The Bray-Barron House is one of Alabama's better examples of a mid-nineteenth-century middle-class town house. The Greek Revival house was built before 1850 by Nathan Bray, one of four brothers who came to Eufaula from New England; all four served in the Confederate Army, and Nathan was assigned to receive arms and ammunition from manufacturers and deliver them to the army. Members of the Bray family lived in the house until 1963.
71000093.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000157.summary: The Gov. Chauncey Sparks House, built by local architect W. C. Whipple, who sold it in 1857, is an architectural landmark that was home to several prominent Alabama political leaders. Henry Reuben Shorter, a lawyer, Confederate lieutenant colonel, and president of the Alabama Railroad Commission from 1885 to 1897, acquired it in 1865 in trade for 60,000 pounds of cotton; his brother John Gill Shorter was governor during the Civil War. His nephew Reuben F. Kolb, Alabama's second Commissioner of Agriculture and the state's leading Populist, lived here as a child. The house was later the home of Governor Chauncey Sparks, a bachelor.
72000157.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000095.summary: The McNab Bank Building, generally dated to the 1850s, is a fine iron-front example of the North Italian Renaissance Revival style and one of the oldest standing bank buildings in Alabama. It was built by John McNab, a Scottish-born banker who became Eufaula's wealthiest citizen, for his Eastern Bank of Alabama, one of the early free banks chartered under the state's 1850 free banking law, which ended the state monopoly on banking. The two back rooms later served as the law offices of Governor Chauncey Sparks.
71000095.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000097.summary: Wellborn, built in 1837 by George Whipple, is one of the earliest Greek Revival mansions in the Chattahoochee River Valley; though simple and unadorned, it makes excellent use of available materials. It was built for Dr. Thomas Levi Welborn, a Georgia native and Jefferson Medical College graduate who came to East Alabama in 1833 after the Creeks gave up their lands, and who died in 1841 of wounds received fighting in the later Creek uprisings. His son William was one of Eufaula's first commissioners when the town was incorporated in 1857, and Confederate soldiers nicknamed the house "Soldiers Rest."
71000097.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

75000308.summary: The Louisville and Nashville Depot, built in 1907, is the major landmark of Evergreen and is similar to, but somewhat larger than, the depots the L&N built shortly after 1900. Rail service first reached Evergreen when the Alabama and Florida Railroad, connecting Montgomery and Pensacola, was completed in April 1861 with support from Conecuh County subscribers. The L&N acquired the line in 1900 and built the present station seven years later for $14,911. It stands alone on the wide median that divides the town's main business street.
75000308.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82001996.summary: The Kiels-McNab House, built around 1840, is significant for its association with two prominent figures in Eufaula's early history. Elias M. Kiels, who built it as his home, was Barbour County tax assessor before and during the Civil War and later a leader of the Radical Reconstruction faction; his young son was killed in the election riots of November 1874, after which Kiels left the county for good. In 1880 the house was bought by John McNab, an early settler and banker who became one of the city's richest and most influential citizens. The house was first listed in 1973, removed from the Register when it was moved to its present site in 1974, and nominated again at its new location.
82001996.heading: Statement of Significance

70000098.summary: The Tavern, built in 1836 by Edward Williams, was the first permanent building in Irwinton, the forerunner of Eufaula, a settlement founded on the Chattahoochee River as a trading center with the Lower Creeks. Built as an inn, it served travelers when steamboats plied the river. It later served as a residence, as a temporary Episcopal church in 1844, and as a Confederate hospital. It was restored under the Cowikee Mills Foundation and stands on the bluff overlooking Lake Eufaula.
70000098.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000096.summary: The Sheppard Cottage, built in 1837 by Henry H. and Mary R. Field, is the oldest residence in Eufaula and one of Alabama's better examples of a Southern adaptation of the Cape Cod cottage. In 1868 it passed to Dr. Edmund Sheppard, a physician who had settled in the area in the 1830s, served in the Confederate Army, and later ran a smallpox hospital. The cottage was given to and restored by the Eufaula Heritage Association.
71000096.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92000033.summary: The Gainestown Schoolhouse is a fine and intact example of an early twentieth-century two-room schoolhouse; though significantly restored, it keeps its form, framing, weatherboards, windows, and many interior features, including its stage. It dates from about 1919, with a section added in the 1920s. Gainestown, settled in 1817 near George Strother Gaines's trading post on the Alabama River, was one of Clarke County's largest settlements and busiest river ports by 1860, but declined after the railroad bypassed it; the school closed in 1952.
92000033.heading: Statement of Significance

00000132.summary: The J. P. McKee Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel, component-part construction the Lustron Corporation used for its prefabricated houses from 1946 to 1950. It is significant for its association with the prefabricated housing industry and the nationwide housing shortage after World War II. The one-story house, clad in porcelain-enameled steel panels, keeps most of its original metal wall and ceiling panels and built-in cabinets and shelves.
00000132.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

99000889.summary: Gainestown Methodist Church and Cemetery is an intact example of an early twentieth-century rural church, built in 1911 on the foundation of, and with materials salvaged from, the congregation's c. 1854 church after it was destroyed by a tornado. The congregation dates to 1819, in what was then a busy settlement and landing on the Alabama River. The cemetery is a notable local collection of funerary art, with scattered family plots, many enclosed by elaborate late nineteenth-century wrought iron fences, and gravestones with the willow motif popular in the early nineteenth century.
99000889.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

96000046.summary: The Avant House, built around 1914-1920, is perhaps the finest surviving example of Classical Revival architecture in Covington County and keeps a high degree of integrity. The two-story frame house is dominated by a two-story pedimented portico with four fluted Ionic columns. From the 1920s to the 1940s it was the seat of a 525-acre farm with five tenant houses, and for many years it had the only telephone service in the area.
96000046.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78000484.summary: The Wilson-Finlay House is a fine example of the Classical Revival style's influence on rural Alabama houses, seen in its symmetrical facade, pedimented portico, Doric columns, and door and window treatment, and it is one of only two Classical Revival buildings remaining in Clarke County. It was built in 1846 for Dr. Joshua Sanford Wilson as a front addition to a ten-room house built around 1843. Dr. Wilson had come to Clarke County in 1817 with his father, Rev. Joshua Wilson, one of the founders of the Gainestown community. Restoration has returned the facade to its original appearance.
78000484.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73000335.summary: The Coffee County Courthouse in Elba was built in 1903, the latest in a series of courthouses since Elba became the county seat in 1852 after the first courthouse at Wellborn burned. Elba's first courthouse, completed in 1853, was burned in 1863 by "Ward's Raiders," a band of Confederate deserters and bushwhackers; its replacement was finished in 1867, and the first brick courthouse followed in 1882. When that building proved too small even after an 1899 enlargement, the present courthouse was built.
73000335.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

00000136.summary: The Doit W. McClellan Lustron House, built in 1949, is an outstanding example of the all-steel, component-part construction the Lustron Corporation used for its prefabricated houses from 1946 to 1950. It is significant for its association with the prefabricated housing industry and the nationwide housing shortage after World War II. It also shows the qualities of postwar design, including durability, easy maintenance, and built-in conveniences such as metal wall panels, cabinets, shelves, and a vanity.
00000136.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

98000411.summary: Clarke Mills (Vanity Fair Mills), built in 1939, was the first textile industry in Clarke County, the second Vanity Fair plant built in the South, and one of the county's first major industries other than agriculture and timber. The original building was designed in the Art Moderne style by Vanity Fair architect H. B. Bieberstein, an important contribution to the county's architecture. The mill remained an important employer in Jackson and later became the only knitting facility for Vanity Fair's division.
98000411.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

08000455.summary: The Asa Johnston Farmhouse, built in 1842, is an excellent example of a mid-nineteenth-century spraddle roof dogtrot house and the most intact example of its form documented in Conecuh County. Its open dogtrot hall keeps a vaulted wood ceiling that is the only documented example of its type in Alabama. It is one of a small number of surviving works by Ezra Plumb, a local carpenter, designer, and builder prominent before the Civil War. Asa Johnston arrived in 1818, the year Conecuh County was created, and became one of the area's wealthiest antebellum planters.
08000455.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

97000655.summary: The Washington County Courthouse at St. Stephens, completed in 1854 as the seventh seat of government for Alabama's oldest county, served as the county's principal government building until the county seat moved to Chatom in 1907. Of the county's eight seats of government, it is the earliest courthouse still standing. It is also believed to have served as the meeting hall of St. Stephens Masonic Lodge No. 81 since the lodge was organized in 1854, making it a long-standing social center for the community. The simple two-story building housed county offices downstairs and the courtroom and Masonic hall above.
97000655.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

88003240.summary: The Covington County Courthouse, built from 1914 to 1916 to designs by architect Frank Lockwood, has been the seat of county government since then and is one of the oldest courthouses still in use in Southeast Alabama. Built of combed granite with Corinthian columns and decorative moldings, it is an excellent example of the Beaux Arts style that shaped public buildings in the early twentieth century. The Italianate jail, completed in 1916 before the courthouse, is one of the oldest jails in continuous use in the state, and its unusual style makes it unique among county jails.
88003240.heading: Statement of Significance

88003239.summary: The Bank of Andalusia building is a pristine example of classical styling and excellent local craftsmanship from the building boom of the early twentieth century, which was spurred by the arrival of the railroad in Andalusia. It is almost completely intact, and its fine but restrained detailing makes it one of only a handful of high-style buildings of the period that keep their original appearance. The bank was organized in 1904 as an alternative to the First National Bank of Andalusia.
88003239.heading: Statement of Significance
