82002006.summary: The First National Bank Building, built in 1920-1921, is significant as southeast Alabama's only "skyscraper" and as the work of Frank Lockwood (1865-1936), one of Alabama's most noted architects of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The six-story building, constructed by Little, Cleckler and Company of Anniston for $115,000, was Andalusia's first and only building on a skyscraper scale. It is also significant for its association with Andalusia's major banking institutions.
82002006.heading: Statement of Significance

84000606.summary: The Central of Georgia Depot, built in 1899, is a fine example of a small late nineteenth-century board-and-batten train station and the last remaining wooden commercial building in Andalusia. The railroad brought modern transportation and prosperity to the town, allowing it to ship lumber, timber, naval stores, and farm products; new wholesale houses and businesses opened near the depot, and the town's population doubled in one year to 596.
84000606.heading: Statement of Significance

73000339.summary: The William T. Shepard House, built in 1908, is the only remaining structure of Poley, a sawmill town of some 1,000 to 1,500 people built around the Miller-Brent Lumber Company, thought to have been one of the larger sawmill operations in the United States in the early 1900s. Unusually elaborate for this part of the state, the house was built for entertaining and became a social center for South Central Alabama, with balls and orchestras brought in from as far away as Montgomery.
73000339.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

96000594.summary: The Samuel Lawson Dowling House, built around 1870, is a significant example of a vernacular house type, with a central hall flanked by pairs of larger front rooms and smaller rear rooms, brought to southeast Alabama by settlers from South Carolina and Georgia. A late expression of the type, it is a rare, perhaps unique, survivor from the first period of frame house construction in Ozark, between the early log buildings and the high-style houses that followed the railroad's arrival in 1888. Its builder, Samuel L. Dowling, a son of one of the county's founding families, also built Ozark's 1873 Methodist church, now gone.
96000594.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

82002007.summary: The J. D. Holman House, built in 1912 to designs by Frank Galliher, is one of the finest examples of the Neoclassical Revival style applied to a large house in Alabama's Wiregrass region. The largest and most elaborate residence in that part of the state when built, it was very modern for its time, with steam heat and the area's first central vacuum system. It is associated with Jesse DeCosta Holman (1872-1960), a prominent businessman who made his fortune trading mules and horses and later acquired a Buick dealership and the Ozark Cotton Mills, one of the first mills in the Wiregrass and the first in Ozark.
82002007.heading: Statement of Significance

00000141.summary: The Isaac Nettles Gravestones, concrete grave markers in the Mt. Nebo Baptist Church cemetery near Carlton, are significant for their association with the African American heritage of Clarke County and as important works of folk art. Isaac Nettles is probably unique among African American folk artists in Alabama for decorating gravestones with death masks, a "frozen face" motif folklorists link to African-derived symbolism. His first such markers followed the deaths of his mother and wife in 1933; the largest is a life-size half figure of his mother, Selena. The gravestones show how a talented resident expressed creativity and honored the dead within the economic limits of a rural Black community during the Depression.
00000141.heading: Statement of Significance

76000321.summary: Claybank Log Church, built in 1852, is one of the few remaining log churches in Alabama and the only one within the limits of a town; it is believed to be the oldest standing structure in Dale County. It replaced a first log building of 1829-30, a non-denominational church on land donated by Elisha Matthews that the Claybank community also used for other gatherings. Though less sophisticated than the McIntosh Log Church, it is a fine example of log construction. As membership declined, by 1900 it was used only for occasional revivals and annual picnics.
76000321.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

73000336.summary: The Boll Weevil Monument, unveiled on December 11, 1919, is the only known statue built to honor a destructive insect. The citizens of Enterprise erected it in appreciation of the boll weevil's role in ending the county's dependence on cotton: after the weevil devastated crops in 1915 and 1916, farmers turned to other cash crops. The county's soil proved well suited to peanuts and soybeans, and within a few years the Wiregrass region became the world's leading peanut producer.
73000336.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000405.summary: The Seaboard Coastline Depot is one of the oldest wooden buildings in Enterprise and one of the oldest transportation landmarks in Southeast Alabama, where railroads were more responsible for development and settlement than anywhere else in the state. The Alabama Midland Railroad reached Enterprise in 1898, and the town grew rapidly at the expense of nearby communities. The Atlantic Coast Line built the station in 1903, shortly after acquiring the line; as the town's population grew to 2,322 within seven years, the depot was enlarged in 1916 to its present size.
74000405.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

78000489.summary: The Kennedy House, built in 1870, is one of the oldest remaining buildings in Abbeville and an unusual example of a Creole cottage in an inland area, a type common along the Gulf Coast. It keeps one of the earliest features of the type, the absence of a central hall. It was built by Dr. William Calvin Bethune, a prominent physician wounded in the Civil War, and was bought in 1885 by William and Mollie Kennedy, Henry County farmers.
78000489.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

89000164.summary: The Oates House is locally significant as the only residential example of the Classical Revival style in Abbeville, the Henry County seat. It was built in 1900 as a one-story house by Ephraim Oates (born 1826), who by 1890 owned more than 5,000 acres and was the county's largest and most successful farmer. In 1910 it was extensively remodeled in the Classical Revival style, with a massive full-height pedimented portico on Tuscan columns, a symmetrical facade, a second-story balcony, and a hipped roof.
89000164.heading: Statement of Significance

80000684.summary: The Rawls Hotel is one of the most elaborate buildings in Coffee County. Built about 1903 by Japheth Rawls and remodeled and enlarged in 1923 by his nephew Jesse P. Rawls, it stands across from the train station and has long been a landmark and gathering place in Enterprise. It is also significant for its association with the Rawls family, important in the city's early growth: the elder Rawls helped develop the county's turpentine industry, while his nephew built the first electric system in Enterprise and operated one of the city's largest and oldest mills.
80000684.heading: Statement of Significance

74000409.summary: The Oates-Reynolds Memorial Building, a girls' dormitory built in 1922, is the only remaining building of the Baptist Collegiate Institute, one of the oldest educational landmarks in the Wiregrass region of southeastern Alabama, southwestern Georgia, and northern Florida. Founded in Newton in 1898, when Alabama's public schools were poorly organized, the institute was typical of the many private and denominational schools of the era and made a significant contribution to education in the region; by 1918 it had 250 students. After the school burned in the early 1920s, this building was built along with a new classroom building. Brick buildings were still rare in the area at the time.
74000409.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000439.summary: The McIntosh Log Church, known as Andrews Chapel, traces its origins to the beginnings of Methodism in Alabama, when the noted preacher Lorenzo Dow came to the Tombigbee River area in 1803, followed by preachers sent by the South Carolina Methodist Conference from 1808. The chapel was built shortly after John G. Rush and his wife donated the site in 1860 and was named for Methodist Bishop James O. Andrews. After a new church was built in 1952, the log chapel served as a Sunday school for several years.
74000439.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

80000687.summary: The Seaboard Coast Line Railroad Depot, built in 1893, is one of the oldest wooden buildings in Headland and one of the oldest railroad depots in Southeast Alabama, and its board-and-batten design is typical of small-town stations of the period. It was one of four depots built by the locally organized Abbeville Southern Railway, whose 26.9-mile line ran from Abbeville Junction (now Grimes) to Abbeville; the first train reached Headland in late September 1893. The line later became part of the Plant System and was absorbed into larger railroads in 1901.
80000687.heading: Statement of Significance

88001352.summary: Montgomery Hill Baptist Church, built in 1853-54 by John Blake under a contract for $1,450, is one of only two surviving antebellum churches in Baldwin County. Its Greek Revival detailing, slave gallery, and interior graining are rare in the county's architecture. The original building contract survives, showing that the church saw few changes until about 1970.
88001352.heading: Statement of Significance

86001160.summary: The Commercial Hotel (Hart Hotel), built in 1904-05 as a residential hotel near the depot, is significant for its association with the early growth of Flomaton, which began as Pensacola Junction, where two major lines met during the L&N Railroad's rapid expansion after 1879. Built to capture business from rail passengers and crews, it was one of five hotels that predated the town's 1908 incorporation and is the only hotel building of that era surviving in the county. The two-story frame building shows late Victorian or Queen Anne influence.
86001160.heading: Statement of Significance

88001350.summary: Latham United Methodist Church, built in 1906 on donated land for $1,500, is the best of three surviving frame vernacular Gothic Revival religious buildings in Baldwin County. It is also significant for its almost complete lack of alterations: its original ceilings, walls, and pews remain, and changes are limited to new steps, aisle carpeting, and light fixtures. The one-and-a-half-story frame church has a front gable and a two-story corner tower with a pyramidal roof.
88001350.heading: Statement of Significance

93001519.summary: The Atlantic Coastline Railroad Passenger Depot, built in 1908, served as Dothan's passenger station until 1979. The two-story brick depot, with large brackets supporting a broad overhanging hipped roof typical of stations of the period, represents Dothan's physical and economic growth in the early twentieth century. Rail routes, especially the line to Montgomery, linked Dothan economically, socially, and politically to larger cities and made it easier to ship farm and industrial products, helping the town grow from a simple crossroads into the central town of the Wiregrass.
93001519.heading: Statement of Significance

16000835.summary: The Water Works Standpipe (Dothan Dixie Standpipe) was Dothan's first water storage tank and provided the city's first water service when it went into operation in 1897, bringing potable water and fire protection to the young town. Its riveted steel shell, holding 150,000 gallons of artesian well water, is a prime example of late nineteenth-century engineering, and only four other water towers were built in Alabama before 1920. The standpipe became the center of early Dothan as development grew around it. Its construction is largely credited to Mayor J. R. Young, who arranged municipal bonds to fund the tower, the well, and the city water works.
16000835.heading: Summary Paragraph

100007191.summary: Moody Hospital, built in 1916 with additions in 1922 and 1929, is the only remaining example of the private hospitals developed in Dothan by local physicians in the early twentieth century, when hospitals were changing from places that mainly cared for the poor into modern facilities serving whole communities. It provided modern medical care to Dothan's white population, while Black patients were served in a separate facility that no longer stands. It served the region for five decades until it closed in 1965.
100007191.heading: Summary Paragraph

13000406.summary: Howell School, built in 1902 and designed by J. W. Baughman, is an excellent example of the eclectic blend of Late Victorian styles popular in Alabama institutional buildings around the turn of the twentieth century. It is also significant for its role in Dothan's post-World War II industrial development: after the Chamber of Commerce actively promoted the city to industry, the building served as a textile factory from 1947 to 1997.
13000406.heading: Summary Paragraph

74000412.summary: The Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse in Dothan, completed in 1911 at a total cost of $85,000, is a three-story Classical Revival building on a granite base with a modified Doric portico. Congress authorized funds for a courthouse and post office in 1906, and the building was located in Dothan through the efforts of postmaster Byron Trammell and B. G. Farmer Sr. It served as both courthouse and post office until a new post office was built in 1964, and then continued as a courthouse and federal office building.
74000412.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

77000204.summary: The Dothan Opera House, completed in 1915, was the most noted of a series of public improvements that marked Dothan's change from a small country town into a city of importance in the Wiregrass region. Designed by an Atlanta architectural firm, the three-story masonry building reflects the revival of classical styles in early twentieth-century public buildings and draws heavily on Italian Renaissance models. It was built as a municipal auditorium and meeting place for theatrical entertainment and is largely unaltered in plan and exterior appearance.
77000204.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

90001315.summary: The Dothan Municipal Light and Water Plant, completed in 1913, was the only coal-fired power plant in Alabama's Wiregrass region at the time. It provided electric and water service to the area until 1949, when the Alabama Power Company took over electric service. Built during the city's boom period, the plant added generators to keep up with Dothan's growing population and is a reminder of the city's municipal growth in the early twentieth century.
90001315.heading: Statement of Significance

82001616.summary: The Purcell-Killingsworth House, built in 1889-1890, is significant for its association with William Henry Purcell (1845-1910), who came from North Carolina after the Civil War and became one of Columbia's leading businessmen and later a local politician. Over 45 years he ran the town's principal river landing and warehouse and was involved in planting, cotton, and insurance. The house, a good example of simplified Victorian taste with an octagonal turret, is the finest residence in this small town and one of only two two-story houses in the area.
82001616.heading: Statement of Significance

100009568.summary: The Bank of Columbia is locally significant for its role in the economic development of Columbia in the later twentieth century. Built in 1912 and extensively remodeled in 1964-65, the building housed the bank until 1977, when it moved to a new building. Through loans to local businesses, independent farmers, and larger farming operations, the bank was instrumental in the town's economic survival and provided stability during uncertain times, as local banks were essential to year-round farming and business in rural areas.
100009568.heading: Summary Paragraph

88001356.summary: Stockton Methodist Church, built in 1929, is significant as an intact rural house of worship. Though the most recent building in its thematic group, it reflects an earlier Classical Revival aesthetic, making it a formal architectural statement in a community of simple vernacular buildings. The one-story frame church has a front gable and a recessed porch across the full facade.
88001356.heading: Statement of Significance

85002163.summary: The Alabama Midland Railway Depot in Ashford, built in 1892, is one of the oldest remaining depots in Southeast Alabama and a particularly fine example of a late nineteenth-century small-town frame depot, one of three of similar design built by the railroad in the 1890s that remain on their original sites. The Alabama Midland was a major force in developing sparsely settled Henry and later Houston counties, opening distant markets to the area's lumber, naval stores, and later farm products. Access to the railroad drew settlers to Ashford and spurred the town's growth.
85002163.heading: Statement of Significance

89002453.summary: The N. Q. and Virginia M. Thompson House, built in 1905, is the finest example of Neoclassical architecture in Citronelle and one of the best in Mobile County outside the city of Mobile. Though Citronelle has other grand houses, this is the only one of its importance in the style, and it has been a focal point near the center of town since it was built. The contractor-builder was George Tyrrell of Illinois, who probably built several other buildings in Citronelle.
89002453.heading: Statement of Significance

73000359.summary: The Ellicott Stone, inscribed with the date 1799 and the words "U.S." on its north face and "Dominios de S.M. Carlos IV" on its south face, is the only remaining marker placed by Andrew Ellicott along the 31st parallel, which he surveyed between 1797 and 1800. Spain had accepted the 31st parallel as the northern boundary of its Florida territory in the Treaty of San Lorenzo in 1795, and President George Washington appointed Ellicott American commissioner of the joint boundary survey in 1796. The stone is the point of origin for land surveys in southern Alabama and Mississippi, and townships in the area are numbered from it.
73000359.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

95000556.summary: The Killcreas House, built from 1900 to 1906 by farmer John Killcreas on land his family acquired in 1881, is an intact example of a rare Folk Victorian house type found only in rural north Baldwin County, with a prominent shingled gable portico and steep main roof; it is one of only eight such houses remaining in the county. Its central hall and back hall plan is a rare arrangement in south Alabama vernacular houses. The lumber was sawn on the property, and the house keeps original plantings and remains of its original fence.
95000556.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

88001349.summary: The First Baptist Church of Bay Minette, built in the mid-1910s, is the earliest surviving example in Baldwin County of a church built of brick and stone. Its masonry construction reflected the congregation's means, matched new building in the prosperous county seat, and contrasted with the congregation's earlier frame churches. A two-story rear annex was added around 1925, and the congregation left the building in 1962.
88001349.heading: Statement of Significance

89002454.summary: The Willis G. Clark House, built around 1865, is one of the two best examples of the Greek Revival cottage in northern Mobile County, notable for an asymmetrical interior and an interconnecting-room plan recalling the Creole cottage. It was built by Willis G. Clark, editor and owner of the Mobile Daily Advertiser, who achieved state and local significance for his work in public education. He was instrumental in founding the Mobile public school system, the first in Alabama, which opened at Barton Academy in 1852, and helped secure state funds for the University of Alabama as a trustee. He was also active in Democratic Party leadership during Reconstruction.
89002454.heading: Statement of Significance

88000112.summary: The Jacob Magee House (Magee-Sturtevant House) achieved national significance as the place where Confederate General Taylor and Union General Canby met on April 29, 1865, and laid the groundwork for the surrender of Confederate forces in the Department of Alabama, Mississippi, and East Louisiana, which in effect brought the Civil War to an official close; Taylor surrendered at Citronelle on May 4. Built in 1846-47, the house is also architecturally significant for its unique blend of a South Atlantic coastal plan with the local Gulf Coast cottage, the only known example of the type in Mobile County.
88000112.heading: Statement of Significance

08000429.summary: The Tanner Farmhouse is a rare intact example of the vernacular housing that characterized the social and economic development of Alabama's Longleaf Pine region, built by carpenters of local materials during rural Alabama's shift from a nineteenth-century farm economy to the early twentieth-century railroad and industrial boom. Its construction likely began around 1886 under owner James B. Cowart and was completed no later than 1908, possibly with repairs after the hurricane of 1906. The house has a center-hall, one-room-deep plan with a rear ell, and a kitchen was added in 1932.
08000429.heading: Summary

75000323.summary: The Gulf, Mobile, and Ohio Passenger Terminal, completed in 1907 at a cost of $400,000, is one of only two large-scale railroad stations in Alabama, and its massive, ornate design reflects the importance of railroads and of Mobile in that era. Designed by P. Thornton Marye, it is one of the earlier and finer examples of the Spanish Colonial Revival style in the city. It served the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, chartered in 1848 to link Mobile with the Mississippi River and the Midwest and one of the first two railroads in the nation to receive a federal land grant, a precedent with great impact on the later nineteenth century.
75000323.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

88001354.summary: St. Patrick's Catholic Church, built in 1924 and later used as the Loxley Public Library, is one of three ornamental concrete block churches in Baldwin County. Its size, scale, and loose medieval stylistic references are rare in rural Loxley. Its original windows and doors remain, though the interior was adapted for library use.
88001354.heading: Statement of Significance

100004131.summary: The Mobile Seamen's Club Building, completed in 1949, illustrates the evolution of local efforts to promote the welfare of white sailors in Mobile, Alabama's only port city. The Seamen's Club began as a Christian organization focused on sailors' moral well-being and grew to serve the domestic needs of the merchant marine. The building is also significant as one of the modern works of noted Mobile architect John Platt Roberts and was hailed at its opening as one of the few shining examples of modern design; its terrazzo lobby floor reflects its nautical theme.
100004131.heading: Statement of Significance

91000842.summary: Saint Francis Xavier Roman Catholic Church is a rare surviving vernacular Catholic church in Mobile, where the Catholic building tradition is overwhelmingly high style; though built of frame, it has a formal plan, stained glass windows, and interior vaulting. The parish in the old suburb of Toulminville was established on land given in 1868 and was briefly served from 1877 to 1879 by Father Abram Joseph Ryan, the famous poet-priest of the Confederacy. The present church replaced the original, which was destroyed by a hurricane in 1916.
91000842.heading: Statement of Significance

08000458.summary: Aimwell Baptist Church, built over six years from 1940 to 1946, is significant in the African American heritage of Mobile. Its planning and construction reflect the growth of African American churches in the northern part of the city during segregation, and it housed the congregation's community work, including an active missionary department, daycare, and educational programs. It represents the institutions and facilities that supported the separate African American communities of the era. The church, with crenellated corner towers and Gothic-arched windows, is also architecturally significant.
08000458.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

78000503.summary: The Emanuel Building (Staples-Pake Building) has both architectural and commercial significance. It was built in the 1850s as a three-story brick office building, typical of late Federal architecture in Mobile, by Jonathan Emanuel, a cotton broker who later became president of Mobile Mutual Insurance Company; in 1852 nine cotton brokers were listed at the building. In 1903 it was remodeled for the Bank of Mobile by prominent Mobile architect George B. Rogers, and it is one of the few documented buildings he designed.
78000503.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82001611.summary: The Coley Building is architecturally significant as an unusual blend of styles: built around 1836 as a Federal-style commercial building, it was updated around 1870 with Beaux-Arts elements, including cast iron decoration, a mansard roof, and a first-floor colonnade of fluted Corinthian columns. The two styles blend interestingly while keeping their distinct origins, making it a unique commercial building. It is one of only two buildings in Mobile with a cast iron front.
82001611.heading: Statement of Significance

78000504.summary: The First National Bank building, completed in 1906, was designed in 1905 by the Mobile firm of Watkins, Hutchisson and Garvin and is one of the few remaining examples of their work. Its white glazed brick Neoclassical facade is a significant example of a style popular for public buildings in the early twentieth century. It represents the growth of Mobile's banks after 1900 and was the third building occupied by the First National Bank since it opened in May 1865.
78000504.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

08000964.summary: The United States Court House and Custom House, built in 1933-34 near the Alabama State Docks with a 1939-40 addition, stands as a symbol of the federal presence in Mobile, one of the nation's oldest port cities and Alabama's only Gulf port. Designed by the local firm of Carey and Dowling, with the addition designed under Supervising Architect Louis Simon, it is a good example of 1930s federal architecture in the Modern Classical style, combining Neoclassical Revival, Renaissance Revival, and Art Deco details.
08000964.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

75000322.summary: The Battle House Hotel, completed in 1908, is the fourth hotel on its site and the second called the Battle House; designed by F. M. Andrews and Company of New York, it was one of the earliest buildings in Alabama to use steel-frame construction. The first Battle House, designed by noted Greek Revival architect Isaiah Rogers and opened in 1852, burned in 1905, and leading citizens raised $1,350,000 to rebuild it. President Woodrow Wilson was entertained at the hotel in 1913 after announcing his corollary to the Monroe Doctrine to the Southern Commercial Congress.
75000322.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

85001749.summary: Stone Street Baptist Church is significant as an eclectic, vernacular reworking of an earlier frame church, carried out during the Depression by the church's deacons, who drew on other churches in Mobile and sought an exotic, "Asiatic" look for the building. The site has been used continuously by a Black Baptist congregation since the 1840s: in 1843 the trustees of the St. Anthony Street Baptist Church bought the lot "for the use and benefit of the African Branch" of the church, and title passed to the trustees of Stone Street Baptist Church in 1870. According to its cornerstone, the church was rebuilt in 1909.
85001749.heading: Statement of Significance

73000361.summary: The Brisk & Jacobson Store, built in 1866, is one of the largest and most ornate buildings in Mobile's old commercial district and shows the city's continuing prosperity despite the Civil War. An excellent example of mid-nineteenth-century Classical Revival architecture based on sixteenth-century Venetian palaces, its north front is covered by an exquisitely detailed cast-iron facade, described as the only one remaining in Mobile. From 1869 to 1893 it was the elegant store of Brisk & Jacobson, dealers in men's clothing, and later housed various businesses until 1972.
73000361.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87000937.summary: The Dave Patton House, built around 1915, is the only primary structure known to be associated with Dave Patton (1879-1927), a particularly successful Black businessman in early twentieth-century Mobile whose hauling and wrecking business was described in 1910 as employing 40 mules and 80 workers. It survives as evidence of a successful Black-owned business at a time when most failed. The house is also a particularly fine example of early twentieth-century domestic architecture rarely associated with Black ownership in the period; oral history attributes its design to Mobile architect George B. Rogers.
87000937.heading: Statement of Significance

92000628.summary: The Joseph Jossen House, built in 1906 and later known as the World Trade Building, is a rare brick example of modified Queen Anne architecture in Mobile. It also shows the persistence of nineteenth-century styles, having been built long after the Queen Anne style's peak. It was built during a year of major construction in Mobile that included a large new railroad station, the city's first skyscraper, and three new hotels.
92000628.heading: Statement of Significance

76000345.summary: The Pincus Building, completed in 1891 for local merchant Abraham Pincus, is a fine example of commercial late Victorian Eclecticism and one of two remaining such buildings in Mobile designed by Rudolf Benz. Benz, a graduate of the Polytechnic School of Stuttgart who had worked in Chicago, St. Louis, and New York, designed several Mobile buildings, including the Mobile Cotton Exchange. The building housed the E. O. Zadek Jewelry Company for many years and remained in the Pincus family until 1970.
76000345.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

11000407.summary: The Davis Avenue Recreation Center traces its origins to the Davis Avenue Community House, established in 1921 as Mobile's first recreation center for African Americans. The present building was constructed in 1936 to meet growing demand and is significant for its athletic programs for African Americans living along Davis Avenue, now Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Avenue. It is also the only recreational facility for African Americans in Mobile built with WPA funding, and it uses early modernist design elements.
11000407.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

83003459.summary: The Davis Avenue Branch of the Mobile Public Library, designed in 1930 by George B. Rogers as the library's first branch, is an excellent example of his Neoclassical style. It repeats the massing and general design of the main library Rogers designed in 1928, on a smaller scale and without the pilasters. Though small, the building achieves a monumental effect through formal balance and proportion rather than standard classical moldings.
83003459.heading: Statement of Significance

11000408.summary: The International Longshoreman's Association Hall, built in 1949, is significant in Mobile's African American heritage. The ILA local, established in 1936, represented African Americans in one of the few relatively well-paid occupations open to them during segregation, and it needed a larger hall as the port expanded during World War II. The hall served as a social gathering place where famous African American entertainers performed and as a focal point for civil rights gatherings; Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. made his only appearance in Mobile here on January 1, 1959. The building is also an example of Art Moderne design.
11000408.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

08000459.summary: Mt. Olive Missionary Baptist Church No. 1, built in 1916 and enlarged with a two-story wing in 1952, reflects the establishment of separate African American institutions in northwestern Mobile during segregation and the growth of the community along Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Avenue. It housed the congregation's community work, including a missionary department, ministry to the poor, daycare, and educational programs. The building is also a good, intact example of African American church design of its period.
08000459.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

05000289.summary: This boundary increase expanded the Church Street East Historic District in downtown Mobile to include Veets, a two-story commercial building at 66 South Royal Street with an ornamental concrete block facade, which had been left out of the 1983 district nomination. Built around the turn of the twentieth century, it keeps its historic integrity and is similar to other commercial buildings in the district. The adjoining building at 68 South Royal Street was also included but does not contribute because its storefront has been altered.
05000289.heading: Boundary Increase Narrative

78000505.summary: State Street A.M.E. Zion Church, built in 1854, is one of the most imposing buildings erected for a Black congregation in Alabama before the Civil War and the oldest Methodist church building in Mobile. Its congregation, founded in 1829 as the African Church of the City of Mobile, rebuilt here after its first church burned; as a mission of the Methodist Episcopal Church, it had 500 full members by 1855, making it one of Alabama's most successful Black churches of the time. When the congregation voted in 1865 to join the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, challenged its right to the building. Rev. Wilbur G. Strong, a pioneer of the A.M.E. Zion Church in the Gulf States, was among its distinguished pastors.
78000505.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000690.summary: St. Francis Street Methodist Church, built in 1896, is the only surviving High Victorian religious building in Mobile and represents an important period in the city's architectural history, with strong contrasts of dark red pressed brick and white stone trim. Its massing and detail are unchanged except for the loss of the upper half of its spire in the hurricane of 1916. The congregation grew out of the Franklin Street Methodist Church, founded in 1824, which was the "beehive" from which several other Methodist congregations developed.
84000690.heading: Statement of Significance

84000689.summary: The Phillippi House, built in 1850 by Antonio Phillippi, is the only remaining example in Mobile of a mid-nineteenth-century two-story brick townhouse with a cast iron balcony over the sidewalk, a once-common type. It has a typical side-hall, double-parlor plan and a deeply recessed entrance with Greek key framing. Its high water table is an unusual feature for Mobile.
84000689.heading: Statement of Significance

84000682.summary: The Neville House, built in 1896, is a late nineteenth-century free adaptation of the Italianate style, in which individual design replaced the strict revivalism of earlier decades. It has the typical massing of a two-story brick inner-city house rising directly from the sidewalk, and it carries forward Italianate features such as a bay window, bracketed eaves, and paneled parapet. Its large window panes, geometric cast iron, and other details reflect later Victorian taste.
84000682.heading: Statement of Significance

69000034.summary: Mobile City Hall was built in the 1850s, during the term of Mayor Jones M. Withers, on the site of the city's open-air public market, which had operated there from 1823 until courts ordered such markets removed. The Greek Revival building of stuccoed brick continued to serve as a market and was used as a militia armory during the Civil War, when reserve troops drilled in its courtyard. After the war municipal offices moved into the upper floors, shops continued to operate in parts of the building until about 1940, and it eventually became the center of city government.
69000034.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

08000460.summary: The Turner-Todd Motor Company building, built in 1926 with an addition in 1940, stands on St. Louis Street, known to longtime Mobile residents as "Automobile Alley." It is a significant local example of early twentieth-century Commercial Style architecture, with a flat facade, large first-floor display windows, a recessed entry, and an open floor plan for displaying merchandise. It also shows how this common style was adapted to the needs of the automobile trade, including a concrete ramp at the rear.
08000460.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

84000694.summary: The Scottish Rites Temple, built in 1921-22 to designs by George B. Rogers, is a distinctive example of Egyptian Revival architecture, with sloping walls rising unbroken for 65 feet, pylon-like entrances, a cavetto cornice, and stylized sphinx figures. Although the style drew interest at several times, especially after the opening of Tutankhamen's tomb in the 1920s, few such buildings were built and fewer survive. It is the only building in Mobile, and the only one on the Gulf Coast, designed entirely in the Egyptian style. Rogers was the first Mobile architect named a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects.
84000694.heading: Statement of Significance

82001610.summary: The Cavellero House, built in 1835, is the oldest surviving Federal-style building in downtown Mobile. Despite alterations to its facade, it keeps its overall massing and scale. It represents the once-common arrangement in which shopkeepers ran businesses on the ground floor and lived on the floors above.
82001610.heading: Statement of Significance

98001027.summary: This third boundary increase added a duplex at 310 St. Francis Street, along with a vacant lot, to the Lower Dauphin Street Commercial District in downtown Mobile. The two-story frame duplex, built around 1905 in a loosely Classical Revival style with inset porches and monumental boxed columns, had been left out of the original nomination and earlier expansions. It was added because it contributes to the district in location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, feeling, and association.
98001027.heading: Boundary Increase Narrative

86000083.summary: USS Alabama, a South Dakota-class battleship launched in February 1942 and commissioned on August 16, 1942, served in both the Atlantic and Pacific theaters of World War II and earned nine battle stars. Although the aircraft carrier replaced the battleship as the Navy's principal capital ship, battleships like Alabama did important service bombarding enemy-held shores and escorting carriers with dense antiaircraft fire. Decommissioned in 1947, she remained unaltered until she was transferred to the State of Alabama as a war memorial in 1964, and she keeps her World War II integrity.
86000083.heading: Statement of Significance

84000665.summary: The Dahm House, built in 1873, is an excellent example of a transitional building that draws on traditional forms while showing early Victorian characteristics. Its cubic massing, dentil cornice, three-bay facade, and side-hall plan with double parlors resemble the Federal and Italianate houses of the nearby DeTonti Square Historic District. Its colored leaded glass and geometric cast iron porch, contrasting with the flowing forms of earlier ironwork, announce the Victorian period.
84000665.heading: Statement of Significance

84000672.summary: The Meaher-Zoghby House, built in 1901, combines late nineteenth-century vernacular influences found in Mobile with distinctly early twentieth-century elements. Its broken massing of receding planes suggests the Queen Anne style without turrets or complex chimneys, and its brickwork, including alternating quoins, is excellent. Its restrained design marks a clear change from the complexity and exuberance of the Victorian era, and it stands on its original site.
84000672.heading: Statement of Significance

73000363.summary: The Kirkbride House, also called the Conde-Charlotte House, is one of Mobile's older standing buildings and one of the city's more architecturally interesting houses. The Federal-period building, possibly built as early as 1822 by Peter Hobart on the site of old Fort Condé (later Fort Charlotte), reputedly served as the city's first jail and courthouse; a sophisticated Greek Revival portico was added in the 1840s. Jonathan Kirkbride, a builder from New Jersey, bought it in 1849 and adapted it as a residence. It became the property of a Mobile historic preservation society in 1940 and served as a U.S. Navy officers' club during World War II.
73000363.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92001885.summary: Government Street Presbyterian Church, built in 1836 and credited to James Gallier with Charles and James Dakin, is one of the oldest and least-altered Greek Revival houses of worship in the United States and is notable for its intact Greek Revival interior. It has been called a candidate for the title of America's most beautiful Greek Revival church. Its two-columned Ionic portico set between walls (distyle in antis) is one of the earliest surviving uses of that form for an American church, a design later adopted for countless churches. The church was among the first outside New York to reflect the influential New York school of Greek Revival design of Ithiel Town, Alexander Jackson Davis, and Minard Lafever.
92001885.heading: Statement of Significance

85000446.summary: The Hunter House, built in 1878, is an exceptional example of nineteenth-century residential architecture in Mobile built as a Black-owned home; the two-story Italianate house matches comparable white-owned houses of the period in scale, character, and detail. It is also significant for its association with Bettie Hunter (c. 1852-1879), an affluent Black businesswoman who reputedly built her wealth through a successful hack and carriage business in downtown Mobile. The house, its contents, and a flattering obituary reflect wealth and influence exceptional for Black residents in the nineteenth century.
85000446.heading: Statement of Significance

70000109.summary: The Bishop Portier House, a Creole cottage with Federal-style details, was the residence of the ranking prelates of the Roman Catholic Church in Alabama from 1833 until 1914. Bishop Michael Portier, a native of France, became the first Bishop of Mobile in 1829, moved into the house four years later, and served until his death in 1859, overseeing the Catholic Church in Alabama and all of Florida. During his tenure he led the building of the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception and founded Spring Hill College (1830), Visitation Convent and Academy, St. Mary's Orphan Asylum, and a number of other schools.
70000109.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

69000033.summary: Fort Condé, built of brick in 1717 on the site of Bienville's 1711 wooden stockade, was the first masonry fort built by Europeans on the Gulf Coast. Renamed Fort Charlotte under British rule after 1763 and kept by the Spanish, it was the center of military, commercial, and governmental activity for the French, British, and Spanish empires in the Gulf region for about 100 years. Congress authorized the sale of the old fort in 1818, and later development obliterated even its exact location until archaeological excavations reidentified the site, uncovering the foundations of the southwest bastion, the moat, and the casemates of the south wall.
69000033.heading: Statement of Significance

84000675.summary: The Metzger House, built in 1875, is an excellent example of a one-story brick middle-class house in inner-city Mobile, continuing the 1860s local tradition of combining classical and Italianate features, while its floor-length shuttered porch windows give it a Gulf Coast feel. It reflects the period after the Civil War and Reconstruction, when demand for large, expensive houses declined and middle-class housing came into prominence. Its refined porch details show that skilled craftsmen built even modest homes of the era, and the house is largely unaltered.
84000675.heading: Statement of Significance

86000086.summary: USS Drum was the first Gato-class submarine completed by the United States before World War II; the Gato class was the standard American fleet submarine early in the war and, with its successor class, bore the brunt of the fighting against Japan. Drum conducted 13 war patrols and sank 15 Japanese ships totaling more than 80,000 tons. American submarines, though never more than two percent of naval personnel, sank much of Japan's warship and merchant tonnage and created a blockade that cut off the raw materials Japan needed to continue the war.
86000086.heading: Statement of Significance

83003462.summary: Fire Station No. 5, built in 1851 for a volunteer fire company at a cost of $5,500, is an excellent example of a functional building designed in the Greek Revival style. Its first story uses a Doric two-columned (distyle in antis) arrangement, and its fine proportions, simple moldings, and interior Greek key door frames give it distinction. Like other nineteenth-century volunteer fire company buildings, it is two stories of brick, with the equipment on the ground floor and a social and recreation room above.
83003462.heading: Statement of Significance

76000347.summary: St. Louis Street Missionary Baptist Church houses one of only four Black congregations established in Alabama before 1865 and is the second oldest Missionary Baptist church in Mobile. The congregation was organized in 1854 by ten members of Stone Street Baptist Church who wished to sponsor a statewide missionary program. The present Eclectic building, with Renaissance and Neoclassical Revival elements, was completed in 1872 at a cost of $24,000 and renovated in 1897 and 1910. In 1874 it hosted the Colored Baptist Convention session that voted to found Selma University.
76000347.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

11000898.summary: Caldwell School opened in 1947 as a segregated public school offering primary and secondary education to African Americans. It was one of only eight public schools for African Americans in Mobile, one of five offering both levels, and one of three serving the segregated northwestern part of the city around Davis Avenue, known as "the Avenue." It served in that role until 1969, when a federal mandate ordered the complete integration of Mobile County schools.
11000898.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

70000108.summary: Mobile City Hospital, dedicated in 1831, served as the city's hospital until 1966. It cared for hundreds of victims of yellow fever epidemics from 1839 to 1897; in the 1873 epidemic more than 40 percent of those treated there died. It was a center for the care of wounded Confederate soldiers in the closing months of the Civil War, especially during the Battle of Mobile Bay in August 1864.
70000108.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

71000103.summary: The Martin Horst House, built in 1867-68 by builder George Woodward Cox at an estimated cost of $19,000, represents the finest residential architecture of its time in Mobile; it is Italianate with some Greek Revival details and stands in the Church Street East Historic District. Martin Horst, a prosperous German immigrant businessman, served as mayor of Mobile in 1870-71 and is credited with ending carpetbagger rule early in Reconstruction. Cox also built a number of other fine buildings in Mobile.
71000103.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

87000853.summary: Emanuel AME Church, built in 1890 and unaltered since, is Mobile's only example of a Gothic Revival church built for a Black congregation. It is an excellent example of the work of architect James F. Hutchisson, who used brick corbeling to tie together three asymmetrical facade bays into a unified design. Like Mobile's other major Black congregations of the nineteenth century, Emanuel AME grew out of Black members' desire to continue worship as white parent churches separated from their Black memberships.
87000853.heading: Statement of Significance

74000428.summary: The U.S. Marine Hospital is one of the oldest public buildings in Mobile and a good example of the city's limited number of Classical Revival buildings. The Marine Hospital Service, created by Congress in 1798 to care for sick and disabled seamen, bought the site in 1838, and the first patients were admitted in 1843. Confederate soldiers were treated there from 1861 to 1865; after Union forces took it in April 1865, it returned to its original purpose in 1870.
74000428.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000668.summary: The Charles Denby House, built in 1873 and restored in 1981, is a good example of a purely vernacular design developed without reference to Mobile's Federal, Greek Revival, or Gulf Coast cottage styles. Its traditional central-hall plan, simple interior trim, and one-story brick construction are a valuable record of middle-class housing of the 1870s. It and the nearby Metzger House are the only two one-story brick middle-class houses of the period left in the inner city.
84000668.heading: Statement of Significance

91000841.summary: Saint Joseph's Roman Catholic Church is an important high-style example of the Second Gothic Revival in Mobile, typical of the city's Catholic architecture in its design, quality materials, and workmanship. Designed by Diboll and Owen of New Orleans and completed in 1908, it was praised by the Mobile Daily Register as one of the handsomest churches in the state, notable for its open interior without columns. Its contemporary rectory is more closely matched in style to its church than any other in the city. St. Joseph's Parish, Mobile's third oldest, was formed in 1857 to serve mainly German immigrants.
91000841.heading: Statement of Significance

91000845.summary: The Convent of Mercy, built in 1908 to designs by New Orleans architect A. H. Downey with an ancillary building of 1928, is locally significant for combining two early twentieth-century styles, English Baroque Revival above and Neoclassical below, in a design not found elsewhere in Mobile. The Sisters of Mercy, who came to the area in the 1880s and opened St. Joseph's School, established their motherhouse and a high school in Mobile in 1895. The school closed in 1968, and the sisters moved to Spring Hill the next year.
91000845.heading: Statement of Significance

83003474.summary: The Vickers and Schumacher Buildings at 707-711 Dauphin Street are the last surviving buildings in Mobile where carriages and wagons were manufactured, though the city once had numerous carriage makers. The Schumacher Building dates from 1866 and the Vickers Building from about 1904, both in a severe, unornamented style suited to a carriage factory that relies on brickwork for visual interest. Carriage makers used the buildings until 1914, when they became a storehouse for the Mobile Electric Company; their large carriage openings, though infilled, remain intact.
83003474.heading: Statement of Significance

82001613.summary: The Weems House, a one-story frame house built in 1870 by Louis H. Weems, is a good example of the sympathetic reuse in the 1870s of Greek Revival elements popular in Mobile from the 1830s to the 1850s. It keeps the dignity and proportions of the Greek Revival, including a front porch integrated into the overall design and a street-facing pedimented gable. Details such as the dentil molding along the rakes of the pediment amplify the earlier vocabulary and set it apart from true Greek Revival houses.
82001613.heading: Statement of Significance

84000671.summary: The Hawthorn House, built around 1853 by Joshua K. Hawthorn, was unusual among the Spring Hill houses of its time in being a year-round rather than summer residence. It is a simply detailed Gulf Coast cottage that shows Greek Revival influence in its central-hall plan and square porch posts. It used older building methods, such as hand-hewn lumber, wooden pegs, and internal corner braces, at a time when builders in Mobile were using machine-cut lumber and cut nails.
84000671.heading: Statement of Significance

70000110.summary: Admiral Raphael Semmes, the most famous Confederate naval hero, lived in this house from 1871 until his death in 1879. Semmes commanded the Confederate raiders Sumter and Alabama; the CSS Alabama captured more than 60 Union ships between 1862 and 1864 before it was sunk by the USS Kearsarge off France in June 1864. Rescued by British seamen, Semmes returned to the South and became possibly the only man in modern military history to hold the ranks of both admiral and brigadier general.
70000110.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

82002061.summary: The Tscheiner House (Damus School), built in 1866 by F. Tscheiner, a ladies' shoemaker, is an early and very good example of the Carpenter Gothic style in Mobile, with especially fine detail and careful craftsmanship. Built when most Mobilians were building in the Italianate style, it foreshadowed later Victorian styles, and its designs were likely copied from a popular pattern book such as Downing's The Architecture of Country Houses. It is also significant as the home of the Damus School, a prominent school for young women, from 1867 until the early twentieth century.
82002061.heading: Statement of Significance

73000364.summary: The Protestant Children's Home, built in 1845, is one of the earliest buildings in Alabama built for philanthropic purposes and served as an orphanage for 125 years. The Protestant Orphans Asylum Society was incorporated by the legislature in 1840 to care for children orphaned by Mobile's yellow fever epidemics. The building, said to have cost $4,000, is attributed to Henry Moffat, a Philadelphia-born carpenter and builder.
73000364.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

91000839.summary: St. Vincent de Paul Church (now St. Vincent de Paul-Prince of Peace), built in 1874, is an important high-style example of the Gothic Revival in Mobile. Patterned after St. Patrick's Church in Albany, New York, it is one of the city's best interpretations of the style and has some of the finest brickwork in Mobile. The parish, the second oldest in the city, was founded by Bishop Michael Portier in 1847 to serve Catholics in southern Mobile, and a church school operated there from 1847 to 1963.
91000839.heading: Statement of Significance

93000420.summary: The U. J. Cleveland House (Cleveland-Smith House), built in 1853, is an intact Gulf Coast cottage with an unusual interior plan; its back hall dining room arrangement is extremely rare in Mobile. It was built by U. J. Cleveland on a thirty-acre parcel on what was then the sparsely settled outskirts of the city. The house was moved in 1893 when Charles Street was extended through the property.
93000420.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

72000168.summary: The Bragg-Mitchell House is significant for both its owners and its architecture. Built in 1847 for William H. Pratt, it is one of the finest Greek Revival mansions in Mobile and was designed by Thomas Simmons James, one of the city's outstanding architects, who also worked in Natchez, Jackson, and New Orleans. It was the home of Judge John Bragg and later of his brother, General Braxton Bragg.
72000168.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

72000170.summary: Georgia Cottage, a Greek Revival house, is best known as the home of novelist Augusta Evans Wilson, said to be the first woman in America to earn more than $100,000 from her writing. Born in Columbus, Georgia, in 1835, she lived here from 1857, when her father bought the house, until her marriage to Lorenzo M. Wilson in its front parlor in 1868. While living here she wrote three of her novels, Macaria, St. Elmo, and Vashti, using the right wing as her study.
72000170.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

74000427.summary: The Gates-Daves House is a mid-nineteenth-century frame country cottage with long, low proportions, a type uncommon in Mobile, and it is probably the best remaining example. Local tradition says it was built by Hezekiah Gates, who bought the property in 1841, though the purchase price suggests a house may already have stood there. The Daves family owned it from 1856 to 1926, when part of the property was sold and the house was divided into two dwellings.
74000427.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

76000346.summary: The South Lafayette Street Creole Cottages are a notable group of three restored houses, the March-Erickson House (1852) and the Dorgan-Holmes and Hobbs-Harris Houses (both 1868), that formed the nucleus of a middle-class neighborhood that grew after 1850 as one of Mobile's major western suburbs. They are fine examples of the Creole cottage with strong Greek Revival influence, and the March-Erickson House, built by Henry March, is one of Mobile's oldest Creole cottages. Most earlier buildings on the street have burned or been demolished, and the restoration of these houses played a significant role in the area's renewal.
76000346.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

92000629.summary: The Amelia Stewart House (Hallett-Stewart House) is a notably intact Greek Revival country house and a copy of Oakleigh, showing that house's influence on local architecture and the persistence of the Greek Revival style. It combines two parts: a raised rear section built in 1835 as a garçonnière, or separate quarters, for a house that later burned, and a front section added in 1871.
92000629.heading: Statement of Significance

91000860.summary: The Ernest Megginson House, built in 1927 by druggist Ernest Megginson, is a typical middle-class expression of the Spanish Revival style and perhaps one of the most elegantly styled Spanish Revival houses in Mobile, with stucco walls, a ceramic tile roof, and an interplay of interior and exterior arches. It stands in Florence Place, a suburb platted in 1926, where early efforts to require an all-Spanish Revival neighborhood were defeated by the Depression.
91000860.heading: Statement of Significance

71000104.summary: Oakleigh, built in 1831-1832 by James W. Roper, is one of Alabama's largest, oldest, and finest examples of the T-shaped, off-center hall plan, a regional type valued for the light and ventilation it provided in the humid climate. Its curved exterior staircase rising to the portico beside the front door is a unique feature. Alfred F. Irwin bought the house in 1852; during the Union occupation of Mobile at the end of the Civil War, Mrs. Irwin, who was of Irish descent, flew a British flag from the front gallery, which kept Union officers from quartering there.
71000104.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

91000862.summary: The Jacob VanderSys House, built in 1927 by local builder and contractor Jacob VanderSys, is a typical middle-class expression of the Spanish Revival style, with stucco walls, a ceramic tile roof, and interior and exterior arches. It stands in the Florence Place subdivision, platted in 1926 in one of Mobile's growing suburbs, and was first used as a rental house.
91000862.heading: Statement of Significance

91000859.summary: The J. E. Paterson House, built in 1929 by J. E. Paterson as a rental house, is a typical middle-class expression of the Spanish Revival style, with stucco walls and casement windows. It stands in Florence Place, a Mobile suburb platted in 1926 by George Fearn and Son, where early efforts to require an all-Spanish Revival neighborhood failed because of buyer resistance and the Depression.
91000859.heading: Statement of Significance

91000857.summary: The Arthur VanderSys House (VanderSys-Cloninger House), built in 1926 by Arthur VanderSys as his own home, was one of the earliest houses in its development and is a typical middle-class expression of the Spanish Revival style, with stucco walls, a ceramic tile roof, interior and exterior arches, and an unusual arched wing wall. It stands in Florence Place, a Mobile suburb platted in 1926 by George Fearn and Son, where early efforts to require an all-Spanish Revival neighborhood failed because of buyer resistance and the Depression. Deed restrictions required houses costing at least $4,000 and a uniform 25-foot setback.
91000857.heading: Statement of Significance

91000861.summary: The George Levy House, built in 1927 for Mobile cotton buyer George Levy, is a typical middle-class example of the Spanish Revival style, with stucco walls, parapeted rooflines, and sophisticated tilework on the porch deck. It stands in Florence Place, a Mobile suburb platted in 1926 by George Fearn and Son, where early efforts to require an all-Spanish Revival neighborhood failed because of buyer resistance and the Depression.
91000861.heading: Statement of Significance

84000680.summary: Monterey Place, built in 1898 by Charles M. Shepard, is one of the best examples of High Victorian Queen Anne residential architecture in Mobile, where many such houses have been lost to commercial encroachment; its elaborate form and fanciful detail are rivaled by only a few other houses in the city. In the early 1900s Kate Shepard and her sister ran the "Misses Shepard School" on the second floor, teaching primary through high school courses to many Mobilians. Originally called the Shepard House, it took its present name after Monterey Place was cut through in 1910.
84000680.heading: Statement of Significance

100002768.summary: Blue Bird Hardware and Seed, designed in 1954 by Arch Winter and built in 1955, is architecturally significant as a representative of Winter's mid-century modern style and approach in Mobile. Winter was a partner in Ellis & Winter, which became the most prolific mid-century modern architectural firm on the Gulf Coast; he was named a Fellow of the American Institute of Architects and received the first Alabama Distinguished Architect award in 1996. Its blend of form, function, technology, and style makes the one-story concrete block and glass store architecturally unique in Mobile.
100002768.heading: Summary Paragraph

91000856.summary: The Joseph M. Walker House, built in 1927 for Joseph M. Walker, a manager, is a hollow tile and stucco Spanish Revival house with a tile porch that has remained substantially unaltered. It stands in Florence Place, a Mobile suburb platted in 1926 by George Fearn and Son, where early efforts to require an all-Spanish Revival neighborhood failed because of buyer resistance and the Depression. Deed restrictions required houses costing at least $4,000 and a uniform setback.
91000856.heading: Statement of Significance

91000858.summary: The Wade Askew House (Askew-Engerson House), built in 1927 for Wade Askew, an assistant freight manager, is a typical middle-class expression of the Spanish Revival style, with stucco walls, a ceramic tile roof, and exterior arches, and it has no significant changes. It stands in Florence Place, a Mobile suburb platted in 1926 by George Fearn and Son, where early efforts to require an all-Spanish Revival neighborhood failed because of buyer resistance and the Depression.
91000858.heading: Statement of Significance

90001240.summary: Trinity Episcopal Church, built in 1853, is the finest Gothic Revival church in Mobile and one of the best high-style examples in Alabama. It was designed by the nationally known New York architects Frank Wills and Henry Dudley, who also designed St. John's in Montgomery and the Church of the Nativity in Huntsville. It was a solid expression of the ecclesiological movement, which championed Gothic architecture as truly Christian. Its interior integrity is excellent, and its spire was replaced after Hurricane Frederic in 1979.
90001240.heading: Statement of Significance

83002966.summary: The Greene-Marston House, also known as Termite Hall, is a good example of a small antebellum farmhouse updated and expanded in the early twentieth century, with the early cottage incorporated into the first story of the present house. Its late Victorian wraparound porch, gable decorations, and chimneys are good local examples. The oak paneling added inside in the 1910s is possibly the finest example of Jacobean-style paneling in Mobile.
83002966.heading: Statement of Significance

84000081.summary: The Center-Gaillard House contains some of the earliest surviving construction in the Spring Hill summer community, with its oldest section dating from 1827 and a cottage addition from about 1837; its growth from a small cabin to a house can be traced in its rooflines, flooring, and siding. Its old kitchen house, the oldest yet found in the Mobile area, is the best surviving example of the simple board-and-batten dependency that was probably the most common type of its time.
84000081.heading: Statement of Significance

84000120.summary: The Pfau-Creighton Cottage, built in 1862, is an excellent example of an early farm dwelling, though it dates from a time when more sophisticated styles had emerged; its style and workmanship suggest a rural carpenter who kept building in the manner he knew. It is the only house in the nineteenth-century Spring Hill neighborhood group without a central hall, with two rooms across and two deep. Its original owner was Philip J. Pfau, a bootmaker with his own shop.
84000120.heading: Significance

81000131.summary: The Carlen House, built around 1843, is a very good example of a simple Gulf Coast or Creole cottage and one of the few such cottages remaining in Mobile without highly refined detailing; it is also noted for its unusually heavy, well-crafted braced framing. It is one of the few remaining early farmhouses tied to the small produce farms that encircled the city and supplied fresh vegetables. Michael Carlen, a small farmer, bought the land in 1842, and his family sold the house and land to the Mobile County School Board in 1923.
81000131.heading: Statement of Significance

84000078.summary: The Beal-Gaillard House, built in 1836-37, is an excellent example of a large country house built before architects such as Dakin, Gallier, and James brought sophisticated moldings and columns to Mobile, and it keeps a fine setting of open spaces, old trees, and azalea-lined paths. It typifies the westward movement of the 1830s, when well-to-do Mobilians could afford a country house as well as a city residence. Its builder, Mr. Beal, invested heavily in the development of Spring Hill and lost his fortune in the panic of 1837. Wings were added by later owners, including one in 1903 by Samuel P. Gaillard.
84000078.heading: Significance

84000123.summary: St. Paul's Episcopal Chapel, incorporated in 1859 and dedicated in 1861, is an excellent example of a small mid-nineteenth-century board-and-batten chapel and the only surviving church in the area built with this type of siding. Its eclectic design combines classical elements, such as a three-stage tower, Tuscan porch columns, and rounded window frames, with Gothic Revival features popularized by A. J. Downing. Its founders included many leading Spring Hill residents.
84000123.heading: Significance

86001065.summary: The Paterson House, built in 1927 for William and Patty Paterson and designed by Mobile architect Platt Roberts, is one of the few monumental Mediterranean Revival houses in southern Alabama and perhaps the only grand estate in Mobile that remains intact with its original acreage, outbuildings, and landscape. It shows outstanding craftsmanship and materials, some made by the owner's own business; Paterson was president of the Robinson Land and Lumber Company and owned the Paterson Clay Company. It stands on Government Street, which became the location of many of Mobile's grand estates as the city expanded westward.
86001065.heading: Statement of Significance

91000855.summary: The George Fearn House, built in 1904 and later the Century 21 Building, is one of the earliest high-style Spanish Revival houses in Mobile and an example of the work of Mobile architect George Rogers. It keeps a high degree of integrity, including its original art glass, light fixtures, bath fixtures, and mantels. It was built when Mobile architecture was dominated by Victorian and Neoclassical styles, as new suburbs to the west offered builders new stylistic choices.
91000855.heading: Statement of Significance

88000108.summary: Azalea Court Apartments, built in 1928-29 by the Apartment Realty Company, is the only large-scale Mission-style apartment building constructed in Mobile in the 1920s. Its locally unique scale, plan, and design are the work of architect J. Platt Roberts, who used elements of the national style, including a red tile roof, arched openings on large square piers, stuccoed quoins, decorated windows, and parapets imitating Spanish Colonial missions. It is unlike any other surviving Mobile apartment building of the 1920s and 1930s.
88000108.heading: Statement of Significance

73000365.summary: Spring Hill College, founded in 1830 by Michael Portier, first Bishop of Mobile, and chartered by the legislature in 1836, is one of the oldest operating institutions of higher learning in Alabama. Its Quadrangle includes six buildings: Moore Hall (1866), the only building surviving from the original campus; Main Hall, built soon after the campus fire of 1869; the dining hall and kitchen (1885); a second kitchen and Yenni Hall dormitory (both 1905); and St. Joseph's Chapel (1909).
73000365.heading: STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE

84000124.summary: Stewartfield is a Greek Revival raised cottage built in 1849-50 and enlarged before 1857, part of the nineteenth-century Spring Hill neighborhood group of historic resources. With offset wings and a semicircular rear ballroom, its plan forms a Greek cross. The long oak- and azalea-lined lane leading to the house once formed the central axis of an oval racetrack, a remnant of which survives in the circular front drive. The house keeps its original siding, a front gallery with fluted Doric columns, and a delicate dentil course along the cornice.
84000124.heading: Description

84000122.summary: Sodality Chapel, a very simple chapel built for private worship around the middle of the nineteenth century, is the oldest surviving frame building on the campus of Spring Hill College, which Bishop Michael Portier founded in 1830. Its spartan design, relieved only by a semicircular fanlight and cross patterns made by two colors of window glass, reflects the needs of the Sodality that built it. The chapel has remained essentially unchanged except for a possible later rear sacristy.
84000122.heading: Significance

82002060.summary: The Miller-O'Donnell House, built in 1837 for James P. Miller, is an exemplary surviving Gulf Coast cottage of the 1830s, with a frame upper story raised high above a masonry foundation and a high central stairway that gives the small house a monumental quality. Built and lived in by small farmers who sold produce at the City Market, it is one of the few farmhouses left within Mobile's city limits and represents the many small produce farms that once encircled the city. It later passed to the O'Donnell family, who stopped farming it early in the twentieth century.
82002060.heading: Statement of Significance

84000087.summary: The Collins-Robinson House, built in the late 1830s or early 1840s and enlarged in 1889, is an early and interesting example of a raised Gulf Coast cottage, with a central hall and square Tuscan porch posts but an otherwise simple, restrained design. Its French doors flanking the entrance and ground-floor casement windows were uncommon in Mobile and recall early French Creole houses. Records suggest it began as a two-room house entered directly from the front porch, in the earliest Gulf Coast tradition, with separate buildings for dining, cooking, and guests.
84000087.heading: Significance

91000863.summary: The James Arthur Morrison House, also called the Morrison-Walker House, is one of the finest Spanish Revival houses in Mobile and a rare high-style residential example, with stucco walls, a Mission parapet, round-headed openings, iron grillwork, and tile porches. Restaurant owner James Arthur Morrison bought the lot in Country Club Estates, an exclusive Spring Hill development platted in 1924, and began building in 1926. The house was built in the Mission Revival style, like the country club house going up at the same time.
91000863.heading: Statement of Significance

73000362.summary: Carolina Hall is the outstanding example in Mobile of the late Georgian refinements that spread to the Gulf states from Charleston, South Carolina, and nearby Atlantic seaboard areas. It was built by William Dawson, a wealthy Charleston cotton merchant, and completed in 1840, and is said to have closely resembled the Dawson family home in Charleston. Later owners included Spring Hill College (1904-1917) and Dr. and Mrs. William C. Perdue, who received a Mobile Historic Preservation Society award in 1959 for restoring it.
73000362.heading: Statement of Significance

91000840.summary: Saint Matthew's Catholic Church, dedicated on September 21, 1913, is the finest Mediterranean Revival religious building in Mobile, showing a high degree of style and workmanship in superior materials. The parish was formed around 1900 as the southern sections of Mobile began to grow, and early Masses were held in a single frame building; by 1913 the parish had about six hundred members. The parish also ran a school from 1938 to 1974.
91000840.heading: Statement of Significance

84000083.summary: The Collins-Marston House, built around 1832, is an early Gulf Coast cottage typical of the small summer houses built in Spring Hill in the middle of the nineteenth century, with four rooms off a central hall and square Tuscan porch columns showing classical influence. It remained a summer residence until 1900, when the Marston family added two rooms and a kitchen. With its additions, it illustrates how Spring Hill cottages changed from summer homes to year-round residences.
84000083.heading: Significance

91000854.summary: The Robert L. Spotswood House, also called the Spotswood-Glenn House, is one of the finest Spanish Revival houses in Mobile, with stucco walls, round-headed openings, and a red tile roof. It was built in Country Club Estates, a Spring Hill development platted by George Fearn and Son in 1924 around a golf course and country club, whose deed restrictions ensured substantial houses. Robert L. Spotswood, a solicitor for the Mobile Press Register, and his wife Martha bought the lot in 1925, and the house was finished by 1927.
91000854.heading: Statement of Significance

08001252.summary: The Ross Knox House, built in 1929 and designed by architect John Platt Roberts, is one of the finest Tudor Revival houses in Mobile, with steeply pitched gables, casement windows, a prominent chimney, and ornamental half-timbering. It is also significant for its intact interior, which carries Tudor Revival themes into its doorways, hardware, and fireplace. It stands in Country Club Estates, a 1920s Spring Hill development that grew as automobiles made the area more accessible from downtown.
08001252.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

94000789.summary: Dragonwick, also known as the Roberts House, was built in 1929 by local builder J. F. Pate and is one of the finest Tudor Revival houses in Mobile, with multiple steeply pitched gables, casement windows, a prominent chimney, and Tudor arches. Its intact interior carries Tudor themes into its doorways, hardware, and fireplace. It was built in the 1920s Spring Hill residential, golf course, and country club development south of Old Shell Road.
94000789.heading: Statement of Significance

90000929.summary: The Lewis Starke House in Daphne, built around 1850, is one of the finest Gulf Coast/Greek Revival cottages in Baldwin County. Its octagonal columns, classical dormers, and eared door and window surrounds are rare high-style elements in a county dominated by vernacular building, yet it remains within the Creole/Gulf Coast cottage folk tradition. These cottages are significant as distinctive regional forms of Alabama vernacular architecture.
90000929.heading: Statement of Significance

90000930.summary: The George W. Cullum House in Daphne is one of the finest Gulf Coast/Greek Revival houses in Baldwin County, with a formal arrangement, eared door and window surrounds, and marble mantels that are rare in a county dominated by vernacular building. It began in 1846 as a one-and-a-half-story Gulf Coast cottage, and about 1855 owner William Jones added flanking wings that turned it into a more formal Greek Revival house. It remains within the Creole/Gulf Coast cottage tradition, a distinctive regional form of Alabama vernacular architecture.
90000930.heading: Statement of Significance

80000679.summary: The Methodist Episcopal Church, South, now Daphne United Methodist Church, built in 1858, is one of two remaining antebellum churches in Baldwin County and a good example of a country adaptation of the Greek Revival style, built long after the style's national peak. It stands on land owned by Mr. and Mrs. William Howard since 1833, and grave markers from 1847 in its graveyard suggest an earlier church may have stood there. Though damaged in the 1979 hurricane and given a replacement belfry in 1916, it keeps its basic exterior and interior appearance.
80000679.heading: Statement of Significance

88002817.summary: The Texas, also called the Texas-Dryer-Brunell House, built in 1835, is one of the oldest buildings in Baldwin County and a rare two-story mix of Gulf Coast and Creole cottage features. It was one of the cottages, along with the California, the Long Branch, and the Homestead, that William L. Howard built with a large guest house in 1835 as a hotel on the bluffs of Mobile Bay's Eastern Shore, in the community later named Daphne. The house was moved less than a quarter mile in 1907 and has changed little since.
88002817.heading: Statement of Significance

88002812.summary: The McMillan House, also called the McMillan-O'Neal-Nordmann House, built about 1835, is the oldest Gulf Coast cottage in Baldwin County. The slight kick of the eave over its recessed front porch, which serves as a rain porch, shows local adaptation to the Gulf Coast climate. William McMillan built the house on the high bluff at Daphne, then a popular summer retreat for Mobilians, and after his death in 1869 it was sold to James O'Neal, with whom it is most closely associated.
88002812.heading: Statement of Significance

88002810.summary: The Captain Adams House, also called the Captain Adams-Stone House, built about 1850, is the finest high-style Gulf Coast cottage in Baldwin County, combining a central hall plan and raised brick piers with strong Greek Revival details. It is also significant for its two outbuildings, rare survivals in the county. Steamboat captain James J. Adams built it as a summer home after buying the land in 1849, and he entertained former President Millard Fillmore there in 1850.
88002810.heading: Statement of Significance

88002818.summary: The Walker House, also called the Walker-Goldsby-Warren House, built about 1850, is one of two high-style Gulf Coast cottages in Baldwin County, with a central hall and raised brick piers typical of the type and Greek Revival windows and entablature.
