Its single outbuilding is a rare survival in the county. Mobile businessman Daniel Walker built it as a summer house on land overlooking Mobile Bay, and it became a year-round residence in 1907.
88002818.heading: Statement of Significance

100004134.summary: The Manly-Strong House is a high-style Gulf Coast cottage on the Eastern Shore in Daphne, with a one-and-a-half-story gable roof over a recessed full-width porch, an early rain porch, a central hall, and exterior chimneys. Its exact construction date is unknown: local residents say it was built before 1858, and previous owners say the 1830s. Local history holds that it was built by a captain, suggesting ties to the nineteenth-century maritime trade along the Eastern Shore.
100004134.heading: Significance Summary

01001410.summary: The State Bank of Silverhill, built in 1927 as a community financial and business center, is significant for the services it provided to the residents of Silverhill. It is an excellent, intact example of an early twentieth-century masonry building in a vernacular style combining Classical Revival and Craftsman elements. Its hollow terra cotta tile walls with brick veneer, new at the time, made it nearly fireproof, and it is one of the highest-style vernacular buildings in Silverhill.
01001410.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

97000096.summary: People's Supply Company, built in 1902, was Silverhill's general store in the early twentieth century and the community's only source of dry goods and farm supplies; as a place where mail was sent and picked up, it was a nerve center for the town. With its gable front, board-and-batten siding, wraparound porch, and dormers, it is a distinctive example of the free-standing gable-front store, a type of which few survive in Baldwin County.
97000096.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

85000443.summary: The Svea Land Company Office, built in 1897 and later the Oscar Johnson Memorial Library, is associated with the large influx of immigrants into rural Baldwin County in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The second building and first non-residential structure in Silverhill, it was the center of the colonization of Silverhill by Swedish immigrants through the Svea Land Company, formed in Chicago in 1890. Around 1900 the one-room building became the community's first school.
85000443.heading: Statement of Significance

90002176.summary: The Martin Lindsey House, built in 1915 by Mobile lumber magnate Martin Lindsey, is the last surviving bay house within the city of Mobile. With its wraparound porch, central hall, tall ceilings, and interior transoms, it was designed to catch breezes off the bay. The bay house was a logical outgrowth of the nineteenth-century Greek Revival and Creole cottage, and by the early 1900s such houses were being built along the shores of south Mobile County.
90002176.heading: Statement of Significance

05000841.summary: The Henry Stuart House in Montrose is significant for its unique design, which embodies the philosophy of simple living held by its builder and first owner. It is a small, circular concrete-block building with a domed roof; Stuart hand-poured and dated each block, recording its construction from November 1925 to September 1926. Set partly below ground and well ventilated, it stays comfortable year-round, and its single room held Stuart's books, a loom, and a bed hung from the ceiling. Stuart lived a solitary life there tending his gardens from 1925 to 1944, which earned him the name "the hermit of Montrose."
05000841.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

97000649.summary: The Axil Johnson House in Fairhope, which Johnson built and finished for himself in 1940, is associated with the most prominent local craftsman in plastering and cement finishing in Fairhope during the first half of the twentieth century. Johnson worked in Fairhope from 1900 to World War I and again from the early 1940s, mostly with local materials, and his house displays his skill in its finely stuccoed exterior and plastered interior. It is also one of the last Craftsman-style houses built in Fairhope and one of the town's largest homes of its time, with a separate rental apartment.
97000649.heading: Statement of Significance

85000442.summary: Whittier Hall, built in 1905 for summer boarders, is associated with the early twentieth-century development of Fairhope as a popular health and vacation resort. Fairhope, on the highest hill on the eastern shore of Mobile Bay, is best known as the oldest and largest Single Tax colony in the country. By 1905, according to the Fairhope Courier, the town led all the towns on the bay in boarding accommodations.
85000442.heading: Statement of Significance

88001002.summary: The Golf, Gun & Country Club building, also called the Country Club-Manning House, built in 1922, reflects the entertainment and recreation values of Fairhope in the 1920s, with a spacious wraparound porch and a large interior room with a fireplace for social gatherings and a full basement for equipment storage. It served as a clubhouse and social gathering place from 1922 to 1938, hosting community teas, dances, and dinners as well as golfers. The surrounding golf course was subdivided for housing in the 1950s.
88001002.heading: Statement of Significance

88001005.summary: The Carl L. Bloxham Building, built in two phases in 1932 and 1946 as a real estate and insurance office, is a rare Baldwin County example of the Art Deco style. It shows the style in its geometric floral ornament, fluting, zigzag roofline motif, and smooth wall surfaces, and it was the first building in Fairhope in this new style. It was built by the prominent local contractor M. Dyson and Company.
88001005.heading: Statement of Significance

88001001.summary: The former U.S. Post Office in Fairhope, later known as the Courier Building, built in 1932, is the finest example of the Italian Renaissance Revival style in Baldwin County, with a low hip roof, symmetrical recessed facade, pedimented entrance, and columned portico. It is also associated with prominent local contractor Marmaduke Dyson, who built it to his own design and also built the Bank of Fairhope (1927) and the Gaston Building (1924).
88001001.heading: Statement of Significance

88001008.summary: The Bank of Fairhope building, later the Press Register Building, built in 1927, is one of the finest commercial buildings in Fairhope, a good local example of the Neoclassical style, and one of very few buildings in town designed by an architect, William March, with M. Dyson and Company as builder. It housed the Bank of Fairhope from 1927 to 1938, the only bank in Baldwin County to come through the Depression without closing. Its loans to farmers and families materially improved Fairhope's prospects.
88001008.heading: Statement of Significance

88001004.summary: The Gaston Building, built in 1924 by contractor Marmaduke Dyson, was the headquarters of the Fairhope Single Tax Corporation and the offices of the Fairhope Courier from 1924 to 1938. It was the center of both the intellectual case for and the practical business of putting Henry George's economic philosophy into practice in Fairhope, and the Courier, created to promote the Single Tax theory, circulated among supporters worldwide. It is also the least-altered early twentieth-century brick commercial building in Fairhope.
88001004.heading: Statement of Significance

88001007.summary: The Beckner House, also called the Beckner-Baker House, built in 1906, is an exceptional early example of a Fairhope house built for year-round living at a time when summer resort houses were the norm. It is also a pristine example of the Fairhope house type, which was usually stuccoed in the 1920s. J. M. Beckner, a 63-year-old Single Taxer from Indiana who came south to join the Fairhope experiment, hired Minneapolis contractor E. D. Brann to build it.
88001007.heading: Statement of Significance

88001006.summary: The Zurhorst House, also called the Zurhorst-Maumenee House, built in 1906 by Charles E. Littlefield, is the finest example of concrete-block construction in Baldwin County and an unusually exuberant building for Fairhope. Concrete block, common in Fairhope from about 1905 to 1930 because it stayed cool in summer and warm in winter, is used here for latticework, quoins, elaborate window and door surrounds, and Greek key and dentil trim. Its owner, John Zurhorst, was a German immigrant and ardent Single Taxer from St. Louis who moved to the Fairhope colony after following it through the Fairhope Courier.
88001006.heading: Statement of Significance

88001351.summary: Lebanon Chapel AME Church in Fairhope, begun in 1923, is the finest example of concrete-block construction in a religious building in Baldwin County, and its central tower, quoins, dentils, and belt course make it the highest-style building in the local Black neighborhood. The congregation of some twenty members built it under the supervision of member Warren B. Pearson, a mechanic and builder from nearby Volanta, whose use of ornamental concrete block followed Fairhope's building tradition of the time.
88001351.heading: Statement of Significance

88001358.summary: Twin Beach AME Church near Fairhope, built in 1925 by Black craftsman Axal Johnson, is one of three ornamental concrete-block churches in Baldwin County, and its medieval-inspired twin towers and buttresses make it the highest-style building in the area. The congregation was formed as Zion Chapel in 1867 by Black residents near Battles Wharf, before Fairhope existed, and worshiped in a brush arbor and then in buildings lost to fire and storms. Its more than two hundred members chose concrete blocks molded to resemble stone for the present church.
88001358.heading: Statement of Significance

88001353.summary: St. Mark's Lutheran Church in Elberta, built in 1927, is the best Medieval Revival religious building in Baldwin County, with a squat tower, buttresses, Gothic windows, and brick walls, and it was a more permanent building in a rural community where frame buildings predominated. Elberta was settled in 1906 by German immigrants, many of whom came by way of the Midwest to take up truck farming. The congregation was organized in 1908 with fourteen charter members and first worshiped in German in a simple frame church dedicated in 1909.
88001353.heading: Statement of Significance

88002816.summary: The Street House in Point Clear, built in 1906, is a classic Gulf Coast cottage with a central hall plan, gable roof, dormers, recessed porch, and slight elevation, plus an attached rain porch, a local adaptation common on Point Clear houses. It is also unusual for Point Clear as a year-round inland residence rather than a summer house on the bay. Farmer William Street built it for his family after the September 1906 hurricane destroyed their home on Weeks Bay.
88002816.heading: Statement of Significance

88001357.summary: Swift Presbyterian Church, built in 1907, is one of three remaining frame Gothic Revival churches in Baldwin County and the highest architectural expression in the Miflin community, where simple construction was the rule. Miflin was a lumber community on the north end of Wolf Bay that had a school and many houses but no church by 1905. Lumberman C. A. Swift provided the land and lumber for the church.
88001357.heading: Statement of Significance

88001355.summary: St. Paul's Episcopal Church in Magnolia Springs, begun in 1901 and consecrated in 1902, is one of three frame vernacular Gothic Revival churches in Baldwin County. It is also significant for its unaltered interior, with a cathedral ceiling of exposed trusses, beaded-board walls, and a cross of magnolia leaves. Magnolia Springs was founded in 1871 by Midwesterners drawn by its springs and climate, and for many years it had no church; St. Paul's then remained the only church in town for nearly fifty years.
88001355.heading: Statement of Significance

00001027.summary: The Moore Store, a one-story clay tile building built in 1923, is significant for its commercial role in Magnolia Springs as the oldest and only survivor of a series of small general stores that served the rural community. It served as both a general store and a service station, with a storefront on one side and a garage door on the other. It replaced an earlier store lost to fire, and the Moore brothers bought it soon afterward and ran it well into the 1960s.
00001027.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

95001019.summary: The Brunell House in Magnolia Springs, built around 1910, represents a modest type of rural building of the Neoclassical period, notable for standing in a resort community known for larger homes and hotels. Located away from the river and springs that drew visitors, it was built in the style of its day and finished in elegant curly pine, a local material that likely exceeded local expectations for such a house. It was probably a rental house for Mr. Brunell, whose own home was also finished in curly pine.
95001019.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

98000111.summary: The Sunnyside Hotel in Magnolia Springs, built in 1897, is an intact and rare Baldwin County example of a small resort hotel. Although south Baldwin County has been a popular resort area since about 1900, few historic hotels survive; in the 1920s, a peak decade for local tourism, the county had only five hotels, and the Sunnyside is one of three still standing. With its wraparound porch, wall dormers, steep roof, transoms, and curly pine beaded-board interior, it is an important survivor of the county's early twentieth-century resort years.
98000111.heading: Narrative Statement of Significance

00001031.summary: The Governor's Club in Magnolia Springs is an intact and rare Baldwin County example of a small resort hotel from the 1920s, a peak decade for local tourism, when the county had only five hotels. Its spacious wraparound porch with turned posts and balusters, floor-to-ceiling windows, and fine interior details make it an important survivor of the county's early twentieth-century resort years. The property was assembled from 1901 to 1908 as the estate of Chicago businessman Frank Brunell, and in 1924 it was conveyed to the Governor's Club to run a recreation resort.
00001031.heading: Statement of Significance

74000429.summary: The Middle Bay Light, called the Mobile Bay Light in its nomination, is one of Alabama's few navigational landmarks and by far the most interesting. The one-and-a-half-story hexagonal structure was built as both a residence and a light, reputedly as a replica of the Hooper's Strait Light off Maryland, and is thought to be one of only a few such lights remaining. Funded by an 1883 act to mark the newly completed Mobile ship channel, the station was established in December 1885; the light was automated in 1935, and concerned citizens saved it from demolition in 1967.
74000429.heading: Significance

88000106.summary: The Hiram B. Austin House on Mon Louis Island, built around 1837, is the earliest and best example of the bay house known in Mobile County and the only identified antebellum house on the western shore of Mobile Bay. It is an excellent Gulf Coast cottage, with a full-length front porch, large windows and doors suited to the climate, a central hall, early Greek Revival details, and peg construction. It replaced earlier houses that fell into the bay as the eroding bluff collapsed, and it is tied to a family line reaching back to the earliest history of Mobile County.
88000106.heading: Statement of Significance

88002811.summary: The Hamner House, also called the Hamner-Roberts House, in Bon Secour, built around 1885, is a relatively unaltered, full-sized Gulf Coast cottage with a gable roof, recessed porch, central hall, and a five-bay facade, which is rare among inland examples. It was built by Will C. Hamner, who bought the land in 1881 and sold it in 1896. Its original brick piers have been replaced by tall pilings to meet local flood control rules.
88002811.heading: Statement of Significance

88002815.summary: The Orrell House, also called the Orrell-Burnette House, in Bon Secour, built around 1900, is an unaltered rural example of the Gulf Coast cottage, with a recessed porch, gable roof, exterior chimney, and central hall plan. It stands on land once owned by William R. Orrell, a late nineteenth-century settler who took advantage of the farming and timber opportunities along the Bon Secour River.
88002815.heading: Statement of Significance

16000814.summary: The Swift-Coles House in Bon Secour is an exemplary early twentieth-century Gulf Coast residence, now a public house museum. It began in 1882 as a simple four-room dogtrot cabin and was enlarged in 1902 and again in 1908-1910, with cross-breezes through the interior and double galleries suited to the Gulf Coast climate before air conditioning. Charles and Susan Swift bought the property in 1898 and moved to Bon Secour to go into the lumber business, and the house grew to sixteen rooms for their expanding family.
16000814.heading: Summary Paragraph

85000255.summary: Bishop Manor Estate in St. Elmo, built around 1925 by Steven Bishop, is the only known surviving example in Mobile County of the extravagant estates built in the South by wealthy Northern families in the early 1900s, and it survives essentially intact. Its well-proportioned main house draws heavily on Mediterranean architecture and uses exceptional materials, including basswood paneling and a curved staircase, a cherry stair rail, marble fireplaces and floors, and glazed tile. The estate also includes a cement pool and bathhouses.
85000255.heading: Statement of Significance

88002809.summary: The Allen House, also called the Allen-Marshall House, on the Bon Secour River, built around 1880, is a fine nineteenth-century Creole cottage, with a recessed front porch, gable roof, two front doors, and no central hall. Its Tuscan porch columns and mirrored mantels show the embellishments possible on this simple house form. It was built by James Allen, an English-born oysterman, and his wife Louisa, who bought the lot in 1877.
88002809.heading: Statement of Significance

90000917.summary: The George Leatherbury House in Coden, built in 1912, is the best example of the bay house on Portersville Bay in Mobile County. Bay houses, an important regional type usually built as summer homes, have extensive galleries, large rooms, and many windows and doors, and this house carries on a tradition dating to the mid-nineteenth century. Coden was a turn-of-the-century resort community, and few of its bay houses survive. Leatherbury was a Mobile lumber broker and mill owner.
90000917.heading: Statement of Significance

100001878.summary: The Dauphin Island School, built in 1931, was the only school building on Dauphin Island and remained in use until 2016, serving as the only source of formal education for local children. Keeping a school on the island was challenged for decades by Mobile school system decisions and by storms, but the school stayed open, and it has long been a local landmark where alumni gather for reunions. It replaced the island's first schoolhouse, a frame building built in 1898.
100001878.heading: Summary Paragraph

75000305.summary: Sand Island Light, completed in 1873, is the older of Alabama's two remaining lighthouses and the third light built on this site, where a light has marked the entrance to Mobile Bay and the Mobile Ship Channel since 1838. The previous brick tower of 1858 was destroyed by Confederate forces in 1862 to keep Union forces from using it as a lookout, and the present tower was first lit on September 1, 1873. The island eroded steadily, and the 1906 hurricane destroyed the keeper's house and drowned the assistant keeper and his wife. The light was automated in 1947 and extinguished and abandoned in 1971.
75000305.heading: Statement of Significance

75000306.summary: The U.S.S. Tecumseh, an ironclad monitor built by Charles A. Secor and Company of Jersey City and designed by John Ericsson, who also designed the original Monitor, lies upside down in about 29 feet of water roughly 300 yards northwest of Fort Morgan. Chosen to lead Admiral David Farragut's Union fleet into the Battle of Mobile Bay, it struck a mine and sank on the morning of August 5, 1864. Of the nine Canonicus-class monitors, it was the only one sunk in battle and is the only survivor. It illustrates the Navy's transition from sail to steam, from wood to iron armor, and from fixed broadsides to revolving turrets, and its gear is expected to remain stored as it was in battle.
75000306.heading: Statement of Significance

66000146.summary: Fort Morgan, overlooking the entrance to Mobile Bay, commemorates the Battle of Mobile Bay in August 1864, which closed one of the last two Confederate ports of the Civil War; the fort played a crucial part in the unsuccessful defense of the bay and surrendered only after siege and constant shelling had reduced it to rubble. Designed by Simon Bernard, a French engineer and former aide to Napoleon who joined the U.S. Army in 1816, the star-shaped fort is a remarkable example of a very large early nineteenth-century masonry fort with especially fine brickwork. Mobile Point was reactivated during the Spanish-American War and both World Wars, and the site includes batteries built around 1900 as well as the nearby wreck of the U.S.S. Tecumseh.
66000146.heading: Statement of Significance

14001042.summary: Carrollton Hall, also known as Folly Quarter, is a grand Greek Revival country villa built in 1831-32 by Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the only Catholic signer of the Declaration of Independence and by then its last surviving signer. He built it on about 1,000 acres of his Doughoregan Manor estate for his granddaughter Emily MacTavish. Baltimore architect William F. Small, who had apprenticed under Benjamin Henry Latrobe, designed the 2½-story house of smooth granite ashlar, with matching Greek Doric porticos on the west and east fronts. Inside are a coffered barrel-vaulted saloon and a domed second-floor room lit by an oculus. Planned hyphens and wings were never built. The house stayed a country estate until 1924, and Franciscan friars bought the mansion in 1928.
